title: Size-4 numerators are PROVED in F_q[T]: F_4[T] with A=T, F_2[T] with A=T²
connection: The two function-field analogues whose numerator has the same norm as 4 (|A| = 4: q=4,deg A=1 and q=2,deg A=2) are theorems (FUNCTIONFIELD_ES Thm 6.1, 6.3), proved by a FINITE congruence covering. Over Z a finite covering is impossible (Mordell square classes).
why: Pinning down exactly which Z-obstruction each FF proof dodges isolates the one ingredient Z lacks; it is the cleanest 'proved twin' of ES.
first_step: Tabulate for Thm 6.1/6.3 every covering family and mark which uses char-2 cancellation vs absence of the square-class obstruction (FUNCTIONFIELD_ES §6 'Why this exists over F₂').
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Sign-subgroup world: positivity = leading coefficient in a subgroup H ≤ F_q^*
connection: Monic (H = 1) is Hayes' choice; H = F_q^* is the trivial sign-free problem. Taking H = squares (index 2) mimics Z, whose sign group {±1} has index 2 in nothing but whose 'positive' half is index 2 in Z∖0.
why: Interpolating H shows whether hardness is controlled by the index of the cone; an index-2 cone FF problem might be the most faithful model of ℕ ⊂ Z.
first_step: Run the existing ffl_* search with leading coefficients restricted to squares for q = 3,5,7, deg P ≤ 8, and compare failure counts to the monic version.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Profinite sterile points: FF x* in ES₃(T²) vs non-square sterile profinite integers
connection: FF_STERILE_* constructs a profinite point x* of ES₃(T²) where every covering family fails (Haar-null set). Over Ẑ the odd squares are sterile for certificate lines; are there non-square sterile points in Ẑ?
why: If Ẑ has only square-type sterile points, ES reduces to squares-plus-growth; if it has others, they are new candidates for hard primes.
first_step: Mirror the FF construction in Ẑ: run the certificate-line covering tree mod 840·k and look for profinite branches avoiding all lines that are not square classes.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Positivity at a finite place: cone = polynomials with constant term 1
connection: Replace 'monic' (sign at ∞) by 'X(0) = 1' (sign at the place T). This cone is multiplicatively closed but contains elements arbitrarily close to 1 T-adically, i.e. it is not discrete at its sign place.
why: The other_rings principle predicts collapse to a finite covering when the cone is not discrete at the sign place; checking it in a new world tests the principle.
first_step: Search for e with e = 1/U + 1/V, U,V in the cone, e ≡ 'class 3' modulo the analogue of 4 (T²?) — try q = 3,5 by brute force.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Sign groups at ∞: {±1} for Q versus F_q^* for monic F_q[T] in ray class groups mod m·∞
connection: With the sign at ∞, the ray class group mod m of F_q[T] is (F_q[T]/m)^* (Carlitz), and dropping the sign quotients by F_q^*; for Q the analogous groups are (Z/m)^* and (Z/m)^*/{±1}. (The narrow class groups themselves are trivial in both cases, since every ideal has a positive/monic generator.) So the 'sign part' of ray class groups has size 2 over Q and q − 1 over F_q[T].
why: ES-type certificate conditions are ray-class conditions; if FF hardness scales with the size of the sign part, Q (sign part of size 2) sits in the most constrained-sign regime.
first_step: Compute, for q = 3, 4, 5, 7, the failure rate of ES_q(T, P) at deg P = 6 against q − 1; fit.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Mordell–Schinzel proves ES FALSE over Z[T] (eventual positivity) at P = mT + r² (gcd(m, r) = 1, odd values)
connection: Over Z[T] with cone 'positive leading coefficient', a solution at P = mT + r² with gcd(m, r) = 1 (and P taking odd values; e.g. 4T + 4 = 4(T+1) is trivially solvable: 4/(4T+4) = 1/(2T+2) + 1/(4T+4) + 1/(4T+4)) would be a polynomial identity covering a square class, excluded by Mordell–Schinzel. So Z[T] is an analogue world where ES is provably false.
why: It certifies that any proof over Z must be non-uniform in n (cannot come from a single polynomial family per class); Z[T] is the 'false twin' to set against the FF 'true twins'.
first_step: Check whether the Mordell–Schinzel argument extends to Z[T] with merely eventual positivity of denominators (not positivity for all T ≥ 0).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Two-variable identities for primes represented by a non-principal binary form
connection: Primes p = f(S,T) for a non-principal form f (e.g. disc −23, h = 3) form a non-congruence set. A polynomial identity 4/f(S,T) = Σ 1/X_i(S,T) in Z[S,T] would cover a non-abelian Chebotarev set.
why: It would be a certificate family outside the abelian (congruence) world where Mordell's obstruction lives; the obstruction then concerns which forms represent squares.
first_step: Search ansätze X_i quadratic/quartic in (S,T) for f = 2S²+ST+3T² by solving coefficient equations with a Gröbner basis or LLL.

title: Nagao amalgam: SL₂(F_q[T]) is not finitely generated — the words form of ES changes shape
connection: ES ⇔ certain short SL₂(Z) words; SL₂(F_q[T]) is an amalgam (Nagao) of GL₂(F_q)-type and Borel pieces and is not finitely generated, so word length is replaced by degree.
why: If the FF words problem is trivial via the Borel piece, it shows that ES words over Z draw their difficulty from SL₂(Z)'s finite generation.
first_step: Translate the SL₂ word form of ES to SL₂(F_q[T]) and check whether Borel elements produce solutions for all P.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Katz monodromy for Kloosterman/Salié-type sums in ES Type II counts at q → ∞
connection: Type II counts at fixed P are sums of incomplete Kloosterman/Salié-like sums; over F_q[T] with q→∞, Katz's equidistribution gives square-root cancellation with known monodromy groups.
why: If the relevant monodromy is computed, it predicts the fluctuation law of the fixed-p count over Z (Katz–Sarnak style) and so the lower-tail behaviour.
first_step: Identify the exact exponential sum in the FF Type II count (FUNCTIONFIELD_ES §4) and look up its geometric monodromy in Katz 'Gauss sums, Kloosterman sums and monodromy groups'.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: F_q[T] with q = p prime vs prime power: does F_4 behave like F_2 or like F_3?
connection: Thm 6.3 (F₄, A = T) and Thm 6.1 (F₂, A = T²) are both char 2. Comparing F₄ with F₉ (char 3) and F₂₅ isolates characteristic from field size.
why: Disentangles 'char 2 cancellation' from 'small q', which decides whether the |A| = 4 analogues are char artefacts.
first_step: Run the existing covering-tree search for q = 9, A = T (|A| = 9) and q = 3, A = T² to deg 8 and report covering success.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Chowla over F_q[T] (proved for large q) ↔ parity barrier in ES sieve arguments
connection: ES lower-bound sieves hit the parity barrier; FF Chowla (Sawin–Shusterman, large q) breaks parity in FF. If an FF ES statement follows from FF Chowla, the integer statement needs a Chowla-type input.
why: Clarifies whether parity is the precise barrier for a sieve proof of ES.
first_step: Check whether the FF ES counting function at fixed P can be written with a Möbius/Liouville twist that Chowla controls.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Polynomial ES over Z[T] for P of degree 2: 4/(T² + 1)
connection: Primes of the form T²+1 are ≡ 1 (mod 4) when T even. An identity for 4/(T²+1) over Z[T] with eventually positive denominators would cover them; T²+1 is never a square for T>0, so Mordell–Schinzel's square obstruction does not apply directly.
why: A quadratic-polynomial identity would be a non-linear certificate family; existence/non-existence probes whether the obstruction is genuinely about squares.
first_step: Search for 4/(T²+1) = 1/X + 1/Y + 1/Z with X,Y,Z ∈ Z[T] of degree ≤ 4 (or with T in a fixed class mod M) via linear algebra on coefficients.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Exponential-polynomial identities: denominators in Z[T, 2^T] or Z[T, p^T]
connection: Allow denominators that are exponential polynomials in an auxiliary parameter (e.g. identities in which a variable exponent k enters as 2^k or 3^k). Such families are not quasi-polynomial in n and escape Mordell–Schinzel's formal framework.
why: Growing families with exponential parameters (power ladders) are one of the few certificate shapes outside B1; the identity world Z[T, a^T] is their natural home.
first_step: Formalize POWER_LADDER_ES families as identities over Z[T, 2^T] and ask whether any covers a full square class mod 840 for all T.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Function-field ES with A of degree k and P of degree < 2k (small-height regime)
connection: When deg P is close to deg A the problem is like m/n with m comparable to n; the FF small-height regime can be fully enumerated.
why: Exact enumeration of the small-height regime gives the FF analogue of the 'U(n) exceptions' list (105, 2961, ...) and may show a common structure.
first_step: Enumerate all failures for q = 3, deg A = 2, deg P ∈ {3,4,5} and inspect their factorization patterns.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: FF Thm 6.3 search technique (covering trees) on Z with growing modulus
connection: The computer-assisted FF proofs used a covering tree whose leaves are congruence classes with identities. Over Z the same tree never closes (squares), but its growth rate measures the 'certificate deficit'.
why: The FF/Z comparison of tree growth quantifies the gap; a sub-exponential growth over Z would suggest a growing-family proof is plausible.
first_step: Run the FF covering-tree code verbatim on Z (moduli 840·k) to depth 6 and record the number of open leaves per depth vs the FF case.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Artin–Schreier identities in char p: the 'Frobenius twist' certificate family
connection: In char p, X ↦ X^p is additive, so identities like 1/X^p − ... interact with Frobenius; e.g. (P+1)^p = P^p + 1. Certificate families using P^p are unique to char p.
why: A Frobenius-twist family that covers an FF class unreachable otherwise shows a char-p-only mechanism; over Z its only shadow is Fermat's little theorem congruences (power ladders mod p).
first_step: Search char-3 identities where a denominator is (P + c)^3 or P^3 + c and see whether they cover classes the linear families miss.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES over F_q[T][1/T] (S-integers in FF) — analogue of Z[1/3]
connection: Inverting a prime T in F_q[T] gives units T^k; the other_rings Lemma 3.1 then supplies universal divisors e | 1 + T^k with e in the 'class 3' analogue, collapsing ES.
why: Confirms the cone-discreteness principle in FF and quantifies how many units are needed (smallest k).
first_step: Find smallest k with a divisor of 1 + T^k in the needed class mod A for q = 3, A = T²+1.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Function-field ES with A irreducible vs A reducible (4 = 2·2 is reducible)
connection: 4 = 2² over Z; FF analogues with A = T² (reducible, proved over F₂) vs A irreducible of degree 2. If the reducible case is systematically easier, ES's numerator being a prime square is relevant.
why: Points at whether 4 = 2² structure (square of the dyadic prime) is used by any Z mechanism.
first_step: For q = 3, compare failure sets for A = T² vs A = T² + 1 (irreducible) at deg P ≤ 8.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Smooth-numerator relaxation is trivial: 4/n = 2/n + 1/n + 1/n
connection: Allowing numerators that are S-units (S-integer denominators) trivializes ES already with numerators (3, 3, 1) — the depth-1 identity. Even 4/n = 2/n + 1/n + 1/n works, so the least smoothness bound is ≤ 2; the relaxation is uninformative unless the number of non-unit numerators is restricted (see ν(p) item).
why: Filter: prevents a wasted computation and redirects to the 'one non-unit numerator' world, which is weighted ES (1,1,ℓ).
first_step: None beyond recording; pursue the ν(p) / weighted (1,1,ℓ) items.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Trace descent: Galois-sum an O_K solution to get an integer identity with numerator 8
connection: If 4/n = Σ 1/x_i with x_i ∈ O_K (K real quadratic), adding the conjugate equation gives 8/n = Σ Tr(x_i)/N(x_i). When Tr(x_i) | N(x_i) for each i, this is a 3-term unit-fraction representation of 8/n.
why: Turns the proved real-quadratic world into an integer statement for numerator 8 (Schinzel-type), with an explicit divisibility condition to engineer.
first_step: For the D = 2 identity of Prop 3.3, compute Tr and N of each denominator as polynomials in n and check the divisibility Tr | N on residue classes.

title: Two-term ES over norm-Euclidean Z[√d] (Bradford–Ionascu Thm 3.1) ↔ divisor ≡ 3 mod 4 criterion
connection: Bradford–Ionascu show even 4/n = 1/a + 1/b holds over Z[√d] for d ∈ {2,3,5,…,73} (no positivity). Over Z, 4/n = 1/a+1/b needs a divisor of n in a class mod 4; in O_K prime splitting supplies more divisors.
why: Identifies the step as 'enough divisors in the right ray class'; the integer replacement is the e-slice divisor condition on a p-tied integer.
first_step: Read §3 of arXiv:1405.4025 to extract the ray-class condition used, then state the Z analogue for 4Cp + 1.

title: Non-rational totally positive n in Q(√5): uncovered classes as a 'square obstruction' in O_K?
connection: other_rings: for D = 2, 5, 7, 13 some non-rational classes of (O_K/4)^* are not hit by the unit mechanism in the search box. Are these the square classes (a T1 analogue over K)?
why: If the missing classes are exactly squares mod 4O_K, T1 has a number-field generalization; if not, a new obstruction type exists.
first_step: Rerun scripts/bs_ff_rings.py for D = 5 with a larger box and compare the missing classes with the squares in (O_K/4)^*.

title: Semiring cone Z_{≥0}[√2]: discrete at one real place, not at the other
connection: C = {a + b√2: a, b ≥ 0} ∖ {0} is multiplicatively closed, ≥ 1 at the identity embedding, but conjugates a − b√2 can be tiny. Intermediate between ℕ (fully discrete) and totally positive O_K (unit-rich).
why: Tests whether discreteness at ONE place suffices for hardness; if ES over this cone is again 'lottery', the archimedean crux is one-place.
first_step: Search the unit-sum mechanism in C: find e ∈ C, e ≡ 3 (mod 4O_K) with e = 1/u + 1/v, u, v ∈ C (note units 1+√2 ∈ C but (1+√2)^{-1} ∉ C).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES over Z[√−d] orders (non-maximal) with Gaussian-style cones
connection: Non-maximal orders (e.g. Z[2i], Z[√−3]) are not integrally closed; unit fractions behave differently at the conductor. ES for rational n in Z[2i] with Re, Im ≥ 0 sits between Z and Z[i].
why: Conductor primes give extra local constraints, a toy model of 'local obstruction at 2' that ES has with numerator 4.
first_step: Compare solution counts for rational p ≤ 10^4 in Z[i] vs Z[2i] cones.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Hurwitz quaternions with positive-definite cone: non-commutative ES
connection: In a definite quaternion order, 1/x = x̄/N(x); require denominators with positive real part or in a cone. Non-commutativity gives more solutions per norm.
why: Quaternion norms connect ES to sums of four squares and Eichler orders; repo QUATERNION_ES treats an equivalent form — the cone version is a separate world.
first_step: Read QUATERNION_ES.md, then test 4/p = Σ 1/x_i with x_i Hurwitz quaternions of positive real part for p ≤ 1000.

title: Group rings Z[C_m] with cone N[C_m]: ES in a ring with zero divisors
connection: Z[C_m] ≅ order in ∏ Q(ζ_d); the cone N[C_m] (non-negative coefficients) is multiplicatively closed and discrete in the trivial-character coordinate but not in others.
why: Combines several cyclotomic components with one positive coordinate; tests whether a single 'augmentation' coordinate carrying positivity suffices for hardness.
first_step: For m = 2 (Z[C_2] ≅ order in Q × Q), determine positive ES for n·1 and compare with ES over Z × Z.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Imaginary quadratic fields with class number > 1: ES for principal vs non-principal primes
connection: Over O_K with h > 1, a rational prime p ≡ 1 mod 4 may split into non-principal primes; then 4/p has fewer 'divisor' options among principal elements. With a sector cone this is a new hard world.
why: Measures the role of class group in the divisor-in-class lottery; Z has h = 1.
first_step: Take K = Q(√−5), sector cone, test ES for rational p splitting into non-principal primes vs principal ones.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Ring of algebraic integers Z-bar with totally positive cone: ES trivially true?
connection: In the ring of all algebraic integers, every element has square roots etc.; with a totally positive cone, the unit-sum mechanism has infinitely many units, so ES should collapse.
why: A sanity endpoint of the classification (infinite-degree world).
first_step: Note as corollary of Prop 3.3: Z-bar ⊃ Z[√2]; any rational n has a totally positive solution. Record.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Global sign patterns of ES solutions vs local predictions (Legendre symbols of x, y, z mod small primes)
connection: For each global solution record (x/ℓ), (y/ℓ), (z/ℓ). If some locally allowed pattern never occurs globally at hard primes, that is a hidden global constraint (reciprocity-type).
why: Hidden global constraints are exactly what T1 is; finding more of them maps the obstruction landscape.
first_step: Using existing solution data for p ≤ 10^6, tabulate patterns at ℓ = 3, 5, 7 and test against local frequencies.

title: Matrix ES over M₂(Z) with the cone of matrices with positive entries
connection: Matrices with positive entries form a multiplicatively closed cone discrete at ∞ (entries ≥ 1). Inverses are rational; ES: (4/n)·I = X⁻¹ + Y⁻¹ + Z⁻¹ with X, Y, Z positive-entry, invertible over Q.
why: This cone links ES to SL₂(N)-type monoids and continued fractions (the repo's SL₂ words form); it might reproduce ES exactly or relax it.
first_step: Check: does a solution with positive-entry X, Y, Z force a solution of ES? Compute small cases n = 5, 13, 17.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Eichler orders / quaternion algebras ramified at ∞ and p: ES via ideals of norm p
connection: In the definite quaternion algebra B_{p,∞}, left ideals of norm p correspond to supersingular data; ES-like equations among ideal classes appear in Brandt matrices.
why: Brandt matrices give exact counts of ideal-class relations with Ramanujan bounds; if ES solutions map to Brandt-matrix entries, positivity of counts follows.
first_step: Read bsC_supersingular_transfer.md and check whether any ES count equals a Brandt-matrix entry for small p.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Gaussian cone ES for Gaussian primes vs ES over Z: is there an injection of solutions?
connection: A solution of ES over Z for p is a solution in the Gaussian cone (real denominators are in the cone). Conversely, from a Gaussian-cone solution for rational p, taking norms or real parts may give integer data.
why: If 'Gaussian cone ES for rational p ⇒ integer ES' via a projection, the Gaussian world would be a strengthening to attack.
first_step: Test: for each Gaussian-cone solution of 4/p (p ≤ 1000) check whether real parts or norms yield an integer ES solution.

title: ES in rings of integers of CM fields with cone from the maximal real subfield
connection: For a CM field K with totally real K⁺, use denominators in K whose relative norm to K⁺ is totally positive. Units of K⁺ (rank ≥ 1 when [K⁺:Q] ≥ 2) make the unit mechanism available.
why: Another family where infinite units collapse ES; confirms that only Q and imaginary quadratic K (unit rank 0) are hard.
first_step: For Q(ζ_8), test the unit mechanism with units of Q(√2).

title: Dual numbers Z[ε]/(ε²): the tangent-space ES
connection: 4/(n + mε) = Σ 1/(x_i + a_i ε) ⇔ ES for n plus the linear condition Σ a_i/x_i² = 4m/n². The a_i are free integers, so the dual-number world asks which ES solutions have a solvable linear tangent condition.
why: Tangent conditions measure how rigid ES solutions are; a 'deformation' world might connect to counting solutions with multiplicities.
first_step: For p ≤ 10^4 and each solution compute gcd conditions for Σ a_i/x_i² = 4m/p² to be solvable for all m.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES over a Dedekind domain with infinitely many units but no order: positivity replaced by a norm bound
connection: Replace the cone by 'all |x|_v ≥ 1 at archimedean places' (a norm-bounded set, not multiplicatively closed by inverses). This is the 'height-positivity' world: denominators must have all conjugates ≥ 1.
why: Unlike totally positive, this excludes small units; it may restore lottery behaviour in fields with units, giving hard twins with richer arithmetic.
first_step: In Z[√2], require |x|, |x'| ≥ 1 and search ES for rational p ≤ 10^4; compare with the totally-positive collapse.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Positive ES in Q(√−1) with the cone 'Re > 0 and Im ≥ 0' (half-closed quadrant) vs both-sign cones
connection: Bradford–Ionascu's cone is Re, Im of equal sign; a strict first quadrant is multiplicatively closed only up to 90° sums (it is not closed: i·i). Clarify which quadrant-like sets are closed and which make ES non-trivial.
why: Cone design determines the world; misdesigned cones give trivial or empty problems.
first_step: Check closure of the equal-sign cone (product of two first-quadrant elements can leave the quadrant) — note Bradford–Ionascu's cone may not be multiplicatively closed, and record what they actually require.

title: Egyptian integral domains (Guerrieri–Loper–Oman, Epstein): ES as a 3-term refinement
connection: An Egyptian domain is one where every element of the fraction field is a finite sum of distinct unit fractions. ES is the 'length 3 for numerator 4' refinement. The Egyptian-domain literature classifies which domains have the unrestricted property.
why: Their techniques (e.g. using units or integrality over Egyptian subrings) might yield length bounds, i.e. 'Egyptian length' functions whose Z-value at 4/n is ES.
first_step: Read 'From ancient Egyptian fractions to modern algebra' and Epstein 2303.15685; look for any length-bounded statement.

title: Tropical/valuative cone over F_q((1/T)): ES 'at ∞' is a leading-coefficient problem
connection: Over the completion F_q((1/T)) with monic cone, ES is the leading-coefficient equation (Lemma 1.1); over R the analogue is just inequality x > n/4. Comparing the completed worlds isolates what is local at the sign place.
why: Shows that in FF the sign place gives a discrete leading-coefficient constraint while over R it gives only an inequality — a structural difference to keep in mind for dictionaries.
first_step: Write both local problems and their solution sets; record as a dictionary entry.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Forced elements of M(p): p + 1, p + 2, 2p + ... — which large numerators are always available?
connection: (p+1)/p = 1 + 1/(2p) + 1/(2p) shows p + 1 ∈ M(p); similarly (p+2)/p = 1 + 1/p + 1/p and 3 ∈ M(p). A large forced element divisible by 4 would prove ES via divisor-closure.
why: Any identity m(p)/p = Σ 1/x_i(p) valid for all p with 4 | m(p) proves ES; Mordell–Schinzel-type arguments should forbid polynomial m(p) at square classes, so this pins the obstruction in the m-direction.
first_step: Enumerate polynomial families m(p) = ap + b with uniform identities (b small) and list their m mod 4 for p ≡ 1 mod 4; check whether all forced ones are ≢ 0 mod 4 (T1-type).

title: Norm denominators: all x, y, z sums of two squares — fails at 16 primes below 4000
connection: Requiring every denominator to be a norm from Z[i] (sum of two squares) fails at p = 41, 137, 233, 241, 601, 769, … (16 of 269). This is the 'Gaussian-norm' constrained world.
why: A constrained world with visible failures is a laboratory: if its failures have a local/reciprocity explanation it is a cousin of T1; if not, it is a lottery world at a lower expected count.
first_step: Up to 2·10^4: 40 failures among 1125 primes (data/z52b/analogues_constraints_20000.txt). Test whether failures are density-zero, and check whether a local obstruction (e.g. mod 8 or mod 3) explains them.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Odd-denominator ES is impossible (2-adic): the archetype of a constrained-world local obstruction
connection: If x, y, z are odd, xy + yz + zx is odd and xyz odd, so the reduced fraction has odd numerator, while 4/n (n odd) has numerator 4. So no solution. Likewise exactly one even denominator is impossible by 2-adic valuations (the computation confirms).
why: Gives the template for 'congruence-subgroup denominators' worlds: local obstructions are trivial to detect and separate from genuine lottery failures.
first_step: Generalize: for which multiplicative sets H ⊂ (Z/ℓ^k)^* of allowed denominator classes is there a local obstruction? Tabulate for ℓ ≤ 7.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Pairwise coprime denominators: impossible for n ≥ 2
connection: If gcd(x,y) = gcd(y,z) = gcd(x,z) = 1, the fraction (xy+yz+zx)/xyz is already reduced, so xyz = n·t and xy + yz + zx = 4t with t = 1, impossible for positive integers. All solutions need shared factors among denominators.
why: Every solution has a 'gcd skeleton'; the repo's Type I/II parametrisation is exactly the description of that skeleton. A constrained world with exactly one coprime pair is a natural middle case.
first_step: Count, for p < 4000, solutions with exactly one coprime pair vs none (the computation shows 'all pairs share a factor' never fails).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Sierpiński 5/n: the m = 5 twin of ES (verified to 10^18 per Pomerance's notes)
connection: 5/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z is open in exactly the same way: almost-all (Vaughan) and polynomial identities except square classes. Comparing hard classes of m = 4 and m = 5 separates numerator-specific from universal obstructions.
why: If a mechanism proves 5/n but not 4/n (or vice versa) it isolates a numerator-specific ingredient — e.g. the dyadic structure of 4.
first_step: Compute the mod-M uncovered classes for m = 5 after all small Type I/II identities (like Mordell's 840 for m = 4) and compare with T1 squares.

title: Mordell–Schinzel for general m: are square classes obstructed for every numerator?
connection: For m = 4 square classes mod M admit no polynomial identities. Check whether the same holds for every m (and whether additional obstructed classes appear for composite m such as 8 or 12).
why: A uniform obstruction across m confirms that T1 is about squares, not about 4; extra obstructed classes for some m would be new phenomena.
first_step: Run the identity-coverage search for m = 5..12 modulo 840·k and list uncovered classes; compare with squares.

title: Rav's two-term criterion: ES ⇔ ∃x, two divisors of nx summing to 0 mod (4x−n)
connection: a/b = 1/y + 1/z is solvable iff there are divisors d₁, d₂ of b with a | d₁ + d₂ (Rav 1966). With a/b = (4x−n)/(nx), ES(n) ⇔ ∃ x ∈ (n/4, n/2]-ish and divisors d₁, d₂ | nx with (4x − n) | d₁ + d₂.
why: It turns ES into additive combinatorics of divisor sets modulo m = 4x − n: 'the divisor set D(nx) satisfies D + D ∋ 0 mod m'. Sumset tools (Cauchy–Davenport, Kneser) are native.
first_step: For p < 10⁶ and each x, check whether |D(px) mod m| is large enough that Kneser/Cauchy–Davenport would force 0 ∈ D + D (mod m), and how often that alone certifies.

title: Best underapproximation of 4/n by three unit fractions (Kovač / Nathanson / Chu) — ES ⇔ gap 0
connection: The 'best k-term underapproximation' literature studies max{Σ_{i≤k} 1/x_i ≤ q}. ES ⇔ the 3-term underapproximation of 4/n is exact. Structure theorems for best underapproximations (eventually greedy) might constrain when exactness is possible.
why: If best 3-term underapproximations of 4/n are 'eventually greedy' in a way that forces a particular x, ES reduces to a single e-slice — testable.
first_step: Read Kovač 2406.07218 and Nathanson 2202.00191; compute the best 3-term underapproximation of 4/p for p ≤ 10^4 and check whether greedy first term works.

title: Odd unit fractions for 4/n: parity forces an EVEN number of terms (2 is sometimes enough)
connection: A sum of k odd unit fractions has numerator Σ_i Π_{j≠i} x_j ≡ k (mod 2) over an odd denominator; since 4/n (n odd) has even numerator, k must be even. k = 2 sometimes works (4/15 = 1/5 + 1/15); otherwise k = 4 is the next option.
why: A 4-term odd-denominator ES ('4/n = four odd unit fractions') is a natural open-looking twin; determine whether it is always solvable when the 2-term version fails.
first_step: Compute for odd n ≤ 10^4 whether 4/n is a sum of two, else four, odd unit fractions; look for obstructions mod 8.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Semiprime denominators: 4/p as a sum of three reciprocals of semiprimes
connection: Recent work shows every natural number is a sum of distinct semiprime unit fractions (Shisheng Li). The 3-term version for 4/p is a constrained ES with a natural density of allowed denominators ~ log log x / log x.
why: Probes how ES's solution count scales when denominators are thinned to a density-zero but not too sparse set.
first_step: Brute force for p ≤ 10^4; record failure density; compare with lottery prediction.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Rado/partition regularity of 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/w
connection: Brown–Rödl-type results transfer Rado's theorem to reciprocal equations. Is 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/w partition regular (monochromatic x, y, z, w in any finite colouring)? The linear counterpart x + y + z = 4w is not regular (no zero subset-sum of coefficients), but reciprocal equations can behave differently.
why: Partition regularity would be a robust 'many solutions' statement for the ES variety across all w, a Ramsey strengthening of 'ES has solutions'.
first_step: Check the reciprocal Rado literature (Brown–Rödl; Gaiser 2306.04029) for 1/x+1/y+1/z = c/w; try 2-colourings by computer for small ranges.

title: Four-term ES with distinct denominators is trivial — but four-term with a size cap is not
connection: 4/n as a sum of 4 unit fractions is easy (e.g. via 3/n splitting). With all denominators ≤ C·n (no huge denominators), the 4-term problem becomes a lattice/lottery problem again.
why: Size-capped multi-term ES might be provable for k = 4 with C large while ES (k = 3) remains open, giving a tunable intermediate theorem.
first_step: Compute, for n ≤ 10^4, the least C such that 4/n has a 4-term representation with max denominator ≤ C n; test boundedness.

title: Egyptian fractions with restricted prime support (Chen–Elsholtz–Jiang; Czenky–McGovern–Plavnik)
connection: Representations of 1 with denominators in S(p_1,…,p_t) (S-units) are studied; ES in Z[1/S] relates. For ES over ℕ with denominators S-smooth except for factors of p, the count is finite and computable.
why: Gives an explicit finite-world version of ES (bounded prime support) where complete enumeration is possible and failure structure can be studied exactly.
first_step: For S = {2,3,5,7}, enumerate solutions of 4/p = Σ 1/x_i with x_i ∈ p^{0,1}·S-units, p ≤ 10^6; find which p are covered.

title: Mixed: 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z² (one square denominator)
connection: One square denominator keeps the problem 2-dimensional but couples to quadratic residues. It is a sibling where the T1 square obstruction might be amplified or cancelled.
why: If it is always solvable via an identity involving z² ≡ something, it gives a new certificate type over Z.
first_step: Brute force n ≤ 10^4; for each solvable n record the class of z mod small primes.

title: Rational numbers representable with three unit fractions: density among a/b with b ≤ N
connection: Most rationals a/b with a large are not 3-term sums. ES says all 4/n are. Placing 4/n in the 2D picture (a, b) shows ES is on a 'ray' where the density is 1 conjecturally.
why: If density along the ray a = 4 is provably 1 (Vaughan) and along a = c log b provably 0, the transition curve is a precise target for heuristics.
first_step: Compute, for b ≤ 2000, the proportion of representable a/b as a function of a; plot transition.

title: Greedy / Engel / Sylvester expansions as dynamical systems on rationals
connection: The greedy (Fibonacci–Sylvester) algorithm and Engel/Pierce expansions are dynamical maps on ℚ ∩ (0,1). ES asks for a 3-step orbit-like decomposition, not necessarily greedy.
why: Odd greedy and other algorithms have termination theorems and counterexample families. An algorithm with provable 3-step termination on 4/p would prove ES.
first_step: Test 'greedy with a bounded look-ahead' algorithms (choose x among the first K candidates ≥ ⌈p/4⌉) for 3-term termination at all p < 10⁸; find the minimal K(p) growth.

title: Derived-set (accumulation) structure: 4/n is never an accumulation point of 3-term sums except via 2-term limits
connection: The set E₃ of 3-term sums is closed with accumulation points in E₂ (2-term sums). 4/n ∈ E₃ is a statement about an isolated vs limit point.
why: If 4/n lies in the closure of E₃ for trivial reasons (approximations from above/below), quantifying the approximation rate may force membership for arithmetic reasons.
first_step: Compute dist(4/p, E₃ ∖ {4/p}) for p ≤ 10^4 and compare with the expected spacing.

title: Triangle groups of covolume 2π(1 − 4/n)
connection: ES(n) for n ≥ 5 ⇔ there is a hyperbolic triangle group Δ(x,y,z) whose orbifold area is 2π(1 − 4/n), equivalently a hyperbolic triangle with angles π/x, π/y, π/z and area π(n−4)/n.
why: The covolume spectrum of Fuchsian groups is classically studied (Siegel's minimal covolume, signature theory). ES becomes 'every number of the form 2π(n−4)/n is a triangle-group covolume'.
first_step: Check whether 'areas of hyperbolic triangle orbifolds' as a set of rationals has been studied (search 'orbifold Euler characteristic triangle group which rationals'); list areas for arithmetic triangle groups.

title: Brieskorn–Pham log canonical thresholds: ES ⇔ 4/n = lct(x^a + y^b + z^c)
connection: For the diagonal singularity x^a + y^b + z^c, lct = min(1, 1/a + 1/b + 1/c). So ES(n) ⇔ 4/n (< 1 for n ≥ 5) is the log canonical threshold of a 3-variable Brieskorn–Pham polynomial.
why: Birational geometry studies the set LCT₃ of 3-dimensional lcts (ACC, accumulation points); ES asks whether all 4/n lie in the Brieskorn–Pham stratum. Other quasi-homogeneous types give natural relaxations.
first_step: Check the known description of LCT for quasi-homogeneous isolated singularities in 3 variables (Arnold's types) and list which rationals arise from each type.

title: Exact Seifert/pretzel form: ES(n) ⇔ a Seifert space M(0; (x,1),(y,1),(z,1)) with Euler number −4/n (double cover of the pretzel link P(x,y,z))
connection: The Seifert space over S² with unnormalised invariants (x,1),(y,1),(z,1) has rational Euler number e = −(1/x + 1/y + 1/z) and |H₁| = xy + yz + zx. It is the double branched cover of the pretzel link P(x,y,z), with det P = xy + yz + zx. So ES(n) ⇔ some positive pretzel link P(x,y,z) has det = 4xyz/n ⇔ some such Seifert space has e = −4/n.
why: It is an exact translation of the original equation into 3-manifold/knot language. The fields have structure theorems for pretzel knots (sliceness, genus, Heegaard Floer) and for Seifert invariants, with n appearing as the Euler number.
first_step: Tabulate, for n < 200, the pretzel links P(x,y,z) realising ES solutions; check whether Type I/II solution families correspond to natural pretzel families (e.g. one strand dividing another) and whether T1 square classes relate to slice pretzel knots (Greene–Jabuka; det must be a square).

title: Weighted star trees with central weight k: determinant xyz(k − 3 + Σ 1/x_i) — ES with integer offset
connection: Torrente-Lujan allows central diagonal entry k; the determinant becomes xyz(k − 3 + 1/x + 1/y + 1/z) (k = 2 recovers xyz(Σ 1/x_i − 1); e.g. k = 3, arms (2,2,2) gives 12). Different k shift the target by integers, giving 'ES with integer offset'.
why: Integer offsets are trivial arithmetically but the matrix world might impose inertia/definiteness constraints that select ES-relevant triples.
first_step: Read arXiv:2605.23011 for the determinant formula with general k and record the induced Egyptian equation.

title: Rectangle tilings: ES ⇔ an n×4 rectangle split into three horizontal strips, each a row of equal squares
connection: A strip of width W tiled by x equal squares has height W/x; three strips stacked give height W(1/x+1/y+1/z). Thus ES(n) ⇔ the rectangle of aspect n : 4 is tiled by three such strips.
why: Tiling theory (Dehn's theorem, Laczkovich–Szekeres tilings with similar rectangles) studies which aspect ratios are tileable under constraints; ES is a 3-strip constrained tiling.
first_step: Formalize and check whether allowing strips to be split further (two-level tilings) yields a known Dehn-type characterization that ES is a restriction of.

title: Landau's class equation and fusion-category Egyptian equations: 1 = Σ 1/|C(g_i)|
connection: Integral modular categories and finite groups yield Egyptian equations for 1 (Landau; Bruillard–Rowell). A group with 4 conjugacy classes gives 1 − 1/|G| = three unit fractions, an ES-type equation with numerator |G| − 1.
why: Shows ES-like equations arising from algebraic structures where existence is guaranteed by constructions; the analogous numerator family (N−1)/N is a sibling world.
first_step: Enumerate (N−1)/N = 1/a + 1/b + 1/c solutions and compare with groups having 4 classes (Z₄, V₄, D₅, A₄); note which equations are 'realized'.

title: Dessins d'enfants of type (x,y,z) with χ = 4/p − 1: ES certificates as Belyi maps
connection: Finite-index subgroups of Δ(x,y,z) ↔ dessins (bipartite maps) with all white-vertex degrees dividing x, etc. ↔ an ES certificate is the 'type' of a dessin whose Euler-characteristic bookkeeping involves p.
why: Dessins carry a Galois action; if an ES certificate could be read off a canonical dessin attached to p (e.g. from a Belyi map of a curve with p-torsion), existence would be algebraic. Speculative.
first_step: Look for a natural Belyi map attached to p (e.g. on the Fermat curve of exponent p, or X(p)) whose passport (ramification type) gives (x,y,z) with 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/p; X₀(p)-type modular curves have ramification (2,3,∞) — check others.

title: Spherical / Euclidean / hyperbolic trichotomy as a 'phase diagram' of numerators
connection: 1/x + 1/y + 1/z > 1 (spherical: the infinite family (2,2,r) plus finitely many others), = 1 (Euclidean: (3,3,3),(2,4,4),(2,3,6)), < 1 (hyperbolic). ES with 4/n < 1 sits in the hyperbolic regime; numerators m/n > 1 give the spherical lists.
why: The classification for sums > 1 (one infinite family plus a finite list) is the archetype of an 'Egyptian classification' theorem; ES is the infinite hyperbolic regime where no classification is possible but density is.
first_step: Record as context; check whether 'which rationals in (1, 3] are 3-term sums' (finite-ish lists per denominator) gives a useful contrast for heuristics.

title: Platonic-style Euler equation 1/p + 1/q = 1/2 + 1/E as the 2-term cousin
connection: Regular maps {p,q} satisfy 1/p + 1/q − 1/2 = χ/(2E). Two-term Egyptian equations arise from Euler's formula; ES is the analogous three-type (hypermap) equation.
why: Suggests that ES-type equations with an extra 'defect' term are realizable by maps on surfaces with prescribed χ; maps exist abundantly, so realizability is not the issue — the integrality is.
first_step: Context only; record the hypermap equation N/x + N/y + N/z − N = χ as the general form.

title: Weighted projective planes P(a,b,c) and Egyptian conditions for Fano/Kähler–Einstein
connection: Well-formedness and Fano conditions for P(a,b,c) and for hypersurfaces in weighted projective space are linear/Egyptian conditions on weights (e.g. Σ w_i > d for Fano hypersurfaces). Reid's 95 K3 families arise from such equations.
why: Classification lists of weighted hypersurfaces are generated by Egyptian-type inequalities; an equality version '1/a + 1/b + 1/c = 4/n' may describe a specific family (e.g. degree conditions), giving a geometric home for ES triples.
first_step: Look for weighted hypersurface conditions of the form Σ 1/w_i = r (equality) in Reid's/Iano-Fletcher's lists; match with 4/n.

title: Birational automorphism group of the ES surface S_n
connection: S_n: 4xyz = n(xy + yz + zx) ⇔ (after 1/x = X etc.) the plane X + Y + Z = 4/n, a linear plane; integrality is what makes it hard. The 'hidden' automorphisms preserving integrality are the Type I/II reparametrizations.
why: Explicit automorphisms mapping integral points to integral points at different n (n ↦ n') would be 'transport' maps between ES problems (repo: TRANSPORT_LAW).
first_step: List all integral-structure-preserving maps among Type I/II parametrizations and check for maps with n' ≠ n (scaling, Möbius in parameters).

title: Ford circles / Farey: 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/n as a tangency/curvature condition
connection: Farey neighbours and Ford circles encode 1/(qq') differences; three unit fractions summing to 4/n can be read as a chain of Farey steps. The repo's Farey/forest forms are instances.
why: Already explored (forests); keep as a pointer to the Farey world where SL₂(Z) acts.
first_step: Pointer only; check BRAINSTORM/farey_ford_cf.md.

title: Cluster algebras / friezes: unit fractions from Conway–Coxeter friezes
connection: Friezes encode continued fractions and SL₂ words; ES₅/SL₂-word forms suggest a frieze pattern of width ≤ 3 that produces 4/p. The repo has FRIEZE_ES.
why: Pointer: cluster mutation is a natural 'transport' between solutions.
first_step: Check whether the ES₅ length-3 words correspond to 3×(width) frieze patterns with entries tied to p, per FRIEZE_ES.md.

title: Squared rectangles: 4/n via Kirchhoff networks with three parallel branches of integer conductance
connection: Brooks–Smith–Stone–Tutte: a squared rectangle corresponds to a planar network with currents = square sizes. Three parallel branches each a series of identical resistors give the strip-tiling item; richer networks give 'generalized ES'.
why: Networks with a fixed small number of edges realizing n/4 form a hierarchy of relaxations whose first non-trivial level is ES.
first_step: Enumerate series-parallel networks of ≤ 3 integer resistors realising p/4 and identify which topologies are always solvable (series ones trivially) — clarifies ES as the 'all-parallel' corner.

title: Probability: 1/x + 1/y + 1/z as the rate of the minimum of three exponentials
connection: If T_i ~ Exp(mean x_i) are independent, min T_i has mean 1/Σ(1/x_i). ES ⇔ the minimum of three exponential clocks with integer means has mean n/4. Equivalent for discrete clocks: the first success among three periodic processes.
why: Reformulation only; might suggest probabilistic couplings to count solutions.
first_step: Low priority; note.

title: Integral fusion rings of rank 4 with Egyptian dimension equations (Alekseyev–Bruns–Dong)
connection: Classification of integral Grothendieck rings and modular data uses Egyptian-fraction equations with constraints, solved by computer to high rank. Their algorithms enumerate Egyptian solutions under divisibility constraints efficiently.
why: Their enumeration techniques (Bruns' Normaliz, divisibility pruning) could be reused for exhaustive constrained-ES censuses.
first_step: Read the algorithm sections of arXiv:2507.07023 and arXiv:2302.01613; assess reuse for ES censuses.

title: ES is false in a model of open induction (via Mordell–Schinzel in a discretely ordered ring)
connection: Discretely ordered rings like Z[T] with T infinitely large (and Shepherdson-type models of IOpen built from Puiseux polynomials) are models of weak arithmetic. ES in Z[T] with this order is the eventual-positivity polynomial world, where Mordell–Schinzel rules out n = mT + r².
why: Would show ES is unprovable in open induction, so any proof needs induction on non-open formulas — a precise statement about the logical strength of ES proofs (it is Π₁, so true-if-unprovable in PA).
first_step: Check that a suitable ring (e.g. Shepherdson's model, or Z + T·Q[T] variants) satisfies IOpen and that the Mordell–Schinzel argument applies there (denominators may have rational non-constant coefficients).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Ultraproduct of Z/pZ? No — ultraproduct of Z[1/S_k] with growing S: ES transfers by Łoś
connection: Since ES holds over every Z[1/ℓ] (odd ℓ < 3000 checked), it holds in ultraproducts of these rings; but these ultraproducts are not Z. Łoś only transfers first-order sentences true in almost all factors, giving nothing for Z.
why: A clean negative showing that proved S-integer worlds cannot transfer to Z by compactness; useful to prune approaches.
first_step: Record the negative; double-check that 'positive' is first-order definable in Z[1/ℓ] (it is, via sums of four squares).

title: Random-set analogue: replace '4Cp + 1' by a random integer of the same size and test ES-type existence
connection: The lottery model treats divisors of 4Cp + 1 as random. Simulating with genuinely random integers N_C ≈ 4Cp gives the 'random world' where ES holds with probability → 1 but fails sometimes.
why: Comparing failure rates in the random world with the actual (none known) quantifies how much structure real ES has beyond randomness.
first_step: Simulate: for random 'p' replace 4Cp + 1 by uniform random integers in [4Cp, 4Cp + 4C·p^{0.5}] and measure failure frequency at p ~ 10^6.

title: Algebraic combinatorics: q-analogue of ES (q-integers [n]_q) and its solvability
connection: Replace n by [n]_q = 1 + q + … + q^{n−1}: 4/[n]_q = Σ 1/[x_i]_q in ℚ(q)? ↔ q-deformations sometimes make problems rigid.
why: If a q-analogue has polynomial-identity solutions, specialising q → 1 might give ES; Mordell–Schinzel suggests obstruction persists, but the q-world has extra freedom (cyclotomic factorisations of [n]_q).
first_step: Search x, y, z ≤ 60, n ≤ 60 for exact identities in Q(q) using polynomial arithmetic.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Cross-world hard primes: 241 and 2521 fail in several constrained worlds
connection: 241 fails 'all even' (m = 8), 'a denominator ≡ 0 mod 4' and 'all denominators sums of two squares'; 2521 fails 'z = lcm' and 'sums of two squares'. Primes failing several strengthenings may be intrinsically hard for ES.
why: If a small set of primes is hard across worlds, studying its structure (e.g. 241 = 15·16 + 1, 2521 = 2520 + 1 = lcm(1..10) + 1!) may reveal what structure makes p hard.
first_step: Note 2521 = lcm(1,…,10) + 1 and 241 = 240 + 1 (240 = 2⁴·3·5); test whether p − 1 highly composite (many small factors) correlates with failing strengthenings.

title: Size-capped ES: max denominator ≤ p²/8 fails at 45 primes below 2·10^4 (incl. 5, 13, 17, 29)
connection: The cap z ≤ p²/8 removes the largest solutions (Type II with z ≍ p²); 45 primes then fail. The failure set shows which primes depend on the 'extreme' solutions.
why: Size-capped worlds quantify how much ES relies on huge denominators; the threshold cap c(p) = min over solutions of z/p² is a new invariant.
first_step: Compute c(p) = min_solutions max(x,y,z)/p² for p < 2·10^4; check whether c(p) → 0 or stays bounded below for infinitely many p.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Probabilistic 'Schinzel world': random rationals a/b with b prime — what fraction are 3-term sums?
connection: Luca–Pappalardi/Mond–Portier give x(log x)³ ≪ Σ_{p≤x} A₃(p) ≪ x(log x)³(log log x)², i.e. A₃(p) is about (log p)⁴ on average over primes (up to loglog); heuristically a random numerator a ≤ p is representable with probability ≈ (log p)⁴/p (an average-based heuristic, not a theorem about individual p). ES says a = 4 always is: 4 is special because small numerators have more representations.
why: Makes precise that ES is about the small-numerator end of a distribution whose bulk is sparse; methods that see only averages over a cannot reach a = 4.
first_step: Compute #representations of a/p as a function of a for fixed p ~ 10^4; fit decay in a.

title: Computability world: ES for 'computable reals'/Turing degrees — category error check
connection: Considered: 'ES over computable reals' is meaningless (no integrality). Kept only the meaningful variant: ES restricted to n in a decidable set is decidable for each n, and the set of ES-failures is co-c.e.
why: Confirms nothing beyond the Π₁ item; record to avoid revisiting.
first_step: None (closed).

title: ES for elements of Z_p (p-adic) with 'positivity' from an embedding into R — not well-defined
connection: Category-error check: Z_p has no archimedean embedding, so positivity cannot be imported; the meaningful p-adic analogues are local solubility (always) and p-adic cones (items in batch B).
why: Record the closed item to avoid repeated consideration.
first_step: None (closed).

title: Modular hyperbola XY ≡ 1 (mod p) with X ≡ Y ≡ −1 (mod t) and XY = tp+1
connection: Words ↔ points (X,Y) = (A, A*) on the modular hyperbola XY ≡ 1 mod p with X, Y ≡ −1 mod t and the exact archimedean condition XY = tp+1. Shparlinski's survey covers point counts in boxes via Kloosterman sums.
why: Native results give points of XY ≡ c mod m in boxes of side ≥ m^{1/2+ε}. ES needs a hyperbola-shaped region (XY exactly tp+1), and that shape is the whole difficulty.
first_step: Compute the fraction of integral Type II hyperbola points in each mod-4cd class and compare with the modular hyperbola's equidistribution.

title: ES in 'Z with a different order': positive cone = {n : n ≡ 1 mod 4 or …} is not multiplicatively closed — design check
connection: Orders on Z other than the usual one don't exist (Z has a unique ordering as an ordered ring). So 'other positivity on Z' must be a semigroup restriction (constraint worlds), not a new order.
why: Closes a tempting but empty direction; constraint worlds (batch C) cover the meaningful variants.
first_step: None (closed).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Gaussian-norm constrained world: failures are NOT explained by mod 8 or the quartic character of 2
connection: Failures of 'all denominators sums of two squares' below 2·10^4 (40 primes) occur in both classes 1 and 5 mod 8, in non-square classes mod 840 (e.g. 709, 829), and 17 of 40 have 2 as a quartic residue (vs 48% overall among p ≡ 1 mod 8). So no simple local/reciprocity explanation is visible.
why: This world therefore looks like a genuine lottery world with fewer tickets than ES — a test bed for the lottery model where failures actually occur, calibrating predicted vs observed failure rates.
first_step: Compute the lottery-model expected number of norm-constrained solutions per p (densities of sums of two squares among Type I/II denominators) and compare predicted with observed failure frequency.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Ternary Goldbach (proved) vs binary Goldbach (open): where ES sits
connection: Ternary problems with power-size expected counts are proved by the circle method; binary ones are open. ES at fixed p has expected count ≍ log²p, smaller than binary Goldbach's ≍ p/log²p — ES is 'sub-binary', so circle-method-type methods are not expected to work pointwise.
why: Calibrates expectations: pointwise ES needs structure (algebraic identities, reciprocity) rather than analysis; analytic methods only give almost-all.
first_step: Context; record the comparison of expected counts in the memo header.

title: Conlon–Fox–He on an Erdős–Graham question about Egyptian fractions
connection: Recent work resolves an Erdős–Graham question on Egyptian fractions (details to read). It belongs to the modern 'Egyptian existence' toolkit along with Bloom and Liu–Sawhney.
why: Any new technique giving existence of Egyptian representations with structural constraints is a candidate input for constrained ES worlds.
first_step: Read arXiv:2404.16016 abstract and main theorem; note the technique.

title: Odd perfect numbers and abundancy: Σ_{d | n} 1/d = 2 as an Egyptian constraint
connection: σ(n)/n = Σ_{d|n} 1/d; perfect numbers solve an Egyptian equation with denominators forced to be all divisors. Bounds on odd perfect numbers (Nielsen) use unit-fraction inequalities.
why: Shares the 'Egyptian equation + multiplicative constraint' shape; techniques bounding solutions there bound ES-like constrained worlds.
first_step: Low priority: note as sibling.

title: Least quadratic non-residue (Burgess/Vinogradov) ↔ least ES certificate
connection: ES certificates are found by searching small parameters (e.g. least C with 4Cp + 1 having a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C). The least quadratic non-residue problem has a GRH bound O(log² p) and unconditional p^{1/(4√e)}.
why: If the least certificate behaves like the least non-residue, ES is implied by a GRH-type character-sum bound — exactly where the repo's EXSET_LINNIK memos look.
first_step: Compute the least certificate parameter C(p) for p ≤ 10^7 and compare its growth with log² p; check EXSET_LINNIK.md.

title: Markoff surfaces: strong approximation for almost all primes (Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak, W. Chen)
connection: For Markoff, the integral points mod p form a single orbit except for a small set of p, proven for all large p by W. Chen via a divisibility argument (degree of the mod-p orbit). ES has no Vieta group, but a different group action on its integral points could play the same role.
why: Chen's argument ('the size of every orbit is divisible by p') is a pointwise-for-all-primes technique arising from group actions — the only such technique in sibling worlds.
first_step: Search for any nontrivial correspondence/group acting on ES solutions mod p (beyond permutations); see UNIT_ORBIT_ES.md.

title: Cox 'primes of the form x² + ny²': certificate at level d as a ring-class-field splitting condition
connection: A Type I/II certificate at level d is equivalent to p having a specific representation or splitting behaviour in a ring class field of an order in Q(√−d) (QUATERNION_ES / LATTICE_MEETING). Cox's book gives the exact class-field criterion for such representations.
why: It turns 'certificate at level d' into 'Frobenius of p lies in a set S_d of a Galois group'. ES ⇔ p's Frobenius lies in ∪_d S_d, an infinite union of Chebotarev conditions (the B2 shape).
first_step: For d ≤ 10, write S_d explicitly (ring class field of the relevant conductor) and compute the density covered; compare with the Mordell residue-class picture.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Sierpiński's 5/n, Schinzel's m/n: almost-all results (Vaughan) are uniform in m — what uniformity is known?
connection: Vaughan's density result covers every fixed m. The dependence of the exceptional-set bound on m is the quantitative sibling link between ES and its numerator neighbours.
why: A bound uniform in m up to (log n)^A would show the numerator-ladder (4 | 8 | 16) exceptional sets shrink together.
first_step: Read Vaughan 1970 for m-dependence; record.

title: Lattice-point/hyperbola methods (Dirichlet divisor problem) for fixed-p ES counts
connection: ES counts at fixed p are sums of divisor-counting functions over arithmetic progressions; the Dirichlet hyperbola method with exponent pairs gives error terms.
why: Comparing the main term ≍ log²p with error terms shows whether any pointwise statement is within reach of classical exponent-pair technology (likely not).
first_step: Count factor pairs of the fixed-x product equation in the required residue classes using divisor bounds and compare across x.

title: Primitive prime divisors (Zsigmondy/Bang) as the integer replacement for 'units' in proved worlds
connection: In Z[1/ℓ] the universal divisor comes from 1 + ℓ^k; Zsigmondy guarantees new prime factors of a^k ± 1. Over Z the corresponding p-tied integers (4Cp + 1) have no such algebraic factor structure.
why: If p-tied integers with Zsigmondy-like algebraic factorizations exist (e.g. p^k + 1 or 4p^k + 1 families), they supply 'universal divisors' p-dependently — power-ladder certificates.
first_step: List ES certificate families involving p^k ± 1 or similar (power ladders); check POWER_LADDER_ES.md for the state of the art.

title: Andrews–Dyson-type partition identities as 'identities in growing families'
connection: Partition theory has infinite families of identities (Rogers–Ramanujan type) with growing parameters, proved by q-series. ES needs growing certificate families whose union covers all p; q-series identity machinery (Bailey chains) generates infinite families systematically.
why: Bailey-chain-style generators for ES identities (indexed by a growing parameter) would be a systematic way to produce non-B1 families.
first_step: Low priority; look for an ES identity family indexed by k with a recursive (chain) structure, e.g. from power ladders.

title: Real cyclotomic field Q(ζ_p)^+: cyclotomic units tied to p supply ES solutions; descend by trace
connection: Q(ζ_p)^+ has totally positive cyclotomic units (e.g. squares of (1 − ζ^a)/(1 − ζ) suitably normalized) and p is totally ramified. Positive ES for 4/p holds there by the unit mechanism; tracing a solution down to Q gives 2(p − 1)/p = Σ Tr(1/α_i), an Egyptian-type identity with trace numerators.
why: Provides an explicit p-indexed family of algebraic solutions whose descent might be engineered (choice of unit) to have unit-fraction traces — an algebraic source of p-dependent certificates.
first_step: For p = 5, 13, 17 compute a totally positive cyclotomic unit η ≡ −1 mod an inert-type prime and the resulting solution; compute traces of the denominators.

title: All denominators divisible by 3 ⇔ 12/p is a 3-term sum: fails at 15 primes below 8000
connection: Analogous to all-even ⇔ 8/p: 'all denominators ≡ 0 mod 3' ⇔ 12/p = Σ 1/(x_i/3). Failures: 5, 13, 29, 37, 73, 97, 193, 433, 577, 1129, … (15 of 499).
why: The numerator ladder m ∈ {4, 8, 12, 16, …} gives nested strengthenings with growing (apparently finite?) exceptional sets; their structure across m (Schinzel) tells how robust ES is.
first_step: Extend to 10^5 and check whether the m = 12 exceptional set stabilizes (finite) or keeps growing; compare with m = 8 ({17, 241}).

title: Size cap max ≤ p^{3/2}: fails at 359 of 499 primes — most primes need a denominator > p^{3/2}
connection: Most p ≡ 1 mod 4 have no solution with all denominators ≤ p^{3/2}; ES genuinely needs large denominators (Type II with z ≍ p²/k).
why: Shows that size-restricted ES is false for most p at exponent 3/2; the critical exponent θ (all denominators ≤ p^θ always possible) lies in (3/2, 2]. Determining θ is a precise new question.
first_step: Compute, for p < 10^5, min over solutions of log(max denominator)/log p; plot its distribution and limsup/liminf.

title: ES over Z_(p) (all primes except p inverted, ordering inherited from Q): trivial
connection: Z_(p) ⊂ Q inherits the usual order. Since 4 is invertible in Z_(p) for odd p, 4/p = 1/(p/2) + 1/p + 1/p with positive denominators p/2, p, p ∈ Z_(p). So inverting everything but p trivializes ES — the complementary extreme to Z[1/p].
why: Boundary marker for the localization family; the interesting worlds are finite S (Z[1/ℓ]) where structure remains.
first_step: None (closed).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Integer statement from the Gaussian twin: ES with denominators of the form a² + b² and a 'sector' constraint
connection: A Gaussian-cone solution for rational p projects (via norms) to an integer equation with denominators that are sums of two squares. The norm-constrained integer world fails at 40 primes below 2·10^4, so any projection must lose this constraint somewhere.
why: Quantifies what the Gaussian world can and cannot give back to Z: norms alone are too restrictive.
first_step: For a few p in the norm-failure list (41, 137), check whether Gaussian-cone solutions exist (if yes, the projection is not via norms).

title: ES for Gaussian n = π with π ≡ 1 mod 4 in Z[i] but denominators in Z (rational): mixed world
connection: Ask for 4/π = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with x, y, z ∈ Z[i] but two of them rational integers. Mixing rational and Gaussian denominators interpolates between ES and the Gaussian twin.
why: Mixed worlds test whether a single 'extra' algebraic denominator suffices to dissolve difficulty (one complex degree of freedom).
first_step: Brute-force for Gaussian primes of norm ≤ 2000 with two rational denominators.

title: ES on average over number fields: for random real quadratic K, how often does rational ES need units?
connection: For many K, rational ES solutions over O_K may be integer solutions (no units needed). Statistics of 'units needed' across K measure how often integer ES is the bottleneck.
why: If, for a positive proportion of K, all p have non-unit solutions of a new type (genuinely quadratic denominators without units), these give a new integer-adjacent mechanism.
first_step: For D ≤ 100 and p ≤ 1000 count solutions with non-rational denominators not using units (bounded height).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Thinned-denominator worlds (norm forms, forbidden primes): failure rates vary hugely with the thinning
connection: (Not what was computed: the census used NORM denominators, which allow primes ≡ 3 mod 4 to even powers.) Norm-thinning results: sums of two squares fail at 40 primes below 2·10^4; Eisenstein norms fail at 451 of 499 below 8000; x² + 2y² norms at 276 of 499. The strict 'no prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4' world is still to be run.
why: The failure rate varies hugely with the thinning set; a quantitative lottery model must predict 40/1125 vs 451/499 vs 276/499 correctly — a sharp test of the model.
first_step: Fit the lottery model's per-p expected count for each thinning (density of allowed denominators ~ C/√log) and compare predicted vs observed failure fractions.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES with denominators in a fixed coset of squares: 4/n = Σ 1/(c·s_i²)
connection: Denominators c·s² (c fixed squarefree): 4/(cn)… reduces to 4c'/n = Σ 1/s_i², the square-reciprocal world (batch C). A coset choice c = p makes it p-tied.
why: Square-reciprocal worlds are very sparse; their solvability for specific c might be governed by genus theory, giving a quadratic-forms handle.
first_step: For c ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 6} compute which n admit 4/n = Σ 1/(c s_i²) up to 10^5.

title: ES in the max-denominator-minimizing world: optimal solutions and their arithmetic
connection: For each p choose the solution minimizing max(x,y,z). The optimal solution is a canonical object; its Type (I/II) and parameters form a function of p whose structure may be simpler than the full solution set.
why: A canonical solution map p ↦ s(p) could be guessed (e.g. 'smallest C with a certificate') and proved by showing the guess always works.
first_step: Compute s(p) for p ≤ 10^5; tabulate its type and parameters; look for a rule.

title: ES over finite rings Z/p^kZ lifted with Hensel: number of solutions mod p^k as k → ∞ (p-adic density)
connection: The p-adic density of the ES surface at the target prime p (σ_p) controls how Type I/II split solutions. Its exact value (as function of p) enters the singular series and might vanish to higher order at p for structural reasons.
why: A small σ_p would explain why ES counts at p are only polylog; a closed formula is cheap to derive.
first_step: Count solutions of 4xyz ≡ p(xy + yz + zx) (mod p^k) with x, y, z in suitable unit/non-unit patterns for k ≤ 3, small p.

title: Bounded-slice world: ES with e = 4x − p ≤ E fixed — false for each fixed E (Mordell), find growth of needed E
connection: For fixed E, the union of slices e ≤ E is a finite covering by congruence classes, so fails at square classes. The least E(p) is the true complexity measure; ES ⇔ E(p) < ∞.
why: Bounds on E(p) like O(log^A p) would be a precise and plausible (GRH-like) target; repo memos study it.
first_step: Compute E(p) to 10^7 and fit growth; compare with the least-certificate item.

title: ES over the semiring of Pythagorean triples / norm-one elements: Z[i] units of infinite order? none — use Q(i)^×/torsion
connection: Category check: Z[i] has finite units, so a 'norm-one cone' is finite; using Q(i) norm-one elements gives non-integral denominators. Not a meaningful world; recorded as closed.
why: Avoids a dead end.
first_step: None (closed).

title: Lattice of solutions: the Z-span of solution vectors (1/x, 1/y, 1/z) as p varies
connection: For each p the solutions give rational vectors with coordinate sum 4/p. Their Z-span or the lattice generated by the denominators across p might show hidden linear relations (e.g. always containing a fixed vector).
why: A fixed vector in all solution spans would be a 'universal certificate' in disguise.
first_step: Compute for p < 2000 the lattice generated by (lcm/x, lcm/y, lcm/z) and look for invariants.

title: Prime-denominator world (Luca–Pappalardi title world): 4/p with all denominators in {p, primes, 2·primes}
connection: Denominators restricted to primes or twice primes is a very sparse world; 'x prime' alone fails at 260/499 below 8000. Full prime-type restriction probably fails almost always.
why: Gives a lower anchor for lottery calibration (very few tickets → mostly failures).
first_step: Compute for p < 8000 the 'all denominators in {primes, 2·primes, p·small}' world.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Coding-theoretic world: ES as a weight-enumerator identity for three cyclic codes of lengths x, y, z
connection: A cyclic code of length x has 'density' 1/x for a single codeword position class; a disjoint union of three such position classes with total density 4/n is the AP packing reformulation in coding language.
why: Mostly a rephrasing of the AP packing world; little added value.
first_step: Low priority.

title: Graph world: the bipartite graph primes ↔ certificate families; ES ⇔ no isolated prime
connection: Build a graph with primes p on one side and certificate families (Type I/II parameter sets) on the other, edges when the family solves p. ES ⇔ every p has degree ≥ 1. Random-graph thresholds (isolated vertices vanish at log-degree) model ES.
why: The isolated-vertex threshold in random bipartite graphs is sharp (expected degree ~ log of size); ES's degree ~ log²p is above threshold, matching 'ES true but barely'.
first_step: Compute degree statistics and compare with the isolated-vertex threshold for matching random graphs.

title: Word-map monodromy (finite flat covers t,u,v ↦ tuv − u − v) has no integer analogue — find one?
connection: EXSET_FUNCTION_FIELD 7′ uses monodromy groups of word covers (CFSG ⇒ Alt) to bound large-q exceptional densities by exp(−Ω(n²)). Over Z, the analogue would be a 'Galois group' for the factorization of n + v as tuv − u − v… — no known integer analogue.
why: Integer 'monodromy' could be modelled by Chebotarev in the splitting fields of the polynomial family X·Y·Z − Y − Z − n over Q(n) (Hilbert irreducibility); its Galois group controls the density of n with a word of a given shape.
first_step: Compute the Galois group over Q(n) of the polynomial system defining words of a fixed shape and compare with the FF G_{n,p}.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES_q(T) has no finite linear covering for q = 3^r, r ≥ 2 (FF_ODD_ABSENCE Cor 2.3) — a proved FF 'Mordell'
connection: The FF analogue of Mordell's no-covering result is PROVED for q = 9, 27, … (computer-assisted); in contrast F_4 and F_2 have finite coverings. This maps exactly which q behave like Z with respect to coverings.
why: Characterizing q with/without finite coverings (char 2 yes, 3^r no) gives a criterion whose Z-analogue is Mordell; the char-2 exception is the cancellation mechanism.
first_step: Tabulate known covering status for q ∈ {2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9}; guess the criterion (char 2 ⇔ covering?).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES over F_q with a cone = an index-2 subgroup (squares): the 'quadratic positivity' finite world
connection: In F_q, require x, y, z to be non-zero squares. Solvability of 4/n = Σ 1/x_i with squares is a question about the diagonal quadric Σ a_i w_i^{−2}… — solvable for q large by Weil; failures only for small q.
why: Small-q failures of 'quadratic positivity' indicate how much a sign-type restriction can obstruct in a finite world — a calibration of T1-like effects at the level of a single prime.
first_step: Brute force for q ≤ 50: for which q and n does 4/n = Σ 1/x_i with x_i nonzero squares have no solution?
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Signed ES with exactly one negative term and all |denominators| ≤ C·n²: does it always hold?
connection: Signed ES (one minus sign) is trivially solvable with denominators ≍ n² (4/(4k+1) = 1/k − 1/(k(4k+1)), split one more). Bounding all three denominators by C·n² keeps it easy; bounding by n^{3/2} may make it a lottery.
why: A signed analogue with a size cap is a tunable world: its threshold exponent vs the positive ES threshold (> 3/2 from data) compares sign freedom with size freedom.
first_step: For n ≤ 10^4 compute the minimal max-denominator over signed (one negative) 3-term representations of 4/n; compare growth with the positive case.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Signed ES as the 'char-2 shadow': cancellation of equal-size terms ↔ difference of nearly equal unit fractions
connection: In F_2[T], 1/X + 1/(X + δ) has a cancelled leading term; over Z, 1/x − 1/(x + δ) = δ/(x(x+δ)) is small. Signed integer identities in which the negative term is the partner of a positive term mimic F₂ identities.
why: Lifting F₂-proofs to Z would produce signed identities; a 'positivity repair' lemma (replace 1/a − 1/b by positive terms when structure allows) would complete the transfer.
first_step: Take the F₂[T] covering identities (FUNCTIONFIELD_ES §6), substitute T ↦ 2 or T ↦ integer with signs, and see which become signed integer identities for 4/n.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Merging step: from a 4-term solution to a 3-term one (when do two unit fractions sum to a unit fraction?)
connection: 1/a + 1/b = 1/c iff (a − c)(b − c) = c². Given many 4-term solutions of 4/n, ES follows if some pair satisfies this. The density of 'mergeable pairs' among 4-term solutions is a computable statistic.
why: Reduces ES to a statement about 4-term solutions (easier to construct) plus a quadratic coincidence; a 4-term family with a built-in mergeable pair would be a Type I/II family in disguise.
first_step: For n ≤ 2000 enumerate 4-term solutions with bounded denominators and count mergeable pairs; check whether every n has one (it must, since ES holds there).

title: Matrix ES in M_2(Z) with X symmetric positive-definite and det X = x: projective version
connection: For PD integral X with det X = x, (X⁻¹)_{11} = X_{22}/x. Summing (1,1) entries: 4/n = Σ X_i,22/x_i — numerators X_i,22 ≥ 1, so the (1,1)-projection gives a 'numerator-weighted ES'. Matrix ES ⇒ weighted ES with weights X_{22}.
why: Weighted ES with weights ≥ 1 is easier (weights 2 trivialize), so matrix ES is likely easy; this pins how the matrix world relaxes ES.
first_step: Check whether k = 2 matrix ES is trivially solvable via weighted identities (e.g. one matrix contributing weight 2).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Gaussian-cone ES for rational p counted by Hecke characters
connection: Solutions in Z[i] with sector constraints correspond to Gaussian integers in angular sectors; counts of Gaussian primes/integers in sectors are given by Hecke Grössencharacters (Kubilius). A sector-count formula for Gaussian-cone ES would use equidistribution of angles.
why: Angular equidistribution is proved (Hecke); if ES's Gaussian twin reduces to 'some solution in a sector', equidistribution of all solutions' angles would prove it for large norm.
first_step: Compute angles of all Z[i] solutions of 4/p (no cone) for p ≤ 1000 and check whether some lies in the cone; test equidistribution.

title: p-adic cone 1 + p^kZ_p: locally OBSTRUCTED, not collapsed
connection: If all denominators lie in 1 + p^kZ_p (k ≥ 1), each 1/x_i is ≡ 1 mod p^k, so the sum is ≡ 3 (mod p^k) and is a p-adic unit; 4/n with p | n has negative valuation. So this cone gives a local obstruction (congruence-subgroup type), not a collapse.
why: Corrects a tempting misapplication of the cone principle: cones of local units impose congruence obstructions; the collapse mechanism needs elements that are small at a sign place.
first_step: Record with the congruence-subgroup obstruction family (batch C items on odd / 1 mod 3 denominators).

title: Numerator 4 over F_q[T] with A = T² + 1 irreducible of degree 2 (an 'odd 4')
connection: F_q[T] with q odd has |A| = q² for degree-2 A. Choosing A irreducible makes the numerator 'prime', unlike 4 = 2². Comparing A = T² and A = T² + 1 (q = 3) tests whether a reducible numerator matters (batch A item) — this is the companion run.
why: If irreducible A has more exceptions, the reducibility 4 = 2·2 helps over Z (e.g. via 2-adic structure).
first_step: Run the existing FF search for q = 3, A ∈ {T², T² + 1, T² + T + 2} for deg P ≤ 10.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Hilbert's 10th / Diophantine sets: the set of ES-failing n is Diophantine (co-r.e.) — trivial but formal
connection: {n : ¬ES(n)} is Π₁-definable, hence its complement {n : ES(n)} is Diophantine (Σ₁) by MRDP; a polynomial whose positive values are exactly ES-good n exists. Nothing new arithmetically, but gives a 'polynomial certificate world'.
why: Mostly formal; MRDP polynomials are huge. Recorded to close the logic direction.
first_step: Note; skip unless a logician collaborator is interested.

title: ES for squares n = p²: always true from ES(p), but certificate lines are empty (T1) — the 'derived' world
connection: ES(p²) follows by scaling a solution for p. Yet no certificate line covers odd squares (T1). So squares are the archetype of 'true but uncertifiable by lines' — solutions come only by inheritance from p.
why: Suggests a general mechanism: hard primes might also be 'inheritance-only' from some related integer (e.g. a solution of 4/(pk) scaled?). Search for inheritance relations ES(m) ⇒ ES(p) with p ∤ m impossible, but p | m possible: ES(p) ⇐ ES(pk) is false direction… check carefully.
first_step: Clarify which inheritance directions exist (ES(d) ⇒ ES(n) for d | n) and whether a p-solution can be 'generated' from solutions at multiples of p by some descent.

title: Dyadic splitting type across imaginary quadratic twins: 2 ramified (Z[i]), inert (Z[ω]), split (Z[(1+√−7)/2])
connection: The numerator 4 factors differently: (1+i)⁴, 2² (inert), (αᾱ)² (split). If ES-type difficulty in cone worlds depends on how 2 splits, the dyadic structure of ES (I3 coordinate 4Z ∪ (8Z − p), m = 8 coincidence) is the integer shadow of that dependence.
why: Gives a controlled experiment on the role of the prime 2 with three otherwise similar worlds.
first_step: Define comparable cones in the three rings (discrete, multiplicatively closed) and compare failure statistics for rational primes p ≤ 2000.

title: Random thinning: keep each integer as a denominator independently with probability ρ — threshold ρ_c(p)
connection: With #ES(p) ≈ c log²p solutions, a random ρ-thinning keeps each solution with probability ρ³; the expected surviving count is c ρ³ log²p, so failures appear when ρ ≲ (log p)^{−2/3}.
why: A purely probabilistic world with an explicit threshold; comparing with the observed failure rates of structured thinnings (norms, Beatty) shows which thinnings are 'random-like'.
first_step: Simulate ρ ∈ {0.5, 0.3, 0.2} on all solutions for p < 2·10^4 and compare failure fractions with the Poisson prediction exp(−ρ³ #ES(p)).

title: Transfer statement D (from Mordell–Schinzel in Z[T]): any proof must be non-uniform in n
connection: Since ES is false over Z[T] (eventual positivity) at square classes, no argument that also works verbatim for 'polynomial n' can prove ES. Proof strategies must use a property of integers that fails for polynomials (e.g. archimedean size of specific values, primality, bounded height search).
why: A meta-filter for proof ideas: test each idea by asking whether it would also 'prove' ES over Z[T].
first_step: Add this filter to the evaluation checklist of later waves (not applied here per brief).

title: Lifting from mod-p solutions: Hensel/approximation world 'ES over Z/p^kZ with archimedean box'
connection: A solution mod p^k with representatives in the box (p/4, 3p/4] × [1, p²] × [1, p³] and k large enough is an integer solution (the equation is exact once p^k exceeds the size). So ES ⇔ a box-solution modulo a large modulus.
why: Recasts ES as a box problem in a finite ring where character-sum methods apply; the box is tiny relative to the modulus, which is why it's hard.
first_step: Quantify: the box volume vs modulus at which heuristics predict a solution (= log²p expected count); compare with known small-solution theorems.

title: Hardy field world: ES for n = n(t) a function of a real parameter with eventual positivity
connection: Generalizing Z[T]: n(t) in a Hardy field (e.g. exp-log functions), denominators integer-valued exp-log functions eventually positive. Mordell–Schinzel's obstruction might weaken when exponentials are allowed (power ladders live here).
why: Gives the natural home of 'growing families': identities in exp-log functions of an auxiliary parameter k that cover square classes would have to evade T1 via exponential growth.
first_step: Test whether T1 at odd squares still blocks exp-log identities: does an identity in (k, 2^k) evaluate to certificate lines at squares?

title: Cone worlds in Z[√2]: compare four cones (ℕ, N[√2], height-positive, totally positive)
connection: A family of four cones in one ring, only partially ordered by inclusion (e.g. √2 ∈ N[√2] is not totally positive), with expected behaviour hard, ?, hard?, easy. Measuring solution counts per cone for rational p gives a direct map of how cone size controls ES.
why: The cleanest single-ring experiment for the cone principle.
first_step: Implement one search with four filters; output solution counts per cone for p ≤ 1000.

title: ES for Hurwitz quaternions of prime norm p: does every p have a quaternion solution with commuting denominators?
connection: Commuting quaternion denominators lie in an imaginary quadratic subfield; so quaternion ES with commuting denominators = union over imaginary quadratic orders inside the quaternion order of cone-ES there.
why: Gives a union-of-imaginary-quadratic-twins world: ES over many Gaussian-like rings at once; existence in at least one might be easy.
first_step: For p ≤ 500, search for quaternion solutions with all denominators in a common Z[√−d] ⊂ Hurwitz order.

title: Sato–Tate-type world: distribution of ES solution 'angles' (x/p, y/p², …) as p varies
