connection: Normalized solution coordinates (x/p ∈ (1/4, 3/4], log y/log p, …) may equidistribute w.r.t. a limiting measure as p → ∞, like Sato–Tate angles. Hard primes would be those whose solutions avoid the bulk of the measure.
why: A limiting measure gives a precise heuristic for the probability that no solution falls in the 'admissible region' — the ES lower-tail question.
first_step: For p < 2·10^4 histogram x/p over all solutions and test convergence of the empirical measure.

title: Effective Hilbert-irreducibility world: ES-good p as values outside thin sets of a parameter family
connection: Each Type II family is a rational map from parameters to p; p is ES-good iff it is a value of some family. 'Values of a polynomial map in all primes' is Hilbert-irreducibility territory (value sets of covers). ES ⇔ the union of value sets of countably many covers contains all p ≡ 1 mod 4.
why: Value-set theorems for covers (e.g. Müller, Dèbes) might give density statements with better error terms than sieve methods.
first_step: Formalize Type II families as covers P¹ ← C and look up value-set results for families of covers of growing degree.

title: FF analogue of hard-prime structure: P with P − 1 'smooth' (many small-degree factors)
connection: Over Z, constrained-world failures cluster at p with smooth p − 1 (601, 1801, 2521). In F_q[T] the analogue is P with P − 1 (or P + c) having many small factors; FF exceptional P's can be checked for this property.
why: If the same 'smooth shift ⇒ hard' pattern appears in FF where proofs exist, the FF proofs explain how such P are still covered — a template for Z.
first_step: From FF exception lists (EXSET_FUNCTION_FIELD data), compute the factorization degree profile of P − 1 for failing vs non-failing P.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Sign-twisted FF world: monic denominators but numerator A with leading coefficient c ≠ 1
connection: With A of leading coefficient c, Lemma 1.1 forces lc relations; choosing c a non-square (q odd) twists the 'colour' at ∞ — an FF analogue of changing the numerator's sign class (4 vs −4 or 4 vs 4·non-square).
why: Over Z the analogous twist is numerator −4 (signed) or 4·(−1) — trivial; in FF the twist by non-square c is non-trivial and may model T1's sign layer.
first_step: Run ES_q(cT, P) for q = 3, c = −1 (non-square), deg P ≤ 10; compare with c = 1.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Union-of-slices world with a 'budget': ES restricted to the first B slices — false for each fixed B, but by how much?
connection: Each fixed set of B slices is a finite covering ⇒ fails on a positive-density set (square classes and more). The density of failures f(B) as B grows measures how fast ES's certificate supply converges.
why: f(B) → 0 is equivalent to Vaughan-type almost-all; its rate is a concrete function to compute and model (e.g. f(B) ≍ exp(−c√B)?).
first_step: Compute f(B) for B ≤ 200 using p < 10^7; fit decay.

title: Catalog: odd n = p + 2^a + 2^b + 2^c (Sun's conjecture: every odd n > 8)
connection: odd n = p + 2^a + 2^b + 2^c (Sun's conjecture: every odd n > 8) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ log² n — same order as ES. Obstruction: none known. Status: open (conjectured by Z.-W. Sun, arXiv:0901.3075). Mechanism: none; numerics only.
why: Exact twin of ES in expected count (log²) with additive instead of multiplicative witnesses; any proof or disproof calibrates ES directly.
first_step: Check whether Crocker's construction extends to three powers (search 'p+2^a+2^b+2^c exceptions'); compute min witness count / log² n up to 10^9.

title: Catalog: Brier numbers (both Sierpiński and Riesel)
connection: Brier numbers (both Sierpiński and Riesel) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: divergent log. Obstruction: simultaneous coverings. Status: exist (explicit large k). Mechanism: two coverings.
why: Simultaneous covering of two linear families is possible — relevant if ES were reduced to two simultaneous divisor conditions.
first_step: Check the size of the smallest known Brier number and the covering moduli used.

title: Catalog: n = p + F_k (prime + Fibonacci number)
connection: n = p + F_k (prime + Fibonacci number) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: O(1). Obstruction: covering congruences on the Fibonacci orbit (periodic mod m, Pisano period). Status: check whether: positive proportion represented and an AP of failures known (Wu–Sun style). Mechanism: Pisano periodicity makes covering possible.
why: Any linear-recurrence witness sequence is periodic mod m, enabling coverings; ES witnesses are divisor-type, not recurrence-type.
first_step: Search 'sum of a prime and a Fibonacci number covering' to confirm the AP-of-failures result.

title: Goldbach's other conjecture and explicit finite exceptions

title: Catalog: m/n = 1/x + 1/y (two unit fractions; Stewart 1964 criterion)
connection: m/n = 1/x + 1/y (two unit fractions; Stewart 1964 criterion) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: O(d(n)) — tiny. Obstruction: local+multiplicative: needs coprime divisors a,b of n with m | a+b. Status: fully characterised; for fixed m almost all n work, asymptotic for exceptions (Elsholtz 1998, Huang–Vaughan 2011); 4/p never works for p ≡ 1 mod 4. Mechanism: divisor criterion: exceptions = n whose prime factors lie in a subgroup of (ℤ/m)^× avoiding −1.
why: The k = 2 analogue of ES is completely understood: failure ⟺ prime factors in a subgroup avoiding −1. ES's E1/E2 events are this criterion applied to p-tied auxiliary integers.
first_step: Recast ES as: ∃ auxiliary integer N(p, params) whose prime factors are NOT confined to a subgroup avoiding −1 mod 4C; list which subgroups are forced at squares (T1).

title: Odd greedy algorithm as a cautionary every-n problem
connection: The odd greedy expansion (always choose the smallest odd denominator) is conjectured to terminate for every rational with odd denominator, but this is open even though Breusch/Stewart show odd representations exist. ES has the same split: existence vs a specific algorithm. Keep proofs about existence, not about a fixed procedure (consistent with B1's bounded-procedure barrier).
why: Prevents investing in 'prove algorithm X always succeeds' routes that are harder than existence.
first_step: Run the odd greedy algorithm symbolically on 4/n and determine the exact condition under which it terminates within three terms.

title: Catalog: Hensley's conjecture (δ_A > 1/2 ⇒ almost all q)
connection: Hensley's conjecture (δ_A > 1/2 ⇒ almost all q) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: q^{2δ_A − 1}. Obstruction: congruence obstruction for A = {2,4,6,8,10}. Status: false as stated (Bourgain–Kontorovich); corrected forms open. Mechanism: local obstruction mod small moduli.
why: Count crossing 1 at δ_A = 1/2 is the exact dividing line for power-count orbits; ES sits at count log², i.e. 'δ = 1/2 + logarithmic'.
first_step: Find an alphabet A with δ_A = 1/2 (critical) and look at what is known: is ES₅ a 'critical-exponent' thin orbit problem?

why: Diagonal-action rigidity controls simultaneous multiplicative approximations, the structure of 4/n − 1/x ≈ product-type quantities.
first_step: Check whether ES's second step (4/n − 1/x = 1/y + 1/z) can be phrased as a multiplicative approximation problem for a diagonal action.

Status: 100% of n ≡ 5,6,7 mod 8 (Smith); all such n conditional on BSD. Mechanism: Selmer group distribution (Smith's method) + parity.

title: Feature: free (untied) witness parameter
connection: Dividing-line feature 'free (untied) witness parameter'. ES has a partially free parameter C (4Cp+1) but the modulus 4C moves with it (B2). To supply it one could: freeze the modulus: restrict to C in a fixed finite set and use many p-tied integers simultaneously (fixed-modulus character events, F3)
why: Least-witness theorems under GRH need fixed moduli; ES's moving modulus is the precise lack.
first_step: List fixed-modulus sub-events of ES (C fixed) and compute the fraction of p ≡ 1 mod 24 solved by C ≤ 10 — how many fixed C are needed empirically?

title: Feature: composition law on targets
connection: Dividing-line feature 'composition law on targets'. ES LACKS prime-to-prime composition (only ES(n) ⇒ ES(kn)). To supply it one could: look for a bilinear map on ES certificates: from certificates at q₁, q₂ build one at q₁q₂ that 'descends' to a prime factor (as in Euler's four-square descent)
why: Four squares and two squares are proved by composition + descent.
first_step: Check whether the quaternion-order reformulation (QUATERNION_ES.md) carries a multiplicative norm compatible with certificates.

title: Feature: class-group parametrisation with positivity
connection: Dividing-line feature 'class-group parametrisation with positivity'. ES LACKS (certificates are not known to biject with a class group or genus). To supply it one could: seek a binary/ternary quadratic form Q_p whose representations of a fixed number correspond to ES solutions; then class number > 0 / genus would force existence
why: Three squares, x²+ny² representations: count = class-number-weighted, positivity from Dirichlet's L(1,χ) > 0.
first_step: Write ES Type I solutions as representations by the binary form 4ad·x − f·y patterns; check for a discriminant D(p) attached naturally.

title: Feature: root-number / parity forcing
connection: Dividing-line feature 'root-number / parity forcing'. ES LACKS a parity-forced object. To supply it one could: attach an L-function or Selmer group to p (e.g. from a genus-one fibre of the ES surface) whose root number is −1 for all p ≡ 1 mod 24
why: Parity of Selmer ranks proves 100% results (Smith) and conditional pointwise results (BSD).
first_step: For the elliptic fibrations of the ES surface over Q(p), compute root numbers of a few fibres for p ≡ 1 mod 24 and see whether a sign is forced.

title: Feature: finite escalation / certificate threshold (290, 451, Graham's 77)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'finite escalation / certificate threshold (290, 451, Graham's 77)'. ES LACKS (U(n) has sporadic failures to 978145; ES itself has no known threshold theorem). To supply it one could: find a reformulation where an escalation lemma holds: 'if ES-shape S solves all p < B then all p' — unlikely, but record the precise failure
why: Universality theorems for forms are finite-check because of modular-form bounds; ES has no modular generating function.
first_step: Look for a generating series Σ R(n) q^n with modular or mock-modular properties (theta quotients in repo).

title: Feature: exceptional set has a canonical shape (AP / squares / sparse algebraic)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'exceptional set has a canonical shape (AP / squares / sparse algebraic)'. ES HAS one canonical bad shape (odd squares, T1) and sporadic U(n) values. To supply it one could: prove that ES failures, if any, avoid every other structured shape (polynomial values, Crocker-type sparse families, APs)
why: Proved/failed problems both display structured exception sets; classifying admissible exception shapes narrows disproof routes.
first_step: Check ES numerically on dense structured families: p = a²+1, p = 2^k·m+1, p = Fermat-like numbers up to large sizes; record min R(p)/log² p per family.

title: Feature: independence of witness events
connection: Dividing-line feature 'independence of witness events'. ES UNCLEAR: certificate families share the integer p, correlations not controlled. To supply it one could: measure empirically the pairwise correlation between Type I families (a,d) and (a',d') as events over p, and bound them by large-sieve arguments
why: Crocker-type failures exploit strong correlation; Poisson heuristics need weak correlation.
first_step: Compute the covariance matrix of the 50 most frequent certificate families over p ≡ 1 mod 24 ≤ 10^7.

title: Feature: thin-orbit expansion (SL₂ spectral gap)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'thin-orbit expansion (SL₂ spectral gap)'. ES LACKS: ES₅ is a fixed-length-3 word problem, no growing word length. To supply it one could: allow longer words with a constraint that collapses them to length 3 (as Zaremba's alphabet size tunes counts); check if a 'length-collapsing' identity exists
why: Zaremba / Apollonian density-one results need orbits whose size grows as a power.
first_step: None new (ZAREMBA_TRANSFER.md).

title: Feature: parameter family crossing the dividing line
connection: Dividing-line feature 'parameter family crossing the dividing line'. ES IS the endpoint m = 4 of Schinzel's m/n family (Pomerance–Weingartner transition at p ≈ exp(m^{1/2+o(1)})). To supply it one could: prove a monotonicity/interpolation statement: solvability of m/p for m' < m at all large p; or uniform-in-m count lower bounds
why: Families that cross (5x+1 vs 3x+1, Hensley δ, m/n) localise where proof techniques stop.
first_step: Compute R_m(p) for m = 4..20 and the same p; check whether R_m(p)·m/(log p)³ is stable (PW heuristic) and whether m = 4 shows anomalous excess.

title: Feature: reciprocity obstruction at a thin set (T1 at odd squares)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'reciprocity obstruction at a thin set (T1 at odd squares)'. ES HAS it, like Apollonian (HKRS), Rickards–Stange, flea orbits, Conjecture H at squares. To supply it one could: exploit it: obstruction theory often comes with a 'reciprocity-corrected' local-global principle that is provable in fat cases (Rickards–Stange)
why: In the proved fat case, knowing exactly the obstruction gives the full answer; ES's analogue would be 'ES fails only for those certificate lines at squares'.
first_step: Compute, for n = m² (m odd), the full set of certificate shapes that survive T1 and check that ES(m²) is always solved by non-line shapes (it is, trivially, since m² composite) — find the prime-level analogue.

title: Feature: effectivity of known partial results
connection: Dividing-line feature 'effectivity of known partial results'. ES Vaughan-type bounds are effective; no ineffective input in sight. To supply it one could: allow ineffective inputs (Siegel zeros) — maybe a dichotomy: either no Siegel zero ⇒ ES for p ≫ 1, or Siegel zero ⇒ ES via Deuring–Heilbronn
why: Some pointwise results (ternary forms, Linnik) are proved via Deuring–Heilbronn dichotomies.
first_step: Check whether a Siegel zero would help ES (exceptional character makes primes ≡ some class rare — helps or hurts divisor-in-class events?).

title: Feature: strong approximation / integral points on homogeneous spaces
connection: Dividing-line feature 'strong approximation / integral points on homogeneous spaces'. ES the ES surface is not a homogeneous space. To supply it one could: find a homogeneous space (e.g. SL₂ or a torus) fibration over a parameter of the ES surface; integral points on fibres then follow from strong approximation
why: Markoff mod p, ternary forms (spin groups) use strong approximation on groups.
first_step: See STRONG_APPROX_ES.md for prior work.

title: Feature: monotone structure in the number of terms k
connection: Dividing-line feature 'monotone structure in the number of terms k'. ES ES is k = 3; k = 2 completely classified (Stewart); k ≥ 4 has power counts. To supply it one could: use the k = 2 classification as a sieve: ES(p) holds if some explicit p-tied integer N has a coprime-divisor pair (a,b) with 4 | a+b … i.e. reduce to many k = 2 problems
why: Interpolating between a classified and an open case is a classic route.
first_step: Formalise: ES(p) ⟺ ∃x: 4/p − 1/x is a 2-term fraction; apply Stewart's criterion to (4x − p)/(px) for x in [p/4, 3p/4].

connection: Selmer's cubic 3x³ + 4y³ + 5z³ = 0 ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: 0 rational points. Obstruction: Sha / Brauer–Manin on the curve. Status: proved Hasse failure. Mechanism: descent.
why: Classical local–global failure with nothing local wrong; ES has no BM obstruction (Bright–Loughran), so failures would have to be non-BM (integral/positivity).

title: Catalog: Cassels–Guy cubic surface 5x³ + 9y³ + 10z³ + 12w³ = 0
connection: Cassels–Guy cubic surface 5x³ + 9y³ + 10z³ + 12w³ = 0 ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: 0. Obstruction: Brauer–Manin. Status: proved Hasse failure. Mechanism: BM obstruction.
why: Cubic surfaces can fail Hasse; ES's cubic surface has no BM obstruction — conjecturally rational points satisfy Hasse (Colliot-Thélène), but ES is integral/positive.
first_step: None.

title: Catalog: Melfi: every even number is a sum of two practical numbers
connection: Melfi: every even number is a sum of two practical numbers ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: large. Obstruction: none. Status: proved (Melfi 1996). Mechanism: practical numbers are dense-ish (≍ x/log x, Weingartner) with multiplicative closure.
why: Practical numbers are the Egyptian-fraction-friendly integers; a 'Goldbach' for them is provable via their multiplicative structure.
first_step: Look at whether ES for p holds trivially when p+something is practical with suitable divisor sums; formalise 'practical-number' certificates.

title: Catalog: Euclid–Mullin sequence contains every prime
connection: Euclid–Mullin sequence contains every prime ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: heuristic yes. Obstruction: none. Status: open. Mechanism: none.
why: Pointwise-every-prime statement with no structure; control.
first_step: None.

title: Catalog: Klurman–Shparlinski–Teräväinen: small primes generate (ℤ/q)^× for almost all q
connection: Klurman–Shparlinski–Teräväinen: small primes generate (ℤ/q)^× for almost all q ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: (log Q)^{1+ε} primes. Obstruction: —. Status: proved almost all q. Mechanism: averaging over q.
why: Shows subset-product generation by small primes is provable on average; ES needs it at one tied integer.
first_step: None new.

title: Catalog: Every prime p > 3: p = a + b with a, b ≥ 1 and ab a square? (trivial cases) vs p = x² + y² + 1? (Linnik: p − 1 = x² + y²)
connection: Every prime p > 3: p = a + b with a, b ≥ 1 and ab a square? (trivial cases) vs p = x² + y² + 1? (Linnik: p − 1 = x² + y²) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: power. Obstruction: none. Status: proved (Linnik). Mechanism: dispersion.
why: Linnik's p − 1 = x² + y² is a pointwise-prime theorem via dispersion over primes (averaging over primes!).
first_step: Control: the averaging is over p, not pointwise in a fixed n.

title: Catalog: Gauss's Last Entry / Kummer's conjecture on cubic Gauss sums
connection: Gauss's Last Entry / Kummer's conjecture on cubic Gauss sums ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: —. Obstruction: —. Status: Kummer's conjecture false-as-stated; distribution proved (Heath-Brown–Patterson). Mechanism: metaplectic forms.
why: Distribution vs pointwise: Gauss sums equidistribute but individual sign/argument unknown — metaplectic links (METAPLECTIC_ES.md).
first_step: None new.

title: Lonely runner: simultaneous Diophantine approximation
connection: Lonely runner shares F01,F06,F24,F32: integer parameters must admit a witness time, there are no evident local obstructions, and approximation supplies constructive witnesses. ES likewise needs a pointwise witness despite local solubility.
why: A transference principle between simultaneous approximation and congruence choices might provide a useful model for pointwise witness selection.
first_step: Inspect the survey’s reduction to a finite set of simultaneous inequalities; ask whether ES’s divisor-in-residue condition admits a comparable finite approximation statement.

title: Catalog: Goldbach for Gaussian integers / number fields (Mitsui)
connection: Goldbach for Gaussian integers / number fields (Mitsui) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: power. Obstruction: —. Status: almost all. Mechanism: Hecke L-functions.
why: Control.
first_step: None.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Catalog: Erdős–Straus for 4/n with x ≤ y ≤ z and z ≤ n^k bounded exponent
connection: Erdős–Straus for 4/n with x ≤ y ≤ z and z ≤ n^k bounded exponent ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: count depends on k. Obstruction: —. Status: unknown; ES solutions can have z ≍ n² (Type I). Mechanism: —.
why: Size-restricted variant gives a tunable count; dividing line in k.
first_step: Compute min over p of the minimal max-denominator exponent log z / log p for p ≤ 10^7.

title: Between: Are all exceptions of p + 2^a + 2^b structured (Crocker-type) or are there 'random' ones?
connection: Pan proves ≫ x^{1−ε} exceptions; classify numerically the exceptions ≤ 10^9 by whether they lie in algebraic families.
why: If log-count failures are always structured, then ES (log², and failures provably not AP-structured) gains heuristic support.
first_step: Enumerate odd n ≤ 10^8 not of the form p + 2^a + 2^b; test membership in known families; look at residues mod small primes.

title: Between: Why is m = 12 so exceptional in the Pomerance–Weingartner table?
connection: m = 12 has 24 exceptions up to 10^12 vs 9 for m = 10 and 13 for m = 13; the count per m should correlate with an arithmetic singular series (structure of (ℤ/m)^× and −1).
why: An 'ES singular series' S(m, n) that predicts the m-dependence would be the right object to bound below at m = 4.
first_step: Compute heuristic expected counts E_m(p) = Σ_{Type I/II shapes} densities for m = 4..15 and correlate with exception counts.

title: Sporadic exceptions U(n) = {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145} vs. Ramanujan's 2719
connection: Ramanujan's form had sporadic exceptions explained by a finite computation + GRH. The finite U(n) exception list might be sporadic in the same sense, or the start of a structured family (a reciprocity family as in Apollonian packings).
why: Deciding 'sporadic vs structured' tells whether U(n) is a good proxy target for ES.
first_step: Check whether sporadic values share a factor pattern (105 = 3·5·7, 2961 = 3·987=3·3·7·47 …) and compute class numbers / Legendre symbols to see a governing invariant.

title: Between: ES with a prime denominator
connection: Require one of x, y, z to be prime. Expected count ≈ log² p / log p ≈ log p — a Crocker-scale count inside ES.
why: If ES-with-prime-denominator fails infinitely often in a structured family, the structure is informative; if it holds to 10^9 that is evidence log-count can hold here.
first_step: Search p ≡ 1 mod 24 ≤ 10^7 for representations 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with z (or x) prime; list failures.

title: Between: Explicit (deterministic) thin additive basis with r(n) ≍ log n
connection: Erdős's construction is probabilistic; check whether an explicit construction with r(n) ≍ log n is known (Kolountzakis gave algorithmic constructions; Jain 2024 discusses open aspects).
why: ES = 'a deterministic log²-count system covers every prime'. Whether explicit log-count bases can be certified is the purest derandomisation analogue.
first_step: Check whether explicit/derandomised constructions with r(n) ≍ log n exist (search Kolountzakis 1995; arXiv:2405.08650).

title: Between: Ternary Egyptian for numerators m with all denominators in an AP
connection: 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with x,y,z ≡ r mod q: local obstructions appear; which (q,r) still look universal?
why: Maps local obstructions vs global failures in a controlled family.
first_step: Compute for q ≤ 12 the residues r for which all n ≤ 10^6 coprime to stuff are solvable.

title: Between: ES with x, y, z pairwise coprime-to-p structure (Type I only / Type II only)
connection: Is every p solvable by Type I alone? by Type II alone?
why: If one type alone fails for some p, ES's robustness depends on two independent mechanisms — an interesting structural fact.
first_step: Compute R_I(p), R_II(p) separately for p ≡ 1 mod 24 ≤ 10^8; list p with R_I = 0 or R_II = 0.

title: ES as an infinite congruence 'covering' of the non-squares; distortion-method analysis
connection: Hough and Balister–Bollobás–Morris–Sahasrabudhe–Tiba bound the uncovered density of covering systems via a distorted-measure sieve. ES Type II (★): the classes p ≡ −(u+B) (mod 4uB) over all (u,B) must cover every prime; they never cover odd squares (T1). Study the uncovered set of the subsystem with moduli ≤ M within [1, X] as M grows.
why: The distortion method controls the uncovered set precisely for systems with many moduli; ES's system is explicit and its uncovered set is known to contain squares.
first_step: Compute the uncovered set of {−(u+B) mod 4uB : 4uB ≤ M} in [1, X] for M up to 10⁵, X up to 10⁸; compare its size with #squares + #(small sporadic) and track how fast non-squares disappear.

title: Feature: witness = divisor in a class (multiplicative) rather than prime value (additive)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'witness = divisor in a class (multiplicative) rather than prime value (additive)'. ES HAS multiplicative witnesses; parity barrier is not obviously relevant. To supply it one could: use multiplicative-function machinery (Halász, Matomäki–Radziwiłł) on indicator-type functions of 'has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C'
why: Problems with prime-valued witnesses hit the parity barrier; divisor-in-class problems are governed by Stewart-type subgroup criteria instead.
first_step: Express 1[N has a divisor ≡ −1 mod q] in terms of characters of (ℤ/q)^× via the subgroup criterion and check if Halász-type bounds apply when N runs over 4Cp+1, C ≤ X.

title: Feature: Linnik-constant bound (smallest witness ≤ n^A)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'Linnik-constant bound (smallest witness ≤ n^A)'. ES UNKNOWN for ES; known witnesses are small in practice. To supply it one could: prove a conditional (GRH) bound on the smallest certificate parameter, turning ES into a finite check per p
why: Least-witness theorems (Linnik, Bach) are among the few pointwise polylog results, though conditional.
first_step: Compute max over p ≤ 10^9 of the minimal Type I parameter a·d (or C) and compare with log² p.

title: Feature: Galois-theoretic forcing of divisor classes (cyclotomic/Lucas)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'Galois-theoretic forcing of divisor classes (cyclotomic/Lucas)'. ES LACKS: ES needs divisors ≡ −1 mod 4C of linear forms, which no cyclotomic structure forces. To supply it one could: use Lucas sequences U_n(P,Q) with discriminant D: primitive divisors r of U_n satisfy r ≡ (D/r) mod n, so negative D gives r ≡ −1 mod n for inert r — choose (P,Q) depending on p
why: Zsigmondy/BHV force divisors in classes ±1 mod n; a −1 mod 4C class appears naturally for inert primes.
first_step: Construct for given p a Lucas sequence whose n-th term equals (or divides) 4Cp+1 or a related ES integer; check whether its primitive divisors can be forced inert.

title: Feature: self-reducibility to smaller instances
connection: Dividing-line feature 'self-reducibility to smaller instances'. ES HAS ES(n) ⇐ ES(prime factor) (downward), LACKS upward/sideways reductions among primes. To supply it one could: find 'sibling' implications ES(q) ⇒ ES(p) for q related to p (e.g. q | 4p + 1)
why: Inductive proofs need sideways reductions; four-squares uses n ↦ prime factors and composition.
first_step: Test numerically: is there a rule mapping each p to a smaller prime q with ES(q)'s solution transforming into ES(p)'s? (SIBLING.md)

title: Transfer: trial-count × success-probability profile
connection: Classify thin problems by (#trials, success probability per trial): Goldbach (power, 1/log²), p + 2^k (log, 1/log), ES (C ≤ X gives X trials but success ≈ 1/C-ish ⇒ Σ ≈ log² X).
why: ES has power-many trials but harmonically decaying success: a distinct profile from both 'power reservoir' and 'log trials'. Problems with the same profile and their status would be the right comparison class.
first_step: Find other problems with harmonic success profiles: e.g. 'n has a divisor d ≡ −1 mod k for some k ≤ X' (Stewart-type), and check what's known pointwise.

title: Transfer: Type I through binary quadratic forms of discriminant −4d
connection: f | 4a²d + 1 = (2a)²d + 1 means f is primitively represented by a form of discriminant −4d; Type I at (a,d) ⟺ p ≡ −f (mod 4ad) for such f. ES becomes a union of genus/class conditions on p modulo 4ad.
why: Brings class groups and genus theory of Q(√−d) into ES; class-group positivity is a proved-side mechanism.
first_step: For d ≤ 50, compute the set of residues −f mod 4ad realised by represented f, and check how quickly the union over (a,d) covers all classes mod lcm (local covering) vs primes.

title: Transfer: Kneser/Olson subset-product theory for gate G4
connection: Stewart's criterion: a fraction fails 2-term representation iff the prime factors of the relevant integer lie in a subgroup H avoiding −1. Kneser/Olson/Davenport-constant bounds describe when subset products must hit −1.
why: ES failure ⟺ for every C, all prime factors of the relevant auxiliary integers lie in subgroups H_C ∌ −1 — a simultaneous confinement over many C.
first_step: Quantify: for random integers N ≡ 1 mod q, the probability of H-confinement ≈ (log N)^{−(1−1/[G:H])}; multiply over independent C to get the heuristic failure rate; compare with data.

title: Rosser–Iwaniec semi-linear sieve for 'no divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4C)'
connection: For C = 1, 'N has no divisor ≡ 3 (mod 4)' iff all odd prime factors of N are ≡ 1 (mod 4): a half-dimensional sifted set (Landau–Ramanujan). For general C, ES failure at N requires the prime factors of N to avoid generating −1 in (ℤ/4C)^×.
why: The semi-linear sieve gives sharp upper and lower bounds for such sifted sets; summing over C at fixed p could bound the failure probability.
first_step: For fixed p, compute #{C ≤ X : 4Cp+1 has no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C} and compare with the semi-linear sieve prediction ∏(1 − 1/ℓ)^{1/2}-type density.

title: Transfer: hyperbolic lattice-point counting in log-size regions
connection: Type II solutions are integer points on a quadric-type variety in a region whose volume grows only like log² p; equidistribution theorems (Duke–Rudnick–Sarnak, Eskin–McMullen) need power-size regions.
why: Explains in a geometric language why ES sits below the 'counting with error term' regime; points to effective equidistribution in small regions as the needed input.
first_step: Identify an explicit quadric Q and region R_p with #(Q(ℤ) ∩ R_p) = R_II(p); compute vol(R_p).

title: Transfer: Halász / Matomäki–Radziwiłł for confinement indicators
connection: The indicator that N has all prime factors in H ⊂ (ℤ/q)^× is multiplicative in N; Halász-type theorems give mean values over short intervals / sequences.
why: Pointwise confinement over the sequence N_C (C ≤ X) is a mean of a multiplicative function along an AP 1 mod 4p — Matomäki–Radziwiłł style results along APs may bound it.
first_step: Check whether MR-type results apply to multiplicative functions along APs with modulus as large as 4p and length X ≈ p^θ.

title: Transfer: Heegner points on modular curves X₀(N) with N tied to p
connection: Look for CM points of discriminant −4p or −p (for p ≡ 1 mod 4 one has Q(√−p)) on a curve mapping to the ES surface.
why: Heegner constructions give O(1)-count pointwise existence at every prime in a class.
first_step: Determine whether the ES surface over Q is rational (it is a cubic surface with rational points, so likely rational) and look for curves of genus ≥ 1 in it parametrised modularly.

title: Transfer: Poisson / Janson model calibrated on Schinzel's m/n family
connection: Use Pomerance–Weingartner's m-family as a training set: fit a model P(no solution | p, m) and extrapolate to m = 4.
why: A model that correctly predicts exceptions for m = 8..15 (where exceptions exist) and predicts none for m = 4 would be a strong calibrated heuristic.
first_step: Implement R_m(p) counting for m ≤ 15 and p ≤ 10^7; fit log P(R=0) against (log p)³/m.

title: Transfer: Bertrand-style exact extraction from a binomial-type integer
connection: Find an explicit p-tied integer M(p) (product of many N_C, or a binomial/Gauss-period quantity) whose p-adic/multiplicative structure provably contains a factor in the needed class.
why: Bertrand's postulate is proved by bounding C(2n,n) from both sides: a thick deterministic object with exact extraction.
first_step: Consider M = ∏_{C ≤ X} N_C and compare its size with the maximum possible size of an H_C-confined product: can size alone force escape?

title: Transfer: Two-squares decomposition p = a² + b² as a forced object
connection: p ≡ 1 mod 4 has a unique a² + b²; check whether 4/p has certificates expressible in a, b (e.g. via (a ± b), a² − b², ab).
why: If a fixed finite set of polynomial-in-(a,b) formulas solved ES, it would bypass Mordell–Schinzel (those are polynomial in p, not in a,b).
first_step: For p ≡ 1 mod 24 ≤ 10^6, test whether some x ∈ {a, b, a+b, a−b, ab, a²−b², …}·small multiples gives 4/p − 1/x a 2-term fraction (Stewart test).

title: Transfer: Class number h(−p) / h(−4p) parity as a lever
connection: For p ≡ 1 mod 4, h(−4p) is even (genus theory); 2-power divisibility depends on representations like p = x² + 32y². Correlate ES certificate shapes with 2-power class group data.
why: Ties ES to Rédei-type structure where governing-field and Smith methods exist.
first_step: Tabulate h(−4p) mod 8 and the minimal ES certificate shape for p ≡ 1 mod 24 ≤ 10^6; look for dependence.

title: Catalog: Every large odd n = prime + practical number (Pomerance–Weingartner, Margenstern's conjecture)
connection: Every large odd n = prime + practical number (Pomerance–Weingartner, Margenstern's conjecture) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: large (practical numbers ≍ x/log x). Obstruction: none. Status: proved for large odd n (arXiv:2007.11062). Mechanism: distribution of practical shifted primes + sieve.
why: Practical numbers are Egyptian-fraction-friendly; a Goldbach-type pointwise theorem with a log-thin witness set is provable because the set has density x/log x.
first_step: Look for an ES reformulation with 'practical' or 'smooth-divisor-rich' auxiliary integers (if p + k is practical with suitable divisors, a certificate exists?).

title: Catalog: Hardy–Littlewood second conjecture π(x+y) ≤ π(x) + π(y)
connection: Hardy–Littlewood second conjecture π(x+y) ≤ π(x) + π(y) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: —. Obstruction: —. Status: incompatible with prime k-tuples (Hensley–Richards 1973). Mechanism: admissible dense tuples.
why: Plausible numerically, but structurally false under a stronger conjecture — calibrates that ES numerics to 10^18 constrain only 'random' failure mechanisms.

connection: Dirichlet's theorem on primes in APs ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: x/(φ(q) log x). Obstruction: local (gcd). Status: proved. Mechanism: L(1, χ) ≠ 0.
why: Existence from nonvanishing of an L-value: does ES have an L-value whose nonvanishing would force a certificate?
first_step: Look for a Dirichlet series D_p(s) = Σ_C w(C, p) C^{−s} encoding certificates whose analytic behaviour at s = 1 detects existence.

connection: Hilbert irreducibility ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: —. Obstruction: —. Status: proved. Mechanism: thin sets.

connection: Goldbach–Linnik numbers in short intervals ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: power. Obstruction: —. Status: almost all. Mechanism: zero density.

connection: Vinogradov's least-QNR conjecture n(p) ≪ p^ε ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: —. Obstruction: —. Status: open. Mechanism: Burgess barrier.

connection: Erdős–Woods numbers ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: —. Obstruction: —. Status: infinitely many known (constructive). Mechanism: CRT constructions.

connection: Every even n = difference of two primes (in infinitely many ways) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: power. Obstruction: —. Status: open; bounded gaps give some even numbers. Mechanism: Maynard sieve.

title: Catalog: Darmon–Granville generalised Fermat finiteness
connection: Darmon–Granville generalised Fermat finiteness ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: finite. Obstruction: —. Status: proved finite for 1/p+1/q+1/r < 1. Mechanism: Faltings.
why: Hyperbolic signature 1/p + 1/q + 1/r < 1 — a unit-fraction condition governing Diophantine finiteness; the ES surface boundary geometry may have an orbifold-signature reading.
first_step: Compute the orbifold/log-geometry signature of the ES boundary (as in Campana orbifolds) to see if ES lies in a 'Campana-special' class.

title: Minimal pair: 3x+1 (open, almost-all) vs 5x+1 (false)
connection: 3x+1 (open, almost-all) vs 5x+1 (false): they differ essentially in one feature — sign of the random-walk drift. ES's position: ES's analogue of drift is the expected count log² p → ∞ (positive 'drift'), on the true side.
why: Minimal pairs isolate the feature responsible for crossing the dividing line; each is a precise question about ES.
first_step: Define an ES 'drift': d(p) = log E[R(p)] and check monotone growth in data.

title: Minimal pair: Hensley alphabet {2,4,6,8,10} (false) vs Zaremba alphabet {1..5} (claimed true)
connection: Hensley alphabet {2,4,6,8,10} (false) vs Zaremba alphabet {1..5} (claimed true): they differ essentially in one feature — a congruence obstruction from the alphabet; both have δ > 1/2. ES's position: ES has no local obstruction at primes (only T1 at squares), so sides with Zaremba on this axis.
why: Minimal pairs isolate the feature responsible for crossing the dividing line; each is a precise question about ES.
first_step: None.

title: Minimal pair: Fermat two squares at p ≡ 1 mod 4 (proved, count 1) vs ES at p ≡ 1 mod 4 (open, count log²)
connection: Fermat two squares at p ≡ 1 mod 4 (proved, count 1) vs ES at p ≡ 1 mod 4 (open, count log²): they differ essentially in one feature — rigid algebraic structure (Gaussian integers, involution) vs none. ES's position: Larger count but no structure: the dividing line is structure, not count.
why: Minimal pairs isolate the feature responsible for crossing the dividing line; each is a precise question about ES.

title: Minimal pair: Markoff mod p (proved) vs Markoff integral Hasse for k (false i.o.)
connection: Markoff mod p (proved) vs Markoff integral Hasse for k (false i.o.): they differ essentially in one feature — finite field (strong approximation + orbit divisibility) vs integers with reduction theory. ES's position: ES is trivially solvable mod every prime power (no local obstruction) — the integral side is everything, as for Markoff k.
why: Minimal pairs isolate the feature responsible for crossing the dividing line; each is a precise question about ES.

connection: Apollonian (false: reciprocity) vs Zaremba (claimed true): they differ essentially in one feature — reciprocity obstructions present vs absent (for the standard alphabet). ES's position: ES: reciprocity obstruction present at squares only.

connection: Ramanujan's form x²+y²+10z² (finite exceptions, GRH) vs x²+y²+z² (proved by genus): they differ essentially in one feature — class number of the genus > 1 (spinor genus not a single class). ES's position: ES has no class-number parametrisation at all; closer to the harder member.

title: Universal torsor of the ES surface and its integral points
connection: The ES surface U_n is a (log) del Pezzo/ toric-type surface; universal torsors linearise counting (Salberger, Heath-Brown) ↔ Type I/II parametrisations are torsor coordinates.
why: If the ET parametrisations are exactly the universal torsor, then ES(p) ⟺ an integral point on an affine variety with a free torus action — and the variety might have extra structure (e.g. be a cone over a known variety).
first_step: Compute Pic of a smooth compactification of U_n and compare the ET variables (a,b,c,d,e,f) with Cox ring generators.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Feature: variance / second moment control
connection: Dividing-line feature 'variance / second moment control'. ES KNOWN on average (Elsholtz–Tao moments). To supply it one could: use the second moment Σ_p R(p)² with Cauchy–Schwarz pointwise in short families (primes in a residue class mod a large modulus)
why: Romanoff-type and almost-all results come from second moments; pointwise needs higher moments or rigidity.
first_step: Read Elsholtz–Tao's moment computations; check whether higher moments (k-th) are computed.

title: Feature: uniformity in an auxiliary large parameter
connection: Dividing-line feature 'uniformity in an auxiliary large parameter'. ES PARTIAL (PW uniform-in-m Vaughan bound). To supply it one could: introduce an artificial large parameter (m, or modulus Q of restricted classes) where uniform results give pointwise results at a special point
why: Function-field large-q results and PW's uniformity show how an extra parameter can be leveraged.
first_step: Ask: is ES(p) implied by a uniform-in-m statement for m/(kp) with k varying (scaling ES(n) ⇒ ES(kn))?

title: Feature: structure of the exceptional set at composite n
connection: Dividing-line feature 'structure of the exceptional set at composite n'. ES ES at composites reduces to prime factors (trivial). To supply it one could: use the fact that U(n)-type variants have sporadic composite failures (105 = 3·5·7, …) to locate which sub-certificate families matter
why: Composite sporadic failures of variants show which certificate families are 'load-bearing'.
first_step: Factor U(n) sporadic list and check whether each prime factor's variant certificates are 'incompatible' under scaling.

title: Feature: p-adic / archimedean transition (local densities at ∞)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'p-adic / archimedean transition (local densities at ∞)'. ES positivity region is bounded (finitely many positive solutions). To supply it one could: view the positive solutions as integral points in a compact region of a non-compact surface; volume of region ~ log² p (matches count)
why: Counting in bounded regions with volume → ∞ slowly is the generic 'small count' regime; proofs require effective equidistribution at log scale.
first_step: Compute the volume of the positivity region in Haar/log measure and compare with R(p) on average.

title: Feature: fixed-point-free action ⇒ even count
connection: Dividing-line feature 'fixed-point-free action ⇒ even count'. ES UNKNOWN. To supply it one could: if a natural involution on solutions of 4/p has fixed points exactly at special solutions, R(p) parity encodes existence of special solutions
why: Parity-of-count arguments are the cheapest pointwise mechanism (Zagier).
first_step: Compute R(p) mod 2 for ordered/unordered triples and correlate with existence of solutions with x = y or y = z.

title: Meta: build the dividing-line table as a feature matrix and fit a decision tree
connection: Encode each catalog problem by features (count order, obstruction type, witness type, rigidity, reservoir, periodic parameter, symmetry group) and outcome; fit a tiny decision tree and see where ES lands and which feature flips it.
why: A crude but systematic way to read off the dividing line from data; the splits are candidate 'missing features'.
first_step: Export catalog tags from data/z52b/dividing.jsonl to a CSV, hand-correct features, fit sklearn DecisionTreeClassifier with depth ≤ 3.

title: Meta: search Guy's UPINT D11 and Erdős problems site for unit-fraction problems with known 'dividing' resolutions
connection: Erdős problems database (erdosproblems.com) lists many unit-fraction problems, some recently resolved; each resolution mechanism is a data point for the dividing line.
why: Recent AI-assisted resolutions are concentrated in abundance regimes; listing which unit-fraction problems remain open sharpens the line.
first_step: Scrape erdosproblems.com tag 'unit fractions' and record status + mechanism for each.

title: Catalog: n = p + k! (prime plus factorial)
connection: n = p + k! (prime plus factorial) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ (log n/log log n)·(1/log n) → 0. Obstruction: none. Status: density zero of representable n (expected count → 0); not a theorem I verified. Mechanism: count tends to zero.
why: Extreme of the count axis: below O(1) existence fails generically — anchors the bottom of the dividing scale.
first_step: Check whether a density-zero theorem for p + k! is in the literature (search 'sum of a prime and a factorial').

title: Catalog: n = 2^a·3^b + p (prime plus 3-smooth)
connection: n = 2^a·3^b + p (prime plus 3-smooth) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ log n (#3-smooth ≤ n ≈ log²n/2 log2 log3) × 1/log n ≈ log n. Obstruction: covering possible (periodic orbits of 2^a3^b). Status: unknown to me (check). Mechanism: —.
why: Log-count with periodic two-parameter witnesses; covering may or may not be available in two parameters — informative for the covering mechanism's reach.
first_step: Search for coverings that kill all n − 2^a3^b; compute exceptions ≤ 10^8.

title: Greedy set-cover growth of primes by ES certificate families
connection: Order Type I/II families (by modulus) and compute the minimum number of families needed to cover all primes ≡ 1 mod 24 up to x. Finite coverings are impossible (B1); the growth rate (log x? log² x?) measures 'how infinite' ES's covering is.
why: Compare with covering systems (finite) and with p + 2^k (no covering of the complement). A slow (≈ log x) growth would suggest a structured infinite covering.
first_step: Implement greedy set cover over families with modulus ≤ M for primes ≤ 10^7; plot cover size vs x.

title: Sieve-limit (parity-type) model for ES
connection: Selberg's parity example shows sieves cannot distinguish primes from integers with λ(n) = −1. Ask for an analogue: a set S with the sieve statistics of primes (level of distribution, local densities) on which every ES certificate family fails — odd squares are such a set for certificate lines (T1).
why: If such a model exists, sieve-only proofs of ES are impossible; if the statistics of primes already exclude it, a sieve route exists.
first_step: Try S = {n : n ≡ 1 mod 24, n = m² or m²·(unit-like)} and generalisations; check which sieve axioms each candidate violates.

title: Turán–Kubilius / Erdős–Kac for the number of certificate families hitting p
connection: If the number of hitting families behaves like ω(n) (Erdős–Kac normal with mean and variance log²-scale), the lower tail would be Gaussian-small, not Poisson-small.
why: Distinguishes two heuristic regimes with very different exceptional-set predictions.
first_step: Compute mean and variance of R(p) in windows; compare variance/mean ratio to 1 (Poisson) vs ≫ 1 (overdispersion).

title: Erdős–Selfridge 'covering with distinct moduli and divergent density' analogue for primes
connection: Known covering results bound minimum modulus (Hough) and handle densities; the ES system has distinct moduli 4ad with multiplicities. Ask for a 'prime covering lemma' with explicit hypotheses.
why: Would give a structural theorem in which ES is an instance — even a conditional one.
first_step: Read Balister–Bollobás–Morris–Sahasrabudhe–Tiba 'distortion method' and see if it bounds uncovered primes for infinite systems.

title: ES and Romanoff-type 'positive lower density for restricted families' as a stepping stone
connection: Prove: for a fixed finite set of certificate families, the set of primes they solve has positive relative density in the hard classes (trivially true by Dirichlet). The interesting stepping stone is 'density → 1 as family set grows, with an explicit rate' (Vaughan-type).
why: Clarifies which partial results are new vs trivial.
first_step: None; tag as a calibration.

title: Stevenhagen-type conjecture for ES: exact density of p solved by families with modulus ≤ M
connection: Stevenhagen predicted the negative-Pell density via a Markov chain on 2-ranks, later proved (Koymans–Pagano). For ES, a Markov-chain model over growing family sets could predict exact densities at finite M.
why: Exact finite-M densities are provable (Chebotarev); comparing them with a model checks the model's dependence structure.
first_step: Compute exact densities of primes solved by families with 4ad ≤ M for M ≤ 200 (finite CRT computation) and fit decay of the unsolved density.

title: ES over ℤ[1/S] (S-integral ES)
connection: Allow denominators in ℤ[1/S] — i.e. x, y, z rationals with S-unit denominators. For S ∋ 2 or 3 does ES become provable for all p via identities?
why: Moving between integral and rational points one prime at a time locates the integrality obstruction.
first_step: Find the smallest S for which a polynomial identity covers all p ≡ 1 mod 24 with x, y, z ∈ ℤ[1/S] positive.

title: Expander-free 'thin' structure: ES₅ words as length-3 paths in the Farey graph
connection: ES₅ ⟺ λ(p) ≤ 3: a short path in the Farey/Stern–Brocot graph between specific vertices. Graph distance ≤ 3 problems in growing graphs with no expansion argument.
why: Diameter/short-path existence results in arithmetic graphs (e.g. Cayley graphs of SL₂(ℤ/p)) are proved by expansion only at log diameter, not fixed length.
first_step: See BRAINSTORM/bsA_farey_graph_metric.md.

title: Bounded generation of SL₂(ℤ[1/p]) / elementary matrices (Carter–Keller, Vsemirnov)
connection: Bounded generation results (every matrix a product of ≤ N elementary matrices) are pointwise for every element, proved by arithmetic (Dirichlet's theorem) — closest to 'fixed-length word exists for every target'.
why: ES₅ is an existence of a fixed-length word; bounded generation proofs use primes in APs to steer entries.
first_step: Read Vsemirnov / Morgan–Rapinchuk–Sury on bounded generation of SL₂(ℤ[1/p]) and compare the word shape with ES₅'s.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Markoff-surface 'strong approximation' (Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak) adapted to U_n
connection: BGS prove the Markoff graph mod p is connected (almost all p) via Vieta moves; the ES surface U_n has a Brauer group ℤ/2 and no BM obstruction. A Vieta-like group action on integer points of U_n would convert existence into 'orbit meets the integral points'.
why: Repo says no analogous action is known — but a *partial* action (e.g. from the 3 'swap' symmetries plus a cremona transformation of the cubic) may exist and nobody computed its orbits.
first_step: Compute the Cremona/birational automorphisms of the Cayley cubic preserving the ES boundary and build the induced graph on ES solutions mod ℓ for small ℓ.

title: 'p is not a square' as the only input: character-escape lemma
connection: Since T1 kills certificate lines exactly at squares, and a non-square p is a non-residue modulo some prime ℓ ≤ ℓ(p) (least non-residue-type bound), look for a certificate family that is activated precisely by (p/ℓ) = −1.
why: Turns ES into a least-non-residue problem (pointwise under GRH with polylog ℓ, Burgess unconditionally) if each ℓ has a family activated by (p/ℓ) = −1 that always works.
first_step: For each small prime ℓ, list certificate families whose solvability condition is implied by (p/ℓ) = −1 alone — known to fail? (repo F6 'sign layer is easy'; class layer is the problem). Record where it breaks.

title: Result: least certificate-family size s(p) has a p-independent distribution (median 22, 99% ≤ ~200) and the CRT model predicts its maximum
connection: For all 179 468 hard-class primes p < 10⁸ the least s = ad (Type I) or ab (Type II) solving p has median 22, 90% quantile 86, 99% quantile 209 — identical to the < 10⁷ sample (22, 85, 187). The max over p < 10⁷ is 1133 (model n·δ(X) = 1 predicts ≈ 1210); over p < 10⁸ it is 2814 at p = 53049049 (model ≈ 1990, next-largest 1467).
why: Quantifies 'how far' one must search per prime and shows the independence model is calibrated on the extreme-value statistic, not only on averages. EVIDENCE only.
first_step: Push to 10⁹ (≈ 1.6·10⁶ hard primes, model predicts max ≈ 3·10³) and check the record-setters for near-square structure (cf. NEAR_SQUARE.md).

title: Dividing-line reading of the computation: ES is a 'random covering' with log³ intensity, Crocker's problem a 'random covering' with log intensity
connection: In the residue model, ES's hit intensity grows like (log X)³ (families up to X), so failures become rarer than any power of X; p + 2^a + 2^b has intensity ≈ log n, giving failure probability ≈ n^{−c}, compatible with infinitely many structured failures.
why: Places ES and Crocker's problem on one axis (intensity growth) where ES is comfortably on the 'all n' side, provided independence holds; the open question is only correlation/structure.
first_step: Compute the analogous residue-model intensity for p + 2^a + 2^b + 2^c (expected log²) to complete the axis.

title: Catalog: Primes p with p = x² + y² and x prime (Fouvry–Iwaniec)
connection: Primes p with p = x² + y² and x prime (Fouvry–Iwaniec) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ √p/log p. Obstruction: none. Status: proved infinitely many (Fouvry–Iwaniec 1997). Mechanism: bilinear forms over Gaussian integers.
why: Thin restriction on a two-squares representation still provable in the family aspect; not pointwise.
first_step: None.

title: Catalog: Least prime p ≡ 1 mod q with additional splitting (Chebotarev least prime, Lagarias–Odlyzko)
connection: Least prime p ≡ 1 mod q with additional splitting (Chebotarev least prime, Lagarias–Odlyzko) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: power of discriminant. Obstruction: none. Status: proved (bounds ≪ d^{C}). Mechanism: zero-free regions.
why: Least-witness in growing fields; ES's growing-level union is a union of such Chebotarev conditions.
first_step: None.

title: Connection: 'every prime splits in some member of a family of fields' problems
connection: Examples: every prime p is ≡ 1 mod some small prime ℓ (trivial), every p is a QNR mod some small ℓ (least non-residue), every p splits in some Q(√d) with d small (least QR prime). ES is a non-abelian-free but class-valued version.
why: These 'some member of a family' problems are proved pointwise exactly when the family has a forced member (Burgess / pigeonhole); identifying the forced member is the crux.
first_step: List such problems with their least-witness bounds and check which have unconditional polylog/power bounds.

title: Connection: sum-product phenomena mod q for 'p ≡ −e mod 4ab, e | a+b'
connection: Type II couples a product (4ab) with a sum (a+b) through divisibility; sum-product estimates force mixed sets to cover residues, but the problem's residue question is trivial locally — the content is integrality and size.
why: Records that sum-product tools address local covering (already free for ES) — a dividing-line non-feature.
first_step: None; note only.

title: Connection: ES with 'one denominator a prime power of p' only (x = p^k·u)
connection: Restricting which denominators carry p changes the family set (Type I vs II). Pure Type I or pure Type II counts are each ≍ log³-intensity in the residue model?
why: If one type alone has intensity growing fast enough, ES could in principle be proved within one type; the computation can split intensities by type.
first_step: Modify scripts/z52b_dividing_avoid.py to run Type I only and Type II only; fit exponents separately.

title: Connection: the m/p family in the residue model
connection: Run the same CRT-avoidance computation for m = 5..15 (Type I: f | m a² d + 1, m a d | p + f; Type II: e | a+b, m a b | p + e) and compare δ_m(X) with PW's exception tables.
why: If δ_m(X) predicts the observed largest exceptions for m = 8..15 (e.g. 241 for m = 8), the residue model is validated on cases with actual failures — the strongest available heuristic check for m = 4.
first_step: Parametrise scripts/z52b_dividing_avoid.py by m; note PW's exceptions are for all n, not just primes.

title: Large sieve inequality applied to the exceptional set with the C-form classes as the sifting classes
connection: Classical large sieve: if a set S ⊂ [1, X] avoids ω(q) residue classes mod q for each q ≤ Q, then |S| ≤ (X + Q²)/L with L = Σ_{q ≤ Q} μ²(q) Π_{p|q} ω(p)/(p − ω(p)). For the C-form, S = exceptional set avoids, for each prime a ≡ −1 (mod 4C), the single class r_{C,a} mod a — ω(a) = #{C : 4C | a + 1} = τ((a+1)/4)-ish. So L ≈ Σ_{a ≤ Q} #{C: 4C | a+1}/a ≈ Σ_a τ((a+1)/4)/a ≈ (1/2) log²Q. Hence |exceptions ≤ X| ≪ (X + Q²)/log²Q — with Q = √X: ≪ X/log²X. A quick, elementary exceptional-set bound; weaker than Vaughan but *structurally* it shows the exceptional set has density 0 with a log² saving that mirrors the log²p count.
why: Elementary, and its proof shape (large sieve with ω(a) ~ τ(a+1)) might extend to a *weighted* large sieve giving more; and it exhibits ES's exceptional-set bounds as a special case of sieving by 'divisor-many' classes.
first_step: Verify the computation of L carefully (sum over prime a only, or all a via the full large sieve with multiplicative ω); compare with Vaughan's exp(−c(log N)^{2/3}); check whether larger Q (via Montgomery–Vaughan with Q up to X^{1/2}) or Type II's extra (c,d) classes improve the exponent.

title: Result: ES difficulty tracks the least quadratic non-residue n(p) ('pseudosquare-ness')
connection: For hard-class primes < 10⁸ (n(p) ≥ 11 is forced by the classes), corr(log s(p), log n(p)) = 0.42; median least family size is 17, 29, 53, 74 for n(p) in [11,13), [13,20), [20,30), [30,50). But the overall record (s = 2814 at p = 53049049) has n(p) = 17, so n(p) is not the whole story.
why: Primes that look like squares to many small quadratic characters are harder — T1 at actual squares is the limit of this trend. A proof route: 'ES-hardness ≤ function of quadratic-character pattern', with genuine non-squares eventually escaping. EVIDENCE.
first_step: Replace n(p) by the number of primes ℓ ≤ 100 with (p/ℓ) = +1 and by the full character vector; fit s(p) with a regression or tree; look at the residual for the 2814 record.

title: Connection: Type I families carry a quadratic-character condition: Type I at (a,d) needs (d/p) = −1
connection: Elementary: every prime r | f | (2a)²d + 1 has (−d/r) = 1, so the Kronecker character χ = (−4d/·) has χ(f) = 1; p ≡ −f (mod 4d) then gives (−4d/p) = χ(−1) = −1, i.e. (d/p) = −1 for p ≡ 1 mod 4. Hence a Type I solution at (a,d) exists only if d is a non-residue pattern for p, so the least Type I parameter has d ≥ n(p)-type size, and Type I is dead at squares (T1 for Type I).
why: Explains the correlation result (families sharing d share the character condition) and the n(p) trend in one line. Almost certainly the campaign's 'sign layer' (F6) in different notation.
first_step: Check the analogous condition for Type II (e | a+b, 4ab | p+e) and confirm against T1_TEMPLATE.md; then re-run the correlation test within fixed-d groups.

title: Catalog: Pseudosquare primality tests (Lukes–Patterson–Williams)
connection: Pseudosquare primality tests (Lukes–Patterson–Williams) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: —. Obstruction: —. Status: proved: primality certified by pseudosquare conditions (under hypotheses). Mechanism: quadratic residuosity patterns.
why: Pseudosquares are where 'looks like a square to all small characters' is quantified; proofs use them as deterministic certificates.
first_step: See pseudosquare connection item.

title: OEIS anchors for 5/n and 6/n: A226644, A226645
why: The m-family is the Sierpiński/Schinzel generalisation; missing entries for m ≥ 7 are a gap a curator could fill and a sign the m-family data is unexplored.
first_step: Submit U_m(n) for m = 7..13 to OEIS (data in data/z52b/raw/m*_4000.txt) after checking against a second implementation.

title: Least prime with U(p) = 6 is 193 (a Type-A failure)
connection: The sequence 'least prime p with U(p)=k' begins 2,5,3,13,–,193,7,97,11,89,19,–,53,…; 193 (López Type-A failure) is the first prime with exactly six solutions.
why: Hard primes for one certificate family show up as the first occurrences of small U-values, i.e. the count sees the same arithmetic.
first_step: Tabulate, for each k ≤ 40, the least p with U(p)=k and check whether these are enriched in p ≡ 1 (24) and in the m/p-failure sets (data/z52b/raw/m*_pr1e5.txt).

title: 2521 = lcm(1..9) + 1 is the hardest prime ≤ 2·10⁵
connection: 2521 = lcm(1,…,10)+1 minimises U(p)/log²p over primes ≤ 2·10⁵ (U=9); the primes lcm(1..k)+1 = 7, 13, 61, 421, 2521 have ratios 1.85, 0.61, 0.65, 0.44, 0.15 — monotone towards hard.
why: p ≡ 1 mod every small prime power makes every small prime a QR mod p and kills all small-modulus covering identities simultaneously; this is the extremal configuration for Mordell-type coverings.
first_step: Compute U, R, Uv for the next such prime 232 792 561 = lcm(1..19)+1 (≈ 1–2 h with the count program; words sieve to 2.4·10⁸ is cheaper) and test whether it is a (★) or b=1 failure.

title: U(p) at least-QNR-record primes is only moderately small
connection: At the least p≡1(4) with least QNR q (q=11..47), U(p)/log²p = 0.40,0.37,0.54,0.53,0.36,0.29,0.60,0.53,0.55,0.67,0.61 — below typical (≈1–2) but not record-hard; 2521 (least QNR 11) is far harder (0.15).
why: Shows hardness is not a function of the least QNR alone: p−1 smoothness / p ≡ 1 mod higher prime powers adds a second axis — useful for designing a two-parameter hardness model.
first_step: Regress log U(p) on log L(1,χ_p) and log(σ(p−1)/(p−1)) jointly; check which explains 2521 vs 87481.

title: Type II count k₂(p) prefers L(1,χ_{−4p}) large (α ≈ +0.21)
connection: Solutions with two denominators divisible by p (k₂) correlate positively with L(1,χ_{−4p}) = πh(−4p)/(2√p) (ρ=+0.37) and negatively with L(1,χ_p) (α ≈ −0.20); Type I (k₁) sees only χ_p (α ≈ −0.34, χ_{−4p} gain ≈ 0).
why: The two ET types live on different quadratic twists (χ_p vs χ_{−4p} = χ_{−1}χ_p at odd q): a natural 'complementarity' — when one type is starved by its character, the other may be fed.
first_step: Test the complementarity: correlation between k₁ and k₂ residuals; is min(k₁,k₂) ever 0 at p ≡ 1 (4) and if so, is the other large?

title: U(p) uncorrelated with a_p of non-CM elliptic curves
connection: Spearman of U(p)-residual with a_p(11a1)/2√p is +0.004, with a_p(37a1)/2√p −0.005, with |a_p(32a1)|/2√p +0.007, with Ramanujan τ(p)/p^{5.5} +0.006 (n≈9 000).
why: Null result: no detectable dependence on these Hecke eigenvalues, so a naive 'ES count tracks a fixed non-CM form' fingerprint is not supported; the detected dependence is through quadratic characters/L-values.
first_step: Repeat with weight-2 newforms of level 4·d for d | 840 and with weight-3/2 forms (Shimura lifts) where class numbers do appear.

title: (7/p) anomaly: U(p) does not see the character at 7
connection: Residual Spearman of U(p) with (2/p), (3/p), (5/p) is −0.55, −0.31, −0.28 but with (7/p) only −0.013, although Mordell's classes p ≡ 3,5,6 (mod 7) are covered by identities.
why: Suggests the mod-7 identity contributes O(1) solutions while 2,3,5 contribute families ∝ log p; identifies which local primes matter for the count — relevant to any weighted covering.
first_step: Split U(p) by p mod 7 class and by whether the mod-7 identity solution exists; check whether the 7-family has bounded size.

title: U(p) vs τ(p−1) and σ(p−1)/(p−1): ρ ≈ −0.53
connection: More divisors of p−1 ⇒ fewer ES solutions (ρ(τ(p−1)) = −0.53, ρ(σ(p−1)/(p−1)) = −0.53, ρ(φ(p−1)/(p−1)) = +0.42).
why: Smooth p−1 means p ≡ 1 modulo many small numbers — the Mordell-class obstruction; links ES hardness to the Erdős–Pomerance world of smooth shifted primes.
first_step: Test whether τ(p−1) remains significant after controlling for L(1,χ_p) (partial correlation).

title: Real quadratic regulator log ε_p anticorrelates with U(p) (ρ = −0.44)
connection: log ε_p and log ε_p/√p correlate −0.44 / −0.51 with U(p)-residual; h(p) alone ≈ 0 (−0.04); CF period of √p −0.27.
why: By the class number formula, 2h(p)R/√p = L(1,χ_p) (R = log ε_p): the regulator carries the L-value since h(p)=1 mostly; a direct ES ↔ fundamental unit link is the CF/Pell side of the CF-length forms of ES (ES₅).
first_step: Correlate the five-slice / λ(p) ≤ 3 certificate counts with the CF period of √p and with the regulator.

title: Uv(p) (U-certificates) ~ U(p): ρ = +0.64; R(p) only +0.24
connection: The ES count U(p) correlates +0.64 with the U-certificate word count Uv(p), +0.46 with I3(p), +0.32 with W(p) but only +0.24 with the (★) count R(p).
why: R(p) is a thin slice with its own character (χ_{−4p}); Uv tracks the whole count. Useful when choosing which certificate family to attack for a lower bound proportional to U(p).
first_step: Compute what fraction of each p's ES solutions correspond to (★), U, I3 words via the explicit maps; check whether the fraction is stable.

title: Height growth: max_{p≤X} minz(p)/p
connection: Record values of minz(p) occur at 2,3,5,7,11,13,17,23,29,31,37,53,… (nearly every prime early on); record minz(p)/p would measure the worst certificate height.
why: An upper bound minz(p) ≤ p^{1+θ} for all p is equivalent to ES with a height bound; empirical θ guides which 'bounded C' statement to aim for.
first_step: Compute max_{p ≤ X} log(minz(p)/p)/log p for X up to 10⁷ and fit.

title: Greedy-failure composites: 49, 169, 361, 553, … (squares and products)
connection: The composite members of the x=(n+3)/4 failure set include many odd squares ≡ 1 (24) (49, 169, 361, 961, 1369, …) but not all (25 is certified: 4/25 = 1/7 + 1/70 + 1/350 with 7 = (25+3)/4), and non-squares like 553 = 7·79, 721, 793, 889.
why: Squares are over-represented (a T1-like effect for a single identity family) but not uniformly obstructed; non-square composite failures show the obstruction is not only quadratic.
first_step: List non-square composite members ≤ 10⁵ and check whether each factors into primes that are themselves failures (multiplicativity test).

title: Easy primes: U(p) records eventually all ≡ −1 (mod 840)
why: Mirror of the hard primes (≡ 1 mod 840): ES-easiest primes are ≡ −1 modulo highly composite numbers (5039 = 7! − 1 = 2·2520 − 1). The count is a function of p's position relative to smooth numbers.
first_step: Note 55439 = 2·27720 − 1 and 5039 = 2·2520 − 1 are records; test the next candidates 2·lcm(1..k) − 1 and lcm(1..k) − 1 when prime; OEIS search of the record list gave no match.

title: k₂(p) ≥ 1 for every prime p ≤ 2·10⁵
connection: Every prime ≤ 2·10⁵ has a solution with exactly two denominators divisible by p (Type II); min k₂(p) over p ≡ 1 (4) > 1000 is small but nonzero.
why: ET note Type II is the 'easier to count' type; empirical universality of Type II alone is the statement many campaign lines target.
first_step: Record the minimum k₂(p) per dyadic range and list primes with k₂(p) = 1.

title: maxx(p) − p/4 (largest smallest-denominator)
connection: The largest possible smallest denominator maxx(p) has maxx − p/4 weakly tied to least QNR (ρ=−0.19); maxx(p) ≤ 3p/4 always; the sequence is not in OEIS.
why: Measures how 'balanced' the most balanced solution can be (BALANCED_LATTICE.md); balanced solutions are rare and relate to the cubic surface's real-point distribution.
first_step: Plot (maxx(p) − p/4)/p; compare with the balanced-solution census in BALANCED_LATTICE.md.

title: Mordell's six square classes mod 840 are exactly the six ES-hardest classes by count, in the order 1, 121, 361, 169, 529, 289
why: Quantitative refinement of Mordell's theorem: the classes with no polynomial identity are also the classes with the fewest solutions on average, and the ordering inside them (1 hardest, 289 least hard) is a new fingerprint to explain (by 3-, 5-, 7-adic depth: 1 ≡ square of 1 mod everything).
first_step: Group primes ≤ 2·10⁵ by class mod 840 and by class mod 9240 = 840·11, compute mean and min of U(p)/log²p.

title: Hardest 30 primes ≤ 2·10⁵ by U/log² are all ≡ 1 (mod 24)
why: Confirms Mordell's classical reduction quantitatively and shows the hard set inside 1 (mod 24) is further structured by mod-5/7/9/16 conditions.
first_step: Compute the hard list's distribution mod 5, 7, 9, 16, 25 vs all p ≡ 1 (24) to measure each prime power's contribution.

title: 5/n and 6/n: no 3-term failure (primes ≤ 10⁵, all n ≤ 4000)
connection: U₅(p), U₆(p) ≥ 1 for all primes 3..10⁵ and all n ≤ 4000 (6/n trivially follows from 3/n except tiny n).
why: Sierpiński's 5/n is the nearest sibling of ES; joint fingerprints (U₄(p), U₅(p)) can show whether the same primes are hard for both.
first_step: Compute Spearman(U₄(p)/log²p, U₅(p)/log²p) at p ≤ 10⁵ and list primes hard for both.

title: '3-divisible ES': 12/p fails at 22 primes ≤ 10⁵, last 12 241
why: Contains the Type-A failures 193 and 2521 and the R-zero 577: the '3-divisible' sub-problem is hard on the same primes — a sub-ES whose failure set is a fingerprint of global hardness.
first_step: Extend 12/p to 10⁷ (fast: x ∈ (p/12, p/4]) to test finiteness; check whether 66529, 409, 5569 eventually appear (they do not ≤ 10⁵ except as listed).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: '5-divisible ES': 20/p fails at 63 primes ≤ 10⁵, last 90001
connection: No ES solution with 5 | x, y, z at 63 primes ≤ 10⁵, including 1201, 2521, 4201, 4801, 8761, 21841, 24481 (ES-hard) — the last at 90001 = 9·10⁴+1.
why: The 5-divisible failure set mirrors primes ≡ 1 (mod 5^a·…) — a local obstruction at 5 that compounds global hardness.
first_step: Tabulate p mod 25 and mod 125 for 20/p failures vs random primes.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Failure sets are monotone under divisibility of the numerator (sanity + structure)
connection: If m | m′ then fail(m) ⊆ fail(m′) (multiply all denominators of an m′/n representation by m′/m to get one of m/n); verified on all m ≤ 48, p ≤ 10⁵. 'Primitive' failures (not explained by a divisor d ≥ 5 of m) number 0,0,1,6,4,8,3,22,10,8,25,32,17,45,…
why: ES is the bottom of a divisibility lattice of Schinzel problems; primitive failure counts strip out inherited obstructions and are the right 'new difficulty' per numerator.
first_step: Submit primitive-failure counts to OEIS; examine whether primitive failures of 4k concentrate on primes hard for 4/p.

title: R-zeros and Type-A failures across numerators: 193 fails 19 numerators, 577 13, 2521 11, 3361 11, 409 7, 9601 5, 5569 4, 66529 3, 23929 0
connection: Among m ∈ [5,48], the campaign's hard primes fail many m/p; but 23929 (an R-zero) fails none — R-failure is not 'globally hard'.
why: Separates certificate-line hardness ((★) zeros) from intrinsic ES hardness — useful to decide which hard primes are artefacts of a chosen line.
first_step: For each of the 14 R-zeros compute U(p)/log²p and H(p) to rank 'intrinsic' vs 'line-specific' hardness.

title: 10/n fails at {2,3,7,11,43,61,67,181}; 11/n at {2,3,4,37}; 13/n at {2,3,4,5,7,14,53,61,67,79,211,281}
connection: Complete-looking small exception lists (n ≤ 4000 all, primes ≤ 10⁵), none in OEIS; composite exceptions occur (4 for 11 and 13, 14 for 13).
why: Each list is a finite certificate target; the presence of composite exceptions (4, 14) shows the reduction-to-primes fails for m ≠ 4, unlike ES.
first_step: Explain 13/14 and 11/4 failures (why multiplicativity breaks) and check whether any composite n > 100 fails m/n for m ≤ 13.

title: m/p failures are enriched in primes adjacent to 5-smooth numbers
connection: For m=12, 15 of 22 failures have p−1 or p+1 5-smooth (only 182 such primes ≤ 10⁵ in total); m=20: 27/63; m=24: 39/146 — OEIS returns spurious A219669 ('primes neighboring a 5-smooth number') for m=45.
why: Primes next to smooth numbers are ≡ ±1 modulo many small numbers simultaneously — the Mordell-class mechanism; a quantitative version is a 'smooth-neighbour' hardness law.
first_step: Compute failure rate among 5-smooth-neighbour primes vs others for each m; extend to 7-smooth.

title: Number of m/p failures ≤ 10⁵ by m: 0,0,1,6,4,8,3,22,10,9,25,38,17,49,16,63,… (no OEIS match)
connection: The failure-count profile across m (5..48) has strong arithmetic modulation (peaks at m ≡ 0 mod 12).
why: A Fourier/arith analysis of this profile would expose which local factors (mod 3, mod 4) drive Schinzel failures.
first_step: Regress log(#fail(m)+1) on log m and the indicator functions 4|m, 3|m, 5|m.

title: U₁₂(p)/U₄(p): the 3-divisible fraction of ES solutions
connection: U₁₂(p) counts solutions of 4/p with 3 | x,y,z; its ratio to U₄(p) is a 3-adic local statistic; failures at 193, 577, 2521 mean this fraction hits 0 at hard primes.
why: Factorisation of the count into local factors (Euler product over divisibility conditions) would be a strong structural fingerprint (Manin-type).
first_step: Compute E[U_{4k}(p)/U₄(p)] for k=2,3,5 and compare with 1/k³-type local densities on the ES surface.

title: A union conjecture: ES_2 ∪ ES_3 (even or 3-divisible solutions) for all primes p > 3
connection: Since fail(8) ∩ fail(12) ∩ primes = {2,3} ≤ 10⁵, conjecture: every prime p > 3 has an ES solution with 2 | x,y,z or 3 | x,y,z.
why: Each subfamily has a cleaner local structure (2-adic resp. 3-adic) than ES; a proof could exploit that the obstructions live at different primes (analogous to López's Type A ∪ Type B conjecture).
first_step: Extend the joint census; search for the natural certificate lines in each subfamily and check whether their failure sets are disjoint.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Hardest-for-15 vs hardest-for-4: correlation across numerators
connection: Compute Spearman between U₄(p)/log²p and U_m(p)/log²p for each m ≤ 48 (data on disk).
why: If hardness is one latent arithmetic variable (e.g. L(1,χ_p) and p−1 smoothness), correlations should be high for all m and highest for m sharing factors with 840.
first_step: Run the 44 correlations; cluster m by correlation profile.

title: Primes failing ≥ 15 numerators are all < 700
connection: High H(p) occurs only at small p (113, 193, 101, 137, 181, 421, 149, 241, 281, 353, 397, …); for p > 10⁴, H(p) is small.
why: Shows that 'multi-numerator hardness' decays with p — consistent with Vaughan-type almost-all results with explicit m-dependence (PW).
first_step: Plot max H(p) over dyadic ranges.

title: Last 16/p failure 83449 and last 12/p failure 12241: next-term prediction
connection: If ES_k failure sets are finite, the largest elements grow quickly with k; PW-type heuristics would predict last(ES_k) ≈ exp(c k^{1/3}) or similar.
why: A cheap predictive check of the probabilistic model behind PW on the ES-relevant numerators 4k.
first_step: Fit log last(4k) for k = 2..5 and compare with PW's density model; extend 16/p and 20/p to 10⁷ to see if new failures appear.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: I3 zero squares: 1,4,…,1225,1600,19600,2 433 600
why: Squares are over-represented among late I3 zeros, echoing T1 (odd squares kill all certificate lines). A T1-like reciprocity for even squares with I3 would explain 19600 and 2433600.
first_step: Compute I3(m²) for m ≤ 3000 and check whether I3(m²) is systematically small (but nonzero) for m divisible by 4·3·5·…

title: R(n) = 0 at n = 2^k − 1 for k ∈ {2,3,4,5,7,8,13}
connection: The (★) count vanishes at 3, 7, 15, 31, 127, 255, 8191 although R(n) = 0 has density < 0.1% among n ≡ 3 (mod 8); R(2^k−1) > 0 for other k ≤ 21.
why: Mersenne numbers are 'p-tied' obstructions: 4C(2^k − 1) + 1 = 2^{k+2}C − 4C + 1 has restricted divisor classes; a cute but real fingerprint for the divisor form of R.
first_step: Explain via the divisor form R(n) = Σ_C #{d | 4Cn+1 : d ≡ −1 (mod 4C)} with n = 2^k − 1; test R(2^k − 1) for k ≤ 61 with a dedicated divisor search.

title: Composite R-zeros include the pseudosquare 2641 = 19·139
connection: Composite non-square n ≡ 1 (4) with R(n) = 0: 57, 105, 177, 249, 345, 465, 777, 801, 969, 1345, 1465, 1617, …, 2641, …; 2641 is Lehmer's pseudosquare L₁₃ (A002189) and also an x=(n+3)/4 greedy failure.
why: Pseudosquares mimic squares for all small-prime Legendre symbols; T1 kills squares, so pseudosquares should be near-T1 — a quantitative 'approximate reciprocity obstruction'.
first_step: Compute R, U, Uv, I3 at all pseudosquares A002189 up to 10¹⁰ (targeted divisor-form computation) and compare with typical values.

title: BM main term explains the ES count U(p) better than its own (★) count
connection: At 696 primes p≡1(4) ≤ 12 000: residual Spearman(M_BM, U) = +0.65 but residual Spearman(M_BM, R) = +0.10; raw Spearman(R, M_BM) = 0.47 (shared log² growth); mean R/M_BM = 1.31.
why: M_BM is built from χ_p(uB) so it tracks the χ_p Euler product that drives U; R's fluctuations follow χ_{−4p} instead — the BM layer is not the dominant fluctuation term of R, a mismatch worth understanding.
first_step: Recompute on 20 000–30 000 (running: data/z52b/bm_check_20000_30000.json) and decompose R(p) − M_BM(p) into higher-order characters (the X(n) part of FRONTIER §2.1).

title: (★) and Uv and I3 zero rates by n mod 8
why: Concentration of all failures in n ≡ 1 (8) mirrors ES's Mordell structure; any line with failures at n ≡ 3,7 (8) carries extra, avoidable difficulty.
first_step: Tabulate zero rates by n mod 24 and mod 840 for each family; find the family whose zero set is contained in the square classes mod 840.

title: W(n) (all words) has records at 1,3,5,7,11,17,19,23,35,47,59,71,…
connection: Records of W(n) = #{t,u,v ≥ 1 : tuv−u−v = n} are at n with n+1 and 2n+1, 3n+1… all highly divisible (W counts divisors of tn+1 in classes); not in OEIS.
why: W(n) = Σ_t #{d | tn+1 : d ≡ −1 (mod t)} is the unrestricted analogue of the ES certificate count — its extremal behaviour bounds all sub-counts.
first_step: Identify W(n) with a classical divisor-sum (Σ_t τ_{−1 mod t}(tn+1)); submit to OEIS.

title: R(p) is always even — the (u,B) swap involution
connection: R(p) at primes p≡1(4): 2,2,2,4,2,6,4,4,2,8,…, always even (FRONTIER notes it); R(p)/2 = #{u<B}.
why: R(p)/2 is the natural 'unordered' count; parity information beyond this (R(p)/2 mod 2) could come from a second involution as in Zagier's proof.
first_step: Check the distribution of R(p)/2 mod 2 by p mod 8; search for a second involution on (★) triples with computable fixed points.

title: ESC(p) as a certificate count at primes — calibrate ESC(p)/log²p
connection: ESC(p) (words with some coordinate in 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ−p)) is existence-equivalent to ES at primes per CONTEXT, but it is a count of certificates, not a lower bound for the number of solutions (ESC(5) = 6 > U(5) = 2); its residual follows χ_p with α ≈ −0.24 (R²-gain 0.31).
why: If ESC(p)/log²p is bounded below empirically with a cleaner constant than U, it is the better target count for lower-bound heuristics.
first_step: Compute min_{p ∈ [X,2X]} ESC(p)/log²p up to 3·10⁶ and compare its stability to U(p)'s.

title: Distribution of the smallest C in (★) certificates
connection: For each p with R(p) > 0, Cmin(p) = least C contributing; its distribution (geometric? power law?) is a fingerprint of how 'far' the certificate is.
why: Bounded Cmin would be a finite covering; growth of max Cmin(p) over p ≤ X measures the needed modulus range.
first_step: Compute Cmin(p) for p ≤ 3·10⁶ via a C-major sieve and fit max_{p≤X} Cmin(p).

title: min over p ≤ X of R(p)/log²p: does it go to 0?
connection: R has 14 zeros ≤ 10¹⁰, so inf R/log²p = 0 infinitely often is possible; the empirical lower envelope of R(p)/log²p over primes with R > 0 is a separate fingerprint.
