why: If the positive values are bounded below by c·log²p while zeros persist, failures are 'discrete' events (local obstructions) rather than tail events of a smooth distribution — matters for which probabilistic model to use.
first_step: Histogram R(p)/log²p near 0 (values 2, 4, 6) for p ≤ 3·10⁶ and compare with Poisson with the BM mean.

title: Higher-power residue characters of 2,3,5,7 have no detectable effect on ES counts
connection: Within strata of fixed quadratic profile ((2/p),(3/p),(5/p),(7/p)), whether a ∈ {2,3,5,7} is a cubic/quartic/octic residue mod p shifts mean residual log U(p), k₁, k₂, R(p) by |Δ| ≤ 0.03 (largest −0.029; the attached Mann–Whitney p-values are unstratified tests, smallest 0.015 among 48 tests — consistent with null after multiple testing).
why: Data counterpart of the genus/higher-character split (FRONTIER §2.1): order ≥ 3 characters at small primes don't bias counts; all systematic arithmetic dependence is quadratic (plus p−1 structure).
first_step: Repeat with characters of order 3,4 of larger moduli (q ≤ 50) and with the full X(n) decomposition on (★).

title: Quartic residuosity of 2 (p = x² + 64y²) is irrelevant for ES counts
connection: Among p ≡ 1 (8), '2 is a 4th power mod p' shifts residual log U by +0.008 (MW p = 0.10).
why: Rules out a tempting Gauss-type link (p = x²+64y²) to hardness; the Neumann–Setzer form p = u²+64 is a different condition (see next item).
first_step: None needed; record as negative fingerprint.

title: Number of elliptic curves of conductor p (or 4p, 8p, 16p) vs U(p)
connection: LMFDB lists curves by conductor; their number at N = p, 2p, 4p, 8p, 16p could correlate with ES counts if ES surfaces fibre into genus-1 curves (cf. GEOMETRY_ES.md) of these conductors.
why: Fibrations of the ES cubic surface by conics/genus-1 curves have discriminants involving p; the Mordell–Weil ranks of such fibres might govern solution counts.
first_step: Download LMFDB conductor counts for N ≤ 500 000 (Cremona tables) and correlate with U(p) residual at p ≤ 30 000 (N=16p).

title: U(p) residual vs Σ_{d≤8} τ(p+4d) is null (ρ = +0.02)
connection: The b = 1 (López Type A) line asks for a divisor of p+4d ≡ −1 (mod 4d); yet the raw divisor mass Σ_{d≤8} τ(p+4d) is uncorrelated with U(p), while τ((p+3)/4) correlates +0.59.
why: Divisor *mass* of shifts is not what matters — the residue-class restriction is; shows why naive divisor-sum lower bounds don't track solvability.
first_step: Replace τ by the class-restricted count #{e | p+4d : e ≡ −1 (4d)} and recompute.

title: k₂ (Type II) is more sensitive to 3 than k₁: ρ((3/p)) = −0.41 vs −0.25
connection: Residual k₂(p) correlates −0.41 with (3/p) and −0.39 with v₃(p−1); k₁(p) correlates −0.25 and −0.25.
why: Type II solutions come from divisors of p-tied integers in classes mod 4C; C = 3 multiples are cheap — p ≡ 2 (mod 3) helps Type II most.
first_step: Count Type II solutions by C (the c=1 parameter) and check which C carry the 3-dependence.

title: k₂ correlates with spf(p+4) (−0.35)
connection: Smallest prime factor of p+4 anticorrelates with k₂(p): p+4 with small factors → more Type II solutions.
why: p+4 = 4·((p+3)/4)+1… p+4 divisors are the b=1, d=1 line; small factors give many small divisors in classes ≡ −1 (mod 4C).
first_step: Check ρ(k₂, spf(p+4C)) for C = 1..10.

title: U(p) vs CF period of √p (ρ = −0.27)
connection: Longer CF period of √p (larger regulator) ⇒ fewer ES solutions.
why: ES has continued-fraction reformulations (ES₅, λ(p) ≤ 3); the CF of √p is a different object, but the correlation goes through L(1,χ_p) = 2hR/√p.
first_step: Partial correlation of U with CF period controlling for L(1,χ_p); if ≈ 0, the CF of √p carries nothing extra.

title: r₃(p) = 12 h(−4p) for p ≡ 1 (4): ES counts vs sums of three squares
connection: By Gauss, r₃(p) = 12h(−4p) at p ≡ 1 (mod 4); so U's weak correlation with h(−4p) (+0.08 raw, +0.14 normalised) is also its correlation with r₃(p).
why: THREE_SQUARES.md explored ES ↔ ternary forms; data say the three-squares count is only a weak predictor — the right ternary form, if any, is not x²+y²+z².
first_step: Correlate U(p) with representation numbers of other ternary forms of small discriminant (genus theory via Hurwitz numbers H(4p), H(8p), H(3p)).

title: Hurwitz class numbers H(4p), H(8p), H(3p) jointly vs ES counts
connection: Hurwitz numbers are coefficients of weight-3/2 Eisenstein series; a linear combination of H(dp)/√p could match the χ-twist dependence found for k₁/k₂.
why: Would give a modular-form 'shadow' of the ES main term, testable to high precision.
first_step: Fit log k₂ on log H(4p)/√p, log H(8p)/√p, log H(3p)/√p; inspect coefficients for rational structure.

title: Root numbers / L-functions of quadratic twists of 32a1 by p
connection: Compute-and-check: the twist E^{(p)}: py² = x³ − x (congruent-number-type curve) has root number determined by p mod 8; its analytic rank at hard primes vs others.
why: Congruent-number style curves are the classic 'Diophantine via elliptic curves' fingerprint; ES hardness clustered in p ≡ 1 (8) where these twists have root number +1.
first_step: Use pari ellanalyticrank on twists for p ≡ 1 (8) ≤ 10⁴, correlate rank with U(p)/log²p.

title: R-zeros: least QNR and L(1,χ_p) are high (11 of 14 above the 85th percentile)
why: (★) failures sit where small primes are QRs mod p — the same axis as U-hardness — even though R's own fluctuations fit χ_{−4p} better; zeros are an extreme-tail event of the χ_p axis.
first_step: Logistic model P(R(p)=0) vs log L(1,χ_p) and log L(1,χ_{−4p}) on p ≤ 3·10⁶ (12 zeros) — check both coefficients' signs.

title: Type-A failures: 193 has h(−4p) in the bottom 2%, 2521 and 66529 have L(1,χ_p) at the 95th percentile
connection: 193: least QNR 5, h(−4p) quantile 0.019, L(1,χ_p) quantile 0.56; 2521: least QNR 11, L quantile 0.95; 66529: least QNR 13, L quantile 0.95.
why: Type A hardness looks χ_p-driven at 2521, 66529 but 193 is a χ_{−4p} (small class number) case — the two mechanisms both occur among the three Type-A failures.
first_step: Compute both quantiles for all Type-A near-failures (primes where the b=1 line has exactly 1–2 certificates) ≤ 10⁸.

title: Elsholtz–Tao normalisation: average U(p) grows like log³p, not log²p
connection: ET (arXiv:1107.1010, verified abstract) prove N log²N ≪ Σ_{p≤N} f(p) ≪ N log²N log log N (f ordered), i.e. average f(p) ≍ log³p up to log log; our median U(p)/log²p rises 1.33 (p≈10⁶) → 1.54 (p≈10⁷), ratio ≈ log-ratio 1.17, consistent with log³.
why: All hardness rankings across different sizes should use U(p)/log³p (or the fitted Euler-product model); the log² normalisation in several items here is only valid within a narrow range.
first_step: Refit min/median of U(p)/log³p and U(p)/(log³p·loglog p) over dyadic ranges 10³…10⁸ to see which normalisation is flat.

title: Is U(p)/log²p approximately lognormal?
connection: Histogram the residual; tails determine the probability of U(p)=0 under a smooth model — heavy lower tail would make finitely-many-exceptions heuristics fragile.
why: LOWER_TAIL_* memos study the lower tail of (★); the same for U is cheap here.
first_step: Fit normal/skew-normal to the residual and compute the predicted P(U(p) ≤ 5) vs observed (only p ≤ 17).

title: ES hardness vs Wieferich-type / Fermat-quotient data
connection: Compute-and-check: correlation of U(p) with q_p(2) = (2^{p−1} − 1)/p mod p (Fermat quotient) — a p-adic invariant of 2.
why: Would test whether p-adic (mod p²) information about small primes affects ES; expected null, but cheap and a clean negative.
first_step: Compute q_p(2) mod p for p ≤ 2·10⁵, normalise to [0,1), Spearman with residual U.

title: Primes p with p−1 = 2^k·m, m small: Fermat-like primes as hard cases
connection: Fermat primes 17, 257, 65537 have p ≡ 1 mod 2⁴, 2⁸, 2¹⁶ respectively; compute U(p)/log²p for them: the 2-adic depth effect (−9% per level?) would compound.
why: Direct test of whether 2-adic depth effect saturates (32 vs 16 effect was small) or compounds.
first_step: Run z52b_count on 65537, 257, 17 and on primes 2^k·3+1, 2^k·5+1.

title: ES hardness index vs class number of Q(ζ_p)^+? (too expensive; proxy via h(p))
connection: Compute-and-check (proxy): cyclotomic class-number data are unavailable at scale; the quadratic subfield Q(√p) (h(p) null) is the only cheap proxy.
why: Records that the cyclotomic-unit / Vandiver-type world shows no signal at the quadratic level.
first_step: Skip unless a specific cyclotomic mechanism is proposed.

title: Mordell's identity classes as indicator features: which one explains most variance?
connection: For each classical polynomial identity (mod 3, 5, 7, 8, 11, …) define 1[p in identity class] and regress U(p) on all of them.
why: Identifies the identities that matter for the *count*, not just existence — a 'weighting' of the Mordell covering useful for heuristics.
first_step: Encode Mordell's and Vaughan's identity classes (cf. MODEL_SPECIFIC.md) as features and run a LASSO.

title: Linear-algebra fingerprint: rank of the solution set's denominator matrix mod small primes
connection: For each p, collect (x,y,z) mod q (q = 3, 5, 7) of all solutions; the occupied residue patterns form a fingerprint; compare across hard and easy primes.
why: Local solution patterns at q are exactly what covering congruences use; hard primes should occupy few patterns.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁴ (needs solution lists — extend the counter to dump solutions).

title: Composite n: is U(n) multiplicative-ish? (U(pq) vs U(p), U(q))
connection: Compute-and-check: for n = pq ≤ 30 000, regress log U(pq) on log U(p), log U(q).
why: ES for composites is inherited from prime factors; quantifying how the count lifts tells whether the 'solution sheaf' is multiplicative.
first_step: Use f4_all_30000.txt; scatter log U(pq) − log U(p) − log U(q).

title: Per-prime weights of (q/p) in log U(p): q ≡ 2 (mod 3) give a clean Euler pattern q·β_q ≈ −0.35
connection: Regressing residual log U(p) (p ≡ 1 mod 4, n≈8 400) on (q/p) for q < 80: q·β_q = −0.46, −0.35, −0.37, −0.32, −0.26, −0.38 for q = 5, 11, 17, 23, 29, 47 (≈ constant, as an Euler factor would give), but q ≡ 1 (mod 3) give −0.11, −0.05, −0.17, −0.06, +0.30, +0.26 for q = 7, 13, 19, 31, 37, 43 (SE ≈ 0.002·q); stable across ranges and p mod 3.
why: A sharp, reproducible local-weight fingerprint; any heuristic model of ES counts must reproduce the q mod 3 split.
first_step: Explain via (−3/q) (next item); then refit including indicators 1[q | p+3] to see if the dichotomy disappears.

title: The '(7/p) anomaly' is plausibly the same (−3/q) confound
connection: Earlier item: U(p) ignores (7/p) (ρ = −0.013); per-prime fit gives 7·β₇ = −0.11 vs ≈ −0.4 for neighbours; 7 ≡ 1 (mod 3) ⇒ (−3/7) = +1 ⇒ confound with 7 | p+3.
why: If confirmed, removes a false lead (no special role of 7 in ES) and illustrates the shift-character coupling.
first_step: Check after controlling for 1[7 | p+3], 1[7 | p+7], … whether β₇ returns to ≈ −0.06.

title: (★) count R(p): weights β₃ = −0.15, β₇ = −0.08, β₅ = +0.03 (p ≡ 1 mod 4)
connection: R(p)'s per-prime profile differs from U's: dominated by 3 and 7 (both ≡ 3 mod 4) with 5, 17 slightly positive — i.e. R follows (−1/q)(q/p) = χ_{−4p}(q) at q ≡ 1 (4) partially.
why: Pinpoints which local primes the (★) line is sensitive to — a covering argument for (★) should treat 3 and 7 specially.
first_step: Compute the 3-adic and 7-adic local densities of (★) triples (u,B,C) as a function of p mod 3, mod 7.

title: Shift spectrum ρ(U, τ(p+s)) is a mod-3 sign pattern
connection: For p ≡ 1 (4): ρ(U-residual, τ(p+s)) > 0 for s ≡ 1 (mod 3) (≈ +0.1…+0.24), < 0 for s ≡ 2 (mod 3) (≈ −0.05…−0.25); s = 3: +0.48 (the genuine first-step effect).
why: Mostly a confound: 3 | p+s identifies p mod 3, and p ≡ 2 (3) is ES-easy. The residual after stratifying by p mod 3 gives the true shift spectrum.
first_step: Recompute ρ within p ≡ 1 (3) and within p ≡ 2 (3) separately.

title: Composite U(pq) depends weakly on U(p), U(q): log U(pq) ≈ 3.0 + 0.20 log U(p) + 0.11 log U(q) + 0.26 log n
connection: Over 5 668 odd semiprimes pq ≤ 30 000 (p < q), counts at pq are mostly governed by size, mildly by the factors' counts.
why: ES at composites reduces to primes for existence, but counts are 'more than inherited' — composite n have many non-inherited solutions; irrelevant to ES existence but relevant to count heuristics on all n.
first_step: Separate inherited (scaled from 4/p or 4/q) and non-inherited solutions at pq.

title: 2-adic depth effect saturates at 16
why: The 2-adic local density of ES solutions seems to depend on p mod 16 only — a finite local datum, consistent with the 'four-adic input' picture (FOUR_ADIC_INPUT.md).
first_step: Compute the exact 2-adic density of the ES surface at p mod 64 by counting solutions mod 2^k.

title: Binary expansion of hard primes: no signal expected (null test)
connection: Hamming weight / trailing-ones of p in binary for the 40 hardest vs random p ≡ 1 (24): any difference beyond v₂(p−1) would be surprising.
why: Sanity test of the 'digits are irrelevant' prior; only v₂(p−1) (trailing zeros of p−1) is arithmetic.
first_step: Compute and record; expect null after conditioning on v₂(p−1).

title: Five-slice count ES₅(p) vs U(p): fraction of solutions with λ ≤ 3
connection: FRONTIER notes 56% of solutions below 3000 lie outside the five-slice family; fingerprint the fraction per prime and its dependence on χ_p.
why: If the five-slice fraction is stable and bounded below, ES₅ is 'ES with a constant loss' empirically, supporting ES ⇒ ES₅.
first_step: Implement the λ(p) ≤ 3 certificate counter (HJ-length of p/A) and compute ratio at p ≤ 10⁵.

title: k₁/k₂ ratio as a function of p mod 24
connection: Type I : Type II proportions at primes differ by p mod 8 and mod 3 (via the characters above); the ratio fingerprint may reveal which type 'rescues' the hard classes.
why: If for p ≡ 1 (24) Type II dominates, Type II is the natural attack for the hard class.
first_step: Tabulate mean k₁/(k₁+k₂) by p mod 24 and by p mod 840 square classes.

title: Predicting R-zeros from local data: AUC test
connection: Train logistic regression on (q/p), 1[q | 4Cp+1] for small q, C to predict R(p) ≤ 2 (near-zeros) at p ≤ 3·10⁶; evaluate on the 12 zeros.
why: High AUC would show (★) failures are locally predictable — consistent with 'failures are discrete local events' and suggesting a finite covering-by-local-conditions proof might handle all but a predictable sparse set.
first_step: Build features for p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 3·10⁶; R from words_3e6.npy.

title: Carmichael numbers are ES-rich, not ES-hard: U(n) is 3.3–5.7× the neighbour median
why: Although n ≡ 1 modulo each p−1 (the 'hard' congruence shape), having ≥ 3 prime factors multiplies divisor structure; the p ≡ 1 (mod L) hardness mechanism does not survive multiplicatively — hardness is a prime phenomenon.
first_step: Compare with semiprimes pq where both p, q are ES-hard (e.g. 193·241) to see whether hardness compounds at all.

title: Bounded U-certificate size: Vmin(p) ≤ 116 for all primes p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 3·10⁶
connection: Least v ∈ 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ−p), v ≥ 3, with p+v having a divisor ≡ −1 (mod v): records 3 (5), 4 (17), 7 (97), 8 (457), 23 (1009), 87 (2521), 116 (3361) and no further record up to 3·10⁶; 99.9% quantile 31, mean 4.0.
why: A bounded-v version of U ('U_V: some v ≤ V works') is a finite union of single-shift divisor problems; if true for V = 116 it reduces ES at primes to finitely many 'p + v has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod v)' events — exactly the shape where single-shift laws (EXSET_SHIFT_DIVISORS Thm 2.2) apply, though the joint failure probability must still be bounded.
first_step: Extend the Vmin census to 10⁹ at primes; check whether records resume (each single-shift failure has probability ≍ (log p)^{−1/2}, so a fixed finite V must eventually fail infinitely often under independence — the data test that heuristic).

title: (★) certificate size Cmin: records 1,2,5,20,23,39,40,141,149,251,557 then 23105 at p = 184837
connection: Least C with a (★) word at primes p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 3·10⁶: mean 1.94, 99% quantile 9, 99.9% 41; the record jump to 23105 at 184837 is a boundary solution (u = 1, B = 2: 4C−1 = (p+1)/2), i.e. 184837 is an 'almost R-zero'.
why: Boundary-only primes (only u=1 or B=1 certificates) behave like R-zeros for any argument that excludes boundary terms; they enlarge the hard set for interior-only methods.
first_step: List all primes ≤ 3·10⁶ whose (★) words are boundary-only; compare their arithmetic profile with the R-zeros.

title: I3 needs large coordinates: min over I3 words of max(t,u,v) has median 169 and grows (740 at 2.5·10⁶)
connection: At primes p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 3·10⁶ the smallest I3 certificate has max coordinate ≈ 175 on average, records 379 (487 381) … 740 (2 506 373).
why: I3 is cheap in count but expensive in size — unlike U and (★) (bounded small certificates); an existence proof for I3 can't use small-coordinate coverings.
first_step: Fit the record growth (≈ p^{0.3}?) and relate to the t,u,v ≥ 3 constraint geometry.

title: Tail law of Cmin vs independent divisor events
connection: If the slice failures F_C = {4Cp+1 has no divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4C)} were independent, P(Cmin > c) ≈ ∏_{C≤c} P(F_C), where each P(F_C) decays slowly with p (a single-shift failure law, cf. EXSET_SHIFT_DIVISORS Thm 2.2); compare with data. Also compute the full correlation matrix of the events E_C = ¬F_C for C ≤ 20–32 (φ-coefficients; E_C and E_{2C} share structure).
why: Measures dependence between (★) slices C — exactly the 'joint budget' question (JOINT_BUDGET.md) in a cheap observable.
first_step: Compute empirical P(E_C) and P(E_C ∩ E_C′) at p ≤ 3·10⁶ for C, C′ ≤ 20; report the correlation matrix.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: U failures factor as products of small primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) and one larger factor
why: Composite U failures are driven by the composite structure (factors ≡ 3 mod 4 make n+v divisors in the needed class scarce?); 25305 contains 241 (least p ≡ 1 (4) with least QNR 7) — a weak link to pseudosquare-type hardness.
first_step: Test whether U-failure rate among n ≡ 1 (8) depends on the number of prime factors ≡ 3 (mod 4) of n; predict further failures beyond 10⁹ from that profile.

title: Full chain x | y | z fails at 670 primes ≤ 10⁵, starting 73, 193, 313, 337, 409, 457, 577, …
connection: Chains exist for most primes but fail at a sizeable set containing the hard primes 193, 409, 577, 1201 (not in OEIS).
why: The chain sub-family is a 1-parameter-poorer certificate; its failure set is a hardness filter between the full ES and single lines.
first_step: Compute the density of chain failures among p ≡ 1 (24) vs others; is it ≈ constant (then infinitely many failures) or decaying?

title: 241 = 240 + 1 as a universal small outlier
connection: 241 appears in: 8/p failures (last), 16/p and 20/p failures (not 12/p), '4 | some denominator' failures (last), 'no 3' failures (unique), U-hard top 30, greedy x = (p+3)/4 failures, z ≤ p^{1.75} failures (first).
why: p − 1 = 240 = 2⁴·3·5 — 241 ≡ 1 (mod 16, 3, 5) is the smallest prime with simultaneous deep 2-adic and 3,5 structure; a natural test case for every new certificate family.
first_step: Add 241, 2521, 193 to every new family's unit tests; record which families certify them.

title: Primitive solutions (gcd(x,y,z) = 1) fail at 110 primes ≤ 10⁵, all ≡ 1 (mod 12)
connection: No primitive ES solution at 13, 37, 97, 181, 193, 277, 373, 541, 673, 757, 853, 1033, 1093, 1297, 1621, … (last ≤ 10⁵: 98713); share of primitive solutions 7.9%.
why: Primitive points on the ES cubic surface are the integral-point problem proper; failures concentrated on p ≡ 1 (12) show the 3-adic and 4-adic local structure of primitivity.
first_step: Check that all 110 are ≡ 1 (mod 12) and compute failure density in that class (≈ 110/1200?); likely infinite — record as 'primitive ES fails infinitely often?' question.

title: Solutions with x prime fail at 4 597 primes; with some perfect-square denominator at 3 134
connection: Prime smallest denominators (share 0.7%) and square denominators (0.8%) are rare; failure sets start 31, 37, 53, 73, … and 17, 29, 41, 73, 89, … (no OEIS match).
why: Rare-shape sub-families give no ES leverage but are fingerprints for 'random-like' behaviour of denominators (density of primes/squares among x).
first_step: Compare the share of prime x with 1/log x heuristics (≈ 1/log(p/4)).

title: Shares of solution shapes at primes ≈ constants: x | z 0.377, none-div-by-3 0.346, none-div-by-4 0.301, none-div-by-8 0.59, none-div-by-9 0.70
connection: Mean share (over p ≡ 1 (4) > 1000) of each restricted shape among all solutions; these are local-density-like constants of the ES solution set.
why: Stable shares across p would mean the solution set equidistributes in these local conditions (Manin-type equidistribution on the surface) — compare with local densities computed mod 3, 4, 8, 9.
first_step: Compute shares per dyadic range to see whether they converge; compute the local densities predicted by counting solutions mod q.

title: Restricted-ES variant failure sets are mostly NOT in OEIS
connection: Lookups of the failure sets (chain, primitive, coprime-pair, squarefree, height p^{1.75}, prime-x, square-denominator) returned no OEIS match; only the isosceles set matched (A002144).
why: A family of ~10 new, cheaply-defined sequences: submitting them invites outside pattern-matching (e.g. someone may recognise the primitive-failure primes).
first_step: Bundle and submit with definitions, after verifying with an independent brute-force for p ≤ 2000.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Case study 4/2521: no solution has x | z, all have small x ∈ [636, 1026]
connection: The 9 solutions of 4/2521 have x ∈ {636, 638, 644, 652, 658, 748, 1026}, none with x | z; residues mod 3 and mod 4 are mixed.
why: 2521 is the unique lcm-closed failure and the hardest prime ≤ 2·10⁵ by U/log²p; understanding its 9 solutions (5 have 4 | x) is a concrete testbed for 'why is p ≡ 1 (mod 2520) hard'.
first_step: For each solution identify its ET type and the (★)/U/I3 word that generates it; compute what fails for the lcm-closed family (which divisor sums 4z/p = a + b + 1 are missing).

title: Variant engine for m/n: restricted shapes for 5/n and 8/n
connection: Rerun the variant counters for numerators 5 and 8 (one flag) to get Sierpiński / even-ES analogues of the isosceles, lcm-closed and primitive fingerprints.
why: If '4/p isosceles ⟺ p ≡ 3 (4)' has a clean 5/p analogue (p in a class mod 5 or 20?) it reveals the general degenerate-locus law.
first_step: Run z52b_fingerprint_variants with m = 5, 8 on primes ≤ 10⁵.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Does the Type I share fall with L(1,χ_p)? (k₁ responds more strongly than k₂)
connection: Across p ≤ 2·10⁵, k₁ has α ≈ −0.34 on log L(1,χ_p), k₂ only ≈ −0.20, so the Type I share k₁/(k₁+k₂) should decrease as L(1,χ_p) grows; at lcm(1..19)+1 the split is nevertheless typical (k₁/k₂ = 2.3).
why: If the share effect were strong, a proof strategy could split by the size of L(1,χ_p) (Type I when some small prime is inert, Type II otherwise); the residual k₁/k₂ correlation +0.70 and the lcm(1..19)+1 data suggest the effect is modest.
first_step: Fit k₁/(k₁+k₂) against log L(1,χ_p) at p ≤ 10⁷ windows and at pseudosquare primes.

title: Targeted search for record-hard primes via the fitted model
connection: Rank candidate primes p ≡ 1 (mod 840) up to 10¹² by predicted log U (Euler product over q ≤ 50 + 2-adic depth + τ((p+3)/4)) and compute U only for the top predictions.
why: Finds the hardest ES primes at scales where exhaustive counting is impossible — the best stress-test inputs for any proposed certificate family.
first_step: Implement: sieve p ≡ 1 (840) with all q ≤ 23 QR, then rank by τ((p+3)/4) and v₂(p−1); count U at the top 100 in [10⁹, 10¹⁰].

title: The (★) mean constant vs BM mean: R/M_BM ≈ 1.31 (p ≤ 12 000) and 1.22 (20 000–30 000)
connection: Mean ratio of R(p) to the BM main term drifts down with p (M₀ ratio 1.26 → 1.18).
why: If R/M_BM → 1 the BM term is asymptotically the right mean (FRONTIER: M_BM ∼ M₀ under GRH); the drift rate measures the secondary term.
first_step: Compute R/M_BM at windows 10⁵, 10⁶, 3·10⁶ (script scales linearly per prime).

title: Predict per-prime weights β_q from the BM main term
connection: M_BM(p) = Σ (1 − (−uB/p))/φ(4uB): expanding (−uB/p) = ∏_{q|uB} (q/p)^{v_q} predicts how each (q/p) shifts the mean count; compare with q·β_q ≈ −0.35 for q ≡ 2 (3) and the q ≡ 1 (3) confound.
why: A quantitative match would show the BM term is the full explanation of the χ_p fluctuations of U; a mismatch identifies missing terms (e.g. the shift couplings via (−s/q)).
first_step: Compute ∂ E[M_BM | (q/p) = ±1] numerically at p ≤ 30 000 for each q ≤ 47 and plot against fitted β_q.

title: Pell numerology: R-zeros 409 = 408 + 1 and 577 with 577² − 2·408² = 1
connection: The first two (★) failures are 408+1 and 577, the Pell pair (577, 408) for √2; 577 − 1 = 24².
why: Almost certainly coincidence; recorded because √2-convergents p/q give p ≡ ±1 structure and 2 is a QR mod both — test cheaply with the next Pell pairs (3363, 2378), (19601, 13860).
first_step: Check R(p) at primes near Pell numbers (2379, 3361? 3363 is composite; 13861, 19601 composite) — expect nothing.

title: Function-field analogue of 2521: polynomials ≡ 1 modulo all small irreducibles
connection: Over F_q[T], the analogue of lcm(1..k)+1 is P = ∏_{deg ≤ d} (irreducibles) + 1 (or ≡ 1 mod their product); the campaign's F_q[T] ES variants (FUNCTIONFIELD_ES*.md) could be fingerprinted on such P.
why: If F_q[T] ES counts at these P are minimal, the 'p ≡ 1 mod smooth' hardness mechanism is structural and transfers to the setting where proofs exist — a template for transferring arguments.
first_step: Using the existing F_q[T] engines (scripts/*ff*), count solutions at P = 1 + T·∏… for q = 3, 5 and compare with random P of the same degree.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Pseudosquares over F_q[T] (Lehmer analogue) as the hardest ES inputs
connection: Define F_q[T] pseudosquares (non-square P ≡ square-like mod all small irreducibles); predicted hardest ES inputs if the integer picture transfers.
why: Bridges the integer pseudosquare fingerprint to the setting with proved ES variants.
first_step: Generate F_3[T] pseudosquares up to degree 12 and run the ES solvers.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: k-term sibling: 4/p as a sum of 3 unit fractions with all denominators ≤ C·p (bounded height)
connection: The smallest C such that every prime ≤ X has a solution with z ≤ C·p^{a} — with a = 2 every prime ≤ 10⁵ works; find the minimal constant for a = 2 (C = max minz(p)/p²).
why: Effective ES with explicit height is what lattice/geometry-of-numbers approaches would produce; the empirical C is the target.
first_step: Done: max minz(p)/p² = 0.5026 at p = 577 (see the effective-height item); extend to windows at 10⁶, 10⁷.

title: ES hardness vs 'p − 1 practical number' (Erdős–Graham denominators)
connection: p − 1 practical (every m ≤ p − 1 a sum of distinct divisors) is common for smooth p − 1; hard primes have smooth p − 1; Egyptian-fraction representability of 1/p-type fractions is classically tied to practical numbers.
why: Links ES hardness to the practical-number literature (Vose, Saias), where Egyptian fraction lengths are controlled by divisor richness.
first_step: Compute 1[p − 1 practical] and its correlation with residual U(p); check whether all 30 hardest primes have p − 1 practical.

title: ES solution denominators and the Prouhet–Tarry–Escott / Znám problem: category check
connection: Znám's problem (each n_i divides ∏_{j≠i} n_j + 1) and Egyptian-fraction 'improper' problems share unit-fraction identities; ES solutions with x | yz + 1-type divisibilities could be fingerprinted.
why: Low expectation; recorded as a breadth item because Znám-type divisibility is the 'Sylvester sequence' world where unit-fraction identities are exact.
first_step: Count ES solutions at primes with x | yz ± 1 or y | xz ± 1 and see if any family is universal.

title: Hard primes and the Ankeny–Artin–Chowla / large fundamental unit regime
connection: Hard primes have large L(1,χ_p) = 2h(p) log ε_p/√p; with h(p) = 1 typically this means a large regulator (long CF period of √p): compute the CF period of √2521, √66529, √193 vs neighbours.
why: Connects ES hardness to Pell-equation size — and to the CF-length formulations (ES₅) via the same continued-fraction machinery.
first_step: Use the classical_feat data: quantile of CF period at the hard primes.

title: Granville–Soundararajan extreme values: how hard can an ES prime be?
connection: Granville–Soundararajan show L(1,χ_d) reaches ≈ e^γ log log d (up to lower-order terms) for many d; with U ∝ L(1,χ_p)^{−0.3}, the worst primes up to X have U(p) ≳ log³p·(log log p)^{−0.3}… a polylog lower envelope.
why: Heuristic only: if the (unproven, empirically fitted) count law held with lognormal noise, the χ_p mechanism alone would depress counts by at most a (log log)^{O(1)} factor — so ES failures, if any, would have to come from elsewhere; this is a statement about a model, not about ES.
first_step: Formalise as a conditional heuristic: assume U(p) ≈ c log³p L(1,χ_p)^{−α}·(noise); compute P(U(p) = 0) under lognormal noise and sum over p.

title: n mod 840 explains 64% of the variance of log U(n) (all n ≤ 30 000)
connection: Residual log U(n) (after log n, loglog n) has variance explained 0.16 (n mod 2), 0.24 (mod 4), 0.39 (mod 12), 0.42 (mod 24), 0.43 (mod 30), 0.64 (mod 840); primes q ≥ 11 alone explain ≤ 6%.
why: Most of the ES count's arithmetic fluctuation is a periodic function of n with small period — the 'covering congruence' part; the remaining 36% is where pointwise difficulty lives.
first_step: Compute VE for moduli 840·11, 840·13 and the residual's distribution after removing the mod-9240 mean.

title: Ramanujan-sum expansion of the normalised ES count
connection: Compute-and-check: least-squares coefficients a_q in U(n)/log³n ≈ Σ_{q ≤ Q} a_q c_q(n) over n ≤ 30 000.
why: If a_q is (nearly) multiplicative with a_p ≈ −1/p-ish, the count has an Euler-product singular series over n — the all-n analogue of the χ_p law at primes.
first_step: Implement c_q(n) = Σ_{d | gcd(q,n)} μ(q/d) d and fit.

title: Consecutive primes ≡ 1 (4): residual log U correlation −0.09
connection: Slight negative correlation between neighbouring primes' ES residuals.
why: Likely a residue-class artefact (neighbouring primes in different classes mod 3, 8); a nonzero value after conditioning would indicate a 'short-interval' effect relevant to EXCEPTIONAL_SHORT.md-type arguments.
first_step: Recompute after removing class-mod-840 means.

title: Easiest classes mod 840: 557, 277, 653, 53, 317
connection: These classes have the most ES solutions on average (+0.3 to +0.54 in log); they are non-squares modulo several of 3, 5, 8 at once (e.g. 557 ≡ 2 mod 3, 2 mod 5, 5 mod 8).
why: The easy classes are covered by several identities simultaneously; counting how many Mordell identities cover each class and correlating with the class mean tests 'count ≈ number of covering identities'.
first_step: Enumerate Mordell/ET identity families mod 840 and count multiplicities per class; correlate with class means.

title: Kloosterman sums K(1,1;p) vs ES counts (null test)
connection: Normalised Kloosterman sums are Sato–Tate distributed; correlate with residual U(p) at p ≤ 2·10⁴.
why: Kloosterman sums appear in the spectral treatment of divisor problems in progressions (the X(n) part); a correlation at the pointwise level would be surprising.
first_step: Compute K(1,1;p) = Σ_x e((x + x⁻¹)/p) for p ≤ 2·10⁴ and Spearman.

title: Supersingular j-invariants in F_p (not F_{p²}): a class-number quantity
connection: ⌊p/12⌋ + ε counts supersingular j over F̄_p (all lie in F_{p²}); the number lying in F_p is a class-number expression (≈ h(−4p)/2 + … for p ≡ 1 (4), involving h(−p), h(−4p)). Correlate it with residual U(p).
why: Ties a modular-curve count to the class-number data that weakly correlate with ES counts (h(−4p): ρ ≈ +0.14 normalised); expected weak.
first_step: Compute #supersingular j ∈ F_p via the class-number formula (or Sage) for p ≤ 10⁵ and Spearman with residual U, k₂.

title: Tunnell ternary counts as ES predictors
connection: #{x²+2y²+8z² = p} and #{x²+2y²+32z² = p} are weight-3/2 coefficients; their ratio is Tunnell's congruent-number test. Correlate both with k₁, k₂.
why: A weight-3/2 form whose coefficients track ES counts would be the first concrete 'theta lift' fingerprint (Kudla/Shimura direction).
first_step: Brute-force the representation counts for p ≤ 10⁵ (O(p) each with nested loops ≈ fine for p ≤ 2·10⁴).

title: Exceptions are about dispersion, not mean: squarefree-ES (mean 19.8) has 3 exceptions, 20/p (mean 26.4) has 60 still occurring at 9·10⁴
why: Families defined as a 'share' of all solutions (squarefree, lcm-closed, no-3) inherit U's tight distribution and have tiny exception sets; families defined by a multiplicative constraint (k | xyz, the (★) line) have heavy lower tails. For a proof, pick families of the first kind.
first_step: Measure the coefficient of variation of each family's count (residual after log p) and plot last-exception vs CV; test the predicted monotone relation.

title: Sierpiński 5/p hard primes: 8821, 6301, 4201, 12601, 81901, 4621, … all ≡ 1 (mod 20)
connection: Hardest primes for 5/p (residual log U₅) ≤ 10⁵; 4201, 12601, 20521 are also among the hardest for 4/p; residual correlation between U₄ and U₅ is only +0.23.
why: Primes ≡ 1 modulo a smooth number are hard for every numerator (shared 'p − 1 smooth' axis) while the character axes differ by numerator — a decomposition of hardness into universal and numerator-specific parts.
first_step: Fit the Euler-product law for 5/p (per-prime weights) and compare its signs with 4/p.

title: 12601 = 12600 + 1: hardest prime across numerators 4, 5, 7
connection: 12601 has U = 27 (rank 26 of 8 966 primes ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 2·10⁵ by U/log³p), is rank 4 for 5/p and rank 1 for 7/p, and fails 15/p; p − 1 = 2³·3²·5²·7.
why: A natural single test case for 'universal' hardness, smaller than 2521-type examples for other numerators.
first_step: List all ES solutions of 4/12601, 5/12601, 7/12601 and identify common structure (denominators' factorisations).

title: Minimum of U(p)/log³p by decade as the key ES 'safety margin' statistic
why: If m(X) stays bounded below, ES's margin is a constant fraction of the mean — the single number to monitor in any larger census.
first_step: Add U(p)/log³p minima to any future census (count program is ≈ linear in p per prime; windows at 10⁸, 10⁹ feasible).

title: Independent confirmation of OEIS A400619 (records of 4x(p) − p) up to 2·10⁵
connection: Our engine gives records of 4·(least first denominator) − p at primes 2, 5, 73, 1129, 1201, 21169, 118801 (values 2, 3, 7, 11, 23, 31, 59) — exactly the first seven terms of A400619 (Witteveen 2026, searched to 4·10¹¹; next terms 8 803 369, 119 945 383 009).
why: A400619's primes are the 'greedy-hardest' primes; 21169 is also one of our three all-squarefree failures and 118801, 1201 are top-30 U-hard — the greedy-depth record is a strong hardness detector.
first_step: Compute U, R, Uv at 8 803 369 (≈ 4 s with the count program) — note it is close to but different from the R-zero 8 813 281 — and test whether it is an R-zero or U-hard.

title: A392469's empirical bound k(p) < 71 log p vs our certificate-size laws
connection: Gold notes k(a(n)) < 71·log a(n) for all known records; our (★) Cmin has mean ≈ 2 with rare large values (23105 at a boundary case), and Vmin ≤ 116 ≤ 3·10⁶.
why: Logarithmic certificate size is exactly what a 'small-certificate covering' approach needs; comparing the k(p) law with the line-specific laws tells which line has the best size profile.
first_step: Plot max_{p ≤ X} k(p)/log p from mink_pr_2e5.txt and compare with Vmin, Cmin records.

title: Idoneal numbers as natural covering moduli
connection: Euler's 65 known idoneal numbers (largest 1848; the list is complete under GRH, and at most one more could exist unconditionally — A000926) are exactly the D for which x² + Dy² representing p is a congruence condition; Mordell's modulus 840 is one of them.
why: If ES identities can only cover non-principal genera of some form x² + Dy² (a 'genus obstruction' version of Mordell–Schinzel), the idoneal list would indicate where pure congruence coverings of this kind can reach; for non-idoneal D the principal-form condition is no longer a congruence condition (class-group data).
first_step: For D ∈ {1320, 1365, 1848} compute which classes mod 4D are covered by the known identity families and whether the uncovered set is the principal genus.

title: A257843 (Hasler): n where the lexicographically first solution ≠ the max-z solution
why: A 'solution-geometry' fingerprint (shape of the solution set's extremes) — a cheap invariant that may separate hard from easy classes.
first_step: Compute the density of A257843 among p ≡ 1 (24) vs others and correlate membership with residual U(p).

title: OEIS has 2026 ES entries (A392469, A397366, A396825, A400619) — active outside community
connection: Four ES-related sequences were added in 2026 by Gold, van Tol, Witteveen, plus Alekseyev's A287116 (2017); the campaign's hard-prime lists and our variant failure sets are absent.
why: The OEIS ES cluster is an active, low-cost outreach channel; contributing the R-zeros, U failures, I3 zeros, lcm-closed/no-3/squarefree exceptions and the isosceles law would connect to these authors' searches (e.g. Witteveen searched to 4·10¹¹).
first_step: Prepare a batch of 6–8 submissions with b-files and cross-references to A139665, A392469, A400619, A287116.

title: Our ESC zero set ≤ 1369 ⊂ A396825 ∪ {105, 672}
connection: Every n ≤ 1369 with no word having a coordinate in 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ − n) is in van Tol's A396825 except 105 and 672; Uv zeros differ from A396825 by {33, 193, 385} vs {105, 156, 204, 316, 396, 508, …}.
why: Near-containment between independently defined exception sets suggests a common divisor-class obstruction; making it exact would merge two literatures.
first_step: Fetch the A396825 b-file and test containment to 10⁶; analyse 105 and 672 under van Tol's S(n) definition.

title: Σ_{p ≤ N} f(p) / (N log² N) = 0.88, 0.80, 0.77, 0.76, 0.75 (N = 10³…2·10⁵)
connection: ET prove N log²N ≪ Σ_{p≤N} f(p) ≪ N log²N log log N; our ordered counts give a slowly decreasing ratio to N log²N (and 0.45 → 0.30 against N log²N loglog N) — the data favour the lower-bound order, with a constant ≈ 0.7.
why: Suggests (does not pin down) that the log log factor in ET's upper bound may be absent — relevant to which heuristic mean (BM, Euler product) is calibrated correctly.
first_step: Extend to 10⁷ via windows; fit c + d/log N.

title: Lowest-count composites: are they products of hard primes?
connection: Rank composite n ≤ 30 000 by U(n)/log³n; test whether the lowest are products of two primes both in the hard class (p ≡ 1 mod 24) such as 73·193.
why: If hardness multiplies, composite ES-hardness reduces to prime hardness (expected: composites inherit solutions from each factor, so they should be easy).
first_step: Sort f4_all_30000.txt by U/log³n restricted to composites.

title: ES counts on the 'norm form' side: n = a² + b² with a/b fixed angle
connection: For n ≡ 1 (4) prime the Gaussian angle was null; for composite n test whether representations as norms from Z[ω], Z[√−2] (x²+3y², x²+2y²) predict counts.
why: Norm-form representability is the genus/class-field data; for primes it reduces to Legendre symbols (already captured), for composites it adds multiplicities.
first_step: Correlate U(n) with r_{x²+y²}(n), r_{x²+2y²}(n), r_{x²+3y²}(n) at composites ≤ 30 000.

title: Balanced solutions (z ≤ 10x) frequency
connection: Fraction of primes with a solution having z/x ≤ C for C = 10, 100, 1000; BALANCED_LATTICE.md studies balanced points.
why: If balanced solutions exist for all large p with C fixed, geometry-of-numbers on the cubic surface (bounded-height points) would suffice — a strong statement to falsify cheaply.
first_step: Add a min z/x statistic to the count program and record its maximum over p ≤ 2·10⁵.

title: Per-class identity 'signatures' mod 840
connection: For each class a mod 840, the set of limiting ratios (y/x, z/x) of solutions common to all primes in the class is its identity signature; hard classes should have empty signatures (no polynomial identity).
why: Makes Mordell–Schinzel's 'no polynomial identity covers square classes' visible in data, and might expose quasi-identities (identities valid for a positive proportion of the class).
first_step: Group solutions by class and ratio buckets; list buckets present for ≥ 90% of primes in the class.

title: Hard-prime 'twin' structure: p and p + 2520 both hard?
connection: Because hardness depends on p mod 840 and quadratic characters, p and p + 840k share the mod-840 part but not the characters at q ∤ 840; test correlation of residuals at lag 840 among primes.
why: Separates the periodic (mod 840) from the character part: lag-840 correlation among primes estimates their variance shares (cf. 0.60 autocorrelation over all n).
first_step: Compute residual correlation for prime pairs (p, p+840k), k ≤ 10.

title: U(p) and the least prime ≡ 1 (mod p) or the least prime q with p | q − 1 (Linnik-type)
connection: Null-expected cross check: data about primes in progressions modulo p (EXSET_LINNIK.md) should not influence local ES counts.
why: Sanity: separates 'divisor-in-progression' events used in ES (which are about divisors of p-tied integers) from progressions mod p.
first_step: Compute least prime q ≡ 1 (mod p) for p ≤ 2·10⁴ and Spearman with residual U.

title: Fingerprint of 'ES at p' vs 'ES at 4p+1' / 'ES at (p+3)/4'
connection: The (★) divisor form involves 4Cp + 1 and the greedy step (p+3)/4; test whether U(4p+1) or U((p+3)/4) (when composite, often easy) correlates with U(p).
why: Cheap check of whether ES difficulty propagates along the natural 'p-tied integer' maps (a dynamical view: forests in FOREST_*.md).
first_step: Compute Spearman(U(p), U(4p+1)) for p ≤ 7 500 and Spearman(U(p), U((p+3)/4)).

title: Effective height: minz(p) ≤ 0.503·p² for every prime 100 < p ≤ 2·10⁵, extremal at the R-zero 577
connection: max minz(p)/p² = 0.5026 at p = 577 (an R-zero); for p > 1000 the largest log minz/log p is 1.84 (at 6271).
why: An explicit effective-height ES (z ≤ 0.503 p²; minz(577) = 167 330 = 0.50260·577²) holds in range; the extremal prime is again a campaign hard prime, so the height of the cheapest certificate is a hardness detector.
first_step: Track max minz(p)/p² in windows at 10⁶, 10⁷ (count program already outputs minz).

title: Hardest composites are prime squares: lowest U(n)/log³n among composites ≤ 30 000 are 97², 113², 163², 109², 37², 67², 2·71², 173², 103², 61², 73², 89²
connection: Eleven of the twelve are prime squares (eight of them squares of primes ≡ 1 (4); 163, 67, 103 are ≡ 3 (4)) and one is 2·71².
why: Count-level shadow of T1: certificate lines vanish at odd squares and the total count at p² is the lowest among composites — squares are the hard composites, as the reciprocity obstruction predicts.
first_step: Compare U(p²) with U(p)² and with the number of solutions inherited from 4/p by scaling.

title: Tunnell's ternary counts: individually weakly correlated with residual U (ρ ≈ 0.18), Tunnell difference A − 2B null (0.02)
connection: For p ≡ 1, 3 (mod 8), 100 < p ≤ 2·10⁴ (1 115 primes): #{x²+2y²+8z² = p} and #{x²+2y²+32z² = p} each correlate +0.19/+0.18 with residual log U(p); A − 2B (congruent-number criterion) ≈ 0.
why: The weight-3/2 theta coefficients share the class-number/genus signal (both ∝ h(−8p)-type quantities) but the congruent-number combination carries nothing: no congruent-number ↔ ES link at the data level.
first_step: Correlate with h(−2p), h(−8p) to confirm the shared signal is just the class number.

title: Hard-prime fingerprints recur across seven distinct (not statistically independent) detectors
connection: 193, 241, 577, 1201, 2521, 3361, 21169 recur among: U/log³ minima, m/p failures (12, 16, 20, 24), greedy-depth records (A400619), min-k records (A392469), height extremes, variant exceptions (lcm-closed, squarefree, no-3, 4|·), R-zeros/Type-A.
why: A small 'hall of fame' of test primes captures most distinct hardness mechanisms; any new idea can be screened in seconds on it.
first_step: Publish the hall of fame with per-detector membership as a table in the campaign (data/z52b/hard_profile.json + variants).

title: Screening tool: certify-or-not table for any new certificate family
connection: Generalise the variant counter to take a predicate plug-in and output failure sets at primes ≤ 10⁵ in < 1 min (as done for 32 shapes here).
why: Lets other lanes turn 'connection' items into falsifiable data within minutes — the variant runs here found single-exception families (lcm-closed: only 2521) that no theory predicted.
first_step: Refactor scripts/z52b_fingerprint_variants*.c into a predicate-driven engine with a small DSL (divisibility, coprimality, size).

title: Near-isosceles solutions: smallest y − x (or z − y) at p ≡ 1 (4)
connection: Since x = y is impossible at p ≡ 1 (4), the minimal gap y − x over solutions is a fingerprint of how close the hard class comes to the degenerate locus.
why: If the minimal gap is always small (bounded or ≪ log p), near-degenerate families might give uniform certificates.
first_step: Add min(y − x) and min(z − y) to the count program; tabulate at p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 2·10⁵.

title: Moving the first denominator
connection: Connect changes x→x+1 with changes in the residual factor-pair problem, treating consecutive x as coupled rather than independent trials.
why: Neighboring residual numerators differ by four, so their divisor searches share arithmetic structure.
first_step: Tabulate success transitions between neighboring x for 100 primes.

title: Symmetric coordinates
connection: Use s1=x+y+z, s2=xy+xz+yz, s3=xyz and the relation 4s3=ps2 to connect ES to integer-root cubic polynomials.
why: The cubic viewpoint keeps all denominator permutations together and exposes discriminant constraints.
first_step: Search small integer s1,s2 satisfying integral roots of T³−s1T²+s2T−ps2/4.

title: Fraction splitting trees
connection: Connect ES identities to the elementary split 1/a=1/(a+1)+1/(a(a+1)), allowing merges as well as splits.
why: Length-three targets might be reached through longer identities with controlled cancellation or merging.
first_step: Generate a bounded graph of positive unit-fraction identities connected by exact splits and inverse merges.

title: Bilinear determinant encoding
connection: Represent uv−r as a two-by-two determinant and translate ES divisor conditions into determinant equations with congruences.
why: Determinants bring row operations and lattice bases into a directly arithmetic setting.
first_step: Write a residual factor-pair certificate as a determinant condition and list congruence-preserving row operations.

title: Resultants between identities
connection: Eliminate shared parameters from two valid ES families to identify their intersections and potential transition rules.
why: Intersections may show how families cooperate rather than merely duplicate coverage.
first_step: Compute a resultant for two small exact families found by direct denominator ansatz.

title: Birational chart comparison
connection: Cover the ES surface by different rational charts and compare where integer points have manageable denominators.
why: One chart can hide integrality that another makes explicit.
first_step: Write charts obtained by solving for x, y, and a denominator ratio; compare their divisibility conditions.

title: Logarithmic denominator coordinates
connection: Map triples to log(x),log(y),log(z), comparing thin certificate families with the curved positive ES surface.
why: Multiplicative scales become additive and can expose regions systematically missed by bounded boxes.
first_step: Plot normalized log-denominator triples for primes below 1000 using several search cutoffs.

title: Elliptic slices
connection: Intersect the ES surface with simple quadratic constraints and check whether the resulting curves have genus one.
why: A useful slice could carry arithmetic group operations, although positivity and integrality remain separate tasks.
first_step: Try xy=z²+k for small k and compute the genus of the resulting plane curve.

title: Norm equations
connection: Rewrite selected quadratic discriminant conditions as norms in quadratic orders and track the congruences needed for ES.
why: Multiplicativity of norms may combine certificates in ways raw divisor enumeration misses.
first_step: For one Pell-type slice, translate the equation into a norm and record its positivity restrictions.

title: Gaussian integer decompositions
connection: Test whether representing auxiliary factors as sums of two squares helps impose the needed residue class.
why: Norm factors carry extra structure; the connection is a candidate construction, not a universal representation claim.
first_step: For small certificates with a sum-of-two-squares auxiliary factor, tabulate how Gaussian factors determine residues.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Continued-fraction surgery
connection: Study local replacements in continued fractions that change a certificate's congruence data without making its length too large.
why: Equivalent rational expansions can trade coefficient signs, sizes, and parity.
first_step: Enumerate short continued-fraction identities and label which preserve positivity and desired coefficient classes.

title: Stern–Brocot ancestry
connection: Attach each residual rational to its Stern–Brocot path and look for common terminal patterns among successful splits.
why: Path suffixes may encode useful divisibility conditions more compactly than numerator-denominator pairs.
first_step: Record path suffixes of length at most eight for successful and unsuccessful bounded residual searches.

title: Higher power residue labels
connection: Decorate auxiliary divisors with cubic or quartic residue data to distinguish classes invisible to quadratic symbols.
why: Extra labels might reveal a constructive partition even when they do not force existence.
first_step: For primes in suitable congruence classes, compare certificate frequencies across power-residue labels.

title: Chinese remainder optimization
connection: Treat parameter selection as a CRT problem with a cost function on the resulting least positive representative.
why: Congruence compatibility and parameter size are distinct, computable parts of certificate design.
first_step: Combine three small valid congruence conditions and optimize the CRT representative by varying their residues.

title: Lattice basis reduction for residues
connection: Encode simultaneous divisibility and smallness conditions as an integer lattice and use reduced bases to propose auxiliary parameters.
why: Short vectors can suggest candidates even without an existence theorem.
first_step: Build a two-constraint lattice for one residual factor search and compare reduced vectors with brute force.

title: Semigroup holes
connection: Treat attainable certificate parameters under positive identity composition as an affine semigroup and inspect its holes.
why: Eventual saturation is a meaningful possibility even when small exceptions persist.
first_step: Generate the semigroup from a small set of verified composition moves and compute missing points in a bounded region.

title: Subset products in residue groups
connection: Translate selection of a divisor into selecting prime-power factors whose product hits a residue in a finite multiplicative group.
why: This gives an exact finite combinatorial problem once the factorization is known.
first_step: For a factored auxiliary integer, run subset-product dynamic programming and inspect unreachable residue classes.

title: Nonunit residue handling
connection: Separate auxiliary prime factors sharing the modulus from unit factors before applying group-based divisor heuristics.
why: Ignoring nonunits would make the group model false; stratifying valuations repairs it.
first_step: Implement a residue-state enumeration that tracks gcd with the modulus and compare it with unit-only counts.

title: Cyclotomic factor opportunities
connection: Choose auxiliary parameters making a p-tied expression resemble a cyclotomic value with structured factors.
why: Algebraic factorization can manufacture divisors, although the required residue must still be checked.
first_step: Search low-degree substitutions yielding a difference of squares or a cyclotomic factorization in the residual equation.

title: Divisor switching with a moving modulus
connection: Exchange the roles of a target divisor and its complementary factor in the p-tied divisor count.
why: The same certificate can be counted in two ranges, potentially exposing different analytic structure.
first_step: Write both exact summation orders for divisors d≡−1 modulo 4C of 4Cp+1.

title: Local densities as fingerprints
connection: Compute exact residue-level densities for several certificate families and use the vector of densities as a fingerprint of p.
why: Local fingerprints might predict complementary families without asserting a local-global principle.
first_step: Enumerate admissible parameter tuples modulo 8,9,5,7 for three exact identities.

title: Exceptional-prime clustering
connection: Study whether primes with few bounded certificates cluster in arithmetic progressions or short intervals.
why: Structure in the tail could suggest targeted constructions rather than more uniform averaging.
first_step: Define one fixed search budget and compare the bottom count decile across residue classes and intervals.

title: Factorial moments of distinct witnesses
connection: Count ordered tuples of genuinely distinct witnesses rather than powers that include repeated certificates.
why: Factorial moments isolate multiplicity and can test a Poisson-like model cleanly.
first_step: Canonicalize denominator triples and calculate the first three factorial moments by prime range.

title: Dependency graphs for witnesses
connection: Create a graph connecting certificate searches that share prime factors or congruence constraints.
why: Graph sparsity could support more accurate probability models and search schedules.
first_step: For a fixed sample, compare a shared-factor graph with measured success correlations.

title: Entropy of divisor residues
connection: Measure how rapidly the residue distribution spreads as prime-power factors are added to a divisor set.
why: Entropy gives a quantitative description of concentration in a proper subgroup or coset.
first_step: Convolve the two-choice residue measures factor by factor for small factored auxiliary integers.

title: Rough–smooth complementary constructions
connection: Pair a construction exploiting many small factors with one exploiting a single large complementary factor.
why: The two regimes may produce genuinely different certificate mechanisms.
first_step: Partition auxiliary values by largest-prime-factor ratio and compare the successful denominator shapes.

title: Prime divisors in prescribed classes
connection: Study which prime-factor residue patterns of 4Cp+1 are sufficient to produce a target divisor.
why: Some successes may follow from one or two factors rather than the whole divisor set.
first_step: Enumerate minimal sufficient factor-residue multisets for small moduli.

title: Chebotarev questions for family selection
connection: Ask whether a family-selection condition is a Frobenius condition in a fixed finite extension.
why: If it is, an existing distribution theorem might describe which primes select that family, not automatically all primes.
first_step: For one proposed selector, build the extension and check whether its predicate really depends only on Frobenius.

title: Additive energy of log-residue sets
connection: In a cyclic residue group, take discrete logs of available factor residues and measure additive energy.
why: High energy signals a structured subset-product obstruction that can be described concretely.
first_step: Compute sumset sizes and energies for factor-log sets at moduli with cyclic unit group.

title: Expander-inspired residue walks
connection: Use random walks on residue groups generated by available prime factors to estimate how hard a target class is to reach.
why: A walk model can suggest search strategies even when available factor multiplicities prevent unrestricted walks.
first_step: Compare unrestricted walk mixing with exact bounded-multiplicity divisor reachability.

title: Bohr-set parameter windows
connection: Interpret simultaneous near-integral rational expressions in a parametrization as a finite Bohr-set-like condition.
why: Approximate alignment can identify intervals where exact divisibility is worth testing.
first_step: For two explicit rational coefficient conditions, plot simultaneous fractional-part windows over the parameter range.

title: Discrepancy of admissible parameters
connection: Measure deviation of successful parameter residues from uniformity across intervals.
why: A useful discrepancy bound could turn a dense parameter set into an explicit interval witness.
first_step: For a fixed family, compute interval discrepancy at several cutoffs and distinguish local biases from global drift.

title: CRT covering radius
connection: View simultaneous modular exclusions as a periodic subset of integers and ask about its largest parameter gap.
why: The largest gap directly measures how far an auxiliary search may have to travel.
first_step: For several small modulus sets, enumerate the allowed residues over one period and compute maximum gaps.

title: Vector-valued sieving
connection: Keep several certificate-family weights simultaneously rather than collapsing them into one scalar sieve weight.
why: Different families may respond differently to the same local exclusion.
first_step: Tabulate a vector of local survival indicators for three families modulo the first five primes.

title: Logarithmic weights tuned to rare witnesses
connection: Weight certificates by divisor size or auxiliary complexity to reduce domination by primes with many easy witnesses.
why: A better weight may make sparse cases more visible in moment calculations.
first_step: Compare unweighted counts with reciprocal-divisor and inverse-multiplicity weights on the same prime sample.

title: Arithmetic-progression packets
connection: Search for groups of nearby prime parameters in one progression that share a certificate template with varying integer coefficients.
why: Shared templates might support an induction-like construction or explain coverage bursts.
first_step: For a fixed modulus, collect consecutive primes and fit only symbolically verifiable affine parameter relations.

title: Uniform parameter thresholds
connection: Track how the smallest successful auxiliary cutoff grows separately in each arithmetic stratum.
why: A precise growth target can suggest which analytic estimate would actually be sufficient.
first_step: Compute running maxima of the least successful C and report them against log p and powers of p, with bounded-search caveats.

title: Determinantal matching encodings
connection: Ask whether a restricted certificate family can be encoded as perfect matchings with a nonvanishing determinant witness.
why: A matching formulation could import exact combinatorial certificates, but the encoding must avoid spurious solutions.
first_step: Construct a bipartite compatibility graph for a toy factor-allocation problem and test which matchings yield ES triples.

title: Transversal numbers of failure patterns
connection: Represent each observed failure pattern by the families that repair it and study the minimum hitting set.
why: This extracts complementary mechanisms rather than just ranking individually successful identities.
first_step: Compute a minimum hitting set for a bounded family-prime incidence matrix.

title: Epsilon-net search portfolios
connection: Ask whether a small portfolio can hit every sufficiently large witness set in a specified finite parameter universe.
why: An epsilon-net statement would be a finite search guarantee, not a proof for all primes without uniform hypotheses.
first_step: Define the witness-set universe for a bounded experiment and compare greedy nets with random samples.

title: Proof-producing set cover
connection: Compress a finite verified range into exact identity templates plus a certified set-cover computation.
why: The output remains a finite-range proof, but it makes coverage mechanisms auditable.
first_step: Take 100 primes and export the chosen identities with exact substitution witnesses for each covered prime.

title: Ramsey extraction of parameter patterns
connection: Color small parameter tuples by which certificate mechanism succeeds and look for structured monochromatic configurations.
why: Regular patterns can suggest identities, provided each conjectured identity is checked algebraically.
first_step: Color a bounded parameter grid and search for rectangles whose four corners share a symbolic template.

title: Combinatorial word lines
connection: Encode elementary matrix choices as words and ask whether varying one wildcard block preserves an ES-relevant identity.
why: A combinatorial line could package many related certificates into a single construction.
first_step: Enumerate short matrix words with one repeated wildcard and symbolically compute their coordinate expressions.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Base-digit automata
connection: Track a certificate equation digit by digit with carries in a fixed base.
why: Polynomial equalities admit finite carry descriptions under bounded-width restrictions, yielding concrete restricted models.
first_step: Build a base-two carry checker for bounded denominator triples and minimize its state graph.

title: Regular languages of valid matrix words
connection: Describe congruence-admissible matrix words by a finite automaton and distinguish this from their unbounded integer values.
why: Congruence admissibility is genuinely finite-state, providing a rigorous symbolic skeleton.
first_step: Build an automaton for elementary matrices modulo 8 with accepting states matching one required coordinate condition.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Synchronizing words for congruences
connection: Ask whether a shared suffix of elementary operations sends many residue states into a useful target set.
why: Such a suffix would be a reusable congruence repair mechanism, if allowed moves preserve the needed algebra.
first_step: Enumerate short suffixes in the modular transition system and measure the size of their target preimages.

title: Finite-state rational transducers
connection: Search for digit-wise rules mapping p to candidate denominator digits with bounded carry memory.
why: A successful rule on a well-defined input language could become an explicit infinite family.
first_step: Synthesize a transducer for one already verified congruence family and inspect which extra states are needed to enlarge its domain.

title: Transfer matrices for bounded factor states
connection: Count admissible divisor selections with a transfer matrix whose state records residue and used multiplicities.
why: This exactly computes bounded subset-product counts and exposes repeated local blocks.
first_step: Build a transfer matrix for each prime-power factor and multiply them for one auxiliary integer.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Partitions of the reciprocal mass
connection: Connect ES to restricted partition problems after multiplying by a common denominator L: 4L/p=L/x+L/y+L/z.
why: The summands are divisors of L, so this is an exact three-part divisor partition when p divides L.
first_step: For several small multiples L of p, enumerate three-divisor partitions of 4L/p.

title: Partition reciprocity as a sanity tool
connection: Compare positive and nonnegative lattice-point counts in polyhedral relaxations of denominator constraints.
why: Boundary corrections may identify which apparent certificates are merely zero or infinite-denominator artifacts.
first_step: Construct a simple linearized divisor-allocation polytope and compare interior with closed lattice-point counts.

title: Inside-out polytopes for exclusions
connection: Represent linear positivity regions with forbidden congruence hyperplanes or boundary subspaces in a lifted lattice.
why: This separates the bulk feasible region from thin degeneracies.
first_step: For a small linear family, list forbidden hyperplanes and count remaining lattice points at low dilation.

title: Contingency-table factor allocations
connection: Arrange prime valuations in a table indexed by factors and denominator components, with row totals fixed.
why: This creates a familiar integer-fiber problem for the multiplicative part of certificate construction.
first_step: Enumerate valuation tables for an auxiliary integer with three prime factors and compare their induced congruence outcomes.

title: Sandpile groups as residue containers
connection: Investigate whether cokernels of Laplacians appearing in certificate encodings organize denominator congruences.
why: The finite abelian group retains integral information beyond a real determinant.
first_step: For a candidate graph encoding, compute its Smith normal form and compare invariant factors with certificate moduli.

title: Nonbacktracking certificate walks
connection: Forbid immediate inverse moves in a certificate graph and compare the resulting exploration with unrestricted walks.
why: Avoiding trivial reversals may expose genuine cycles and increase search diversity.
first_step: Enumerate nonbacktracking paths of length at most eight in a small verified transition graph.

title: Random spanning-tree exploration
connection: Sample spanning trees of a finite certificate graph to obtain nonredundant exploration routes.
why: The tree removes cycles while retaining reachability within the sampled component.
first_step: Compare the distinct parameter regions visited by depth-first search and random-tree-guided search under equal budgets.

title: Persistent topology of bounded searches
connection: Filter a point cloud of certificates by height and examine components and cycles as the cutoff grows.
why: Persistent features can suggest missing transformations; they are exploratory descriptors, not arithmetic obstructions.
first_step: For one p, compute only sparse graph-based persistence of certificate shapes at several height thresholds.

title: Rewriting confluence
connection: Orient exact identity transformations and ask whether different reduction paths reach a common normal form.
why: Confluence would make duplicate removal and family comparison mathematically cleaner.
first_step: For a finite rule set, enumerate critical overlaps and check equality by cross multiplication.

title: Scheduling complementary searches
connection: Treat each family as a job with a measurable cost and a prime-dependent success profile.
why: Scheduling can improve exploratory reach without confusing computational efficiency with a proof.
first_step: Compare round-robin, least-cost-first, and residue-conditioned schedules on a held-out prime interval.

title: Tilings that encode reciprocal sums
connection: Represent unit fractions as areas of equal-height rectangles after choosing a common grid.
why: A carefully constrained tiling model may turn divisibility and positivity into visible local conditions.
first_step: For a fixed L divisible by p, draw three rectangles of areas L/x,L/y,L/z summing to 4L/p and record grid restrictions.

title: Spin systems for factor selection
connection: Assign a binary spin to each available prime factor and make the total residue the observable of the selected product.
why: This is an exact finite statistical-mechanics model of divisor selection when multiplicities are tracked.
first_step: For a squarefree auxiliary integer, compute the residue distribution by both spin enumeration and divisor enumeration.

title: Zeros of counting polynomials
connection: Study complex zeros of finite certificate-generating polynomials as descriptors of changes in count structure.
why: Root geometry can distinguish count distributions, but no phase-transition or positivity theorem is assumed.
first_step: Compute roots of low-degree count polynomials and check whether unusual root patterns correlate with sparse witness sets.

title: Replica overlap diagnostics
connection: Take two independently sampled certificates for the same p and measure how many factor choices or denominator components they share.
why: Overlap distributions distinguish a broad witness space from many variants of one mechanism.
first_step: Sample bounded certificates uniformly after deduplication and histogram their factor-overlap sizes.

title: Frustration in congruence loops
connection: Identify cycles of local congruence requirements that cannot all be satisfied within a chosen family.
why: Minimal inconsistent loops may indicate which single condition a new family should replace.
first_step: Extract a minimal unsatisfiable set of congruences from a small failed parameter ansatz.

title: Finite-size scaling as a falsifiable heuristic
connection: Compare rescaled distributions of least witness cost across increasing prime ranges.
why: A scaling collapse could propose a growth law; failure of collapse is also informative.
first_step: Fit the scaling on one prime range and test it on a larger disjoint range with identical search rules.

title: Modular energy landscapes
connection: Define an integer energy from violated congruences and exact residual divisibility, with zero energy reserved for checked certificates.
why: The landscape may reveal useful local moves and traps rather than merely a solver score.
first_step: For a bounded parameter box, enumerate energies and locate local minima under unit-coordinate changes.

title: Parallel tempering across families
connection: Allow searches at different energy scales or in different parametrization charts to exchange states through exact chart maps.
why: Exchanges may overcome family-specific traps if the maps are valid and reversible on their domains.
first_step: For two charts with a known overlap, test state exchanges on bounded rational points before imposing integrality.

title: Quenched versus annealed witness counts
connection: Compare the average logarithm of positive count regularizations with the logarithm of the average count across primes.
why: Their gap measures domination by unusually easy instances and helps diagnose misleading averages.
first_step: Compute both statistics for log(1+N(p)) and log of 1 plus the mean N(p) at fixed cutoffs.

title: Arithmetic spectral outliers
connection: Associate a finite operator with residue transitions and ask whether spectral outliers align with quadratic-character sectors.
why: A character decomposition can make a spectral pattern arithmetically interpretable.
first_step: Diagonalize a small convolution operator by characters and compare its modes with observed success biases.

title: Adiabatic encodings of bounded ES search
connection: Encode a bounded certificate search as a finite polynomial binary optimization problem and inspect its low-energy states.
why: The encoding itself may expose useful constraints regardless of whether quantum optimization is practical.
first_step: Build an exact tiny QUBO with explicit carry ancillas and verify its ground states by exhaustive enumeration.

title: Tensor rank of identity families
connection: Represent coefficients of a bounded-degree ES ansatz as a tensor and seek low-rank structure.
why: Low-rank decompositions can propose separable parameter substitutions that are then checked symbolically.
first_step: Form the coefficient tensor of one cleared ansatz and inspect rank-one or rank-two decompositions over the rationals.

title: Lax-pair discovery as an algebraic search
connection: Ask whether a certificate-preserving transformation admits a matrix conjugation description with invariant characteristic polynomial.
why: A Lax representation would expose conserved quantities, not by itself guarantee positive integer orbits.
first_step: For one verified rational map, search two-by-two matrix entries of low degree satisfying the conjugation equation.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Refactorization and Yang–Baxter leads
connection: Search for different factorizations of the same elementary matrix product that exchange parameter triples.
why: Refactorization produces exact rational transformations whose congruence effects can be examined.
first_step: Solve a three-factor matrix equality in two different orders and check whether the resulting map has an ES-admissible domain.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Modular geodesic coding
connection: Compare continued-fraction certificate words with symbolic codes of geodesic segments on the modular surface.
why: Geometric coding may organize word length and cusp excursions, while the ES condition remains arithmetic.
first_step: Translate several short certificate words into matrices and compute their fixed points and trace types.

title: Skew products coupling size and residue
connection: Track a real size coordinate together with a finite residue state under a certificate-related recurrence.
why: This separates growth from arithmetic admissibility while keeping their interaction explicit.
first_step: Build the skew-product map for a short Euclidean or matrix recurrence and plot admissible returns.

title: Periodic-orbit certificate families
connection: Search for parameter recurrences with periodic residue states and nonperiodic integer growth.
why: A periodic modular pattern can preserve admissibility along an infinite arithmetic orbit.
first_step: For one exact recurrence, enumerate cycles modulo 8 and verify which lifted initial points remain positive integers.

title: Arithmetic cocycles
connection: Record a multiplicative scale factor and a congruence correction along each matrix or continued-fraction move.
why: The cocycle may reveal telescoping products that enforce integrality after a whole word.
first_step: Compute the scale cocycle for three verified moves and search short loops with unit total correction.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Adelic height bookkeeping
connection: Combine real denominator size with p-adic valuation penalties in a single explicitly defined height.
why: A balanced height might reveal a descent invisible to the archimedean maximum alone.
first_step: Define a height on one rational parametrization and calculate its change under two exact transformations.

title: p-adic dynamics of parameter maps
connection: Iterate an exact rational parameter transformation over residue rings and inspect attracting or periodic classes.
why: Stable modular behavior could support iterative congruence repair before real positivity is addressed.
first_step: For a verified map, enumerate its defined orbits modulo 3² and 3³ and compare lifting patterns.

title: Stationary points of certificate cost
connection: Minimize smooth proxies such as log(xyz) on the real ES surface under specified denominator ordering and bounds.
why: Critical points indicate where an integer search should concentrate, not where integer solutions must exist.
first_step: Use Lagrange multipliers for one bounded cost and compare its minimizers with actual small certificates.

title: Transport between neighboring prime surfaces
connection: Map real points on the p surface to nearby points on the p′ surface and measure the exact integer rounding defect.
why: The defect may suggest a correction identity linking nearby instances.
first_step: Scale a known triple by p′/p, round two coordinates, and factor the exact residual for the third.

title: Finite Fourier uncertainty
connection: Relate concentration of a divisor-residue distribution to concentration of its Fourier transform.
why: A distribution supported on too few residues must carry detectable spectral structure in a finite group.
first_step: Compute support and Fourier support for exact small examples and identify the characters responsible for concentration.

title: SAT encodings of bounded denominator search
connection: Encode the cleared ES equation and positivity bounds as a Boolean circuit with explicit carries.
why: A satisfying assignment is an exactly checkable finite witness, and the encoding may expose reusable logical constraints.
first_step: Build a tiny bounded instance for p=13 and compare decoded models with direct enumeration.

title: Quantifier elimination for fixed ansatzes
connection: Use real or Presburger quantifier elimination only on subproblems whose language genuinely fits those methods.
why: Exact parameter-region descriptions could simplify one family without pretending general nonlinear integer arithmetic is decidable.
first_step: Choose a linear-congruence ansatz and eliminate one bounded parameter using a Presburger tool.

title: Syntax-guided parametrizations
connection: Define a grammar of gcd, floor, product, and reciprocal operations and search short candidate certificate programs.
why: A restricted grammar makes discovery auditable and encourages explicit formulas rather than opaque predictions.
first_step: Enumerate expressions of depth at most three and test exact identities on a training set before symbolic checking.

title: Abstract interpretation of parameters
connection: Propagate intervals, congruence classes, and sign information through a candidate denominator program.
why: A sound abstract domain can prove that many inputs produce positive integers without enumerating them.
first_step: Implement transfer rules for addition, multiplication, and exact division on interval-congruence pairs.

title: Modular conflict learning
connection: When a parameter box fails for a provable modular reason, store that reason as a reusable nogood.
why: Learned conflicts can apply across many primes sharing the same local labels.
first_step: Extract one sound modular conflict clause from a failed bounded search and test its reuse on other instances.

title: Independent arithmetic verification
connection: Check generated triples by two algebraically distinct routes: cleared products and reduced rational sums.
why: Independent formulations can catch implementation errors or malformed records.
first_step: Write a small verifier specification and test it against deliberately corrupted triples.

title: Algorithmic simplicity of difficult instances
connection: Compare the shortest known certificate-generating program with the smallest numerical certificate.
why: A huge denominator might still have a simple recurrence description, suggesting a different notion of difficulty.
first_step: For a small set of large-height examples, search short recurrences generating their denominator triples.

title: Levin-style program search
connection: Dovetail candidate certificate programs with budgets depending on program length.
why: This gives a systematic discovery baseline and highlights the cost of the chosen expression language.
