first_step: Enumerate a tiny arithmetic-program language and allocate execution steps by a prefix-code weight.

title: Meet-in-the-middle divisor selection
connection: Split prime-power factors into two groups and match complementary target residues.
why: This is an exact algorithmic alternative to enumerating every divisor when modular inverses are handled correctly.
first_step: Implement the split for unit factors of a small auxiliary integer and handle nonunits in separate valuation strata.

title: Bitset propagation of attainable residues
connection: Represent reachable residues by bitsets and update them under each allowed factor power.
why: Bit-parallel operations can make large bounded surveys cheaper without changing the mathematics.
first_step: Benchmark bitset and set-based reachability for moduli below 1000 using the same factorizations.

title: Modular fingerprints for duplicate detection
connection: Use several modular reductions to cheaply reject unequal symbolic or numerical certificates before exact comparison.
why: Fingerprints accelerate deduplication while exact fallback prevents collisions from becoming false identities.
first_step: Design a hash-plus-exact-check pipeline for canonical denominator triples and rational identity expressions.

title: Straight-line certificates for huge denominators
connection: Store denominators by exact arithmetic programs when their decimal expansions are unwieldy.
why: Compact descriptions can make recurrent or compositional families practical, provided equality is still verified exactly.
first_step: Encode a small recurrence family as straight-line programs and compare evaluation and verification costs.

title: Sparse interpolation of parameter relations
connection: Exploit a small expected monomial support when reconstructing relations among certificate parameters.
why: Sparse reconstruction may discover concise algebraic constraints missed by dense fitting.
first_step: Use a low-degree monomial dictionary on a sample of exact certificates and validate any recovered relation symbolically.

title: Hidden-number-style parameter recovery
connection: Treat partial information about modular products as a lattice recovery problem for an auxiliary parameter.
why: The analogy is meaningful only when the available information matches an explicit hidden-number instance.
first_step: Write a toy recovery problem with exact known high bits and compare its recovered parameters with valid certificates.

title: Smooth-order factorization steering
connection: Choose auxiliary parameters whose likely useful factors have smooth multiplicative-group order, then test a p−1-style factoring strategy.
why: This is a construction-and-search heuristic, not a claim that such factors always exist.
first_step: For C≤100, compare certificate usefulness of factors found cheaply by a small smooth-order budget.

title: Product and remainder trees
connection: Use product trees to test many candidate divisors against many auxiliary values efficiently.
why: This supports broad experiments and may reveal unexpectedly reusable factors.
first_step: Design a memory-bounded remainder-tree pass for a small family of auxiliary values and target divisors.

title: Discrete-log coordinates with multiplicity constraints
connection: Use discrete logs only to linearize residues, retaining the bounded exponent ranges of actual divisors.
why: Solving the unrestricted linear congruence alone would create nonexistent divisors; bounded coefficients are essential.
first_step: Compare bounded and unrestricted exponent solutions in a small cyclic unit group and quantify spurious solutions.

title: Certified prime selection for experiments
connection: Separate primality verification of test inputs from ES witness verification so arithmetic strata remain trustworthy.
why: Misclassified inputs could distort experiments about prime-only behavior.
first_step: Specify a test-data format carrying primality evidence or a reproducible deterministic primality procedure alongside each p.

title: Small-bias parameter schedules
connection: Replace unrestricted random residues with a small explicitly generated sample space and measure which character tests it fools.
why: A derandomized schedule may preserve relevant coverage statistics if the test class is identified.
first_step: Construct a tiny small-bias distribution for a selected finite group and compare its character averages with those of uniform sampling.

title: Memory-bounded parallel parameter search
connection: Split the auxiliary domain into deterministic chunks with no shared giant divisor table.
why: A streaming design enables much broader evidence collection without uncontrolled Cartesian-product allocations.
first_step: Specify chunk sizes, per-worker memory caps, and an exact merge key for a bounded search prototype.

title: Permutation-equivariant certificate models
connection: Train predictors on unordered denominator triples using features invariant under all six coordinate permutations.
why: Respecting exact symmetry can reduce spurious distinctions in learned family structure.
first_step: Compare a symmetric feature model with a raw-coordinate baseline on canonicalized bounded certificates.

title: Learning the next family to try
connection: Predict which exact certificate family should be attempted first from cheap features of p.
why: A learned selector accelerates search without becoming part of the correctness argument.
first_step: Compare a small classifier with a fixed family order using measured total arithmetic operations.

title: Symbolic regression of witness costs
connection: Fit simple formulas for least auxiliary size using arithmetic features rather than raw prime magnitude alone.
why: The goal is a testable growth conjecture or selector, not numerical evidence of universal existence.
first_step: Restrict symbolic regression to a small grammar and validate predictions on a disjoint prime range.

title: Counterfactual feature interventions
connection: Alter one arithmetic feature in synthetic parameter data while holding the exact algebraic model fixed where possible.
why: This helps distinguish genuine mechanisms from correlated labels in observational prime data.
first_step: Within one residue-compatible family, vary a single auxiliary prime factor and measure the resulting target-residue change.

title: Uncertainty-guided experiment allocation
connection: Allocate computation to prime strata where count models disagree rather than only to predicted hardest cases.
why: Disagreement can expose model misspecification and broaden the exploratory dataset.
first_step: Compare two simple count models and search a balanced sample of their largest disagreement cases.

title: Out-of-distribution prime tests
connection: Train only on one range or residue stratum and evaluate on genuinely new arithmetic regimes.
why: This detects selectors that memorize local density patterns rather than generalizable mechanisms.
first_step: Hold out an entire congruence class and a larger magnitude range, reporting both separately.

title: Matched prime pairs
connection: Pair primes with nearly identical cheap arithmetic features but very different least witness costs.
why: Contrasts can isolate information missing from a proposed selector.
first_step: Match on residues modulo a small modulus and several character labels, then inspect auxiliary factorizations of the largest-cost contrasts.

title: Embeddings of matrix words
connection: Learn or hand-design representations that place equivalent or easily transformable matrix words near each other.
why: A useful representation could guide discovery of short exact rewrite sequences.
first_step: Compare embeddings based on modular actions with raw word edit distance on verified equivalent words.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Invariant discovery with counterexamples
connection: Search low-degree expressions constant under verified certificate transformations, rejecting candidates on fresh exact examples.
why: A discovered invariant can organize orbit structure and explain why some moves fail to connect families.
first_step: Solve linear equations for quadratic invariants of one transformation and check survivors symbolically.

title: Semantic retrieval of equivalent equations
connection: Search literature by algebraic shape and alternate terminology rather than only by the phrase Erdős–Straus.
why: Relevant results may use norm equations, reciprocal partitions, or restricted divisor sums under different names.
first_step: Form five precise search queries from the equation (ay−b)(az−b)=b² and inspect the returned definitions.

title: A dictionary of incompatible conventions
connection: Translate denominator ordering, primitive conditions, and sign conventions across candidate papers before comparing results.
why: Apparent contradictions or missed equivalences can come from different definitions.
first_step: Build a one-page convention table for three verified sources once located, including exact theorem hypotheses.

title: Parametric proof objects
connection: Represent an infinite family by a polynomial identity proof plus a separate modular integrality proof.
why: This makes the difference between many tested examples and a genuine family theorem explicit.
first_step: Define a record containing symbolic denominators, domain hypotheses, the identity, and integrality certificates.

title: Property-based arithmetic testing
connection: Generate structured random inputs satisfying a family's hypotheses rather than arbitrary integers.
why: This efficiently catches transcription errors while remaining only a development check.
first_step: Design generators for divisibility-compatible parameters and test the cleared identity and positivity separately.

title: Mutation testing for certificate checkers
connection: Deliberately change signs, residues, denominator values, and domain assumptions to test whether a verifier rejects false claims.
why: A checker that accepts corrupted data cannot support trustworthy experiments.
first_step: Create one mutation per required condition and confirm that each is rejected for a mathematical reason.

title: Engel expansions as intermediate representations
connection: Compare multiplicative-denominator Engel expansions of 4/p with ordinary unit-fraction decompositions and possible regroupings.
why: Nested denominator structure may make some exact merges easier to describe.
first_step: Compute short Engel expansions for small primes and test adjacent-term merges into a single unit fraction.

title: Ostrowski numeration of parameter choices
connection: Use continued-fraction-based numeration to encode auxiliary integers relative to p and a chosen modulus.
why: The digits may align with Euclidean recurrences and make congruence repair more local.
first_step: For one rational rotation, write several successful auxiliary values in Ostrowski coordinates and compare their digit patterns.

title: Primary-source identity genealogy
connection: Trace an elementary ES identity backward through citations to learn which substitutions and failed variants accompanied it.
why: Historical derivations may reveal nearby constructions omitted from modern summaries.
first_step: Choose one commonly reproduced identity, locate its earliest accessible source, and record the original parameter restrictions.

title: Two-term and four-term boundary cases
connection: Compare the rigid two-term equation and more flexible four-term constructions with the three-term target.
why: A controlled bridge might identify the exact extra degree of freedom that must be eliminated.
first_step: Start from an explicit four-term identity and solve the exact condition under which two terms merge to one.

title: Characteristic sensitivity of the numerator
connection: Separate characteristics dividing four from those where four is invertible before importing finite-field analogies.
why: In characteristic two the numerator vanishes, so an unqualified transfer would be mathematically misleading.
first_step: Compare the cleared equation in characteristics 2,3,5 and explicitly label degenerate components.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Separable and inseparable parametrizations
connection: Check whether a function-field construction relies on derivatives or Frobenius powers that have no direct integer analogue.
why: Separating these mechanisms can identify the genuinely transferable algebraic part.
first_step: For a candidate polynomial parametrization, compute its derivative and determine whether its parameter map is separable.

title: Cox-ring-inspired monomial bookkeeping
connection: Ask whether divisor classes on a simple compactification suggest a useful multigrading of parameter monomials.
why: A multigrading can explain which substitutions preserve the equation and boundary conditions.
first_step: For a basic rational surface chart, assign formal divisor degrees to denominator factors and check homogeneity of the cleared relation.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Galois actions on factor-allocation types
connection: Study how algebraic conjugation permutes possible factors in a norm-based parametrization.
why: Invariant allocations may descend to rational or integer expressions that are not obvious in split coordinates.
first_step: For one quadratic-field slice, list conjugate factor assignments and compute their invariant products and traces.

title: Rational curves through known certificates
connection: Use a known rational point as the base of a line or low-degree curve construction on the ES surface.
why: A curve through a witness may generate a new family, with integrality conditions available for explicit calculation.
first_step: Intersect lines through a small known triple with the surface and solve for the remaining intersections.

title: Bad reduction of parametrization charts
connection: Identify primes where a symbolic chart or its inverse loses rank or acquires extra components.
why: Those primes may require a different chart and can explain irregular local behavior.
first_step: Compute Jacobian minors and denominator factors for one chart, then list small primes dividing their fixed coefficients.

title: Theta series of congruence lattices
connection: When a certificate subproblem becomes a positive-definite quadratic representation with residue restrictions, encode its counts by a theta series.
why: Theta coefficients are exact representation counts for that specific subproblem; the reduction must be proved first.
first_step: Find one quadratic slice with explicit congruences and compute its first few representation counts directly.

title: Half-integral-weight correspondence leads
connection: Investigate whether a ternary quadratic certificate slice produces a theta series amenable to half-integral-weight tools.
why: The possible connection is through exact representation counts, not a presumed automorphic proof of ES.
first_step: Identify the quadratic form, verify the theta-series hypotheses, and check whether a Shimura-type correspondence addresses its coefficients.

title: Complex multiplication specializations
connection: Look for special quadratic parameters where norm or theta expressions simplify through extra algebraic symmetry.
why: Special values might yield isolated constructive families rather than uniform coverage.
first_step: Choose a small discriminant, compute the associated norm expressions, and test whether the ES congruences simplify.

title: p-adic variation of modular counts
connection: If a valid modular family of representation counts exists, compare its coefficients as an auxiliary weight or level varies p-adically.
why: Variation may reveal congruence relations useful for selecting a family, not universal nonvanishing by itself.
first_step: Choose one verified modular family and check whether its coefficient congruences fit a known p-adic interpolation framework.

title: p-adic integrals for valuation distributions
connection: Express a local valuation histogram as an integral over residue classes and compare it with direct enumeration.
why: This provides a compact language for how divisibility conditions interact across powers of one prime.
first_step: For one auxiliary polynomial, compute the proportions with valuation 0,1,2 modulo a sufficiently high prime power.

title: Newton polygons for valuation branches
connection: Apply Newton-polygon analysis to a one-variable polynomial arising after fixing auxiliary parameters.
why: The slopes can constrain valuations of possible roots and guide which congruence lifts deserve attention.
first_step: For a quadratic or cubic residual polynomial, draw its Newton polygon at a small prime and compare predicted root valuations with exact examples.

title: Sum–product over residue rings
connection: Explore additive and multiplicative expansion in Z/mZ while stratifying by ideals and zero divisors.
why: Composite moduli are intrinsic to many certificate conditions, so field-only models may omit essential structure.
first_step: For m=12,20,24, compute sumsets and product sets of actual attainable residue sets within each gcd stratum.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Dual certificates for relaxed parameter cones
connection: Use linear-programming duality to explain infeasibility of a specific linear relaxation of an auxiliary family.
why: A short dual identity can suggest which constraint must change, while remaining strictly local to that ansatz.
first_step: For one small infeasible linearized instance, compute a rational Farkas certificate and interpret each multiplier arithmetically.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Backward construction from a desired last step
connection: Start with the final exact integrality or positivity lemma a certificate proof would need, then solve backward for parameter choices satisfying it.
why: Backward search can produce identities that forward enumeration misses, with every reverse step checked algebraically.
first_step: Choose a target congruence for a complementary divisor, substitute it into the residual equation, and solve for one remaining auxiliary parameter.

title: Ising model on the modular-hyperbola graph of N
connection: The modular hyperbola xy ≡ −1 (mod e) restricted to divisors of N ↔ an Ising/Potts model whose ground-state energy is 0 iff the e-slice is non-empty.
why: Ground-state problems on frustrated graphs are where spin-glass theory produces sharp phase diagrams; ES asks for 'no frustration' at every p.
first_step: Build the graph (vertices = divisors of N, edges = pairs with ab⁻¹ ≡ −1 mod e) for a few hundred p, compute frustration index vs log p, look for a universal scaling law.

title: Arcsine law for divisors applied to 4Cp+1
connection: Deshouillers–Dress–Tenenbaum: divisors of a typical n are arcsine-distributed on the log scale ↔ ES needs a divisor of 4Cp+1 in a specific residue class −1 mod 4C, for SOME C.
why: Averaging over C (not over p) is a legitimate thick object at a fixed p; the arcsine law tells where divisors cluster, suggesting which C-range to aim at.
first_step: Search 'arcsine law divisors residue class' and check whether a residue-class-restricted DDT theorem exists (Tenenbaum's work on divisors in APs); then test numerically on 4Cp+1, C ≤ p, for fixed p.

title: Integrable lattice model whose conserved quantity is 4/n − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z
connection: Discrete integrable maps (QRT maps, Painlevé discretizations) preserve rational invariants; ask whether U_n: 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is the level set of a QRT-type invariant whose dynamics move integer points.
why: Markoff-type surfaces have Vieta involutions generating all integer points; U_n is a cubic surface too, and an integrable birational map might generate solutions from a seed.
first_step: Search for birational involutions of the ES surface of the form z ↦ (rational in x,y)/z (Vieta for the quadratic in z after clearing denominators) and test integrality.

title: Percolation threshold on the 'divisor-in-class' bipartite graph across C
connection: Build the bipartite graph with left vertices C ∈ [1,X], right vertices residue classes mod 4C, edge if 4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C. ES(p) is 'some left vertex has its target edge'. Percolation thresholds as X grows ↔ how fast the first winning C appears.
why: The first winning C, C_min(p), is a natural 'order parameter'; its growth law (log p? p^ε?) is what any pointwise proof must beat.
first_step: Compute C_min(p) for all primes p ≤ 10⁷ (cheap), fit distribution; check whether the repo already has this (git grep 'C_min' or 'smallest C').

title: Anderson localization analogy: ES certificate as an extended state
connection: The residue-class constraint f ≡ −p (mod 4cd) with f | p²+4c²d resembles a disordered 1-D hopping problem (random 'potential' from the factorization of p²+4c²d); a solution is a resonant state.
why: Localization theory proves existence of extended/localized states for *all* realizations via Furstenberg/Kotani (deterministic, not average), which is pointwise-in-disorder technology.
first_step: Define the transfer matrix M_c = product over prime factors of p²+4c²d of 2×2 matrices encoding the residue mod 4cd, and compute Lyapunov exponents; see if 'λ = 0 at some c' correlates with ES solutions.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Quantum unique ergodicity of theta functions and the 'theta quotient' form of ES
connection: Repo mentions a theta-quotient reformulation. QUE for theta functions (Marklof, Lindenstrauss) gives equidistribution of their values; positivity of a specific theta quotient at a specific point is a pointwise question.
why: Theta functions have exact functional equations (rigidity) — a candidate for mechanism (R).
first_step: git grep -il 'theta quotient' -- '*.md' to find the repo's statement; then check whether the quotient is a ratio of Jacobi forms whose Fourier coefficients have a sign-rigidity (e.g. Kronecker–Hurwitz class-number formula).

title: Pólya's 'random walk on divisors' and first-passage to the class −1 mod 4C
connection: Model the multiplicative group (ℤ/4C)^× as a Cayley graph generated by the prime factors of 4Cp+1; the subset-product set is the set reachable in ≤ ω steps; ES(p) asks that for some C the walk reaches −1.
why: Reachability in Cayley graphs with few generators is studied in expander/diameter theory (Babai conjecture, Helfgott); diameters of abelian Cayley graphs are explicit.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵, compute for each C ≤ 100 the subgroup generated by prime factors of 4Cp+1 mod 4C and whether −1 lies in it; separate 'subgroup misses −1' from 'subgroup contains −1 but subset-product misses'.

title: Casimir / zeta-regularized interpretation of Σ 1/x+1/y+1/z = 4/n
connection: Unit-fraction sums as 'energies' of a vibrating system; zeta-regularized sums 'Σ 1/k' over a finite subset equal 4/n. Totally wild, but 'Casimir energies as Egyptian fractions' might exist in the physics literature.
why: Pure lead-check; cheap.
first_step: Web search 'Casimir energy Egyptian fraction' and 'unit fractions quantum field'; keep only if a nontrivial identity surfaces.

title: Scattering theory: 4/p as a resonance of the Eisenstein series at a cusp
connection: The Eisenstein series Fourier coefficients involve divisor sums σ_s(n); divisor-type counts restricted to residue classes appear in Eisenstein series for Γ₀(4C). The number of divisors of 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C is a coefficient of an Eisenstein series on Γ₁(4C).
why: Converts the tied-modulus divisor count into a modular-form coefficient; sign/positivity of such coefficients across the level is a studied question (for Eisenstein series, coefficients are explicit character sums).
first_step: Write d_{−1 mod 4C}(4Cp+1) as (1/φ(4C)) Σ_χ χ̄(−1) Σ_{d|4Cp+1} χ(d) and see whether summing over C turns the inner twisted divisor sum into something with a known positive main term (repo's M_BM?).

title: Frenkel–Kontorova / devil's staircase of the 'best C' function
connection: C_min(p) (smallest C with a winning divisor) as a function of p may show a staircase structure with plateaus at values tied to Mordell classes; devil's staircases arise from mode-locking in circle maps.
why: Mode-locking = rational rotation numbers = continued fractions, which is already an ES reformulation (ES₅).
first_step: Plot C_min(p) against p for p ≡ 1 mod 24 up to 10⁷; look for plateau structure and its relation to p mod 840.

title: Dimer / Kasteleyn determinant count of e-slice solutions
connection: Solutions on an e-slice are pairs (a,b) with ab | N and ab⁻¹ ≡ −1 (mod e); this is a perfect-matching-like count in a bipartite graph (a's vs b's) and Kasteleyn's method computes matching counts as Pfaffians.
why: Pfaffian expressions give exact, sometimes positive formulas (e.g. Aztec diamond), unlike sieve bounds.
first_step: Construct the bipartite graph for a few N and check planarity (likely not), then check whether the count has a determinant formula anyway via the group structure (it's a convolution over (ℤ/e)^×).

title: Fluctuation theorem / Jarzynski: average over C of exponential weights gives pointwise-in-p identities
connection: Jarzynski's equality turns an average of exp(−W) into a free-energy difference exactly, for every realization of the system. Analogue: an *exact* identity Σ_C w(C)·(#divisors of 4Cp+1 in class) = known function of p would be a 'fluctuation theorem' for ES.
why: Exact identities for weighted divisor sums over C at fixed p do exist (they are class-number-type formulas: Σ_C d_χ(4Cp+1) relates to L-values); positivity then becomes an L-value statement.
first_step: Search for exact formulas: Σ_{C ≤ X} Σ_{d | 4Cp+1} χ_{4C}(d) in terms of class numbers (Hurwitz–Kronecker type); check FRONTIER §2 M_BM derivation for what identity is used.

title: Topological-insulator-style 'bulk-boundary' invariant: Mordell classes as a bulk, squares as the boundary
connection: The 6 square classes mod 840 are the 'boundary' where polynomial identities fail; a ℤ/2 invariant (Brauer class) separates bulk from boundary. Bulk–boundary correspondence predicts protected 'edge states' — here, solutions that exist for a reason that only works away from squares.
why: Pure analogy, but it gives a design principle: look for mechanisms indexed by a ℤ/2-valued invariant that is nontrivial exactly on non-squares (e.g. a Jacobi symbol (p/m) that is +1 at squares).
first_step: List all ℤ/2 invariants of the form 'Jacobi symbol of p w.r.t. something determined by (C,d)' that are identically +1 when p is a square, and check which the known Type I/II identities use.

title: Schwinger–Dyson / loop equations for the generating function of f(n)
connection: Define F(s) = Σ f(n) n^{−s}. Elsholtz–Tao estimate partial sums; a functional equation or 'loop equation' for F (from the multiplicative structure of the Type I/II divisor conditions) might give analytic continuation and thus pointwise info via a Perron formula with explicit kernels.
why: Repo has anal_dirichlet_series.md; the free-lane twist is to look for an algebraic relation among F and its twists rather than estimates.
first_step: git grep -il 'dirichlet series' BRAINSTORM; then compute F(s) numerically for Re s > 1 and test whether F(s)/ζ(s)³ or F(s)/ζ(s)²L(s,χ₋₄) is 'nice' (bounded, Euler product).

title: Gibbs measure on (C, divisor) pairs and a 'free energy ≥ 0' inequality
connection: Weight each pair (C, d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 mod 4C) by w = C^{−s}; the partition function Z_p(s) for s slightly > 1 converges and ES(p) ⟺ Z_p(s) > 0. Positivity could follow from an identity Z_p(s) = (explicit positive L-value product) + (error) if the error is < main term pointwise.
why: The campaign's M_BM is such a main term; the free-energy framing suggests choosing s to maximise main/error ratio, i.e. a 'temperature' optimisation not previously done.
first_step: Numerically compute Z_p(s) for s ∈ {1.01, 1.1, 1.5, 2} and p ≤ 10⁵; see whether the ratio Z_p(s)/E_C[Z] concentrates better for some s.

title: Chaotic scattering: resonances of 4/n − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z = 0 as a 3-body problem
connection: The equation is the condition for three particles with 'masses' x,y,z to have total 'reduced mass' n/4 — reduced-mass combination 1/μ = Σ 1/m_i. Integer reduced-mass problems may have been posed in recreational physics.
why: Pure lead-check.
first_step: Search 'reduced mass integer unit fractions problem'; drop if nothing.

title: Lyapunov-function approach: a potential Φ(x,y,z;n) that strictly decreases under an explicit integer move until a solution is reached
connection: Many existence proofs (e.g. Fermat descent, Vieta jumping, Zagier's one-sentence proof structure) are 'potential + move'. Design a potential on near-solutions of 4/n and a move that decreases it.
why: If a move with a monotone potential exists on a finite set, termination = existence. The known failure at squares must show up as the move being undefined there.
first_step: Take near-solutions (x,y,z) with |4/n − Σ 1/x_i| minimal and try candidate moves (replace z by the nearest integer making the sum exact, then rebalance); check empirically whether any simple rule reaches a solution for all p ≤ 10⁴.

title: Fisher-information / Cramér–Rao bound on how well p mod M predicts f(p)
connection: Treat f(p) as a signal and residues of p mod various M as features; the mutual information I(f(p); p mod M) measures how much of ES is 'local'. Mordell's classes are the M=840 case.
why: A rigorous statement 'f(p) is asymptotically independent of p mod M for all M' would be a theorem of equidistribution type; conversely strong dependence would point to new identities.
first_step: Compute I(f(p) ≥ k; p mod M) for M | 2⁵·3²·5·7·11·13 and p ≤ 10⁷; list the M with highest information per bit.

title: SAT encoding of 'no certificate up to size B' for a symbolic p (bit-blasted) to search for counterexample shapes
connection: Encode: p prime-ish (or just p ≡ 1 mod 840) and ∀ small certificates fail, as a SAT/SMT instance over bits of p ↔ counterexample search.
why: SAT solvers find structured satisfying assignments quickly; UNSAT for bounded p-size would be a verification certificate; SAT gives adversarial p for testing.
first_step: Encode in Z3/bitwuzla: p 64-bit, p ≡ 1 mod 840, and for all (u,C) ≤ 20, (4uC−1) ∤ p+u; ask for a model; then check those p for full ES.

title: Decidability frontier: ES as a Π₁ sentence of bounded-quantifier arithmetic — is it provable in IΔ₀ + exp?
connection: ES is Π₂ (∀n ∃x,y,z) but with the bound x,y,z ≤ n² (true for ES? solutions can be bounded by n² in Type II forms? check) it is Π₁ with bounded search. Reverse-mathematics / bounded-arithmetic questions: which fragment proves the known partial results (Mordell identities are in IΔ₀; Vaughan's sieve needs exp).
why: Proof-theoretic strength calibration tells what style of argument can possibly work: if ES is provable in IΔ₀+Ω₁ then there is a 'polynomial-size certificate' explanation, which constrains the proof shape.
first_step: Check whether there is always a solution with max(x,y,z) ≤ n² (compute for n ≤ 10⁵; known bounds for Type II give z ≤ ...). Then search 'Erdős–Straus bounded arithmetic' / 'unit fractions IΔ0'.

title: Program synthesis (enumerative/DreamCoder) for a 'solution formula' with branching on residues
connection: Search the space of programs 'if p ≡ r mod M then (x,y,z) = (polynomials in p)' with sqrt/floor allowed (non-polynomial! escaping Mordell–Schinzel) that output a valid ES solution on as many primes as possible.
why: Mordell–Schinzel kills polynomial identities on square classes; identities with floor, gcd, or ⌊√p⌋ are not covered by that theorem and nobody has systematically searched them.
first_step: Define a DSL: polynomials in p, ⌊√p⌋, ⌊p/k⌋, gcd(p+a, b), residue branching; run enumerative search (depth ≤ 6) scoring on primes ≡ 1 mod 840 up to 10⁵; report best coverage.

title: Gradient-boosted classifier for 'p has a solution with C ≤ 10' and inspect feature importances
connection: Train a classifier on arithmetic features of p to predict whether a small-C certificate exists; if accuracy is high, the features used ARE a partial identity; if accuracy ≈ base rate, small-C solvability is 'random' w.r.t. all tested features.
why: Cheap, directly reveals structure or its absence in the bounded-C regime (the covering regime).
first_step: Features: p mod 840·k, Legendre symbols of primes ≤ 50, ω and smallest factors of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ 10; target: exists C ≤ 10 with a winning divisor. Train/test on p ≤ 10⁷.

title: Learned certificates: train a model to output C given p, verify by exact arithmetic (AlphaProof-style)
connection: The solution search is 'find C'; a learned prior on C (given features of p) could shrink the search and, more importantly, expose which C-values are 'predictable'.
why: A predictable C-function would be an identity candidate; non-predictability calibrates against covering-type proofs.
first_step: Train a regressor from p-features to log C_min(p); compare against baseline (median); inspect residuals vs p mod 840.

title: Chevalley–Warning / Ax–Katz over ℤ/p: count solutions of 4xyz ≡ n(xy+yz+zx) mod primes to force integer ones
connection: Chevalley–Warning gives p | #solutions mod p of low-degree systems in many variables; the ES equation mod a prime q ≠ p has q² + O(q) points. Can a divisibility invariant on the *integer* solution count (like Markoff's orbit sizes ≡ 0 mod p) be derived?
why: Chen's Markoff proof used an orbit-size divisibility; an analogue 'f(n) ≡ something mod m' with a nonzero RHS would be a parity-type proof of f(n) ≥ 1.
first_step: Compute f(n) mod 2,3,4,6 for n ≤ 10⁵ and check for any forced congruence (e.g. is f(p) always odd for p ≡ 1 mod 24?). Note symmetry: solutions come in permutation orbits, so count orbits.

title: Proof-assistant mining: formalise the Type I/II divisor equivalence in Lean/mathlib
connection: mathlib has Egyptian fraction basics? (check: `Nat.Egyptian`? probably not). Formalising the reduction ES(p) ⟺ divisor condition would be a modest contribution and forces every hidden assumption into the open.
why: Formalisation has repeatedly exposed gaps and suggested generalisations; also a public Lean statement attracts collaborators.
first_step: Search mathlib for 'egyptian' and 'unit fraction'; search GitHub for 'Erdős–Straus Lean'; draft the statement `∀ p, Prime p → p % 4 = 1 → (∃ x y z, 4*x*y*z = p*(x*y+y*z+z*x)) ↔ ∃ c d f, ...`.

title: Gröbner basis / elimination for the system {Type I condition, Type II condition} as polynomial equations with p symbolic
connection: The Type I/II parametrisations are polynomial identities in (c,d,f,p). Elimination ideals over ℤ[p] could expose hidden relations between simultaneous Type I and Type II solutions of the same p.
why: Relations between the two types (e.g. a Type I solution implies a Type II for a related prime) would be a new 'persistence' tool.
first_step: In Singular/Macaulay2, set up the ideal generated by 4xyz − p(xy+yz+zx) with x = pA, etc., and compute elimination ideals; look for any surprise generator.

title: Ramsey-type unavoidable patterns: among any K consecutive primes ≡ 1 mod 24, must one have a solution with C ≤ 2?
connection: Even if not every prime has a small-C solution, maybe 'small-C solvability' has bounded gaps along primes (van der Waerden-ish). Not ES itself but a sub-statement with a combinatorial flavour.
why: Bounded-gap statements can be proved by covering + pigeonhole; data shows which K is plausible.
first_step: Compute the longest run of consecutive primes ≡ 1 mod 24 up to 10⁸ with no C ≤ 2 (resp. ≤ 5, ≤ 10) solution.

title: Hash-function / pseudorandomness: treat (p ↦ prime factorisation of 4Cp+1) as a PRG and ES as 'PRG never outputs the all-miss pattern'
connection: Cryptographic pseudorandomness would *predict* P(miss) ≈ exp(−c log²p) and that misses happen for some p; ES asserts that they never happen — i.e. the map is detectably non-pseudorandom in the lower tail.
why: Forces a clear statement: either ES's 'never' is a coincidence of the small-count regime (and there IS a counterexample), or there is a structural correlation across C. The question 'which' is the campaign's central dilemma; the crypto framing suggests testing *higher-order correlations* across C.
first_step: Measure pairwise and triple correlations between the events 'C wins' and 'C′ wins' for p ≤ 10⁷; compare to independent model.

title: Smallest-solution growth: is min_{solutions} max(x,y,z) ≤ p^{1+o(1)}?
connection: Bounds on the size of the smallest solution are a different pointwise statement than existence; the exponent governs which algorithmic approaches (Coppersmith bivariate: roots up to N^{1/3}…) could be made *provably* complete.
why: If the smallest solution has max coordinate ≈ p^{3/2} typically, then no 'small roots' method is complete; if ≈ p log p, there's hope for a lattice-based constructive proof.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁷ the smallest max-coordinate solution and fit the growth exponent; check repo for existing data (git grep -i 'smallest solution\|max(x,y,z)').

title: Boolean function analysis: Fourier spectrum of the indicator 'C wins for p' as a function of p mod 4C·something
connection: For fixed C, whether 4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C depends on p via the factorisation of 4Cp+1; its Fourier spectrum over p mod M (M a multiple of 4C) measures 'junta-ness'.
why: A low-degree Fourier concentration for all C would be a covering-ish structure; spectrum spread across high frequencies says the event is genuinely 'global'.
first_step: Compute, for C ≤ 20 and M = lcm(4C, 840), the Fourier spectrum (over ℤ/M) of E_p[win_C(p) | p ≡ r mod M] for p ≤ 10⁷.

title: Zero-knowledge-style 'succinct witness' for ES(p): what is the shortest certificate as a function of p?
connection: A solution (x,y,z) is a 3·log p-bit witness; a (C, divisor) is 2·log p bits; the ES₅ CF form is ~log p + small. The minimal witness length (information-theoretically) across p is a 'compressibility of the certificate'.
why: If a witness of O(log log p) extra bits beyond p exists for every p (i.e. 'which of polylog many templates'), ES is 'almost covered' by a polylog-size list — a different proof shape than existing ones.
first_step: Compute, for p ≤ 10⁷, the minimal index of a winning C in the ordering by C; its log is the witness length; compare growth with log log p.

title: Monte-Carlo tree search over 'proof strategies' for small residue classes (AlphaZero for covering systems)
connection: The search for a covering system of identities is itself a game tree; MCTS/RL has found covering-type constructions in other settings (e.g. Wagner's RL for combinatorial counterexamples). Target: maximal density of primes ≡ 1 mod 840 coverable by degree-≤2 identities with moduli ≤ M.
why: Not a proof, but establishes the best achievable 'partial cover' and whether the uncovered set has structure (squares + ?).
first_step: Reproduce the known cover (Mordell + Salez families) as a baseline; implement the RL search over identity templates; report uncovered density vs M.

title: Compressed sensing / sparse recovery: f(p) as a sparse combination of character sums
connection: Express f(p) (or its Type I part) as Σ_χ c_χ χ(p) over characters of various moduli (it's not periodic, but truncated versions are); sparse recovery finds the dominant characters. Dominant terms = the identities that matter most.
why: Quantifies 'how periodic is f(p)' beyond Mordell's mod 840; a sparse spectrum would suggest a near-covering.
first_step: Fit f(p) − A log²p on p ≤ 10⁷ against characters mod M ≤ 10⁴ with LASSO; list top characters.

title: Error-correcting codes: solution sets as codewords, and ES as 'minimum distance ≥ 1 from the zero word'
connection: Define for each p the binary vector v_p ∈ {0,1}^K with v_p[C] = 1 if C wins. ES(p) for C ≤ K ⟺ v_p ≠ 0. The set {v_p} is a 'code'; its minimum weight (over p) and its dual structure may reveal linear constraints among the C's.
why: Linear constraints among win-events (over F₂) would be exactly the parity invariants that could force a win.
first_step: Compute v_p for K = 64 and p ≤ 10⁶; compute the F₂-rank of the matrix and look for low-weight dual codewords (parity checks).

title: Grover-style amplitude amplification is irrelevant, but the quantum query lower bound technique (adversary method) applies to classical 'how many C must be tried'
connection: Adversary bounds give lower bounds on queries needed to find a winning C against a worst-case p; translated classically: any proof that tries C in a fixed order needs ≥ max C_min(p) cases.
why: Makes precise that a 'list of templates' proof must have unbounded length — reinforcing Mordell–Schinzel from an algorithmic angle, but also showing adaptive proofs are not bound by it.
first_step: Just note it; verify unboundedness of C_min(p) numerically (if C_min were bounded a finite cover would exist — contradiction with Mordell–Schinzel only for polynomial covers; so unbounded C_min is a separate empirical question!). Compute max C_min(p) for p ≤ 10⁸.

title: Lattice attack on 'ES with x fixed to the greedy choice': when does greedy-first-term lead to a two-term remainder?
connection: The Fibonacci–Sylvester greedy picks x = ⌈n/4⌉; the remainder (4x−n)/(nx) with 4x − n ∈ {1,2,3} is a two-term sum iff a divisor condition on nx holds. For 4x − n = 1: 1/(nx) is one unit fraction, so greedy gives 2 terms? No: n ≡ 3 mod 4 case gives 1/(nx) — that's the easy class. For n ≡ 1 mod 4, 4x − n = 3 and 3/(nx) must split into two unit fractions.
why: The hard class p ≡ 1 mod 4 is exactly 'is 3/(p·⌈p/4⌉) a sum of two unit fractions, or else choose a non-greedy x'; the two-term criterion for 3/m is classical (3/m = 1/a + 1/b iff m has a divisor pattern mod 3). Making the 'non-greedy x' choice explicit is the whole game and the lattice view (x free, divisor of p²x² in class) is clean.
first_step: Tabulate for p ≤ 10⁶ the smallest x ≥ ⌈p/4⌉ such that (4x−p)/(px) is a two-term Egyptian fraction; study x − ⌈p/4⌉ distribution (is it O(log p)? polylog?).

title: De Bruijn / universal cycle: does a single 'universal' residue sequence of C's cover all primes up to X with O(log X) entries?
connection: Hitting-set problem: find the smallest set S of C's such that every prime p ≤ X has a winner in S. Its growth |S(X)| in X (constant? log X? X^ε?) is the 'covering dimension' of ES.
why: If |S(X)| = O(log X) with a nice structure (e.g. S = {1,2,3,6,...} products of small primes), a 'nested cover' proof shape emerges.
first_step: Greedy set-cover on the prime–C incidence matrix for p ≤ 10⁷, C ≤ 10⁴; report |S| vs X.

title: Verification scale-up as a lead generator: GPU search for primes with anomalously small f(p)
connection: Adversarial search beyond 10¹⁸ for 'hardest primes' (minimum f(p)/log²p) over structured families (p with many small QNRs, p = m² + small); the hardest ones are the stress tests for any candidate mechanism.
why: Repo has adversarial data; extending it with GPU and a better hardness oracle (Legendre-symbol profiles) is cheap and gives a test suite for proposed proofs.
first_step: Define a hardness proxy from Legendre symbols (p/q) for q ≤ 50 (minimising predicted small-C wins); sample 10⁶ primes near 10²⁰ with worst proxy; count solutions on C ≤ 10⁴.

title: Rhind papyrus 2/n table: did the Egyptian scribes' decomposition rules form a covering system?
connection: The 2/n table decomposes 2/n (odd n ≤ 101) into 2–4 unit fractions by patterns depending on n's factors; scholars (Gillings, Abdulaziz) reconstructed the rules. The structure is a historical 'covering by identities' for numerator 2.
why: Recreational/historical lens; the scribes' choice of 'nice' decompositions (small, even denominators) foreshadows the modern preference for Type I/II; cheap read.
first_step: Read Abdulaziz 'On the Egyptian method of decomposing 2/n into unit fractions' (Historia Math 2008) and note whether any rule there generalises to 4/n with 3 terms.

title: Elsholtz–Tao §'open questions' list — re-audit which are now answered and which lead to ES
connection: ET 2013 list several open problems (lower bounds on f(n) for all n? distribution of Type I vs II; polynomial identities). A decade later, some may be resolved in papers not yet in the repo.
why: Cheap literature update with precise targets.
first_step: Re-read ET §1.3–1.4 'open problems'; for each, search arXiv 2013–2026 (citations of ET via Semantic Scholar) and note status.

title: Pólya–Vinogradov-era people: ask Igor Shparlinski about divisor-restricted modular hyperbola points
connection: Shparlinski has many papers on modular hyperbolas and on divisors in residue classes; the exact ES-shaped question (points on xy ≡ −1 mod e with x,y | N) is in his wheelhouse.
why: People item; cheap; he may know a relevant character-sum bound or a reason it's hopeless.
first_step: Email with the e-slice formulation; ask whether 'hyperbola points with both coordinates dividing a given N' has been studied.

title: Thomas Bloom's unit-fractions Lean library as a base for an 'ES data' formal verification
connection: The Bloom–Mehta Lean project has definitions for unit fraction sums; a formally verified 'ES holds for all n ≤ 10⁶ via these certificates' would be a small but citable deliverable and a test of mathlib infrastructure.
why: Formal verification of computations is now routine; cheap.
first_step: Clone the unit-fractions repo; write a `decide`/`native_decide` based checker for 4/n certificates for n ≤ 10⁴ first.

title: Mordell's chapter 30 'the equation 4/n' — the discarded alternative parametrisations
connection: Mordell lists several families beyond the mod-840 ones and remarks on their limitations; the discarded families may be non-polynomial in disguise.
why: Primary-source check; the campaign cites Mordell via secondary literature.
first_step: Read Mordell ch. 30 fully; transcribe every identity and its residue class; compare with the repo's identity census (git grep -il 'identit' -- 'DISCOVERIES.md').

title: Thue's lemma / Brillhart-style two-squares proof pattern applied to p² + 4c²d
connection: The two-squares theorem's elementary proofs (Thue's lemma: for a² ≡ −1 mod p find small x,y with x ≡ ay mod p) produce a divisor from a square root. Type I needs f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p mod 4cd; i.e. a 'square root of −4c²d' structure.
why: Thue's lemma is the canonical rigidity mechanism (R) that produces a pointwise divisor; the question is whether the congruence f ≡ −p (mod 4cd) can be built into the lattice.
first_step: Fix c,d; the condition is f | p² + 4c²d ⟺ p² ≡ −4c²d (mod f); if −4c²d is a QR mod f, Thue gives a representation f·k = u² + 4c²d v² with small u,v; check whether choosing f ≡ −p (mod 4cd) is compatible with the Thue box.

title: Probabilistic method with alterations on the (c,d) grid: a second-moment bound for the tied-modulus count for an *explicit* subfamily of p
connection: Second-moment (Chebyshev) + alterations proves existence for almost all p; the question is whether for *structured* p (e.g. p = 1 + 24m with m having all small primes as factors) the variance is small enough to prove f(p) ≥ 1 unconditionally.
why: 'Almost all' results can sometimes be upgraded to 'all p in an explicit sparse set', which would be a new infinite case of ES (the campaign says no infinite case is proved! Though Mordell identities cover residue classes… those are infinite sets of n but not of primes? Mordell's identities DO cover infinitely many primes; what is open is only square classes). So the target: an explicit infinite set of primes inside the square classes mod 840.
first_step: Check FRONTIER §5 for what is known about explicit infinite subsets of hard primes; then try: primes p with p ≡ 1 mod 840 and 4p+1 ≡ 0 mod 5 … construct a sub-family where a fixed C wins by a *non-polynomial* reason (e.g. p such that 4p + 1 is 5 × a prime ≡ −1 mod 4? that's a prime-value condition, not a residue class — and indeed gives infinitely many p conditionally on Dickson).

title: Is 'no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C' equivalent to 'all prime factors lie in a −1-free subgroup' when the subset-product set is a subgroup? (structure lemma)
connection: Subset products of the prime factors of N generate a submonoid of (ℤ/4C)^×; since the group is finite, the submonoid is a subgroup H; −1 ∉ H iff N's factors generate a −1-free subgroup. So 'C fails for p' ⟺ the prime factors of 4Cp+1 generate a subgroup of (ℤ/4C)^× not containing −1 — IF the subset-product set (with multiplicities) equals the generated subgroup, which needs enough multiplicity. With multiplicity-1 factors it's only the 'subset products', a subset of H.
why: Clarifying exactly when 'generated subgroup' = 'subset product set' (gate G4 in the repo) matters: if the gap is empirically negligible, the failure condition is a clean Galois condition (all factors split in a certain abelian extension), i.e. ES ⟺ 'for some C, 4Cp+1 has a prime factor inert in a subfield' — a Chebotarev-at-a-point shape.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵, C ≤ 50: compute both (subgroup generated contains −1) and (subset product set contains −1); count disagreements.

title: Linnik's theorem and its 'one prime in an AP' nature as the template for 'one divisor in a class'
connection: Linnik: the least prime in an AP mod q is ≤ q^L. It's a pointwise (for every q) statement with polylog... no, with a *power* of q reservoir. ES's reservoir is the divisors of ONE number — but over C there are infinitely many numbers 4Cp+1. Reframe: is there a 'Linnik for shifted multiples': for every p, some C ≤ p^A has 4Cp+1 with a prime factor ≡ −1 mod 4C?
why: With C up to p^A the reservoir IS power-sized, so Linnik-type methods (zero-density, log-free) might apply — this is a *different* (weaker-looking but still ES-implying) target the repo's B3 critique may not cover, since the certificate count over C ≤ p^A is ≫ p^{A−o(1)}... wait, does C ≤ p^A keep the count polylog? The expected number of winning C ≤ X is ≈ Σ_{C≤X} 1/φ(4C)·(something) ≈ log X·const — still only log. Hmm: that's the campaign's point (B3). But Linnik's problem ALSO has only ~q^L/φ(q)·(1/log) expected primes... no, it has many. Record the count honestly and still try: the *prime-divisor* certificate count over C ≤ p^A.
first_step: Search for literature on 'prime factors in residue classes of a fixed integer' (e.g. 'prime divisors of shifted primes in arithmetic progressions', Moree).

title: Ramanujan's 'highly composite' intuition: do primes p for which 4Cp+1 is highly composite for some small C always have solutions trivially? (converse direction for hard primes)
connection: Hard primes should be those for which 4Cp+1 has few prime factors for all small C — i.e. p such that 4Cp+1 is prime or nearly prime for C = 1..K. 'Prime-producing' primes p (4p+1, 8p+1, 12p+1 all prime) are rare (Hardy–Littlewood) but infinitely many conjecturally; are those the only hard ones?
why: If hardness ⟺ 'all 4Cp+1 are nearly prime' then ES failure needs a 'prime constellation' of unbounded length — impossible by sieve upper bounds! (Any fixed length is fine, but failing at ALL C ≤ K with K → ∞ needs 4Cp+1 ∈ {prime or product of primes ≡ 1 mod 4C...}.) Check whether the 'all nearly prime' heuristic for failure matches data.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁷, correlate C_min(p) with Σ_{C ≤ 10} ω(4Cp+1); check whether large C_min ⟺ small ω's.

title: Rational curves of higher degree on U_n/ℚ(n) with floor/sqrt: 'Puiseux identities'
connection: Mordell–Schinzel kills polynomial identities (rational curves over ℚ(n)) on square classes. But identities over ℚ(√n) (i.e. n = m² and x,y,z polynomials in m) are allowed and exist (the m² case has solutions from m). The question for primes: identities over ℚ(n^{1/k}) are not applicable since p is not a k-th power — but identities over ℚ(√(n+a)) could apply when n+a is a square. A 'union over a' cover? Each a covers a sparse set (n = m² − a), total density 0 — so no, unless a varies with n. Record and drop? Keep as an item: 'Schinzel's theorem for algebraic-function identities'.
why: Clarifies what algebraic-function identities can and cannot do; Schinzel may have covered it.
first_step: Search 'Schinzel identities Erdős–Straus algebraic function of n'; read Schinzel 2000 'On sums of three unit fractions with polynomial denominators'.

title: Carmichael's λ and the group structure of (ℤ/4C)^× : choosing C with (ℤ/4C)^× cyclic of small order to make −1 'easy to hit'
connection: For C = 1: (ℤ/4)^× = {±1}; a single factor ≡ 3 mod 4 suffices. For C = p': (ℤ/4p')^× ≅ ℤ/2 × ℤ/(p'−1). −1 is the unique element of order 2 in the cyclic part… the chance a random subset product hits −1 is ≈ 1/φ(4C) per product, but the number of products is 2^ω. Choosing C with φ(4C) small relative to 2^{ω(4Cp+1)}: C prime-power-ish and 4Cp+1 very composite.
why: Optimising the choice of C-family by group structure is a cheap heuristic refinement; could yield a family of C where the win probability is bounded below (e.g. C with 4C | something).
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶, among winning C ≤ 10⁴, histogram φ(4C)/2^{ω(4Cp+1)}.

title: ES in ℤ/mℤ for all m (local solvability) as a finite-automaton: compute the minimal m where local information already determines 'how many lifts'
connection: Local solvability is trivial (Bright–Loughran), but the *number* of solutions mod m with lifting structure (Hensel) gives a 'local density' σ_m(p); the product over m of σ_m is the singular series. For fixed p, the singular series Π_q σ_q(p) is an explicit function of p's residues; its size vs the actual f(p) is the 'global vs local' gap.
why: Singular-series-to-actual-count ratios are informative; if f(p)/S(p) concentrates, the hard part is the archimedean/size part, not local arithmetic.
first_step: Compute S(p) = Π_{q ≤ 100} σ_q(p) with σ_q = (# solutions mod q)/q² and compare to f(p) for p ≤ 10⁵; regress.

title: Stern–Brocot / Farey neighbours: 4/p's Farey parents and the two-term splitting 4/p = 1/x + (4x−p)/(px)
connection: Farey neighbours a/b, c/d with bc − ad = 1 give 1/(bd) = c/d − a/b; a unit-fraction-friendly structure. Writing 4/p as a sum of unit fractions via Farey-neighbour chains of length 3.
why: The repo has Farey items (bsA_farey_*); the free-lane twist: is there a 'Farey path' interpretation where ES = path of length 3 in the Farey graph from 4/p to 0 with unit-fraction steps? That's close to the CF/ES₅ form; worth making explicit.
first_step: git grep -il farey BRAINSTORM | head; then compute for p ≤ 1000 the Farey-graph distance from 4/p to 0 under 'subtract a unit fraction' moves.

title: Adaptive C-choice using the factorisation of the previous failure: C_{k+1} = a prime factor of 4C_k p + 1
connection: If q | 4Cp+1 then 4qp·(something)... consider C′ = Cq: 4Cqp + 1 ≡ 1 − q·(4Cp) ... hmm; since 4Cp ≡ −1 mod q, 4Cq'p+1 for C' = C·k ≡ 1 − k mod q. Choosing k ≡ 1 mod q gives q | 4C'p+1 again with a different cofactor — a way to 'reuse' a prime factor q and search the cofactor's residue. This builds chains of C sharing factors: a tree search with algebraic guidance.
why: Algebraically guided chains may hit −1 mod 4C' faster than blind enumeration; and chain structure might be provable (like Euclid's algorithm steps).
first_step: Implement the chain rule and measure chain length to success vs C_min for p ≤ 10⁶.

title: C-form as an explicit infinite covering system of residue classes (and it provably does NOT cover all primes)
connection: Fix a ≡ −1 (mod 4C), a | 4Cp+1 ⟺ p ≡ −(4C)^{−1} (mod a). So the c = 1 Type II certificates form the explicit system of classes {−(4C)^{−1} mod a : C ≥ 1, a ≡ −1 mod 4C}; full Type II adds classes {−(4c²d)^{−1} mod a : a ≡ −1 mod 4cd}; Type I adds its own. ES ⟺ the union of these explicit infinite systems covers all primes ≡ 1 mod 24. The c = 1 subsystem alone misses 409, 577, 5569, 9601 (C < 1500 checked).
why: 'Does an explicit infinite set of congruence classes with unbounded moduli cover all primes' is a question with its own tools (Erdős covering theory, density of unions, sieve), and the T1 obstruction says the union misses all odd squares — so the full system is a covering of ℕ ∖ {odd squares} ∖ (sporadics?).
first_step: Compute the density of integers covered by the c=1 classes with a ≤ A as A grows (inclusion–exclusion); then add the (c,d) classes; identify uncovered integers ≤ 10⁶ and compare with odd squares + U(n) sporadics.

title: Gaps between consecutive winning C at fixed p: bounded? polylog?
connection: For fixed p, the set of winning C is infinite (e.g. once one C wins, multiples? no — not obviously closed under multiplication; check). The gap structure of winning C's is a 1-D sequence per p whose 'syndeticity' would be a strong structural fact.
why: If winning C's for each p are syndetic with uniformly bounded gaps (say gap ≤ G for all p ≥ p₀), then 'some C ≤ G wins' — a bounded cover, which Mordell–Schinzel suggests is false for polynomial covers but maybe true as a non-polynomial fact. The data decides.
first_step: Compute winning C ≤ 10⁵ for 100 primes near 10⁶; measure max gap; check closure properties (is C winning ⟹ kC winning for some k's?).

title: Involutions on the certificate set: swapping a ↔ b in 4Cp+1 = ab, and the (x,y,z) permutation symmetry
connection: Each Type II certificate (C, a, b) is unordered in {a,b}; each solution (x,y,z) has S₃ symmetry. Counting orbits rather than solutions might reveal parity structure (f(p) odd?) — Markoff's count mod p came from orbit sizes.
why: Involution-counting is the canonical 'rigidity' existence proof; even the failure analysis (no fixed points ⟹ even count ⟹ no info) is worth stating.
first_step: Define the full certificate set S_p = {(C, a, b)} for p ≤ 10⁴; compute |S_p| mod 2 (expect even) and look for another involution (e.g. (C, a, b) ↦ (C', a', b') via the Type I ↔ Type II relation) with a computable fixed-point set.

title: Higher-order relaxations: (ℤ/4C)^× modulo k-th powers for k = 4, 8 — a tower of linear relaxations
connection: Beyond the F₂ (genus) relaxation, consider the quotient by 4th powers (ℤ/4-modules, with 'Rédei symbols'); the Type-II condition mod 4th powers is a ℤ/4-linear condition. The repo has bsB_redei_oddpart; the tower idea is to see at which level the relaxation becomes 'tight' with the true condition.
why: If the condition becomes tight at a bounded level (e.g. mod 8th powers), ES reduces to a ℤ/8-linear statement about Rédei-type symbols — rigid, computable, and maybe provable via reciprocity laws of higher degree.
first_step: Compute, for p ≤ 10⁴, C ≤ 50: level k at which the 'k-th power relaxation' condition agrees with the true win/fail; histogram.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Theta correspondence / Siegel–Weil: representation numbers of p² by ternary forms as a positivity source
connection: Siegel–Weil gives representation numbers of quadratic forms as Eisenstein series values (positive main terms); ternary forms (3 variables) have local–global failures only at finitely many spinor exceptions. Type I: f·g = p² + 4c²d is a quaternary 'norm form' condition. Is there a ternary form Q with Q(c, …) = p² representation ⟺ a Type I certificate?
why: Representation by ternary forms with 'all large n represented' (Duke–Schulze-Pillot) is a proven pointwise theorem with log-size counts — close to ES's shape! It needs the form to be fixed; ES's 'form' varies with (c,d). Still, a fixed-form subfamily (e.g. d = 1 only) might inherit the theorem.
first_step: Fix d = 1: Type I with d = 1: f | p² + 4c² with f ≡ −p mod 4c. The equation p² + 4c² = fg with congruence — compare with representations of p² by the form x² + 4y² restricted by congruences; check whether Duke–Schulze-Pillot's theorem on 'all large n represented by a ternary form with congruence conditions' applies to some auxiliary ternary form.

title: Eichler–Selberg trace formula: Hurwitz class numbers H(4p − t²) sum to traces of Hecke operators — does an ES count hide in a trace?
connection: Σ_t H(4p − t²) = (traces of T_p on cusp forms) + explicit terms (Eichler–Selberg). ES-type counts involve divisors of p² + 4c²d = discriminant-like quantities −(p² + 4c²d) = disc of forms? For Type I, 4c²d + p² ≡ p² mod 4 ≡ 1 mod 4... hmm, −(p² + 4c²d) ≡ 3 mod 4 is a valid negative discriminant! So Type I involves H(p² + 4c²d)-type class numbers summed over c — resembling Σ_t H(4n − t²) with roles of t and n changed (t ↔ p fixed, n ↔ varying c).
why: If Σ_c H(p² + 4c²d) over c in an AP equals a trace of a Hecke operator at p on some space (via a 'reversed' Eichler–Selberg), then positivity/non-vanishing of traces (Deligne bounds give |tr T_p| ≤ (dim)·2p^{(k−1)/2}; not positivity) — more usefully, the trace formula gives an *exact* identity which might convert a 'divisor in class' count into a modular-form coefficient count.
first_step: Search 'Hurwitz class numbers H(p² + 4m) sum' and 'class number sums over quadratic polynomials'; check Eichler–Selberg with weight/level to see if Σ_m H(p² + 4m) (m in an AP) is a known trace.

title: Search for quartic/higher reciprocity obstructions in ES sub-routes
connection: The Apollonian local-global conjecture failed because of quadratic and quartic reciprocity obstructions removing families like squares times constants. T1 is a quadratic one for Type I/II at odd squares. Test sub-routes ((★), b=1, ES₅, windows) for failure sets along families n = k·m², k·m⁴ and quartic-residue conditions.
why: Finds hidden structured obstructions before they ambush a proof; for ES itself any such family would be a counterexample candidate.
first_step: For each sub-route compute failure rates on n = k m² and n = k m⁴ (k ≤ 50) versus random n of the same size and residue class, and (2/p)₄-type quartic symbols on prime failures.

title: Analytic continuation trick: define F_p(s) = Σ_C C^{−s} · #{d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 (4C)} and study its pole/residue at s = 1
connection: If F_p(s) has a simple pole at s = 1 with residue R(p) > 0 computable from local data, then infinitely many C win (for each p) — ES(p) with a vengeance. The residue would come from the 'main term' of the C-average, which the campaign computes as M_BM. The question is whether F_p(s) continues and whether the residue is provably positive — i.e., whether a *Tauberian* argument works at fixed p.
why: Tauberian arguments at fixed p would be a new shape: the Dirichlet series in C at fixed p is a 'vertical' object (like a Dirichlet series of a shifted-divisor problem Σ τ(4Cp+1)C^{−s}, which DOES continue meromorphically with a pole at s=1 — Estermann/Ingham-type). The residue-class restriction d ≡ −1 (4C) is the new feature.
first_step: Study the simpler series Σ_C τ(4Cp+1)C^{−s} (known: continuation via Estermann's treatment of Σ τ(an+b)n^{−s}); then insert the character condition and see if the continuation survives with an explicit residue.

title: Weighted counts: instead of counting certificates, weight each by a function w(C, a) chosen to make the sum provably positive
connection: Counting with weights w ≥ 0 that vanish on 'hard' regions can make the error term smaller relative to the main term; Selberg-sieve weights (λ_d) are the classical example, and Maynard's multi-dimensional weights broke the bounded-gaps problem. For ES: weight certificates by smoothness of a, by C^{−s}, by Legendre-symbol filters.
why: Weight optimisation is a standard move that changed outcomes in sieve theory; the ES count has never (?) been weighted beyond C^{−s}.
first_step: Define a parametrised weight family (e.g. w = Λ-type weights on C or on a) and numerically compute the ratio (weighted count)/(its p-average) for p ≤ 10⁶; find weights minimising the spread of the ratio (i.e. maximising concentration), then analyse the best one.

title: Design theory: do winning (C, a)-pairs form a block design over residue classes of p mod M?
connection: A covering design covers all k-subsets by blocks; here, blocks = {p mod M : (C, a) wins} for each (C, a); ES = covering of all prime residues. The 'covering number' structure of the block system might have a design-theoretic description (e.g. it's a union of cosets of subgroups of (ℤ/M)^×).
why: Design-theoretic regularity (each residue covered equally often) is exactly the kind of structure a uniform argument needs; irregularity points at hard residues.
first_step: For M = 840, compute for each residue r the number of (C, a) pairs with C ≤ 50 that win for ALL primes ≡ r (i.e. polynomial identities) and for a positive fraction; display as a matrix.

title: Use the finite class group of ℚ(√−d) at Type I: choose d so that the class group is trivial (d ∈ {1,2,3,7,11,19,43,67,163}) and the divisor condition becomes a *splitting* condition
connection: For class number 1 fields, ideals = elements; f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p (mod 4cd) ⟺ p + 2c√−d = α·β in O_d with N(α) = f and a congruence on N(α). For h = 1, α is an actual element, so f = N(α) = s² + d t² (or the appropriate norm form) with a congruence on s² + dt² mod 4cd AND α | p + 2c√−d. This makes Type I at Heegner d's completely explicit in terms of representations of p + 2c√−d's divisors.
why: The nine Heegner discriminants give nine fully explicit sub-problems; Type I failures at all nine simultaneously would be a strong constraint on p; maybe the nine cases 'cover' primes by a non-polynomial reason (e.g., p's splitting pattern in the 9 fields = 9 Legendre symbols ⟹ 2⁹ profiles).
first_step: For each Heegner d and p ≤ 10⁶, compute whether a Type I solution with that d exists (c ≤ 10³); tabulate the 9-bit failure vector; check if any profile has all 9 failing.

title: Does ES hold for the square-like composites m² + 24k with small k? (near-square test)
connection: Odd squares are the obstruction for Type I/II; integers *near* squares in the Legendre-profile sense (QR mod many primes) or in size (m² + small) are the natural 'almost obstruction' test; if f(m² + 24) is systematically small, the obstruction has a 'continuity' which a proof would need to respect.
why: Empirical probe of 'how localised' T1 is.
first_step: Compute f(n) for n = m² + 24k, k = 1..5, m ≤ 10⁴ (n not necessarily prime; use Type I/II counts); compare with random n of the same size.

title: Count of representations with multiplicity: Σ_{solutions} 1 vs Σ_{solutions} 1/(stabiliser) — Siegel-mass-style weighted counts might be more 'modular'
connection: Siegel's mass formula is exact for weighted counts (by 1/|Aut|); for ES, 'automorphisms' are permutations of equal coordinates; weighting by 1/|Stab| makes f(n) a 'mass'. If the mass has an exact formula (e.g. a divisor-sum identity) for some sub-count, that's rigid structure.
why: Checking whether any ES sub-count satisfies an exact identity (like r₂(n) = 4Σ χ₄(d)) is cheap and would be a major structural discovery.
first_step: Compute the Type II mass m_II(n) = Σ 1/|Stab| for n ≤ 10⁴; test multiplicativity, test against OEIS, test linear relations with τ(n), σ(n), r₂(n), h(−4n).

title: Reciprocity-law zoo: Eisenstein reciprocity, Rédei symbols, Hilbert symbols — which one is T1 'really', and do its cousins give conditions at non-squares?
connection: T1 is proved by quadratic reciprocity; but the structure 'square ⟹ all certificates vanish' might be a special case of a reciprocity for a 4-term symbol (Rédei) or a Hilbert-symbol product formula (Π_v (a,b)_v = 1). The product formula is an *exact* global identity — if the ES certificate count mod 2 equals a Hilbert symbol product at some place, that's a parity theorem.
why: Parity theorems from the product formula are the standard rigid mechanism in 2-descent; ES's count mod 2 is unexplored (item on involutions).
first_step: Compute f_II(p) mod 2 and f_I(p) mod 2 for p ≤ 10⁶; test against Hilbert symbols (−1, p)_2, (2, p)_2, (p, −C)_q for small C, q; look for an exact parity formula.

title: Finding/lemma: every C-form certificate divisor a of 4Cp+1 is a quadratic non-residue mod p ((a/p) = −1), and this reproves T1 for the C-form
connection: If a | 4Cp+1 with a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) then 4Cp ≡ −1 (mod a), so (4Cp/a) = (−1/a) = −1 (a ≡ 3 mod 4). Quadratic reciprocity gives (C/a) = +1 for a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) (odd part: (C′/a) = (a/C′)(−1)^{(C′−1)/2} = (−1/C′)(−1)^{(C′−1)/2} = 1; 2-part: a ≡ 7 mod 8 when 8 | a+1 so (2/a) = 1). Hence (p/a) = −1 and, as p ≡ 1 mod 4, (a/p) = −1. Verified for all 1798 certificates with p < 3000, C < 80. For p = m² this is impossible ((a/m²) = +1): T1 in two lines. The cofactor b = (4Cp+1)/a is also a QNR mod p (b ≡ a^{−1} mod p).
why: A necessary condition on certificates that is *not* a residue condition on C alone — it couples a with p. It halves the candidate divisors and suggests the exceptional primes (409, 577, 5569, 9601) may be explained by a further forced symbol. It also makes the C-form a purely 'QNR-divisor' problem: find C with a QNR (mod p) divisor a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) of 4Cp+1.
first_step: Do the same computation for full Type II (f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 mod 4cd, ff′ = 4c²dp+1): is (f/p) forced? (Expect (f/p) = (−d/·)-twisted.) Then for Type I. Then try to use the QNR condition positively: among divisors a ≡ −1 mod 4C of 4Cp+1, QR and QNR mod p should be equidistributed by a Pólya–Vinogradov-type argument over C — i.e. the condition costs a factor 1/2, no more.

title: Meta: a standing 'calibration suite' of hard primes for any proposed mechanism
connection: Fix once a list: adversarial primes (DISPROOF_AVENUES), pseudosquare primes, C-form exceptions (409, 577, 5569, 9601), odd squares (must FAIL for Type I/II mechanisms), U(n) sporadics, near-squares. Every new idea is run on the suite first.
why: Turns the T1 test and the adversarial data into a reusable regression test; 10 minutes per idea instead of a lane.
first_step: Write data/calibration_suite.json with the lists and a script that, given a 'mechanism' function p ↦ certificate-or-None, reports hits/misses per category.

title: Meta: crowd-source via Polymath-style wiki a 'census of all known identities with their residue scope'
connection: Mordell, Salez, Cao–Xu (56 families), repo identity census: there is no unified machine-readable list. A JSON file (family, parameters, residue classes covered, type) enables all covering/complement computations in seconds.
why: Foundational tooling; the Cao–Xu 56 families (unverified) can be machine-verified in the process.
first_step: Parse Cao–Xu 2610.32302's families into JSON; verify each symbolically (sympy) and compute the union of residue classes mod 840·k covered.

title: Experimental: histogram of (c, d) parameter pairs of ALL Type I solutions across primes — is the (c,d) 'mass' concentrated on few d?
connection: If most Type I solutions have d ∈ {1,2,3,5,…} small, then Type I is essentially a handful of imaginary quadratic fields; the per-d problem (class group of ℚ(√−d) fixed) is more rigid.
why: Reduces 'infinitely many (c,d)' to 'finitely many d with c varying' for the bulk of certificates — a dimension reduction for proofs.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶, tabulate the fraction of primes whose FIRST Type I solution has d ≤ 10, and the fraction with ANY d ≤ 10 solution.

title: Experimental: 'second-smallest certificate' statistics — gaps between the first and second winning parameters
connection: If the second certificate typically appears soon after the first (small ratio), solutions cluster; if far, they are 'isolated events'. Clustering suggests a local structure around certificates (a 'neighbourhood rule' generating one from another).
why: Cheap, and a neighbourhood rule would be a dynamical structure.
first_step: Compute (C₂/C₁) for the two smallest winning parameters for p ≤ 10⁶; histogram.

title: Analytic: the C-form expected count Σ_{C ≤ X} E[#{a | 4Cp+1 : a ≡ −1 (4C)}] ≈ Σ_C τ(4Cp+1)/φ(4C) — compare with Type II's Σ_{c,d}
connection: Full Type II has modulus 4cd and N = 4c²dp+1: expected count Σ_{c,d} τ(4c²dp+1)/φ(4cd) — summing over c with fixed d gives an extra log factor (Σ_c 1/φ(4cd) diverges like log). So full Type II has expected count ≍ log p·log²X vs the C-form's log p·log X: the c-parameter is where the extra log in log²p comes from. This explains why the C-form misses some primes (its count is smaller by a log).
why: Quantifies the exceptional-prime phenomenon just observed; and it suggests the (c,d) structure is not decorative: the c-direction provides a *second* log, which is the 'thickness' separating 'almost all' from 'all'? (B3 still says polylog.)
first_step: Compute the expected counts numerically for p ≈ 10⁶ and ranges X ≤ 10³: C-form vs Type II vs Type I; confirm the extra log factor.

title: Puzzle: 'three resistors/three lenses' puzzle submissions to recreational columns (Gardner, Dudeney) — any that is ES in disguise with a slick solution for a sub-case?
connection: Dudeney-style puzzles on 'divide a quantity into three unit-fraction parts' exist; a slick trick for a sub-case (e.g. n ≡ 2 mod 3) might be an identity not in Mordell's list.
why: Low probability, cheap.
first_step: Search 'Dudeney unit fractions three' and 'Gardner Egyptian fractions 4/n'; skim.

title: Poisson–Dirichlet model for the factorisation of 4Cp+1 and subset-product coverage of −1
connection: Large prime factors of a random integer follow the Poisson–Dirichlet(1) law (Billingsley). Combining it with uniform classes of factors in (ℤ/4C)^× gives an exact model probability that no divisor is ≡ −1 (mod 4C).
why: It gives a principled per-level failure probability, which can be aggregated over levels with the correlation structure.
first_step: Simulate PD(1) factorisations with random classes for C ≤ 30; compare P(fail) with empirical per-level failure for 4Cp+1, p < 10⁸.

title: Quadratic divisor problem (DFI): Σ τ(n) τ(n + h) and Σ τ(an + b)… the ES count as a 'twisted divisor sum along a quadratic sequence'
connection: Type I: Σ_c #{f | p² + 4c²d, f ≡ −p (4cd)} is a divisor sum along the quadratic polynomial 4dc² + p² in c, with a residue condition tied to c. Divisor sums along quadratic polynomials (Hooley's Σ τ(n² + 1), and the general theory for Σ τ(f(n)) by Hooley, Bykovskii, and recent work by Browning / Sofos) have asymptotics with power savings — *for the unrestricted sum*.
why: The unrestricted Σ_{c ≤ X} τ(p² + 4c²d) has a known asymptotic (Hooley-type) with explicit dependence on the polynomial's discriminant (−16dp²... depends on p!). Pointwise-in-p control of the error is exactly the uniformity question; the literature's dependence on the coefficients is explicit enough to check.
first_step: Read Hooley 'On the number of divisors of quadratic polynomials' (Acta Math 1963) and extract the uniformity in the polynomial's coefficients; apply to p² + 4dc² with X ≈ p^θ.

title: Experimental: generating-function fitting — is Σ f_II(n) q^n a quasi-modular form up to a small error?
connection: Test numerically whether the q-series of ES counts (or sub-counts) is close to a combination of Eisenstein series E₂, E₄ and theta functions: compute the coefficients, fit by least squares to a basis of modular forms of small weight/level, check residuals.
why: If a sub-count is quasi-modular, its coefficients have asymptotic formulas with explicit error (Deligne/Rankin–Selberg), potentially pointwise; a quick fit is the test.
first_step: Compute f_II(n) for n ≤ 5000; fit to the space spanned by divisor-sum functions σ_k(n), σ_k(n/2), r_k(n); report residual norm.

title: Pure analogy: Erdős's '2^n mod n' and 'p + 2^k' problems vs ES — the 'exponential reservoir' difference
connection: Problems with reservoir 2^k (k ≤ log N: only log N candidates) are like ES (polylog candidates) and remain open (p + 2^k not covering an AP — proved by Erdős via covering congruences!). Erdős's covering construction PROVES failure of 'every odd n is p + 2^k' — a negative result via coverings. For ES, is there a covering-congruence construction showing that some explicit residue class of n has NO solution of a restricted shape (e.g. with max(x,y,z) ≤ n²)? That would be a 'restricted-ES is false' result, calibrating which restrictions are safe.
why: Erdős's covering-congruence method is the standard way to prove 'polylog-reservoir' problems FAIL on an AP; applying it to restricted versions of ES tells which restrictions (bounds on x,y,z; Type I only; d = 1 only) are provably insufficient.
first_step: Try to construct a covering of ℤ by classes n ≡ r_i (mod m_i) such that each class forces 'no Type I solution with d = 1' (via a local obstruction like T1 but for the class); if achievable, 'd = 1 Type I' is provably not a complete mechanism on an AP.

title: Gallagher's larger sieve for the ES exceptional set: exploit that exceptions avoid MANY classes mod each a
connection: Gallagher's larger sieve is efficient when the sifted set avoids most classes mod each prime (ω(q) close to q); ES exceptions avoid only one class per (C, a) — so Gallagher is wrong tool; but for the full Type II family, a given a is a modulus for many (c,d) (all with 4cd | a + 1) with DIFFERENT classes r_{c,d,a} = −(4c²d)^{−1} mod a, so the number of avoided classes mod a is #{(c,d): 4cd | a+1} ≈ τ-many distinct classes (are they distinct? −(4c²d)^{-1} for different (c,d) with the same cd... c²d = c·(cd), so different c with the same cd give different classes). Still ≪ a, so the larger sieve doesn't bite. Record as negative.
why: Closes a door cheaply, and the count of 'distinct avoided classes per modulus a' is itself the key quantity for any sieve bound — tabulate it.
first_step: For a ≤ 10⁴, compute ω(a) = #{distinct classes −(4c²d)^{-1} mod a over (c,d) with 4cd | a+1}; its average order vs a.

title: ML: train a model to predict f(p) from the factorisations of 4Cp+1, C ≤ 20, to measure how much of f is 'explained' by small C
connection: f(p) is a sum over all (c,d); regressing f(p) on small-parameter data tells what fraction of the count (and of the variance) is small-parameter — if ~90%, the problem is 'nearly local' in parameter space.
why: Dimension-reduction evidence; directs effort to small-parameter theory (class groups of small d) if the fraction is high.
first_step: Compute f(p) and the small-parameter sub-count for p ≤ 10⁶; R² of the regression; plot residuals.

title: Analogy with 'every integer is a sum of 3 triangular numbers' (Gauss) — a ternary representation theorem proved via class numbers; ES as a 'ternary' problem whose class-number formula is missing
connection: Gauss's Eureka theorem = r₃(8n+3) > 0 via h(−(8n+3)) > 0 — positivity of a class number! ES's Type I count at fixed d is governed by divisors of p² + 4c²d, i.e. by representations in ℚ(√−d); the analogue of 'h > 0' is the existence of an ideal of norm f in the right ray class — i.e., SURJECTIVITY of the Artin map onto a ray class group, which is Chebotarev-existence again.
why: Clarifies that ES's 'positivity' is of Artin-map-surjectivity type (every ray class contains an ideal dividing a specific (p + 2c√−d)) — a statement about ONE element's factorisation, hence B2; but it suggests looking at the *family over c* as a family of principal ideals (p + 2c√−d) whose ideal factors sweep the ray class group as c varies: do they equidistribute in the ray class group mod 4cd? (The modulus grows with c — a 'tied' equidistribution.)
first_step: For d = 1, p fixed, c ≤ X: compute the ray classes (mod 4c) of the ideal factors of (p + 2ci) in ℤ[i]; test equidistribution across c; identify the class containing the certificate.

title: GRH-conditional ES via effective Chebotarev in Kummer-type families: what does the campaign already know?
connection: FRONTIER §5 lists conditional results (GRH, Dickson, Hypothesis H, SEL).
