Check whether 'ES on GRH' is known to fail for a specific reason (e.g. the conductors grow too fast: effective Chebotarev gives a prime of norm ≤ (log D)² where D ≈ (4cd)^{something}; a certificate needs an ideal of norm f ≤ p² + 4c²d dividing a SPECIFIC element — not a free prime — so Chebotarev doesn't apply directly).
why: Prevents duplicating a known dead end; the 'specific element' obstruction is B2 in Chebotarev clothing — record it, but check whether Hooley's trick (sieve over k with GRH) circumvents the 'specific element' issue since Artin's conjecture also concerns a specific element a.
first_step: Read FRONTIER §5 conditional entries; write a half-page comparing Artin (specific a, free q) vs ES (specific p, free (c,d), but the divisor must divide a specific number) and identify precisely where the Artin method's 'free q' is used.

title: CM elliptic curve reading of prime certificates: q ≡ −1 (mod 4C) ⟺ 4C | #E(F_q) for y² = x³ − x at supersingular q
connection: For E: y² = x³ − x and primes q ≡ 3 (mod 4), #E(F_q) = q + 1, so a prime divisor q of 4Cp+1 is a certificate (q ≡ −1 mod 4C) iff 4C | #E(F_q) ↔ the class gate becomes a statement about group orders of a fixed CM curve modulo divisors of 4Cp+1.
why: Elliptic-curve group orders bring ECM-style 'scalar multiplication mod N' tests and division-field Chebotarev structure; a global point/isogeny argument forcing some prime factor of 4Cp+1 to have 4C | #E(F_q) would be a certificate. Speculative but exact for prime certificates.
first_step: Check the claim for q ≡ 3 mod 4 (supersingular ⟹ #E(F_q) = q+1) and extend to composite certificates d (product of primes in ±1 classes); then test whether computing [4C]·P on E mod N = 4Cp+1 detects certificate primes faster than factoring.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Mersenne-adjacent: ES for primes p = 2^{2k} + 1 (Fermat primes) and p = (2^m + 1)/3, etc., via explicit factorisations of 4Cp+1
connection: Fermat primes F_k = 2^{2^k} + 1 ≡ 1 mod 4 (hard class? F_k mod 840: F_2 = 17, F_3 = 257 ≡ 257, F_4 = 65537 ≡ 65537 − 78·840 = 17; 17 is not a square mod 840 class... fine). For p = 2^{2k}+1: 4Cp + 1 = C·2^{2k+2} + 4C + 1; for C = 2^{2k}: = 2^{4k+2} + 2^{2k+2} + 1 = (2^{2k+1} + 2^{k+1} + 1)(2^{2k+1} − 2^{k+1} + 1)? (Aurifeuillean-type factorisation of 4x⁴ + 1 style: x⁴ + x² + 1 = (x² + x + 1)(x² − x + 1) with x = 2^{k+1}: 2^{4k+4} + 2^{2k+2} + 1 — close but not equal; adjust.) Explore Aurifeuillean factorisations giving divisors in the right class.
why: Aurifeuillean factorisations are rigid algebraic identities for special p (not polynomial in p but polynomial in the exponent base) — a loophole in Mordell–Schinzel for special prime families.
first_step: For p = 2^{2k} + 1 (k ≤ 20, prime or not), test C ∈ {2^j} for Aurifeuillean factorisations of 4Cp+1 and check residues mod 4C; generalise to p = a^{2k} + 1.

title: C = 2 parity escape: if 8p+1 = x² − 2y² then C=2 certificate ⟺ some prime factor ≡ 7 mod 8 — and the number of such factors has a parity formula via the norm from ℚ(√2)
connection: 8p + 1 = N(x + y√2) = x² − 2y²: all prime factors are ≡ ±1 mod 8 (or 2, excluded as 8p+1 odd). The C=2 C-form certificate needs a divisor ≡ 7 mod 8 ⟺ at least one prime factor ≡ 7 mod 8 (since the ≡ 1 ones can't help; and any single ≡ 7 factor is a certificate). Number of ≡ 7 factors (with multiplicity) is even (product ≡ 1 mod 8). So C = 2 wins ⟺ 8p+1 is a norm from ℤ[√2] with NOT all factors ≡ 1 mod 8. Is 8p+1 always a norm from ℤ[√2]? No — need (2/q) = 1 for all q ∥ 8p+1 to odd power... So the C=2 analysis splits: either 8p+1 has a prime factor ≡ 3,5 mod 8 — then that factor is not ≡ −1 mod 8 and doesn't directly certify, but a product of a ≡ 3 and a ≡ 5 factor is ≡ 15 ≡ 7 ✓ certifies! So C = 2 wins iff the prime factors of 8p+1 (mod 8) admit a subset product ≡ 7 — i.e. NOT(all factors ≡ 1) AND NOT(all non-1 factors are in a single class {3} or {5} with... ) — exactly the subset-product condition. Enumerate the failure patterns mod 8.
why: For C ≤ 3 the failure conditions are fully explicit finite patterns on the multiset of prime residues; listing them exactly is the base case for the 'failure taxonomy' and for a potential 'C ≤ K failure ⟹ contradiction' argument.
first_step: For C = 1, 2, 3, 4, 6: list the exact failure patterns on multisets of prime residues mod 4C; compute densities; verify against data.

title: History: the 'Straus' in Erdős–Straus — Ernst Straus's own papers on the problem and on Egyptian fractions; was there an approach he favoured?
connection: Straus (Einstein's assistant, combinatorialist) co-posed the conjecture in 1948; his later work on unit fractions (with Erdős: 'On the irrationality of certain series', and on Egyptian fraction denominators) may contain remarks on 4/n.
why: Primary-source history; cheap; might reveal an abandoned heuristic.
first_step: Search MathSciNet/zbMATH for Straus's papers mentioning 'unit fractions' or '4/n'; read remarks.

title: Guy's 'Unsolved Problems in Number Theory' D11 entry: the exhaustive reference list and the 'related problems' (e.g. 5/n, a/n, Sierpiński) as a lead map
connection: Guy's UPINT D11 lists ES with ~50 references and related variants; a systematic pass over each reference for 'method' rather than 'result' is cheap and might surface forgotten approaches (e.g. Bernstein's 1962 Crelle paper, Yamamoto, Terzi).
why: Standard but possibly skipped by the campaign's literature lanes (which focused on 2024–26 arXiv).
first_step: Open UPINT 3rd ed. D11; for each reference not in LITERATURE_2026.md, note method in one line.

title: QNR condition for full Type II: is (f/p) forced for ff′ = 4c²dp + 1 with f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 (mod 4cd)?
connection: Repeat the C-form derivation: 4c²dp ≡ −1 (mod f) ⟹ (c²dp/f)(−1)... (4c²dp/f) = (dp/f) = (−1/f) = −1 since f ≡ 3 mod 4. And (d/f) by reciprocity with f ≡ −1 mod 4d: (d/f) = +1 (same computation as for C). So (p/f) = −1 again, i.e. (f/p) = −1: every Type II certificate factor is a QNR mod p. Check also Type I: f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p mod 4cd — here p² ≡ −4c²d mod f, so (−d/f) = +1 is forced instead (a condition on f, not on p).
why: Extends the lemma to all of Type II (so T1 for Type II is the same two-line argument), and shows Type I has a DIFFERENT forced symbol ((−d/f) = 1, i.e. f splits in ℚ(√−d)) — the two types have structurally different reciprocity signatures, which may be why both are needed.
first_step: Verify numerically for p < 3000: (f/p) = −1 for all Type II certificates; (−d/f) = 1 for all Type I certificates; then check whether Type I has any forced symbol involving p (e.g. (f/p) given f ≡ −p mod 4cd: (f/p) = (−p mod stuff…) — compute empirically the distribution of (f/p) over Type I certificates).

title: Are the C-form exceptions 409, 577, 5569, 9601 exactly the primes p ≡ 1 mod 24 for which some hidden invariant (e.g. h(−4p) ≡ 0 mod 8, or p = x² + 64y²-type quartic condition) holds?
connection: 577 = 1² + 24², 409 = 3² + 20², 5569 = ? , 9601 = ?: compute p = x² + y² and look at 8 | y or 16 | y (which encode (2/p)_4 and higher 2-power symbols); also class numbers h(−p), h(−4p), h(−8p) and their 2-parts; and whether 2 is a quartic/octic residue mod p.
why: The exceptions are a tiny set; a matching invariant would turn 'finite accidents' into a 'quadratic/quartic obstruction' family (à la HKRS), which — since these primes DO have Type II solutions with c ≥ 2 — would show precisely what the c-parameter buys.
first_step: Compute for all primes ≡ 1 mod 24 below 20000 the invariants (x, y with p = x² + y², v₂(y), h(−4p) mod 16, quartic character of 2, p mod 48/96) and find any invariant that separates the four exceptions from the rest.

title: abc-conjecture consequences: does abc bound the size of the smallest certificate or forbid 'all 4Cp+1 nearly prime for C ≤ K'?
connection: abc gives bounds on smooth/powerful values of polynomials; the 'hard prime' heuristic requires 4Cp+1 to be nearly prime (few factors) for all small C — not an abc-type condition. But abc does bound solutions of, e.g., 4Cp + 1 = a·b with a, b both powerful; not relevant. Mostly a negative: abc is about radicals, ES about residues. Keep as a 5-minute check.
why: Rule out quickly; conditional abc results are popular and someone will ask.
first_step: Write one paragraph: why abc (radical-based) is orthogonal to residue-class divisor conditions; note any exception (e.g. Granville's 'abc ⟹ squarefree values of polynomials' would make 4Cp+1 squarefree often — mild help for the subset-product counting).

title: Tool: use Pari/GP's `factor` with `factorint` flags (ECM) to push the C-form census to p ≤ 10⁷ and C ≤ 10⁴ cheaply; publish the exceptional list to OEIS
connection: The C-form exceptional primes (409, 577, 5569, 9601, …) form a natural integer sequence not (apparently) in OEIS; computing it to 10⁷ and submitting it creates a public hook for others.
why: Community/visibility item with a concrete deliverable; OEIS entries attract exactly the kind of elementary-number-theory attention that could explain the exceptions.
first_step: Run the census (Pari, ~hours); check OEIS for the sequence; draft an OEIS submission with the definition 'primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) with no C ≤ 10⁴ such that 4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C'.

title: Which composites fail the C-form? Test whether C-form exceptions are closed under multiplication by squares or by other exceptions
connection: If n fails the C-form, does n·m² fail? (T1-like scaling: for squares the obstruction is via (a/m²) = 1; for n·m²: (a/nm²) = (a/n) — so the QNR condition reduces to that of n; and 4C·nm² + 1 = ab with a ≡ −1 (4C) — different integer.) Empirically test closure properties of the exceptional set E = {n : no C-form certificate}.
why: Structural properties of E (closure, multiplicativity) constrain any eventual characterisation; e.g. if E ⊇ {odd squares} ∪ {409 m² : m odd}, there are infinite non-square families, changing the 'squares + sporadic' expectation for this sub-conjecture.

title: Upper-bound sieve on simultaneous failure for C ∈ {1, 2}: #{p ≤ x : 4p+1 ∈ S₁ and 8p+1 ∈ S₂} ≪ x/(log x)^{1+1/2+δ₂}
connection: Each extra C with an index-2-type failure set adds 1/2 to the sieve dimension; S₂ (mod 8 patterns) has 'dimension' depending on which residue classes mod 8 are excluded from the subset-product condition (computed via the failure patterns). A K-fold simultaneous Landau sieve with dimension κ_K = Σ_C δ_C and explicit constants.
why: For fixed K this is a theorem-level upper bound; the K → ∞ uniformity gives exceptional-set bounds; and comparing with data at K = 2, 3 is a precise calibration of sieve constants vs reality.
first_step: Compute δ_C (the density exponent of S_C) for C ≤ 6 from the failure patterns; run a Selberg sieve numerically for K = 2 to get the constant; compare with the empirical joint-failure count to 10⁷.

title: Could the C-form exceptional set be 'odd squares ∪ {p : (2/p)… something} ∪ finite' with the exceptions explained by a *quartic* reciprocity law?
connection: HKRS's Apollonian obstructions include quartic ones; the C-form's forced (a/p) = −1 is quadratic. A quartic analogue would be: when p ≡ 1 mod 8 and ... the quartic symbol (a/p)_4 is forced to a value that contradicts (a/p) = −1. For p ≡ 1 mod 8 (577, 5569, 9601 all ≡ 1 mod 8!; 409 ≡ 1 mod 8 too: 409 = 408 + 1 = 8·51 + 1 ✓). All four exceptions are ≡ 1 mod 8 — consistent with a quartic (mod 8-sensitive) obstruction acting on a subset of the p ≡ 1 mod 8 primes. Most primes ≡ 1 mod 8 do have certificates, so the obstruction would need another condition (e.g. 2 is a quartic residue, p = x² + 64y²).
why: Concrete, testable hypothesis class for the exceptions.
first_step: Compute for the four exceptions whether 2 is a quartic residue (p = x² + 64y²?) and whether −1 is an octic residue (p ≡ 1 mod 16?); compare to the frequency of these among non-exceptional primes ≡ 1 mod 8 below 20000.

title: Identity families indexed by other binary forms representing p: p = u² + 2v², u² + 3v², u² − 2v², u² + uv + v²
connection: Every p ≡ 1 mod 24 is simultaneously u² + v², u² + 2v² (p ≡ 1,3 mod 8 ✓), u² + 3v² (p ≡ 1 mod 3 ✓), u² − 2v² (p ≡ ±1 mod 8 ✓), u² + 6v²? (needs p ≡ 1, 7 mod 24 ✓!). Each representation gives 2 parameters; polynomial identities in those parameters are not excluded by Mordell–Schinzel.
why: Multiplies the search space of 'legal' identity classes by the number of forms; the combination 'p = u² + 6v²' is special to the hard class p ≡ 1 mod 24.
first_step: Same Gröbner/ansatz search for each form; for p = u² + 6v² in particular (since 24 | 840 structure).

title: ES for n = t² + 1 and n = 4t² + 1: compute identities and check whether the campaign already knows 'ES holds for all n = t² + 1'
connection: n = t² + 1: 4/(t²+1) — try x = (t²+1)/… hmm t² + 1 ≡ 1,2 mod 4; for t even n ≡ 1 mod 4. Is there a known identity? e.g. 4/(t²+1) = 1/(t²+1)·4; want 1/A + 1/B + 1/C. Note (t² + 1) + t² ... Possibly known in the literature on 'Erdős–Straus for n = polynomial values' (e.g. 'all n of the form k² + 1'?). Search.
why: If identities exist for square-avoiding polynomial families, that's an infinite family of hard-class n (not primes necessarily) — and the proof technique (polynomial in t) shows how T1 is dodged; worth 30 minutes.
first_step: git grep -il 't^2+1\|t² + 1\|k^2+1' -- '*.md'; brute-force search for identities with x, y, z ∈ ℤ[t] of degree ≤ 4 for n = t² + 1, 4t² + 1, t² + t + 1.

title: Physics redux: the C-form as a 1-D 'Ising chain in a field' where the field is the character χ and the spins are prime factors — exact solvability (transfer matrix) of the per-C partition function
connection: #{a | N: a ≡ −1 (4C)} = (1/φ) Σ_χ χ(−1) Π_{q^e ∥ N} (1 + χ(q) + … + χ(q)^e) is literally a sum over 'external fields' χ of a product of single-site partition functions — an exactly solvable (non-interacting) model. ES failure = destructive interference across χ. The physics intuition: non-interacting spins in φ(4C) different fields; the total vanishes iff … This is exactly the structure where 'Lee–Yang' and 'sign problem' intuitions apply: the sum over χ is a sum with signs (χ(−1) = ±1 and complex χ(q)).
why: Just the exact formula in physics clothing; but the 'sign problem' analogy suggests looking at |Σ| vs Σ|·| — the ratio measures cancellation; and the structure 'product of single-site terms' means the count is a *Fourier transform of a product* — a convolution on the group, which is where Kneser/subset-sum structure enters (item on additive combinatorics).
first_step: Compute the cancellation ratio (count)/(Σ_χ |Π|)/φ for failing vs winning (p, C); see whether failures are 'maximal cancellation' events with a recognisable pattern.

title: The 'rich non-norm but −1 ∉ D' gap: does the subset-product set D of a rich 4Cp+1 with factors NOT all in one index-2 subgroup necessarily contain −1? Count counterexamples
connection: D is generated (as a subset-product set with multiplicities) by ω ≥ 6 elements of G = (ℤ/4C)^× not all in any index-2 subgroup (i.e. for every odd χ, some factor has χ(q) ≠ 1). Does D ∋ −1? Certainly ⟨factors⟩ ∋ −1? Not necessarily: factors could lie in an index-4 subgroup missing −1 (not index 2) — e.g. G = ℤ/2 × ℤ/4 with −1 = (0, 2) and factors in {0} × ... hmm (0,2) is in ⟨(0,1)⟩. Take G = (ℤ/2)³ (4C = 24: (ℤ/24)^× ≅ (ℤ/2)³, −1 ↔ some vector v); factors in a 2-dim subspace not containing v: index 2 — covered. In (ℤ/2)³ every proper subgroup missing v is inside an index-2 subgroup missing v (hyperplane avoiding v exists iff v ≠ 0 ✓). For general abelian G and element v of order 2: is every subgroup H ∌ v contained in an index-2 subgroup ∌ v? Yes: G/H is a finite abelian group with v̄ ≠ 0 of order 2; there is a character of G/H nontrivial on v̄ (characters separate points); its kernel is a subgroup of index 2 (if the character has order 2) — the character χ with χ(v̄) ≠ 1 has χ(v̄) = −1 (order-2 element), but χ may have order > 2; then ker χ has index > 2 but χ² ... hmm, need an index-2 subgroup: take χ of G/H with χ(v̄) = −1; the subgroup ker(χ) has index ord(χ), may exceed 2. Alternative: the set of characters trivial on H and nontrivial at v̄ — does it contain an order-2 character? In G/H ≅ ℤ/4 with v̄ = 2: the order-2 character χ(1) = −1 gives χ(2) = 1 — fails! So in ℤ/4, the subgroup H = {0} misses v = 2, but the only index-2 subgroup {0, 2} contains v. So: for G with a cyclic ℤ/4 summand in which −1 is the element 2, there are −1-free subgroups (like {0} or ones generated by elements of odd order) not inside any index-2 −1-free subgroup. (ℤ/4C)^× has such summands when e.g. 5 | C ((ℤ/5)^× ≅ ℤ/4). So the 'index-2' dichotomy is incomplete; the correct statement: factors generate a subgroup H ∌ −1 — any index. The sieve then has dimension 1 − |H|/φ ≥ 1/2 anyway (larger for smaller H) — fine. The gap item stands but with 'all factors in some −1-free subgroup H' instead of index 2.
why: Corrects the previous item's formulation (group-theoretic precision matters for the sieve) and shows the sieve dimension is ≥ 1/2 in all cases — the half-dimensional sieve is the WORST case.
first_step: Enumerate for 4C ≤ 400 the maximal −1-free subgroups of (ℤ/4C)^× and their indices; confirm the worst case is index 2 and the sieve dimension is ≥ 1/2.

title: Analogy: Erdős's 'every n > 1 is a sum of distinct unit fractions with denominators ≤ …' — the greedy/Bleicher–Erdős bounds on the number of terms vs denominators; the 3-term boundary
connection: The theory of representing rationals as sums of k unit fractions with denominators ≤ D (Bleicher–Erdős 'Denominators of Egyptian fractions') gives tradeoffs between k and D; ES is k = 3, D unconstrained; maybe a tradeoff theorem 'k = 3 with D ≤ n² always' is provable with the same tools in a weakened form (e.g., k = 3 for all n outside a set of size ≪ N/(log N)^A — the Vaughan line).
why: Historical method check.
first_step: Read Bleicher–Erdős 1976 'Denominators of Egyptian fractions' II and see the structure of their k-term bounds for a/n.

title: Teaching lens: the cleanest 'why ES is hard' demo is p = 409 — build a one-page explainer and use it to brief new lanes/boards
connection: 409 is small enough to hand-check: every 4C·409 + 1 for C ≤ 10 can be factored by hand, each failure explained; yet 16·409 + 1 = 6545 = 5·7·11·17 has the c=2 Type II certificate 7·935 (7 ≡ 935 ≡ −1 mod 8). It shows the congruence-slack of c ≥ 2 concretely.
why: Improves future lane quality (shared concrete example); near-zero cost.
first_step: Write BRAINSTORM/example_409.md with the table of 4C·409+1, C ≤ 12, factorizations, residues mod 4C, and the c=2 rescue.

title: Is the e-slice form ('∃ e ≡ −p mod 4 with −1 ∈ {ab⁻¹ mod e : ab | N}') the right 'primitive' with no exceptions? Compute its exceptional set vs C-form's
connection: The repo's e-slice form is stated as ⟺ ES(p) (FRONTIER §1), with N = (p+e)/4 (Type II) or (pe+1)/4 (Type I). Unlike the C-form it is claimed equivalent; its one-parameter nature (e) vs the C-form's suggests the e-slice packs (c, d) into e. Verify the equivalence numerically and compute the smallest winning e for the exceptions 409, 577, …
why: Establishes which one-parameter form is exact; informs the 'dimension' items.
first_step: Implement the e-slice test; verify against brute-force ES for p ≤ 3000; report e_min for the four exceptional primes.

title: Finding: 'rich' C-form failures are mostly multiplicity-poverty, not subgroup obstructions (61% vs 39%)
connection: For p < 6000, C < 150: of 4182 failing (p, C) with Ω(4Cp+1) ≥ 5, the prime factors generate a subgroup containing −1 in 2531 cases (61%) — the failure is that no subset product with the available multiplicities equals −1 — and generate a −1-free subgroup in 1651 cases (39%). So even with ≥ 5 prime factors the subset-product set D (|D| ≤ 2^Ω ≤ 32 vs φ(4C) up to ~300) is simply too small to be forced to contain −1.
why: Kills the clean 'rich ⟹ Galois-type failure' dichotomy that would have made a sieve-over-norm-conditions proof sketch viable; shows the binding constraint is |D| ≪ φ(4C) (Davenport-constant regime), i.e. the probabilistic regime starts at very small C. Any pointwise argument must live in the regime C ≤ (log p)^{log 2} where 2^Ω can exceed φ(4C), or must be genuinely probabilistic.
first_step: Redo with distinct-prime count ω and with the threshold |D| ≥ φ(4C): find the fraction of (p, C) where D could in principle cover the group; check whether in THAT regime failures are always subgroup-type (which would restore a dichotomy in the only regime where it matters).

title: Visualisation: Ulam-spiral / Klauber-triangle plot of C-form C_min(p) and Type I d_min(p) to spot quadratic-polynomial alignments
connection: Ulam spirals make polynomial families visible as lines; plotting the certificate parameters (or their absence) on a spiral could reveal that exceptions (409, 577, 5569, 9601, 2521) lie on a quadratic curve.
why: Five exceptions is few, but the plot costs nothing and polynomial alignment would be a strong hint toward a Mordell–Schinzel-compatible structure (identities in t with p = Q(t)).
first_step: Generate the plots for p ≤ 10⁶ with colour = log C_min; eyeball; test the exceptional primes against small quadratics.

title: Sturmian words / Beatty sequences: the set of x with ⌊4x/p⌋ jumps, and the 'three-gap theorem' as a structure on candidate denominators
connection: The first denominator x in 4/p = 1/x + … must satisfy p/4 < x ≤ 3p/4 (for 3 terms); the candidate set and the remainders (4x − p)/(px) are governed by the Beatty-like sequence ⌊4x/p⌋; the three-gap theorem (Steinhaus) describes gap structures of such sequences — possibly organising the 'which x leaves a two-term remainder' question.
why: Structural organisation of the x-search; cheap.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁴, mark the x in (p/4, 3p/4] whose remainder is a two-term Egyptian fraction; study the gap distribution between marked x vs three-gap predictions.

title: Ask on the Lean Zulip (#maths) and Terence Tao's blog whether anyone has tried to formalise ES partial results or has unpublished ES notes
connection: Tao co-authored the key counting paper and writes about Erdős problems; the Zulip community has formalised Egyptian-fraction results (Bloom–Mehta). A short, specific question about the single-integer lower tail (FRONTIER §2) might get a comment from Tao or Bloom.
why: People lever; cheap.
first_step: Post a concise question in Zulip #maths (and as a comment on a relevant blog post) with the exact statement and the C-form exception data.

title: Cellular automaton / tag system: encode the greedy-with-backtracking search for 3-term representations as a CA and study its space-time diagram for structure
connection: Rule-based searches sometimes reveal structure via their space-time diagrams (Wolfram's approach); the ES search tree over (x, y) with the two-term test is such a rule system.
why: Recreational/experimental; cheap; near-zero prior of a breakthrough but a possible visual hint.
first_step: Implement and plot for p ≤ 500; stop if nothing visible.

title: Density of winning C for fixed p: is lim inf_X (1/X)#{C ≤ X : win(p, C)} > 0, and is it a continuous function of p's local data?
connection: The expected win probability per C is ≈ τ(4Cp+1)/φ(4C)-ish which → 0 as C grows… so the natural density of winning C is 0; the right normalisation is log density or weights 1/C. Σ_{C ≤ X} win(p, C)/C ≈ c(p) log X? Then c(p) is 'the ES constant of p' and ES(p) ⟺ c(p) > 0 (plus finite checks). Is c(p) an Euler product in p's local data? Compute.
why: Defines a canonical real invariant c(p) whose positivity is ES(p) with infinitely many certificates; if c(p) has an Euler-product formula (plausible: heuristically it is Σ over C-structures of local densities) then ES(p) would follow from the product's positivity — the local factors are explicit and nonzero... the catch is convergence/rigour (this is M_BM at fixed p). Still, measuring c(p) numerically and fitting an Euler product is cheap.
first_step: For 50 primes, compute Σ_{C ≤ 10⁵} win(p, C)/C vs log X; extract c(p); regress log c(p) on Legendre symbols of small primes.

title: Wythoff/Fibonacci game lens: the pair (a, b) with ab = 4Cp+1, a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4C satisfies (a+1)(b+1) = 4C(p + u + v)…: write the Diophantine system as a lattice-point problem in the (u, v) plane under a hyperbola and count by Dirichlet's hyperbola method
connection: p = 4Cuv − u − v ⟺ (4Cu − 1)(4Cv − 1) = 4Cp + 1: for fixed C, solutions (u, v) are lattice points on a hyperbola; summing over C ≤ X, the total count is a 'hyperbola-method' sum Σ_C #{(u,v)}; Dirichlet's method gives main terms with error terms — standard for Σ_{C} τ(4Cp+1) — but here the hyperbola is in (u, v) with the constraint built in. Just the Type II count in the (u,v) coordinates: Σ_{C ≤ X} #{u ≤ v : (4Cu − 1) | 4Cp+1}.
why: A clean reparametrisation: the C-form ⟺ ∃ u ≥ 1: p + u has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4u). This is the same shape (tied modulus) but with the *additive* shift p + u instead of the multiplicative 4Cp + 1 — i.e., the e-slice form with e = u (N = (p + e)/4-ish). It makes the role of u symmetric with v and shows the C-form is a statement about the divisors of p + 1, p + 2, p + 3, … in classes −1 mod 4, 8, 12, …: 'the shifted primes p + u, u = 1, 2, 3, …, cannot ALL avoid divisors ≡ −1 mod 4u'. Verify and record; this is probably the repo's e-slice form in disguise (seen).
first_step: Verify algebraically and numerically: C-form certificate ⟺ ∃u: (p + u) has a divisor a ≡ −1 (mod 4u) [with the cofactor condition automatically satisfied?]. Then for p = 409: p + u for u ≤ 60000 never has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4u?! Check directly — this gives a very concrete statement about 409: '410, 411, 412, … have no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4, 8, 12, …' — e.g. 410 = 2·5·41: divisors ≡ 3 mod 4: none (5, 41 ≡ 1; 2·5 = 10 ≡ 2; …) ✓; 411 = 3·137: need ≡ 7 mod 8: 3, 137 ≡ 1, 411 ≡ 3 — none ✓; 412 = 4·103: need ≡ 11 mod 12: 103 ≡ 7, 206 ≡ 2, 412 ≡ 4 — none ✓ … So 409 is a prime such that p + u never has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4u. A beautiful concrete puzzle.

title: Information from the literature on 'n + u has a divisor in a residue class mod u-dependent modulus' — search specifically for 'divisors of consecutive integers in prescribed classes' and 'Erdős problem on d | n + k with d ≡ ... mod k'
connection: The shifted reparametrisation suggests searching the Erdős problem corpus (erdosproblems.com has ~1000 problems) for anything about divisors of n + k in classes depending on k.
why: Erdős posed many 'consecutive integers' divisor problems; one may be ES-equivalent or ES-adjacent with known partial results.
first_step: Full-text search erdosproblems.com for 'divisor' + 'consecutive' / 'n+k'; read the hits.

title: Exceptional primes vs the 'u = 1, 2, 3 classical identities': 409 + 1 = 410 = 2·5·41 (all odd factors ≡ 1 mod 4), 411 = 3·137 (3 ≡ 3 mod 8, 137 ≡ 1), 412 = 4·103 … — build the 'residue avoidance table' for p + u, u ≤ 50, for 409 and for a random control
connection: A table showing, for each u, the prime factors of p + u mod 4u and why no subset product is ≡ −1 — the 'forensics' item in the additive form, where it is readable by hand.
why: Hand-readable evidence is the fastest route to a conjecture about the obstruction type.
first_step: Generate the table; look for the pattern (e.g., 'every odd prime factor q of p + u satisfies (q/409) = +1 or q ≡ 1 mod 4u' — a Legendre-symbol coincidence pattern).

title: Heuristic repair: the expected-count heuristic for the C-form must be corrected by the forced QNR condition — only divisors a with (a/p) = −1 count, halving the expectation; and if a second hidden constraint exists it halves again — is 409's zero count explainable by a cascade of such 'free' constraints?
connection: Each forced symbol halves the expected count; the observed 0 for 409 at expected ≈ 52 (or 26 after QNR) would need ~5–6 independent forced constraints. Alternatively, a single structural obstruction. Determine which by finding the forced-symbol set empirically: for all C-form certificates (over many p), tabulate the joint distribution of (a/q) for small q, a mod 16, etc., and see which symbols are forced (always equal) vs free.
why: Systematic discovery of forced constraints on certificates is a well-defined computation and could reveal the complete 'reciprocity signature' of the C-form, of which (a/p) = −1 is the first element.
first_step: Collect ~10⁵ certificates (p ≤ 10⁵, C ≤ 200); for each candidate symbol s(a, p, C) in a list of ~50 (Jacobi symbols, residues mod small powers of 2, Kronecker symbols (a/2), (−1/a), (p/u)...), compute entropy of its distribution; list zero-entropy ones.

title: Meta: hand the C-form/Type I c=1 exceptional-set program to a dedicated lane — it is cheap, concrete, and produces test cases regardless of outcome
connection: The program: (i) census to 10⁶–10⁷ of both one-parameter exceptional sets; (ii) forced-symbol discovery; (iii) obstruction proofs for 409 and 2521; (iv) disjointness conjecture; (v) OEIS + MO publication.
why: Of all items in this lane these have the best ratio of concreteness to novelty; the outcome calibrates the whole 'one-parameter vs two-parameter' question.
first_step: Write a one-page brief for a follow-up lane with the five steps and the scripts to start from.

title: Sierpiński 5/n and Schinzel m/n as a family: uniform-in-m translation
connection: The m/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z conjectures (Schinzel: for n ≥ n₀(m)) share U_n's geometry with 4 replaced by m. T1-type obstructions should exist at m-dependent square classes.
why: A translation that works for all m simultaneously (e.g. a fibration over m) might reveal which part of ES is specific to 4.
first_step: Tabulate, for m = 4..12, the per-residue-class solution counts at primes ≤ 10⁶ and locate the m where the minimum count first hits 0.

title: Tao's 2011 blog post comment thread as a mine of unexplored ideas
connection: Tao's blog post on the Elsholtz–Tao paper drew comments with heuristic and computational ideas ↔ campaign may not have harvested all.
why: Cheap source of community-generated angles that were never followed up.
first_step: Read the comments on terrytao.wordpress.com 2011/07 'On the number of solutions to 4/p = …' and extract each distinct idea into this list.

title: Sylvester's sequence and the extremal 1 = Σ1/x_i problem as a dual
connection: Sylvester's sequence gives extremal denominators in Σ1/x_i = 1 ↔ ES's largest denominator is bounded by p²·(…); extremal structure constrains solution shape.
why: Bounding the largest denominator in any ES solution (Curtiss/Soundararajan-type bounds) restricts the search space and may give a finite-check argument shape.
first_step: Compute max(z)/p² over all ES solutions for primes ≤ 10⁵ and compare to Curtiss-type extremal bounds.

title: Vaughan's proof as a fixed point: re-derive with modern large-sieve inequalities
connection: Vaughan 1970 used the large sieve ↔ modern variants (Iwaniec's bilinear, multiplicative large sieve for sparse moduli, Baier–Zhao for square moduli).
why: Campaign has 3/4 exponent; large sieve for moduli of special form (e.g. 4uB) may give a different exponent shape.
first_step: Check whether a large sieve for moduli in the multiplicative semigroup {4uB} (product moduli) exists in literature (search 'large sieve product moduli').

title: Duke–Schulze-Pillot: large integers represented by ternary forms outside spinor exceptions
connection: Every sufficiently large integer (with bounded divisibility at anisotropic primes) locally represented by a positive ternary form's spinor genus is represented by the form (ineffective); ES reformulations via ternary forms would inherit this.
why: This is the classical tool that converts local solubility into global representability pointwise for large n — exactly ES's shape.
first_step: Search the repo's ternary reformulations (THREE_SQUARES.md, QUATERNION_ES.md) for one where ES(p) ⟸ representation of a p-dependent integer by a FIXED ternary form; record why each fails (moving form/moving modulus).

title: Saturation number of Cayley's cubic (arXiv:1406.6963) as an almost-prime ES variant
connection: Saturation results show points on Cayley's cubic with coordinates having few prime factors ↔ ES coordinates have p-adic constraints.
why: If one can force coordinates with bounded Ω on Cayley's cubic, the ES fibre version with one coordinate p·t might be a sieve-reachable relaxation.
first_step: Read 1406.6963 abstract; ask whether its method yields points with a coordinate in a prescribed class mod p.

title: The 'Egyptian fractions with prime denominators' problem (Erdős–Graham) and ES with prime z
connection: Sums of reciprocals of primes equal to 1/n or rationals ↔ ES solutions where denominators are constrained.
why: Constrained-denominator versions sharpen intuition about which constraints are free.
first_step: Count ES solutions of 4/p where y/p or z/p is prime; check whether always ≥1 to 10⁶ (a strengthening that could fail early).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Rav, Schinzel–Sierpiński polynomial identities (no identity for square classes) as a Galois-theoretic obstruction
connection: Mordell–Schinzel: no polynomial identity solves ES on a residue class containing squares ↔ Galois/monodromy of the solution variety over ℚ(n).
why: The obstruction is 'no rational section'; asking for multi-sections of bounded degree or sections over ℚ(√n) or ℚ(n^{1/k}) is a natural relaxation.
first_step: Search for algebraic (non-polynomial) identities: solutions x(n),y(n),z(n) ∈ ℚ(√n) or ℚ(√(n+c)) that specialise to integers for many n.

title: Ahmadi–Bleicher and 'exceptional set has measure zero' line as an independent history thread
connection: Several 1990s–2000s results counted ES solution sets on average ↔ ET 2013.
why: Cheap literature completeness check; may contain a technique (e.g. Bleicher's construction) the campaign lacks.
first_step: Search MathSciNet/zbMATH for 'Erdős–Straus' 1990–2010 and list techniques per paper.

title: Guy's UPINT D11 bibliography completeness sweep
connection: UPINT D11 lists references on ES and related unit-fraction problems ↔ repo LITERATURE_2026.md.
why: Cross-checking a canonical bibliography against the repo's literature file is cheap and catches missed classics.
first_step: Get UPINT D11 references and diff with LITERATURE_2026.md.

title: Erdős–Graham 'bound on the number of solutions' (Browning–Elsholtz upper bounds) as a structural pressure
connection: Browning–Elsholtz bounded the number of solutions of m/n Egyptian 3-term equations from above ↔ lower bound needed.
why: Upper-bound techniques (divisor bounds on a determinantal parametrisation) give the parametrisation used for lower bounds too.
first_step: Read Browning–Elsholtz 'The number of representations of rationals as a sum of unit fractions' (Illinois J. Math. 2011?) and extract its parametrisation.

title: Moree/Pomerance–Weingartner on m/n exceptions as numerator-uniform calibration
connection: Pomerance–Weingartner study the m/n three-unit-fraction exceptions ↔ ES m=4; their density heuristic for exceptions as m grows.
why: Their exception-generation mechanism (n in specific residue classes making all slices fail) is exactly what ES must avoid; reading why it can't occur for m=4 is a structural lemma target.
first_step: Extract PW's mechanism for exceptions at m=8 (n=131, 241) and test whether a 'virtual' m=4 version exists at some modulus.

title: Hensel-lifting history: 'every n locally' proof as a template audit
connection: Local solubility of ES at every prime is easy ↔ global fails only by non-BM obstruction; history of local-global for cubic surfaces (Swinnerton-Dyer, Colliot-Thélène) applies to rational not integral points.
why: Integral Hasse principle on log K3 / log Fano surfaces is where ES sits; recent work (Harpaz, Wilsch) on integral points of log Fano varieties gives counts on average.
first_step: Check Wilsch's thesis/papers on 'integral points of bounded height on log Fano threefolds' for anything about 1/x+1/y+1/z-type surfaces.

title: Strong approximation failure beyond Brauer–Manin: étale-Brauer / descent obstructions for U_n integral points
connection: BL show BM does not explain all failures of strong approximation for U_n ↔ étale-Brauer or descent obstruction might.
why: A computable finer obstruction set would refine which integral 'adelic' points lift; if it is empty at primes, that would be a structural non-obstruction theorem.
first_step: List finite étale covers of U_n (fundamental group of complement) of small degree and test whether their twists have integral points at failing (★)-primes like 409.

title: Fibration method (Colliot-Thélène–Harpaz–Wittenberg) for integral points on families over A¹_n
connection: The total space {4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx)} ⊂ A⁴ fibred over n ↔ fibration method proves Hasse principle for 'almost all fibres' under Schinzel's hypothesis.
why: A Schinzel-conditional statement 'ES for all n in a set of density 1 among primes with explicit exceptions' via fibration method would be new form even if conditional.
first_step: Check if the fibration method has an integral-points version (Harpaz–Wittenberg 'Zero-cycles…'; 'integral fibration method') applicable to cubic fibres.

title: Mordell–Weil-style descent on the 'pencil' S_{n,k} and specialisation k→0
connection: z52 G2 pencil S_{n,k} ↔ Silverman specialisation theorem for families of varieties over the k-line.
why: Specialisation of Brauer groups/Picard ranks along k may detect whether k=0 is a 'jump' fibre.
first_step: Compute the geometric Picard rank of S_{n,k} for generic k vs k=0 (Magma/Sage) and record jumps.

title: Arithmetic of the singular points: the Cayley cubic's four A1 nodes and local data at n
connection: Integral points near nodes correspond to small denominators ↔ local conditions at nodes might be where p's arithmetic enters.
why: Blow-up at nodes introduces exceptional curves; integral points meeting them encode divisibility by p.
first_step: Locate nodes of the ES projective surface for given n and compute which Type I/II solutions reduce mod p to a node.

title: Appell–Lerch sums: Σ_{u,B≥1} q^{4CuB−u−B} as a Lambert-type series
connection: Σ_{u,B≥1} q^{auB−u−B} = Σ_u q^{−u} q^{(au−1)}/(1−q^{au−1}) is a Lambert/Appell–Lerch series ↔ R(p) is the q^p coefficient of Σ_C of these.
why: Lambert series coefficients are divisor sums; Appell–Lerch sums have modular completions which yield exact formulas for coefficients in some cases.
first_step: Compute the series F(q) = Σ_{C≥1} Σ_{u≥1} q^{4Cu−u−1}/(1−q^{4Cu−1})-type expansion and check against R(n) to 10⁴.

title: Weight-1 forms and Kronecker characters: M_BM as a sum of class numbers
connection: M_BM(p) = Σ (1 − χ_{−4uB}(p))/φ(4uB) is an average of characters ↔ L(1,χ) and class numbers of ℚ(√−uB·p)?
why: Swapping sum order may give M_BM(p) as a weighted sum of L-values attached to p; class-number lower bounds (Siegel, Goldfeld) are pointwise.
first_step: Rewrite T(p) = Σ (−uB/p)/φ(4uB) by grouping by m = uB: Σ_m (−m/p)·g(m) with g(m) = #{splittings}/φ(4m); compare with L(1, (−·/p))-weighted sums.

title: Real quadratic fields ℚ(√p): fundamental unit, continued fraction of √p and ES
connection: ES₅ uses continued-fraction length ≤ 3 of something tied to p ↔ the CF of √p (period, palindromes) encodes ℚ(√p) arithmetic.
why: If certificate CFs relate to the CF expansion of √p or (√p+1)/2, the infinite unit group could be a thick reservoir.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵, compare the period of √p with the structure of the smallest ES₅ certificate words.

title: Toric degenerations and Ehrhart counting of ES solutions in boxes
connection: Counting lattice points in polytopes defined by Type II inequalities ↔ Ehrhart quasi-polynomials.
why: The (★) count over a cut-off region is a lattice-point count in a hyperbolic region; Ehrhart theory with dilation p might give exact periodic formulas for partial counts.
first_step: Restrict to u ≤ U, B ≤ V and count solutions mod 4uB to p as function of p; check if it's a quasi-polynomial in p of bounded period.

title: Olson's theorem / Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv for products of divisors
connection: EGZ-type results guarantee subproducts in a coset ↔ ES gate: divisors of N in class −1 mod 4C.
why: Covering targets in multiplicative groups by subproducts is a mature field; ES's issue is target specificity (−1, not identity).
first_step: Restate ES gate as: −1 ∈ Σ*(S) where S = multiset of prime factors of 4Cp+1 in (ℤ/4C)^×; tabulate how often Σ*(S) is the whole group.

title: Rudnev point–plane incidences / Stevens–de Zeeuw in 𝔽_p for modular hyperbola data
connection: Rudnev's point-plane bound and Stevens–de Zeeuw point-line bounds over 𝔽_p give incidence counts beyond trivial; ES Type II solutions are points on modular hyperbolas ff′ ≡ 1 in boxes.
why: Incidence bounds control how many hyperbola points can concentrate, useful for second moments of R(p).
first_step: Count Type II certificate points as incidences between a point set {(f,f′)} and a family of hyperbolas indexed by (c,d) mod p; apply Stevens–de Zeeuw.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Combinatorial Nullstellensatz: ES certificate as nonvanishing of a coefficient
connection: Alon's CN: if a monomial coefficient is nonzero, a nonvanishing point exists in a grid ↔ ES certificates as a grid point avoiding a hypersurface.
why: Repo lists Alon CN in deep-lane catalogue; a specific construction with explicit coefficient computation is the missing piece.

title: Motivic / Grothendieck ring class of the certificate variety
connection: Class of {4uBC − u − B = n} in K₀(Var) ↔ point counts over all finite fields at once.
why: Cheap structural fact; might show the certificate variety is stably rational, giving parametrisations.
first_step: Compute: for fixed n, the variety 4uBC − u − B = n is a smooth affine threefold; determine its class and rationality (solve for C when 4uB ≠ 0: rational).

title: Apollonian packings: Ford circles of 4/p and three tangent circles
connection: Descartes curvatures and Egyptian fractions: Ford circles at a/b have curvature 2b² ↔ 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z as a curvature relation?
why: Apollonian local-global (with reciprocity obstructions, HKRS) is the closest 'thin orbit' analogue; a literal geometric embedding of ES into a circle packing would let one import RS/HKRS results.
first_step: Search for a circle configuration whose curvatures are (x,y,z,p) related by 1/x+1/y+1/z = 4/p (inversion of Descartes-type relations).

title: Farey graph geodesics and ES as a 'triangle' in the Farey tessellation
connection: 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/p ↔ mediants/Farey neighbours: Egyptian splitting a/b = 1/x + c/d occurs along Farey edges.
why: Hyperbolic geometry of the Farey graph might turn ES into a bounded-length path existence between two cusps — geometric group theory tools (Gromov hyperbolicity) apply.
first_step: Express each ES solution as a path in the Farey graph from 4/p to 0 and record lengths/turn sequences for p ≤ 10⁴.

title: Thue's lemma / pigeonhole for x ≡ ay mod p with small x, y and ES
connection: Thue: for any a there exist |x|,|y| ≤ √p with x ≡ ay (mod p) ↔ ES Type II pair form p ≡ −(u+B) mod 4uB.
why: Thue is the prototypical pointwise size-squeeze; Fermat two squares follows. Is there a Thue-type statement with a modulus depending on the variables?
first_step: Search for a fixed modulus M(p) and a residue a(p) such that a small solution of x ≡ a·y mod M yields an ES certificate; test numerically for p ≤ 10⁴.

title: Non-congruence classes: polynomial identities valid on Chebotarev classes of non-abelian fields (e.g. 2 a quartic residue)
connection: Mordell–Schinzel rule out polynomial identities on square classes (congruence classes). Classes like 'p = x² + 64y²' (2 is a quartic residue) are Chebotarev classes of non-abelian fields and are not unions of congruence classes, so identities with p-dependent algebraic parameters (e.g. involving x, y with p = x² + 64y²) could cover them.
why: The repo has NONCONG_LIFTS. Native class-field-theory classes give an infinite supply of new 'families' whose parameters are norms (x,y), sidestepping the congruence-class formulation of B1.
first_step: Search for ES identities in parameters (x, y) with p = x² + y² (or x² + 64y²) of bounded degree, e.g. x = f(a,b) with p = a² + b², by polynomial ansatz + solve; test coverage of the hard class.

title: Elliptic curve E_n: y² = x³ + … attached to 4/n and its rank
connection: Repo has 'ec' data; 1/x+1/y+1/z = 4/n with a fixed ratio gives elliptic curves ↔ positivity of rank / torsion structure.
why: If some explicit elliptic curve over ℚ attached to p has a rational point that yields a certificate whenever its rank ≥ 1, BSD-parity (root number) could force existence for half the primes.
first_step: Inspect data/ec in repo; check whether root number of the associated curve correlates with certificate existence at small size.

title: Heegner points: an algebraic point forced to exist for each p
connection: Heegner points on X₀(N) exist for every imaginary quadratic field satisfying Heegner hypothesis ↔ ES certificate = a forced algebraic object at p.
why: Heegner points exist pointwise by construction (CM theory); they are the archetype of R-type existence. Mapping one to an integer solution would need a 'positivity' extraction.
first_step: Ask: does the CM point of discriminant −4p (or −p) on X₀(4) have any coordinate whose norm relates to 4Cp+1-type integers?

title: Lucas-sequence primitive divisors (Bilu–Hanrot–Voutier) as a source of prime divisors ≡ −1 (mod m)
connection: Primitive prime divisors q of U_m(P,Q) satisfy q ≡ (D/q) (mod m), so q ≡ −1 (mod m) when (D/q) = −1. ES Type II needs a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4C) of 4Cp+1. If 4Cp+1 shares a primitive divisor with a suitable U_{4C}, the certificate follows.
why: BHV give existence of primitive divisors for all m > 30, a pointwise rigidity theorem. The question is whether p-dependent Lucas sequences can be tied to 4Cp+1.
first_step: Find a Lucas sequence u_m(p) with index m ~ 4C such that p-tied integers 4Cp+1 contain u_m's primitive divisor; test small cases.

title: Bunyakovsky/Schinzel H ⟹ infinitely many ES-hard-for-small-menu primes (sanity: unconditional disproof shapes)
connection: Under Schinzel H, for any finite menu of certificate types there are infinitely many p evading it ↔ B1 barrier.
why: This is known (B1). Including as calibration of any proposed proof: it must use an unbounded menu.
first_step: Already in repo (B1); first step: check that every item in this list proposes an unbounded menu or flags otherwise.

title: Siegel's lemma with congruence conditions: a small solution of a linear system tied to p
connection: Siegel's lemma guarantees small integer solutions of underdetermined linear systems ↔ ES Type II linear in C for fixed (u,B).
why: For fixed u, the condition (4uC−1) | p+u is linear in a hidden quotient: p + u = k(4uC − 1); i.e. p = 4uCk − u − k: symmetric bilinear in (C,k)! Siegel can't force bilinear, but the structure is a 'multiplicative Siegel lemma'.
first_step: Note p + u + k = 4uCk: for fixed u, need p ≡ −u − k mod 4uk with C integer. Tabulate minimal u per p and the 'free' parameter k distribution.

title: Random energy model (Derrida) as null model for certificate counts
connection: REM: 2^N independent energies; ground-state statistics ↔ R(p) as count of ≍ p log p rare independent-ish events with polylog mean.
why: REM predicts Poisson zero probability exp(−mean); calibrating ES's zero probability against REM vs correlated models (GREM) quantifies 'how independent' the events are.
first_step: Fit the empirical distribution of R(p)/M(p) over primes ≤ 10⁸ to Poisson vs negative-binomial vs log-normal; report best-fit dispersion.

title: Lee–Yang / stability-preserver view of the window generating polynomial
connection: Lee–Yang (zeros on the unit circle for every ferromagnetic Ising model) and Borcea–Brändén stability preservers prove non-vanishing for every instance via polynomial stability. The window certificate count is a coefficient of Π_i (Σ_{|j|≤a_i} x^{j·g_i}) in the group ring; ask whether a multivariate stable polynomial encodes certificate existence so that stability forces a nonzero coefficient.
why: Stability/interlacing proved 'every instance' theorems where probabilistic arguments only gave typical instances.
first_step: Construct P_p(z) = Σ_{(u,B,C) certificate} z^{u+B+C} for small p and plot zeros; look for regularities.

title: Spectral form factor / pair correlation of 'certificate moduli' 4uC−1 dividing p+u
connection: Quantum chaos tools on number-theoretic sequences ↔ distribution of the set of successful (u,C) per p.
why: Clustering/repulsion of certificates would indicate dependencies affecting zero probability.
first_step: For each p compute the set of successful (u,C); measure nearest-neighbour spacing distribution in log-scale over p ≤ 10⁶.

title: Kinetic/flow interpretation: Euclid algorithm as a dynamical system and ES as short-orbit condition
connection: Gauss map dynamics on rationals ↔ ES₅ continued fraction length ≤ 3 for a p-tied rational.
why: Hensley/Baladi–Vallée transfer operators give distribution of CF lengths of rationals with denominator p; ES asks for one rational in a family with short length.
first_step: Use Baladi–Vallée style counting: number of a/p with CF length ≤ 3 and partial quotient constraints; compare with ES₅ counts.

title: Vieta jumping on the ES surface: z appears linearly, but 4xyz − nxy − nxz − nyz is bilinear in (y,z)
connection: Vieta jumping needs quadratic in one variable; ES is bilinear ↔ after substitution (e.g. y = x + s) a quadratic may appear.
why: Vieta jumping solved IMO 1988/6 (a²+b²)/(ab+1) pointwise via descent; an ES descent would be an R-type extraction.
first_step: Try substitutions y = x + s, z = x + t and look for an equation quadratic in x with integral Vieta partner.

title: Free probability / random multiplicative functions: replace (·/p) by random ±1 multiplicative f
connection: Random multiplicative function models (Harper) ↔ T(p) with Legendre symbol replaced by Steinhaus/Rademacher multiplicative f.
why: Harper's 'better than square-root cancellation' for random multiplicative sums suggests T(p) behaves better than worst case; quantifies M_BM lower bound tightness.
first_step: Simulate T_f = Σ f(u)f(B)·(−1-twist)/φ(4uB) for random multiplicative f and compare distribution to empirical T(p).

title: Entropy/information-theoretic view: bits of p needed to specify a certificate
connection: A certificate (u,B,C) has ~3 log log p bits beyond p ↔ information about p revealed by existence of a certificate.
why: If certificate existence for p were 'hard information', compression arguments (Kolmogorov) could say something; at least clarifies that certificates are tiny relative to p.
first_step: Compute the empirical entropy of the minimal certificate (u,C) distribution conditioned on p mod small moduli; does p mod 840·k predict it?

title: Ergodic theory of multiplicative semigroups: Furstenberg ×2×3 and certificates as orbit points
connection: Furstenberg's ×2×3 rigidity ↔ the multiplicative semigroup of divisors of p-tied integers acting on (ℤ/4C)^×.
why: Rigidity theorems give pointwise density of orbits (every infinite ×2×3-invariant closed set is everything); a finite analogue (Bourgain–Lindenstrauss–Michel–Venkatesh effective) gives 'orbits of 2,3 in (ℤ/q)^× are dense'.
first_step: Check BLMV/Bourgain effective ×a×b results: does {2^i 3^j mod q} hit −1 for all q with small exponents? Then ask if 4Cp+1-divisors contain a fixed multiplicative structure.

title: Billiards / circle rotation: p mod m for consecutive m as a rotation-like sequence
connection: p mod m for m near √p behaves like a quadratic sequence (Dirichlet divisor problem) ↔ ES divisibility events are zeros of p mod (4uC − 1).
why: Near m ≈ √p, p mod m follows parabolic arcs; divisors appear at structured places. Could the ES moduli family hit such arcs?
first_step: Plot (m, (p+u) mod m) for moduli m = 4uC−1 near √p and look for parabolic patterns permitting a forced zero.

title: Thermodynamic formalism for Egyptian fraction expansions (Engel/Sylvester series dynamics)
connection: Engel expansions and Sylvester series have ergodic theory (Rényi) ↔ 3-term Egyptian representations as short orbits.
why: Known metric theory of Engel/Sylvester digits could supply heuristic densities for 'expansions of length 3'.
first_step: Compute the Engel/Sylvester (greedy) expansion of 4/p and its length distribution over primes; correlate with ES difficulty.

title: Records sequence of hardest primes as an OEIS-style object
connection: Sequence of primes p where min certificate size exceeds all previous ↔ OEIS has such records for ES? (check).
why: Records concentrate structure (adversarial primes); their pattern (residues, factorisations of p±small) suggests failure mechanisms.
first_step: Search OEIS for 'Erdos-Straus' sequences; compute records for 'smallest x in 4/p = 1/x+…' and submit/compare.

title: Maximum entropy model for certificate distribution given residue constraints
connection: MaxEnt with constraints p mod q for q ≤ Q ↔ best prediction of R(p) from local data.
why: The gap between MaxEnt prediction and actual R(p) is the 'global' part; if it's small, ES difficulty is local-plus-noise.
first_step: Fit log R(p) ~ Σ_q β_q·1[p ≡ a mod q] by regularised regression and report R² vs Q.

title: Crystallography / Bravais lattices: 1/x+1/y+1/z as Miller-index relation
connection: Miller-index plane equations x/a + y/b + z/c = 1 ↔ the plane through (x,0,0),(0,y,0),(0,0,z) contains the point (p/4,p/4,p/4) ⟺ 1/x+1/y+1/z = 4/p.
why: Geometric reformulation: ES(p) ⟺ some lattice plane with positive integer axis intercepts passes through (p/4)(1,1,1). Lattice-plane counting (geometry of numbers) might apply.
first_step: Use this: count lattice planes through q = (p/4)(1,1,1) with integer intercepts; relate to primitive vectors (1/x,1/y,1/z) scaled — check if this is a known equivalence to ET.

title: Kinetic theory of the 'trial division' process: occupancy problem
connection: Balls-in-bins: each trial modulus m 'catches' p if p ≡ r_m mod m ↔ ES is non-empty-catch.
why: Occupancy problems with heterogeneous bin probabilities have sharp zero-probability estimates (Poisson clumping heuristic, Aldous).
first_step: Apply Aldous' Poisson clumping heuristic to ES with clumps = shared-factor moduli; compute adjusted zero probability.

title: Dynamics on the space of lattices: ES certificates as cusp excursions of a p-indexed orbit
connection: Orbits of diagonal flows on SL₃(ℝ)/SL₃(ℤ) visiting the cusp correspond to small vectors ↔ ES certificates are small vectors in p-dependent lattices.
why: Cusp excursions are governed by Diophantine properties; Littlewood-type pointwise statements are hard but some (Einsiedler–Katok–Lindenstrauss) give measure results.
first_step: Write a 3D lattice Λ_p such that a vector in a specified small cone ⟹ certificate; examine whether the a-orbit of Λ_p is known to enter the cusp region.

title: Bohr sets / Bohr neighbourhoods of p: certificates as elements of a Bohr set
connection: Bohr set B(Γ,ε) = {x : ‖γx‖ < ε} ↔ ES certificates require p/m near −u/m exactly (ε = 0).
why: Additive-combinatorics machinery on Bohr sets gives structure for 'approximate' ES; exact would need ε < 1/m.
first_step: Compute, per p, the approximate certificate count with tolerance ε = k/m for k ≤ K and check if exact count ≈ approximate/(2K+1).

title: Chaotic dynamics: the 'Egyptian map' T(a/b) = a/b − 1/⌈b/a⌉ and its periodic structure mod p
connection: Iterating the greedy step on all a/p, a ∈ (ℤ/p)^× defines a map on residues ↔ ES asks about orbits of length ≤ 3 from a = 4 through rescaled fractions.
why: Graph structure of this map on F_p (functional graph) could have computable statistics (tree sizes) related to ES.
first_step: Build the functional graph of the greedy-remainder map on fractions with denominator dividing p·k for small k; compute statistics.

title: Benjamini–Schramm / local limit of the 'divisor graph' around p
connection: Local weak limits of graphs ↔ the neighbourhood structure of p in the ES certificate graph.
why: Too abstract unless a concrete graph emerges; keep as curiosity.
first_step: Define graph: vertices = primes ≤ X, edge p~q if they share a certificate modulus; compute degree distribution.

title: Shor-type period finding: ES certificate as a hidden-subgroup instance?
connection: HSP over (ℤ/N)^× ↔ ES gate: subgroup generated by divisor classes containing −1.
why: Curiosity mapping; might reveal that certificate-finding reduces to factoring 4Cp+1 (which it does) — so ES search ∈ BQP-easy given factoring.
first_step: Write explicit reduction: ES(p) certificate search ≤ factoring of numbers 4Cp+1 for C ≤ polylog — then note quantum polynomial time.

title: CRT-construction of adversarial p evading all small certificates (Chinese remainder adversary)
connection: Choose p mod Π(4uC−1) avoiding −u for all small (u,C) ↔ B1 barrier; the smallest such p as function of the menu bound.
why: Gives the 'cost' of evading menu of size B; growth rate of the minimal evader vs actual certificate sizes calibrates how big the menu must be at p.
first_step: Compute minimal prime p ≡ 1 mod 840 avoiding all (u,C) with 4uC−1 ≤ B for B = 10..200 via CRT + sieve; plot log p vs B.

title: Pigeonhole (PPP) certificate: injectively map a set of size > N into a set of size N
connection: PPP problems: pigeonhole collisions ↔ ES certificates from a collision in a map from (thick set) to (smaller set) where collisions are certificates.
why: Thue's lemma is a PPP-style argument; ES via a collision would be a G1 'collision' column cell.
first_step: Look for a map from a set of size ≍ p (e.g. residues a mod p) to a set of size < p whose collisions yield (u,B,C) — test candidates on small p.

title: Automata: is the set of p (in base b) with a certificate of size ≤ B a regular language? (Büchi/Cobham)
connection: Sets defined by finitely many congruence conditions are b-automatic ↔ finite menus give automatic sets; ES (all primes) is not automatic but the complement of a finite menu is.
why: Cobham's theorem: automatic in two multiplicatively independent bases ⟹ ultimately periodic. Menus are periodic; any 'digital' certificate rule (digit-carry algorithms, B1 hatch) gives automatic sets in one base only — a way to classify digit-based ideas.
first_step: Take a digit-carry ES rule (repo E2 hatch) and compute its automaton; check whether its success set is periodic (then B1) or genuinely base-dependent.

title: ECM-style randomised factoring of 4Cp+1 tuned to divisors ≡ −1 mod 4C
connection: ECM finds small factors; ES only needs some divisor in a class ↔ certificate search at astronomical p.
why: Engineering: lets adversarial searches reach p ~ 10^100 cheaply (only smooth parts needed).
first_step: Implement: for C ≤ 10⁴, pull small factors of 4Cp+1 by trial division/ECM and test subproducts for class −1 mod 4C; measure success rate at p ~ 10^100.

title: Lattice of exponent vectors: ES certificate as short vector in a relation lattice
connection: Repo gon_lll_relation_lattice ↔ relation lattices among divisor classes.
why: Already explored in repo; listing for coverage. New angle: use LLL to find a subproduct with prescribed class AND size constraint simultaneously.
first_step: Read BRAINSTORM/gon_lll_relation_lattice.md; check whether the size constraint (d < √N) was included in the lattice.

title: Strengthened conjecture: first certificate found within O(log² p) trials in a canonical order
connection: Stronger statement 'ES with an explicit search bound' ↔ like Linnik's constant or least-prime-in-AP bounds.
why: Stronger, more rigid conjectures are sometimes easier to attack (induction/structure) or to refute (giving insight). Also gives a cheap computational target.
first_step: Fix canonical order on (u,C) by 4uC−1; compute max over p ≤ 10⁹ of the index of first success / log² p.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Interactive proofs: verifier checks ES for random p quickly — PCP-style 'ES holds on a dense set' certificates
connection: Probabilistically checkable statements ↔ almost-all ES; verifying 'ES for all p ≤ N' needs a list; can one compress the list into a short certificate (e.g. a few polynomial identities + exceptions)?
why: Compression of the verification certificate is equivalent to finding uniform structure; measuring compressibility (MDL) of the verification list is an experimental structure probe.
first_step: Take the list of minimal certificates for p ≤ 10⁷ and compute how many 'polynomial-family rules' are needed to cover 99%, 99.9%, … (greedy set cover).

title: Symbolic regression (PySR) on minimal ES solution sizes
connection: Symbolic regression discovers closed forms from data; ES minimal solution sizes (min x, min max(y,z)) as functions of p might follow simple laws in residue classes.
why: A clean size law suggests which certificate shapes always exist (e.g. 'some solution with x ≤ p/4 + O(log² p)').
first_step: Run PySR with features (log p, p mod small m, Ω(p+k), Legendre symbols) on 10⁵ primes; report best formulas and residual variance.

title: Neural network certificate generator (learned guessing of (u,C))
connection: Train a model to propose (u,C) for given p, verify exactly ↔ learned certificates.
why: If a small model achieves near-100% top-k accuracy, its learned function may be interpretable (e.g. a rule based on p mod something + a search) — mechanistic interpretability as hypothesis generation.
first_step: Train a transformer on (digits of p) → (u,C) of the smallest certificate for 10⁷ primes; measure top-10 hit rate; probe what it uses.

title: FunSearch-style evolutionary program search for ES certificate heuristics
connection: DeepMind FunSearch used LLM-evolved programs to find cap set constructions ↔ evolve a program mapping p → certificate minimising failures/cost.
why: Evolved programs can reveal compact heuristics; any program with unbounded but structured search may suggest invariants.
first_step: Set up an evolutionary loop (LLM proposes Python functions) scoring by #primes ≤ 10⁶ solved in ≤ k trials; inspect the best programs.

title: Gröbner/elimination for identity families: Mordell–Schinzel boundary computed
connection: Elimination theory can compute all polynomial identity families of bounded degree for 4/n (sections of the ES fibration of degree ≤ d over ℚ[t]).
why: Exhaustive classification of low-degree families tells exactly which classes polynomial identities can reach.
first_step: Set up unknown-coefficient polynomials x(t), y(t), z(t), n(t) of degree ≤ 3 and solve the coefficient system with Gröbner bases (msolve/Singular).

title: Cellular automaton encoding of the sieve of certificate classes
connection: 1D cellular automaton marking residues ↔ pictures of the uncovered set.
why: Visual exploration; unlikely to yield theorems but cheap pattern-finding.
first_step: Render a 2D image: row = modulus m = 4uC−1, column = p mod m, highlight −u; overlay hard primes.

title: Quartic and higher residue symbols as hidden invariants of hard primes
connection: Hard primes are ≡ 1 mod 840 (splitting completely in ℚ(ζ_840)); next-order invariants could be quartic/octic residue symbols ↔ e.g. (2/p)_4, (3/p)_4.
why: If (★)-failures cluster on a quartic-symbol class, it's a new structural fact (like F_q forcing lines but higher order).
first_step: For the 14 (★)-failing primes and hardest ES primes, compute (2/p)_4, (3/p)_4, (5/p)_4, (7/p)_4 and compare with random p ≡ 1 mod 840.

title: Titchmarsh divisor problem with congruence: Σ_{p≤x} #{d | p+a : d ≡ r mod q}
connection: Summing ES certificate counts over p is a Titchmarsh-type divisor problem in progressions (Fouvry, Bombieri–Friedlander–Iwaniec). It controls averages and exceptional sets, as LORENZINI_W used Linnik/Halberstam.
why: This is the native average tool, already in the repo; recorded so the map is complete. BFI-level distribution beyond 1/2 could improve exceptional-set exponents.
first_step: Check whether BFI's level-4/7 results apply to the specific moduli 4C with the −1 class; if so, compute the resulting exceptional-set exponent.

title: Selberg's Λ² upper-bound sieve inverted: lower bound for 'not all events fail' via Turán sieve
connection: Turán sieve gives lower bounds for counts of objects hitting at least one condition from variance ↔ R(p) pointwise needs variance over a p-family — no family at fixed p, but family over (u,C) trials.
why: Turán-type inequality at fixed p: #{success} ≥ (Σ P)²/(Σ_{i,j} P_ij) in a probabilistic model over trials; but the 'probability' at fixed p is deterministic. Identify a randomisation at fixed p (e.g. random auxiliary prime) that preserves certificates.
first_step: Search for an auxiliary random variable at fixed p (e.g. random multiplier λ with certificates for λp mapping back) — check if 4/p certificates can be transported from 4/(λp)-type statements.

title: Divisor function in arithmetic progressions to large moduli (Fouvry–Iwaniec, Heath-Brown τ₃) applied to Σ_C
connection: τ in APs with modulus beyond √x (via Kloosterman, Deshouillers–Iwaniec) ↔ divisors of 4Cp+1 in class mod 4C averaged over C.
why: Average over C at fixed p is a genuine one-variable average (not over p) — exactly the kind of thick average available at a single p. Level-of-distribution results for τ(n) in APs n ≡ a mod q with q ~ n^{2/3} might count Σ_C at fixed p!
first_step: Write Σ_{C ≤ X} #{d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 mod 4C} as Σ_d Σ_C 1[4Cp ≡ −1 mod d, d ≡ −1 mod 4C]; the d-sum with C free: for each d, the C with d ≡ −1 mod 4C ⟺ 4C | d+1. So count pairs (d, C) with 4C | d+1 and d | 4Cp+1 — rewrite and see if it reduces to a count of p in residue classes mod d (averaged over d) — Bombieri–Vinogradov at a single p? Check.

title: When 4Cp+1 is prime, the C-slice of (★) fails; when is 4Cp+1 = q·r with q ≡ −1 mod 4C?
connection: Prime 4Cp+1 kills slice C; semiprimes succeed iff a factor ≡ −1 mod 4C ↔ quadratic-character-like conditions on factors.
why: Breaking R(p) by factorisation type of 4Cp+1 gives a clean probabilistic model: success probability of slice C ≈ Σ over factorisation types.
first_step: Tabulate, over C ≤ 100 and p ≤ 10⁶, the success rate of slice C conditioned on Ω(4Cp+1) = 2, 3, 4…

title: Trivially-forced divisibility at fixed p: 4Cp+1 ≡ 0 mod ℓ for C ≡ −(4p)^{-1} mod ℓ
connection: For each small prime ℓ, some C < ℓ gives ℓ | 4Cp+1 ↔ the divisor ℓ is in class −1 mod 4C only if ℓ ≡ −1 mod 4C — a 'self-levelled' small-prime certificate.
why: This is the cheapest structured certificate family (d = ℓ prime): ES(p) ⟸ ∃ ℓ prime, C | (ℓ+1)/4, ℓ | 4Cp+1. That's p ≡ −(4C)^{-1} mod ℓ — a residue condition mod ℓ for each divisor C of (ℓ+1)/4: density ≈ τ((ℓ+1)/4)/ℓ per ℓ, sum diverges like Σ τ/ℓ ~ log²: matches log² main term!
first_step: Compute the fraction of R(p) coming from d prime (vs composite) for p ≤ 10⁷; if prime d dominate, the problem is 'p in a union of residue classes mod primes ℓ' — classical sieve setting (B1/B2 still).

title: Artin's primitive root conjecture-type heuristic for ES gate (−1 in subgroup generated by divisor classes)
connection: Artin: a is a primitive root mod p for a positive density of p (Hooley under GRH) ↔ ES: classes of prime factors generate a subgroup containing −1.
why: Hooley's GRH-proof technique (Kummer-extension splitting) handles 'subgroup generated by a fixed element' — ES's elements vary with p, but the structure (Chebotarev in Kummer fields) is the tool for 'is −1 in ⟨g⟩'.
first_step: Express '−1 ∈ ⟨g⟩ mod q' as: ord(g) even and g^{ord/2} = −1; check whether certificate primes behave like random elements w.r.t. this event.

title: Exact formula: R(p) = Σ_{C} (τ_{−1 mod 4C}(4Cp+1)) — compute generating Dirichlet series in p
connection: Treat R(n) for all odd n: D(s) = Σ R(n) n^{-s} ↔ analytic properties (poles at s=1 of order 3?) give mean values; Tauberian.
why: Mean value ≍ log² — consistent with triple pole; a factorisation D(s) = ζ(s)^? L(s,…) would expose structure.
first_step: Compute D(s) formally: Σ_{u,B,C} (4uBC − u − B)^{-s}; find its analytic continuation properties numerically or via Mellin–Barnes.

title: Subset products in (ℤ/q)^× of random elements: probability −1 is hit with k elements
connection: Random model: k random elements of (ℤ/q)^×, probability some subproduct = −1 ↔ ES slice success probability given Ω(4Cp+1) = k.
why: Exact probabilities (from group structure: needs −1 in generated subgroup and a subproduct, not just subgroup element) give a refined heuristic for R(p) zero probability.
first_step: Compute exactly for q = 4C ≤ 200, k ≤ 6 the probability that subset products of k uniform elements include −1 (with constraint product of all ≡ −1·something?).

title: Eisenstein integers and 4/p: a slice where p = a² + 3b² helps
connection: Primes p ≡ 1 mod 3 split in ℤ[ω] (all hard primes do, being ≡ 1 mod 840) ↔ a certificate built from p's ℤ[ω]-factorisation.
why: Hard primes split completely in many small fields; their factorisations π·π̄ are canonical objects at p (thick? no, but rigid). A certificate formula in terms of (a,b) with p = a² + 3b² would be an R-type identity on a non-residue-class set — not excluded by Mordell–Schinzel.
first_step: For hard primes p ≤ 10⁶, compute (a,b) with p = a²+3b², a²+b² representation, a²+2b², a²+5b²… and search for linear/quadratic expressions in a,b that give ES certificates for all p.

title: Identities with poles at the T1 locus: rational (not polynomial) parametrisations x(a,b) with denominators vanishing on b = 0
connection: Following the T1 specialisation obstruction: any (a,b)-identity must break at squares; rational functions with b in denominators break exactly there.
why: Integrality then requires b | numerators — a divisibility condition in (a,b) that may hold for all p via a choice among the many representations a² + b² (only one up to sign for primes!) — so only finitely many choices; record as likely-dead but clean test.
first_step: Search rational functions of low degree in (a,b) with denominators b^k for identities 4/(a²+b²) = Σ 1/x_i; then test integrality on primes.

title: Three squares: p = a² + b² + c² representations (r₃ ≍ √p h) as thick object
connection: Odd p ≢ 7 mod 8 are sums of three squares with ≍ √p·L(1,χ) reps ↔ extraction rule to ES certificate.
why: Same G1 logic with an object of size √p tied to class numbers.
first_step: For hard p, enumerate three-square reps and search for any polynomial map (a,b,c) ↦ (x,y,z) yielding certificates on ≥ 1 rep for all p ≤ 10⁴.

title: Cohen–Lenstra heuristics for 'class gate' events
connection: Probability a random abelian group has given structure ↔ (ℤ/4C)^× subgroup generated by divisor classes containing −1.
why: Mostly a modelling tool; could predict which C slices fail more often (those with large 2-rank of (ℤ/4C)^×).
first_step: Compute slice failure rate vs 2-rank of (ℤ/4C)^× for C ≤ 200 over many p.

title: Quadratic reciprocity orientation: F_q is about (q/p); flip to (p/q) and use CRT-based identities
connection: (q/p) = (p/q) for p ≡ 1 mod 4 ↔ F_q becomes a condition on p mod q: p is a QNR mod q ⟹ ES(p). That's a residue-class condition mod q — so F_q is a finite covering statement mod q!
why: Since hard primes are ≡ 1 mod 4, F_q is a union of (q−1)/2 residue classes mod q; Mordell-style identities on these classes would prove F_q — but repo says F₁₁ open with a sterile point; so the classes are not covered by ET identities mod 11·(…). Check sterile point mechanism.
first_step: Read EXSET_CHAR_FORCING.md §7 on x** and determine which QNR classes mod 11 lack an ET identity at all moduli 11·M.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Compactness argument: ES holds for all n iff a certain closed subset of Ẑ contains no positive integers
connection: The set of n ∈ Ẑ not covered by ET identities is closed ↔ positive integers in it must be handled by non-identity (non-local) certificates.
why: Formalising this would define the 'global part' of ES precisely as integers in a profinite closed set (squares in Ẑ are in it). Then ES ⟺ integer points of that set (non-squares) each have a large certificate.
first_step: Define precisely: K = Ẑ minus ∪(open ET identity classes). Compute K ∩ (ℤ/M) projections for M up to 10⁶; check whether K equals the closure of squares or is larger.

title: Overspill: if every prime ≤ N has a certificate of size ≤ (log p)^A, by overspill some nonstandard N too — useless direction; reverse: underspill for counterexamples
connection: Overspill/underspill principles ↔ bounding certificate size uniformly.
why: Mostly logical hygiene: shows 'uniform polylog bound' and 'ES' are equivalent in nonstandard terms only with explicit bounds.
first_step: Skip unless pursuing logic angle; first step: write a paragraph mapping ES's bounded-quantifier form to overspill.

title: ES for all n = 4m² + 1 / m² + 1-type families via Gaussian factorisation
connection: Polynomial values n = f(m) where f has algebraic structure (norm forms) ↔ thin-family proofs à la repo (J)62–(J)80.
why: Each such family that admits a proof is a new PROVED thin family; families with no finite ET covering need a moving window (repo technique).
first_step: Pick f(m) = m² + 1 (odd values?) or 4m² + 1; check if a finite ET covering exists (compute coverage mod M for growing M); if not, try window technique.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Odd-square neighbours in the ES₅ word form: tuv − u − v = m² has no 'interior' words? T1 in word language
connection: ES₅ word certificates should exhibit T1 at squares ↔ word-level proof of T1 might identify an invariant (like a Jacobi symbol of t,u,v) that is constant on words.
why: An invariant constant on words but nonconstant on primes would be a hidden conservation law; T1 says it takes a forbidden value on squares.
first_step: Compute the Jacobi symbol combinations (t/·), (u/v)… on all ES₅ words for small n; look for a combination that equals 1 on all words of non-square n... (check repo first).

title: Sum over t of #{d | tp+1, d ≡ −1 mod t}: the full I3 count as a thick object with t up to p
connection: Allowing t up to ~p gives a sum of ~p log p events; for t > √p, the divisor condition is about tp+1 having a divisor in a class mod t > √(tp) — Lenstra regime (≤ bounded count, decidable fast).
why: In the large-t regime, the condition d ≡ −1 mod t with d | tp+1 forces d small multiple structure: d = kt − 1 with (kt−1) | tp+1 ⟺ (kt−1) | (p + k)·t − (kt−1)·… ⟹ (kt − 1) | p + k: back to Type II trial form. Symmetry u ↔ k — consistent.
first_step: Map the I3 large-t regime onto small-k Type II trials explicitly; confirm the count identity numerically.

title: Shift form: R(p) = Σ_{B≥1} #{s | p+B : s ≡ −1 (mod 4B)} (CHECKED p ≤ 1009)
connection: From p + B = u(4BC − 1): ES-(★) ⟺ some shifted prime p + B has a divisor ≡ −1 modulo 4B ↔ divisors of consecutive integers above p, each with its own tied modulus.
why: Shows the B-variable and C-variable divisor forms (4Cp+1 vs p+B) are two faces; the shift form lives on an interval of integers above p where Erdős–Selfridge/consecutive-integer rigidity tools act, though the modulus 4B is still tied to the shift.
first_step: Verified numerically (scripts/z52b_free_opus_check1.py). Next: compute which B contribute for hard primes (are certificates concentrated at B small, i.e. on p+1, p+2, …?).

title: Bhavik Mehta / Bloom Lean unit-fractions project as formalisation partner
connection: Bloom–Mehta formally verified the unit-fraction density theorem in Lean (b-mehta.github.io/unit-fractions) ↔ ES sub-results (T1, Mordell reduction, thin families) are formalisable.
why: Existing Lean infrastructure for unit fractions lowers the cost of formalising the repo's elementary results.

title: Ask Kontorovich/Stange/Rickards about thin-orbit local-global methods for polylog-count problems
connection: Apollonian/HKRS reciprocity obstructions ↔ T1 dictionary; they know which methods could handle sparse orbits.
why: Direct expert check on whether 'Question R' could ever drop to polylog regime.
first_step: Prepare a one-page summary of the T1 ↔ quadratic-reciprocity-obstruction parallel and ask for pointers.

title: MathOverflow question: the shift form 'p + B has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4B for some B'
connection: Clean elementary restatement of (★) (checked numerically) ↔ community may recognise it from other contexts.
why: Elementary restatements sometimes ring bells in other subcommunities (e.g. combinatorics of consecutive integers).

connection: Talks at e.g. 'Rational points' workshops or Integers conference ↔ feedback from algebraic geometers on the pencil theorem.

connection: Repo's barriers B1–B9 ↔ a public, structured negative-results database prevents others from repeating.

title: Meta: adversarial red-team lane whose only job is constructing hard primes
connection: Disproof search ↔ every proof idea must survive the hardest primes; a dedicated adversary sharpens the frontier.

title: Meta: switch target to ES with 4 replaced by a variable numerator in a family where m = 4 is the boundary
connection: Uniformity in m (E_m results) ↔ find a family statement S(m) true for m ≤ 7 and false for m = 8 whose proof might be easier because it 'knows' the threshold.
why: Threshold-aware statements (e.g. depending on m mod something or size of m) might be provable via local data at m.

title: Recreational: ES puzzle app / daily puzzle for crowd-sourced hard instances
connection: Puzzles like 'write 4/p as three unit fractions' ↔ crowd intuition on hard p.
why: Mostly outreach; humans sometimes find structured solutions faster than search for special forms of p.

connection: Superparticular ratios (n+1)/n compose intervals; Egyptian fractions relate via 1/n differences ↔ decomposing intervals.

connection: Origami folding of fractions (binary folding sequences) ↔ unit-fraction decompositions.

connection: Repo's drop-condition style ↔ formal protocol for testing wild items from this list cheaply.
why: Turns breadth list into actionable triage without depth bias.

connection: REUs produce many small results ↔ thin families and computational censuses are REU-sized.
why: Distributes exploratory work; may yield new thin-family proofs.

title: Meta: canonical certificate database for p ≤ 10⁹ (minimal certificate per form)
connection: Downloadable data ↔ ML items and statistical items in this list need it.
why: Shared data accelerates all experimental items.
first_step: Generate and store compressed minimal (u,C) per prime ≤ 10⁹ (Type II (★)) and minimal Type I; document format.

title: Meta: Bayesian update of P(ES false) using sibling calibrations
connection: Zero-law model ↔ G4 siblings show fewer failures than predicted.
why: Quantified belief guides resource allocation between proof and disproof.
first_step: Fit a hierarchical model on sibling failure data (S_{n,−4}, ES_Q1, 8/n) and output posterior P(ES has a counterexample beyond 10¹⁸).

title: Sidorenko / Blakley–Roy: homomorphism counts of paths in a 'divisibility graph'
connection: Blakley–Roy: hom(P_k, G) ≥ n·d^k in any graph — pointwise lower bound from density ↔ ES certificate as a path of length 2 in a graph whose average degree is computable at p.
why: Gives a pointwise count lower bound purely from the edge count — a rare pointwise mechanism. The difficulty: certificates must be exactly the paths (all paths), which needs a clever graph.
