first_step: Try G_p on vertex set ℤ/M with edges a~b iff ab ≡ (something with p) mod M; check whether 2-paths correspond to Type II certificates for some modulus choice; test on p ≤ 100.

title: Sperner/Tucker on the level × divisor grid
connection: Sperner's lemma forces a fully-labelled cell in any boundary-respecting labelling. Lay out levels C (one axis) and divisor sizes log d / log N (other axis); label grid cells by the class of the divisor relative to −1 (mod 4C); boundary conditions come from trivial divisors (1 and N always in class 1). A fully-labelled cell would be a certificate.
why: Odd, but Sperner-type lemmas give existence from boundary data alone.
first_step: Construct the labelled grid for small p and check whether natural boundary conditions hold and what a fully-labelled cell means.

title: Representation theory of SL₂(ℤ/4C): the Type II condition as a matrix coefficient
connection: SL₂ form [[a,p],[c,d]] with congruences ↔ the count is a matrix coefficient of the permutation representation on cosets.
why: Decomposing into irreducibles separates trivial (main term) and nontrivial (fluctuation) parts — the genus/BM split might be the 1-dim characters; higher irreps carry X(n).
first_step: For small c, compute the permutation representation and its character decomposition; identify which irreps carry the T1 cancellation.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Matroid / independence structure of divisor classes mod 4C
connection: Classes of prime factors as vectors in (ℤ/4C)^× ⊗ F_2 ↔ matroid rank decides 2-part of gate.
why: Ties to F₂-linear-algebra item; matroid union theorems might handle multiple C simultaneously.
first_step: For each C compute matroid of 2-adic character vectors of prime factors of 4Cp+1; study rank deficiency for hard p.

title: Random walks on (ℤ/q)^× generated by prime factors: cutoff and mixing of subset products
connection: Subset products of k random elements of an abelian group G cover G once k ≳ log|G| (Erdős–Rényi random subset products). ES wants −1 covered with k ≈ log log p generators: a 'pre-cutoff' regime.
why: Random-walk theory is precise about pre-cutoff probabilities; combined across many levels C it gives a heuristic failure probability.
first_step: Compute P(−1 ∈ subset-products) for k random elements of (ℤ/4C)^× by exact enumeration; plug into a Poisson model over C ≤ C₀.

title: Additive bases: is the set of 'certificate-friendly' integers an additive basis of finite order?
connection: Define A = {n : ES(n) has a certificate of a simple type}; additive basis results (Schnirelmann) ↔ multiplicative closure of ES (if ES(a) then ES(ka)).
why: ES set is multiplicatively closed upward (multiples); it's a 'multiplicative ideal-like' set — primitive elements are the problem. Primitive sets theory (Erdős primitive set conjecture proved by Lichtman) might apply to 'minimal ES-failures'.
first_step: Note: the set of n failing ES (if any) is closed under taking divisors >1? (If ES(d) then ES(n) for d|n, so failures' divisors fail.) So failures form a divisor-closed set ⊂ primes∪{1}-generated: only primes. Record the clean fact and think about primitive-set density bounds (Lichtman).

title: Geometry: ES as a lattice point on a hyperboloid-like surface in 3D and Minkowski–Hlawka counts
connection: Positive solutions (x,y,z) lie on a smooth surface in ℝ³ (cubic) ↔ counting lattice points on surfaces near the asymptotic directions (where one coordinate dominates).
why: Lattice points on curved surfaces: counts ≍ area / curvature-weighted; ES surface's curvature degenerates at infinity — where solutions concentrate.
first_step: Compute the 'area' of the ES surface patch in the box [p/4, p²]³ weighted appropriately and compare with log² p — a geometric derivation of the main term.

title: Polynomial ES over ℤ[T] (not F_q[T]): 4/f(T) = Σ 1/g_i(T) and specialisation
connection: Solutions in ℤ[T] for polynomial n(T) give identity families ↔ Mordell–Schinzel classification.
why: Systematic: for each polynomial n(T) of degree ≤ 2, decide existence of ℤ[T] solutions; the set of n(T) admitting them maps to proved thin families.
first_step: Enumerate quadratic n(T) = aT² + bT + c with small coefficients and search ℤ[T] solutions with degree ≤ 4 denominators.

title: Hilbert's 10th problem over ℤ with divisibility: Diophantine definability of 'has a divisor ≡ −1 mod m'
connection: The predicate D(N,m) = ∃d | N, d ≡ −1 mod m is existential ↔ complexity of deciding ES-type predicates.
why: Logical classification only; supports TFNP items.
first_step: Note D(N,m) is in NP (certificate d) and coNP? (unknown); state as complexity question.

title: Inverse theorem viewpoint: avoiding −1 forces the subproduct set into an index-2 subgroup coset structure
connection: Subset products avoiding −1 ↔ Kneser/inverse theorems (repo used Kneser at a failing window).
why: Already partially done (Kneser at forced window); generalise to all C simultaneously: −1 ∉ subproducts for every C — a family of inverse conditions on one integer family.
first_step: List, for (★)-failing primes, the index of the subgroup generated by prime factors of 4Cp+1 in (ℤ/4C)^× for C ≤ 50: is it always a subgroup not containing −1?

title: Probabilistic method with alterations: random p-tied object then fix
connection: Erdős's alteration method ↔ choose random C, get N = 4Cp+1 with random factorisation; ES needs the class gate. Alteration: multiply/divide by small primes to fix the class? (not allowed: N is fixed).
why: Recorded as a check that the alteration freedom ES lacks is precisely 'modifying N'. The I3 form with t free gives N = tp+1 for all t — more freedom.
first_step: Compute success probability per t in I3 slices vs per C in (★); confirm the extra freedom quantitatively.

title: Dessins d'enfants / Belyi maps: the ES surface's fibration branched over 3 points?
connection: If the map (x,y,z) ↦ n restricted to some curve is a Belyi map, Galois action on dessins might act on ES solution structure.
why: Speculative; Belyi maps tie combinatorics to Galois action.
first_step: Check whether the map from the curve {y = z} on ES surfaces to the n-line is branched over ≤ 3 points.

title: Kronecker's theorem / three-distance theorem for {p/m}
connection: Three-gap theorem for {nα} ↔ distribution of p mod m over m; hits are zeros of a remainder function.
why: Rigid structure of gaps sometimes forces hits; e.g. in ceiling-remainder form, r_p(m) takes values in structured arithmetic progressions on pieces.
first_step: On each piece q, r = qm − p runs through an AP with difference q; the target r | (m+1)/4 — test whether three-distance-type regularity forces hits on long pieces (small q).

title: B=1 slice of (★) ⟺ (p+1)/2 has a prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4) — a Landau–Ramanujan event
connection: B = 1 slice: need divisor s ≡ −1 mod 4 of p + 1 with s ≥ 3 ↔ p + 1 = 2·odd; odd part has a divisor ≡ 3 mod 4 iff odd part has a prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4 … at an odd power? (product of primes ≡ 1 mod 4 gives ≡ 1).
why: Exact criterion: B=1 slice succeeds iff (p+1)/2 is not a product of primes ≡ 1 mod 4 (i.e. not a sum-of-two-squares-ish with only 1 mod 4 primes). Fails with density ~ c/√log p (Landau) — so B=1 alone handles all but a (log p)^{-1/2} fraction. Simple and illustrative.
first_step: CHECKED (scripts/z52b_free_opus_check2.py): criterion exact for all 8977 primes p ≡ 1 (4) below 2·10⁵; B=1 fails for 13.6% of them. Next: fit the failure fraction against c/√(log p) (Landau–Ramanujan) up to 10⁹.

title: Sieve of 'multiplicatively constrained' shifts: primes p with p+1, p+2, …, p+K all composed of primes in prescribed classes
connection: Simultaneous Landau–Ramanujan conditions on consecutive shifts p+B ↔ sieve of dimension Σ δ_B; such primes exist (heuristically) with density (log)^{−Σδ_B}.
why: Shows quantitatively how a (★)-failure is built: all small shifts must be 'class-constrained' integers. The 14 known failures could be checked against this mechanism.
first_step: For p = 409 and the other (★)-failures, factor p+B for B ≤ 50 and verify each is class-constrained mod 4B; identify the slowest-failing B.

title: Sangaku (Japanese temple geometry) problems with unit-fraction radius relations
connection: Many sangaku give relations like 1/√r = Σ 1/√r_i or 1/r = Σ 1/r_i for tangent circles ↔ ES as an integer-radius configuration.
why: Curiosity/outreach; a configuration with 1/r = 1/r1 + 1/r2 + 1/r3 among mutually tangent circles might connect ES to Descartes/Apollonian integrality.
first_step: Search sangaku collections (Fukagawa–Rothman 'Sacred Mathematics') for a three-reciprocal radius relation and check if it's Descartes-compatible.

title: Signed certificate counts with exact formulas (Jacobi-type): search for a sign ε(u,B,C) making Σ ε an explicit nonzero function
connection: r₂(n) = 4Σ_{d|n} χ₋₄(d) is a signed divisor count with an exact formula ↔ find ε on ES certificates so that S(p) = Σ ε is a class number, a divisor sum of p±k, or a Legendre-symbol expression that never vanishes.
why: If |S(p)| ≥ 1 is forced by an exact formula, R(p) ≥ 1 follows (|S| ≤ R) — the 'exact charge identity' column of G1, pointwise and without lower-tail estimates.
first_step: Compute, for p ≤ 10⁴, S_χ(p) = Σ over certificates of χ(u), χ(B), χ(C), χ(u+B) etc. for all characters χ mod ≤ 24; search each sequence in OEIS / fit to class numbers and divisor sums.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Count congruences of R(p) modulo 3, 5, 8 and of partial counts R_C(p)
connection: G1 'count congruence' column: if R(p) ≢ 0 (mod m) for all p in some class, existence follows ↔ repo tested mod 2/mod 4 (fair coin).
why: Cheap scan of other moduli and of weighted/partial counts (restricted to C in a residue class, or to u ≡ B mod k) for a forced nonzero residue.
first_step: Compute R(p) and partial counts mod m for m ≤ 12 over primes p ≡ 1 mod 24 up to 10⁷; report any residue never taken (especially 0).

title: Signed ES (one negative denominator) as relaxation calibration
connection: 4/n = 1/x + 1/y − 1/z: check whether a polynomial identity solves all n ↔ positivity is the essential ES constraint.
why: If signed ES has identities on all classes, positivity is where Mordell–Schinzel bites; understanding how sign-flips evade T1 (they must) localises the obstruction to the positive cone.
first_step: Search for polynomial identities for 4/n = 1/x + 1/y − 1/z on all residue classes (e.g. via SMT templates); test at odd squares to see which T1 step a negative sign breaks.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Restricted-denominator strengthening: one denominator a power of 2 times something
connection: ES with x ∈ {2^k·m : m ≤ M} ↔ like p + 2^k problems (Erdős: fails on APs).
why: A strengthening expected to fail (B1-style) gives cheap calibration of how much freedom ES needs.
first_step: Find the first prime ≡ 1 mod 24 for which no solution has x a power of 2 times a divisor of something small; tabulate.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Four-term rescue size: minimal largest denominator when a 4th unit fraction is allowed to be huge
connection: 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z + 1/w with w forced large ↔ measures 'ES defect' at p.
why: Gives a continuous difficulty measure even when 3-term solutions are plentiful; correlations with R(p) test whether difficulty is one-dimensional.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵ compute the minimal max(x,y,z) such that the remainder 4/p − Σ is a unit fraction 1/w with w ≤ p³; compare with R(p).

title: Type I / Type II complementarity: are the primes where Type II is scarce rich in Type I?
connection: f_I(p) and f_II(p) counts ↔ correlation across primes.
why: Negative correlation would suggest a conservation-type law (a combined invariant), positive correlation suggests common difficulty driver (local factors).
first_step: Compute Spearman correlation of f_I(p)/log³p and f_II(p)/log³p over primes ≤ 10⁷ (repo data) after removing local-factor main terms.

title: Correlations R(p) vs R(p + 840k): local vs global difficulty
connection: Primes in the same class mod 840 share local data ↔ if R/M is strongly correlated for p, p + 840k, difficulty is local; if not, global randomness.
why: Quantifies the 'lottery' model; complements the ML feature-importance item.
first_step: Compute correlation of R(p)/M_BM(p) and R(p')/M_BM(p') for prime pairs with p' − p = 840k, k ≤ 100.

title: Sierpiński's 1956 monograph on decompositions into unit fractions
connection: Sierpiński 'Sur les décompositions de nombres rationnels en fractions primaires' ↔ early systematic treatment.
why: Classic sources sometimes contain lemmas or conjectures forgotten later.
first_step: Locate a scan (Mém. Soc. Math. France?) and skim for 4/n and 5/n material — check the citation first.

title: Dickson's History of the Theory of Numbers, vol. II, Egyptian-fraction chapter
connection: Dickson collects 19th-century work on unit-fraction equations ↔ pre-ES identities.
why: Cheap, may surface old parametrisations.
first_step: Skim Dickson vol. II chapter on 'sums of reciprocals' (archive.org) for equations 1/x+1/y+1/z = a/b.

title: LLM-assisted literature mining for lemmas of shape 'a fixed integer has a divisor in a residue class'
connection: Semantic search across arXiv for any theorem guaranteeing a divisor of a specific integer in a specified class ↔ ES's core event.
why: Such lemmas are rare and scattered (e.g. in primitive divisor theory, cyclotomy); a targeted mining pass may find a forgotten one.
first_step: Run arXiv full-text search for phrases 'has a divisor congruent to', 'divisor in the residue class', 'prime factor congruent to -1' and screen hits.

title: Fermat's factorisation viewpoint: 4Cp+1 + Y² must be a square X² with X ≡ −1 (mod 2C)
connection: Fermat's method searches X ≥ √N with X² − N square ↔ ES certificate as a Fermat factorisation step landing in a class.
why: Near-square factorisations (d ≈ d') correspond to small Y; the class condition on X is a congruence on a 'quadratic progression' X² − N, amenable to quadratic-sieve-style analysis.
first_step: For hard p, run Fermat-style search on 4Cp+1 for X ≡ −1 mod 2C up to X ≤ √N + K and count hits vs prediction.

title: Pocklington/Proth-style primality certificates as anti-certificates: when 4Cp+1 is prime, slice C fails
connection: Proth: N = k·2^n + 1 primality tests ↔ 4Cp+1 = (4C)·p + 1 is Pocklington-friendly (p | N − 1).
why: Every C with 4Cp+1 prime kills slice C; such C are certifiable cheaply. A counterexample prime p needs many such C or other failure modes; the density of 'Pocklington-prime C' for hard p is a measurable stress quantity.
first_step: Count C ≤ 10⁴ with 4Cp+1 prime for (★)-failing primes vs random primes; compare with Hardy–Littlewood prediction.

title: Hypothesis-H-generated hard primes vs ES: do they also stress Type I?
connection: Dickson-tuple primes kill small (★) slices but Type I slices (divisors of p² + 4c²d) are different ↔ test whether Type I compensates.
why: If Type I is uncorrelated with the tuple construction, ES's union is robust to single-family adversaries — evidence on the 'independent families' model.
first_step: For the record primes from the previous item compute f_I(p) and compare with typical p.

title: Egyptian-fraction 'tree of all solutions' as a graph: connected via common denominators
connection: Graph whose nodes are solutions for all n ≤ X, edges when they share two denominators ↔ moves between solutions of different n.
why: If moves are local (n changes by small structured amounts), the graph could support induction-like arguments (ES(n) from ES(n') via a move).
first_step: Build the graph for n ≤ 10⁴ and study components, degree distribution, and whether each prime connects to a smaller n by a short path.

title: Hereditary closure: ES(n) ⟹ ES(kn), so only primes matter — dualise: does ES(p) follow from ES of all p·q for many q?
connection: Reverse direction: solutions for pq (q varying prime) that are 'Type I in p' might descend ↔ thick family {pq : q prime} at fixed p.
why: This gives a thick object (all primes q) at fixed p; descent condition must be checked. A 'p-primitive' solution for pq with denominators all divisible by q descends.
first_step: For hard p, compute for q ≤ 1000 solutions of 4/(pq) where q divides all denominators (=> descends) vs other; check whether descending solutions exist exactly when ES(p) has certain types.

title: ES words are generalised Frobenius numbers: tuv − u − v = g_t(u,v), the largest integer with ≤ t−1 representations by ⟨u,v⟩ (CHECKED)
connection: For coprime u,v the largest n with at most t−1 representations n = au + bv (a,b ≥ 0) is tuv − u − v (t = 1: Sylvester's uv − u − v) ↔ I3/ES₅ words p = tuv − u − v, and (★) is t = 4C: p = 4C·uB − u − B.
why: Puts ES (★)/I3 inside the Frobenius problem / numerical-semigroup theory: ES(★) ⟺ p is the 4C-th 'k-Frobenius number' of some 2-generated semigroup ⟨u,B⟩. That field has its own tools (Apéry sets, Popoviciu's formula, Ehrhart theory, denumerants) and literature on which integers occur as (k-)Frobenius numbers. Not found in repo by grep.
first_step: Verified for u,v < 12, t ≤ 4 (scripts/z52b_free_opus_check3.py). Next: search literature for 'k-Frobenius number' / 'generalized Frobenius number two generators' (Beck–Robins; Brown et al., J. Integer Seq. 2010 — check) and for 'which integers are Frobenius numbers'.

title: Popoviciu's formula: N(n; a,b) = n/(ab) − {b′n/a} − {a′n/b} + 1 turns (★) into a sawtooth extremality condition
connection: Popoviciu: number of representations of n by ⟨a,b⟩ in terms of fractional parts with a′ ≡ a⁻¹ (mod b), b′ ≡ b⁻¹ (mod a) ↔ n is a k-Frobenius number iff both fractional parts take their maximum (a−1)/a, (b−1)/b, i.e. n ≡ −b (mod a) and n ≡ −a (mod b) (the pair form).
why: Links ES to sawtooth functions ((x)) and hence Dedekind sums and Dedekind/Rademacher reciprocity — reciprocity laws are exactly where T1-type parity information lives (repo's Dedekind–HJ charge was χ-blind; this is a different Dedekind-sum entry point via semigroup counting).
first_step: Write Σ over (u,B) of the Popoviciu sawtooth product for fixed p and check whether summing with weights yields a Dedekind-sum expression with a reciprocity-law evaluation.

title: Counting numerical semigroups by Frobenius number (Backelin, Kaplan, Zhai) as a template for 'every p is a k-Frobenius number'
connection: The number of numerical semigroups with Frobenius number F grows like c·2^{F/2} (Backelin) ↔ here restricted to embedding dimension 2 (polylog many) with k-Frobenius.
why: The embedding-dimension-2 restriction collapses the count to divisor-type size (as expected); but allowing embedding dimension 3 semigroups (three generators) might correspond to richer ES-type certificates — check if a 3-generator k-Frobenius identity gives ES solutions.
first_step: Compute Frobenius numbers of 3-generated semigroups ⟨a,b,c⟩ in families and check whether some family's g(a,b,c) formula yields ES certificates (e.g. Type I parametrisation).

title: Which integers are k-Frobenius numbers of ⟨u,v⟩ with k ≡ 3 (mod 4): a direct elementary question to post
connection: Restating (★) without Egyptian fractions: 'every prime p ≡ 1 (4) except 14 known ≤ 10¹⁰ is the largest integer having exactly 4C−1 representations by some coprime pair u,v'.
why: Semigroup/Frobenius community (e.g. García-Sánchez, Rosales, Ramírez Alfonsín) may recognise it; experts in that field are not in the ES network.
first_step: Draft a short note/MO post in Frobenius language with data, clearly marking that (★) is sufficient for ES but not equivalent (user approval before posting).

title: Chebyshev-bias analogue: are certain classes mod 840·k systematically harder?
connection: Prime number races / Chebyshev bias ↔ per-class average of R(p)/M(p) among the six Mordell-hard classes mod 840 and their lifts.
why: Systematic class biases indicate local factors not yet in M_BM — refinement of the main term or new local invariant.
first_step: Compute mean R(p)/M_BM(p) per class mod 840·11·13 for primes ≤ 10⁸ and test for significant deviations.

title: Sibling: n = xyz − x − y − z (and n = xyz − x − y) universality thresholds
connection: I3: n = tuv − u − v with t,u,v ≥ 3 covers all n > 2 433 600 ↔ sibling shapes xyz − x − y − z, xyz + x + y may have their own exception lists and known proofs.
why: Sibling exception structures calibrate I3_𝒞 (repo's ES-strength conjecture); a sibling with a provable finite exception list would be a method precedent.
first_step: Compute exceptions of n = xyz − x − y − z with x,y,z ≥ 2 up to 10⁷; inspect whether the exception set is finite-looking and whether it has a T1-like obstruction (squares?).

title: Project Euler Egyptian-fraction problems as a source of fast counting algorithms
connection: PE problems on 1/x + 1/y = 1/n and related count solutions fast via divisor enumeration ↔ certificate enumeration engineering.
why: Algorithmic tricks (e.g. enumerating divisors of n² quickly) may speed up censuses.
first_step: Review PE problem forums for unit-fraction problems' best algorithms; benchmark against repo's census code.

title: Odd vs even characters split of the slice count: R_C(p) = even part + odd part
connection: 1[d ≡ −1] = (1/φ) Σ_χ χ(−1)χ̄(d)… = (even-χ sum − odd-χ sum)/φ(4C) applied to Σ_{d|N} ↔ even part = count of d ≡ ±1, odd part = signed difference #(≡ −1) − #(≡ +1) among d ≡ ±1.
why: Since N ≡ 1 mod 4C and d ↦ N/d preserves ±1 classes, the odd part is a signed divisor count (like r₂); if a closed form exists, it's an exact charge identity per slice.
first_step: Compute for each C ≤ 30 and p ≤ 10⁵ the signed count #{d|N: d≡−1} − #{d|N: d≡+1} and look for multiplicative closed forms.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: 2D quantum harmonic oscillator: (★) ⟺ in an oscillator with frequencies (u,B), level p is the highest level with degeneracy 4C − 1
connection: Energy levels n = au + bB of a 2D oscillator with commensurate frequencies have degeneracy N(n; u,B) ↔ ES words p = g_t(u,B) are 'last levels before the degeneracy reaches t' (with particle–hole-type symmetry N(n) + N(g_t − n) = t).
why: Exact physics dictionary; degeneracy-counting via semiclassical (Weyl) asymptotics plus exact Ehrhart corrections is a mature toolkit. Mostly a reframing, but the 'degeneracy jump' language may suggest spectral (trace-formula) approaches to counting all (u,B) at once.
first_step: Write Z(β) = Σ_n N(n;u,B) e^{−βn} = 1/((1 − e^{−βu})(1 − e^{−βB})) and express 'p is a jump level' via residues of Z at roots of unity (Sylvester waves); sum over (u,B) formally.

title: Parity-problem diagnosis: how strongly does slice success correlate with λ(4Cp+1)?
connection: Selberg's parity barrier: sieves cannot detect the parity of Ω ↔ slice C fails whenever 4Cp+1 is prime (λ = −1); if success is strongly parity-correlated, ES inherits the parity problem.
why: If ES-type events are parity-sensitive, sieve-only proofs are excluded for a structural reason (complementing B1/B2); if not, the obstruction lies elsewhere.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶ and C ≤ 50, compute P(slice succeeds | λ(4Cp+1) = ±1) and P(… | Ω = k).

title: Euler-type prime-generating polynomials as thin families (n² + n + 41 and relatives)
connection: Values of n² + n + 41 are prime for n ≤ 39; families with high prime density concentrate primes with special splitting (class number 1 field ℚ(√−163)) ↔ a thin family with rigid arithmetic.
why: Rigid splitting (every small prime is inert in ℚ(√−163)) is exactly the 'all small q are QNR-like' structure that affects F_q forcing lines; checking R on this family probes that interaction.
first_step: Compute R(p)/M_BM(p) for primes p = n² + n + 41 ≡ 1 mod 4 (n ≤ 10⁵) vs random primes.

title: Universal vs per-prime certificate menus: minimal menu covering all primes in [X, 2X]
connection: Set cover over a dyadic block ↔ how menu size must grow with X (B1 says unbounded).
why: The growth law of the minimal menu (e.g. ~ log X or ~ (log X)²) is a quantitative replacement for the qualitative B1 and could be compared with the CRT-adversary cost.
first_step: Greedy set cover for primes ≡ 1 mod 24 in [10^k, 2·10^k], k = 4..8, with menu items = (u,C) pairs; fit menu size vs k.

title: Ask the LLM-board for 'connections we would be embarrassed to have missed' after merging z52b lanes
connection: Cross-model review of the merged list ↔ blind-spot detection.
why: Different models have different associative priors; a short adversarial 'what is missing' round is cheap.
first_step: After merge, run one board round with the prompt 'list 30 connections to ES absent from this list' and dedupe.

title: Symmetric 3-generated semigroups = complete intersections (Herzog): ES as a symmetric-Frobenius representation problem
connection: Herzog: 3-generated symmetric numerical semigroups are complete intersections, i.e. gluings ⟨d·a, d·b, c⟩ with c ∈ ⟨a,b⟩, gcd(d,c) = 1, whose Frobenius numbers are d(ab − a − b) + (d − 1)c. ES words are the slice c = a + b; other c = αa + βb give other trilinear words dab − a(d − (d−1)α) − b(d − (d−1)β).
why: Gives a natural ambient family (all symmetric 3-generated Frobenius numbers = all odd numbers?) containing the ES words; the question 'which (α,β) slices are universal on primes' is a clean ladder of problems, some maybe solved.
first_step: Enumerate, for odd n ≤ 10⁶, which (α,β) ∈ {0,1,2}² slices of d(ab−a−b)+(d−1)(αa+βb) with 4 | d represent n; compare failure sets with U(n)/T1.

title: Feature flip: fixed small t — t ≤ 3 is trivially universal on odd n, fixed t = 4 has a primality-type failure set
connection: The word tuv − u − v with u = 1 gives (t−1)v − 1, so t = 2 or 3 (and t = 1, = Frobenius numbers g(u,v) = uv−u−v, e.g. g(2,n+2) = n) represents every odd n trivially. Fixed t = 4 gives n = 4uv − u − v ⟺ 4n+1 = (4u−1)(4v−1), which fails e.g. whenever 4n+1 is prime. ES needs the union over t ∈ 4ℤ (plus the glued third generator u+v in the semigroup picture).
why: Shows precisely which features (t restricted to 4ℤ, union over levels) turn a trivial or primality-type single-level statement into a plausible universality statement.
first_step: Tabulate which odd n (and primes) fail to be 4Cuv − u − v for each fixed C = 1,2,3,… separately (each level has its own divisor-type failure set) and for unions over C ≤ K.

title: Restrict ES to its σ₂-level sets: (x,y,z) with xy+yz+zx = M and xyz = nM/4
connection: Every ES solution lies on a pair of level sets of elementary symmetric functions σ₂ = M, σ₃ = nM/4; for each M, (x,y,z) are roots of T³ − σ₁T² + MT − nM/4.
why: Turns ES into: find M and σ₁ such that a cubic with these coefficients splits over ℤ with positive roots — a 'split cubic' problem like those handled by discriminant/class-group methods.
first_step: For hard primes p ≤ 10⁶ list the M = σ₂ values of all solutions; look for structure (e.g. M ≡ 0 mod p, M/p values) suggesting a 1-parameter family.

title: Coppersmith lattice method to sample ES witnesses at C ≈ p^{1/4}–p^{1/2}
connection: Coppersmith–Howgrave-Graham–Nagaraj find divisors in a residue class for s > N^{1/4} (with more work). For ES levels C in [p^{1/4}, p^{1/2}] this is a non-brute-force witness finder.
why: Turns the search into a lattice-reduction problem; lattice structure could expose WHY witnesses exist (short vectors) — F31.
first_step: Implement the Lenstra/Coppersmith divisor search for N = 4Cp+1, r = −1, s = 4C at C ≈ p^{0.3}, p = 10¹⁵ primes; count hits vs. expectation.

title: Tenenbaum's divisor concentration / Maier–Tenenbaum propinquity for class-divisors
connection: Maier–Tenenbaum solved Erdős's propinquity problem (most n have two divisors with ratio in (1,2]); ES needs two complementary divisors a,b of N with a ≡ −b (mod e) — 'propinquity in residue classes'.
why: Propinquity-type results (divisors close together) are the multiplicative-interval analogue of ES's residue-class closeness.
first_step: Check whether a residue-class analogue of Maier–Tenenbaum ('almost all N have a divisor ≡ −1 mod q for q ≤ (log N)^c') is in the literature.

title: Granville's corrected Cramér model ↔ BM-corrected Poisson model for R(p)
connection: Granville refined Cramér's model by sieving small primes, predicting larger gaps (ξ ≥ 2e^{−γ}). ES's analogue is replacing the naive density 1/(4uC−1) by 1/φ and then by the BM-corrected main term.
why: A precise 'Granville-type' ES model would predict the maximal size of log P(R = 0 | M) and hence whether finitely many failures are expected.
first_step: Fit P(R*(n) = 0 | M_BM(n)) on odd non-squares ≤ 10⁸ against e^{−cM} with c from a sieved Poisson model.

title: Goldbach–Linnik: even n = p + q + K powers of 2 (K = 8, Pintz–Ruzsa) — adding a sparse structured set makes pointwise possible
connection: Linnik showed finitely many powers of 2 suffice; Heath-Brown–Puchta K = 13, Pintz–Ruzsa K = 8. Shares F01, F05 (binary Goldbach exceptional set) and the strategy 'almost-all + a sparse absorbing set'.
why: ES analogue: show 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z + (sum of K unit fractions from a sparse set S) with K bounded, then try to shrink K — a ladder of weakenings with K = ∞ trivial.
first_step: Define ES_K(S): 4/p − Σ_{i≤K} 1/s_i ∈ {1/x+1/y+1/z} for some s_i ∈ S = {2^j}; compute the least K needed for p ≤ 10⁷.

title: Colliot-Thélène–Xu: spinor exceptions are Brauer–Manin obstructions for integral points
connection: CT–Xu (Compositio 2009) explain many integral Hasse failures for quadratic forms (spinor exceptions on square classes) as BM obstructions. ES has no BM obstruction (BL) yet T1 kills Type I/II at squares.
why: Suggests T1 is a BM obstruction on a different (sub)scheme — the Type I/II torsor — which is exactly what makes the squares special; a CT–Xu-style theorem on a non-obstructed torsor could give existence.
first_step: Identify the scheme whose integral points are Type I/II solutions and compute its Br/BM pairing at n = m² (should reproduce T1).

title: Bilu–Hanrot–Voutier primitive divisors ≡ ±1 mod n supply divisors-in-class for Lucas-type ES families
connection: Primitive prime divisors of the n-th Lucas number u_n satisfy q ≡ (D/q) mod n, and exist for all n > 30 (BHV). That is a guaranteed divisor in a class tied to the index — exactly F10 — for integers in exponential families.
why: The campaign's proved thin families (3·2^s+1, 4^s+105, …) used algebraic factorizations; BHV could give a systematic source of divisors ≡ −1 mod 4C for p-tied integers in Lucas families.
first_step: For the open families 15·2^s+1 and 4^s+297: write 4C·p+1 for small C as a Lucas-sequence value or factor thereof and check whether a primitive divisor lands in the needed class.

title: No diagonal ES solutions at p ≡ 1 (mod 4): the S₃ action on solutions is free
connection: If x = y then 4/p = 2/x + 1/z forces a = 2x − p ∈ {1, p²} and 4 | p + 1, so p ≡ 3 (mod 4); same for y = z. Checked: no diagonal solution for any prime p ≡ 1 (4) below 1500; parity of the unordered count is 50/50 (scripts/z52b_signature_parity.py).
why: Freeness of S₃ means the ordered count is 6× the unordered one and kills simple involution-parity proofs (Zagier-style) — a useful negative datum for F38.
first_step: Look for a non-S₃ involution (e.g. Vieta in the hyperbola fibre) whose fixed points are classifiable; count fixed points for p ≤ 10⁵.

title: Numerator flip 4 → 8: failures at 17, 131, 241 as an anti-overreach test suite
connection: 8/n has genuine exceptions (11, 17, 131, 241 among primes > 3; recomputed by brute force for p < 400) while satisfying the same local/BM features (needs check). Any ES argument must visibly use a property false for 8.
why: Cheapest filter for candidate proofs: run them on 8/131 and 8/241.
first_step: For each tool collected in this lane, write one line: 'does the argument distinguish 4 from 8?'.

title: Equal-denominator / chain sub-problems (x | y | z) as solvable slices
connection: Restricting ES to chains x | y | z or to a fixed ratio y = kx gives two-variable divisor problems with explicit criteria; the diagonal x = y is empty for p ≡ 1 mod 4 (see diagonal item).
why: Each restricted slice is a 'line' in the sense of F34; knowing exactly which primes each slice covers sharpens the infinite-covering picture.
first_step: For k = 2..20 compute which hard primes ≤ 10⁷ admit solutions with y = kx; tabulate densities.

title: Manin–Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel prediction for integral points on the ES threefold vs. Elsholtz–Tao's N log³N
connection: The total space {4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx)} ⊂ A⁴ is a log Fano-type threefold; ET count Σ_{n≤N} f(n) ≍ N log³N (F04). CLT predict exponents from the Clemens complex of the boundary.
why: If the CLT/Wilsch framework reproduces log³ (all n) and log² (primes), the geometric picture explains which boundary strata carry solutions — a geometric handle on where witnesses live.
first_step: Compute the boundary divisor and its Clemens complex for a compactification of the ES threefold; compare max-face dimension + 1 with 3.

title: Hilbert property for integral points (Corvaja–Zannier) applied to the fibration n: X → A¹
connection: ES says the image of X(ℤ)_{>0} under n covers ℤ_{≥2}. Corvaja–Zannier relate the Hilbert property/thin images to fundamental groups. Polynomial-identity families have thin images missing squares (F09).
why: A thin-set theorem explaining why parametrised families must miss square classes would turn F09 into a geometric statement and show what a non-thin covering family must look like.
first_step: Check whether Mordell–Schinzel's impossibility is a special case of a Corvaja–Zannier-type 'images of integral points are thin' statement.

title: Theta-quotient normal form (Thm K) and nonvanishing of Fourier coefficients
connection: METAPLECTIC_ES Thm K writes the ES/ES₅ count as a coefficient of an explicit theta quotient. Nonvanishing of coefficients of modular-type objects is a classical theme: Lehmer's conjecture, Serre's lacunarity, Bruinier–Ono results mod ℓ.
why: If the theta quotient is (mock/mixed) modular of a known type, coefficient nonvanishing results could apply. Repo SIGN_IDENTITY excludes holomorphic forms by size but not mixed/mock objects.
first_step: Identify the precise modularity type of the Thm K generating function: is it a quotient of holomorphic thetas with poles (weakly holomorphic), mixed mock, or not modular? Check Serre's lacunarity criterion for its components.

title: Shrinking-target / hitting-time for the Gauss map: λ(p) ≤ 3 as 'some orbit hits a target in ≤ 3 steps'
connection: ES₅: for each p there is q with p/q of continued-fraction length ≤ 3 (with constraints). In dynamics language: some rational point of denominator p reaches a target set within 3 Gauss-map steps.
why: Effective equidistribution of rationals with denominator p under the Gauss map (Ustinov, Bykovskii) could give counts of such q with a main term ≍ log²p.
first_step: Check Ustinov's results on the statistics of continued-fraction lengths of a/p for fixed p (number of a with length ≤ k).

title: Is finding ES witnesses as hard as factoring p-tied integers?
connection: Witnesses ⟺ divisors of 4Cp+1 in a class (F10). Known fast heuristic (scan small C, factor small numbers). An ES-oracle reveals factors of 4Cp+1 for some C.
why: If ES witnesses are always findable in poly(log p) time by a deterministic method, that method may hide a proof; conversely, a reduction from factoring would explain why no explicit formula exists.
first_step: Measure, for p ≈ 10³⁰, the cost of the cheapest witness search (smallest C with a smooth enough 4Cp+1); check if it ever requires factoring a hard number.

title: Representation of p by x² + ny² for many n simultaneously (Cox) as a model of 'p a square mod everything small'
connection: Hard ES primes are squares modulo many small moduli (Mordell classes mod 840 are squares). Cox's theory characterises p = x² + ny² via ring class fields; the simultaneous version is a Chebotarev condition.
why: If ES-hardness is monotone in 'how many small forms represent p', one could try induction on a class-field tower.
first_step: For hard primes ≤ 10⁸ count n ≤ 100 with p = x² + ny² and correlate with R(p)/log²p.

title: Collatz (Tao 2019): almost all orbits attain almost bounded values via logarithmic density — the exceptional-set-improvement analogue
connection: ∀n conjecture (F01), almost-all known (F05), huge verification (F23), heuristic support (F24). Tao's key was changing the measure (logarithmic density) to gain an approximate invariance.
why: ES's exceptional set bound is stuck at exp(−c(log N)^{3/4}) (F40); a change of averaging measure (logarithmic weights in p, or weighting by the BM main term) might likewise gain invariance.
first_step: Recompute the ES exceptional-set argument with logarithmic density in n and see whether the 3/4 barrier changes.

title: Feature flip F28: forbid Type I (p | exactly one denominator) — Type II alone fails at 14+ primes; union never fails ≤ 10⁸
connection: Restricting the type creates explicit failure sets ((★) fails at 14 primes ≤ 10¹⁰; b = 1 line at 3 primes ≤ 10¹¹); their union survives. Shares the 'two families, each with sparse failures, disjoint failure sets' structure with Heath-Brown's Artin and with Goldbach-type unions.
why: If failure sets of two families can be shown disjoint by a parity/sign argument (one fails ⇒ the other has many), ES follows for large p.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁹ the joint distribution of (R_(★)(p), R_{b=1}(p)) and test for negative correlation at small values.

title: Feature flip F21: problems where a pointwise bound came from averaging over an auxiliary parameter of length ≫ polylog
connection: Pointwise results (Linnik p + x² + y², Vinogradov three primes, Duke ternary) all average over an auxiliary variable of polynomial length. ES's auxiliary variables (C, u, B) have polynomial range but polylog effective mass.
why: Suggests looking for an ES formulation with an auxiliary average of polynomial MASS (e.g. counting weighted solutions with weights growing in C).
first_step: Search for a weighting w(C,u,B) with Σ w·1[event] provably positive and mass ≫ p^δ — e.g. weights from smooth-number counts.

title: Feature flip F20: if only real characters contributed (pure genus count), ES would follow from genus theory
connection: R*(n) = M_gen(n) + X(n); M_gen is genus (order ≤ 2 characters), X the rest. Problems where only genus characters appear (class number one, idoneal discriminants) are solved by genus theory.
why: Idoneal-type phenomena: when the class group is 2-torsion, representation = genus condition. ES-hardness at a prime could be measured by how far relevant class groups are from being 2-torsion.
first_step: For hard primes, compute X(p)/M_gen(p) and correlate with the 2-rank vs. size of class groups of ℚ(√−p·small).

title: Feature flip F35: problems where bounded certificate schemes DO work (Pratt certificates for primality) vs ES's B1
connection: Primality has short certificates (Pratt) found by structured search, but no bounded formula; ES has short certificates (F32) and B1 forbids bounded procedures under Schinzel H.
why: Pratt-style recursive certificates (certificate for p uses certificates for factors of p−1) suggest recursive ES certificates using solutions for factors of 4Cp+1 or p+4d.
first_step: Check whether an ES solution for p can be assembled from ES-like data for prime factors of 4Cp+1 (recursive certificate).

title: Schinzel–Sierpiński: every positive rational is (p+1)/(q+1)? — follows from Hypothesis H; ES's B1 uses H in the opposite direction
connection: Under Schinzel's H many ∀∃ prime statements hold; for ES, H implies every bounded procedure fails (B1 Thm C). Shares F35, F01.
why: Interesting duality: H supplies primes where we want them (for existence) and where we don't (to defeat finite procedures).
first_step: Ask whether H also implies ES (it supplies primes in polynomial families — could it supply divisors in classes?) — likely not, but record why.

title: Hardy–Littlewood Conjecture H (large non-square n = p + k²) / Bateman–Horn: singular series with Legendre-symbol factors
connection: Representation counts whose singular series involve (n/ℓ) — e.g. HL Conjecture H, where squares n are excluded (n − k² factors). ES's main term M_BM has the same Legendre-symbol structure and also degenerates at squares (F20, F08).
why: Lets ES borrow the full Bateman–Horn singular-series machinery for its main term, and the known numerics for its variance.
first_step: Compare M_BM(p)/M₀(p) with a Bateman–Horn-type product ∏(1 − (p/ℓ)/(ℓ−1)) — is it asymptotically such a product?

title: OEIS search: numbers not of the form tuv − u − v (t,u,v ≥ 2) and with 4 | t — is the sequence in OEIS?
connection: U(n)'s failure set (odd squares + {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145}) is an explicit sequence; if it (or its variants) appears in OEIS, cross-references may reveal an independent characterisation.
why: OEIS cross-links occasionally reveal a known theorem behind a computed list.
first_step: Query OEIS for 105, 2961, 3985, 25305 and for the 14 (★) failure primes (409, …, 8813281).

title: Crocker's prime plus two powers of two obstruction
connection: The equation p+2^a+2^b=n has an explicit exceptional/obstruction structure (F01,F08w,F30,F33), contrasting positive-density coverage with universal coverage.
why: Its classification of failures may offer a way to search for structured ES failure families rather than only aggregate counts.
first_step: Read Crocker's construction (check whether his non-represented integers form a sparse family like 2^{2^m}−1 rather than residue classes) and compare its mechanism with the ES residue cover modulo 840 and the failed (★) primes.

title: Zsigmondy's theorem and its finite exceptional list
connection: Every n>1 has a new prime divisor in a cyclotomic difference except explicit small cases (F01,F23); cyclotomic factorization gives a short witness (F32) and finite exceptions (F25).
why: This is a clean example where primitive-divisor algebra turns universal existence into a finite exceptional classification.
first_step: Check whether any ES parametrization yields a cyclotomic factor whose primitive divisor forces d≡−1 mod 4C; begin with 4Cp+1.

title: Tian's rank results for congruent-number curves
connection: A family-wide rank argument yields pointwise conclusions for primes in selected classes (F01p,F29,F31), through Selmer and analytic rank structures rather than direct counting.
why: It is a relevant precedent for exploiting prime congruence classes and 2-descent to obtain a universal witness on a thin arithmetic family.
first_step: Verify Tian's exact residue-class rank theorem and identify the Selmer parity input; test for an analogous parity constraint on ES certificate counts.

title: Heath-Brown's density of integers with two-square prime factors
connection: A density theorem uses quadratic-form factorization to force prime factors of a special type (F05w,F29,F31), matching ES's Gaussian-integer hard case and character-sum averages (F20).
why: It demonstrates how Gaussian factorization can turn average arithmetic information into many explicit witnesses, potentially enriching ES's p≡1 mod 4 analysis.
first_step: Check Heath-Brown's exact two-square-prime-factor result and test its Gaussian-integer decomposition on 4Cp+1.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Schinzel–Sierpiński on primes among shifted linear forms
connection: The existence of primes in structured shifted forms is a pointwise prime-witness problem (F01,F21), and it interacts with the conjectural prime-plus-one/prime-divisor structure of ES (F10,F33).
why: Sieve arguments for simultaneous shifted-prime conditions may be relevant to the prime-tied divisors 4Cp+1, even if the exact theorem is conditional.
first_step: Verify the exact Schinzel–Sierpiński statement intended by (p+1)/(q+1), then test its local admissibility conditions on ES's linear forms 4Cp+1.

title: Apollonian reciprocity obstructions
connection: Apollonian packings have local congruence conditions and global reciprocity obstructions (F06,F07,F18,F31); ES has a prescribed-entry SL₂ matrix formulation plus congruence constraints (F18).
why: Reciprocity obstructions in a group-orbit setting may reveal hidden global constraints or constructive orbit coverage in ES matrix certificates.
first_step: Read Haag–Kertzer–Rickards–Stange's reciprocity criterion and test whether ES's prescribed-entry matrices admit a comparable spinor/reciprocity invariant.

title: Conditional Artin proof versus ES's missing pointwise lower bound
connection: Hooley's conditional result combines a pointwise target with GRH-controlled character sums and a sieve (F20,F21,F22); ES shares the character-sum/sieve signature but lacks its proven lower bound (F36).
why: This is a direct diagnostic comparison of which analytic input turns a character average into strict positivity.
first_step: Map every Hooley error term to an ES analogue in R(p)=Σ_C #{d|4Cp+1:d≡−1 mod 4C}; identify the single term preventing positivity.

title: Linnik dispersion applied to ES divisor counts
connection: Dispersion is designed to derive pointwise existence from averaged arithmetic progressions (F05,F21,F22), and ES's ★ count is itself a sum of progression-restricted divisor counts (F10,F20).
why: It is a concrete analytic bridge between known average estimates and a single-prime lower bound.
first_step: Form the bilinear sum over p and C from R(p), apply Cauchy-Schwarz/dispersion, and check whether off-diagonal terms are bounded by available divisor correlations.

title: Effective conic fibre points for bounded ES searches
connection: The explicit conic-fibration conditions in arXiv:1511.04876 link ES F15's divisor-like hyperbola slices to F32's bounded certificates and F21's pointwise lower-bound need.
why: Even if it only applies after restricting the base, explicit integral-point criteria could yield a new family of guaranteed ES representations.
first_step: Extract the paper's explicit integral-point construction and test it symbolically on the ES slice with one denominator fixed to its smallest admissible value.

title: Weak approximation versus actual ES witnesses
connection: arXiv:2411.02629 analyzes weak and strong approximation alongside semi-integral Hasse principles for Markoff orbifold pairs; this matches ES F06/F07 and F13, while highlighting the gap between local points and positive integral witnesses (F27).
why: Its separation of approximation properties from Hasse existence is relevant to avoiding a false inference from local solubility to ES solutions.
first_step: Identify the paper's examples where approximation holds or fails and translate the obstruction mechanism to the fixed-n ES surface, keeping positivity explicit.

title: Markoff-type K3 integral Hasse counterexamples
connection: arXiv:2504.10992 constructs Markoff-type K3 surfaces with Zariski-dense rational points that fail the integral Hasse principle; this matches ES F07/F13/F27 and flips F06-style local solubility into failure of integral points.
why: It is a verified explicit warning that rational density and local solubility do not settle an integral-point problem on a surface. The obstruction there is Brauer–Manin, which Bright–Loughran (arXiv:1908.02526) show is absent for ES, so look for non-BM ingredients.
first_step: Read the counterexample construction and isolate the integral obstruction; test whether its mechanism has an analogue on an ES fixed-n fibre.

title: Zariski density is not an ES existence theorem
connection: arXiv:2504.10992 gives Markoff-type K3 surfaces with dense rational points but integral Hasse failure, matching ES F13 and contrasting F01/F07; it is a feature-flip from rational abundance to integral scarcity.
why: The distinction helps evaluate whether an ES surface argument controls integral coordinates rather than merely producing rational points.
first_step: Take one explicit surface from the paper and trace a dense rational orbit's denominators; compare with ES's reciprocal-variable divisibility requirement.

title: Spinor-genus representation obstruction with congruence conditions
connection: The ternary quadratic-form and lattice-coset spinor-genus classification in arXiv:2104.08798 matches ES F31/F29/F03 and F21: a representation problem with congruence-restricted integral vectors can have exceptional classes.
why: It supplies a precise quadratic-form framework relevant to ES's Gaussian/quadratic-form reformulations and residue-class restrictions.
first_step: Read the paper's classified spinor exceptions and test whether any ES quadratic-form reduction lands in a corresponding lattice coset.

title: Divisors in residue classes via sign changes
connection: Lenstra's divisor-in-residue-class algorithm, revisited in arXiv:2410.05030, matches ES F10/F15/F21: a tied integer's divisor in a prescribed residue class is the witness-shaped target.
why: This is the closest direct arithmetic match to ES's divisor reformulation, and the abstract reports an algorithmic method based on a sign change.
first_step: Read the algorithm and try its sign-change sequence on the ES tied integer 4Cp+1 with target divisor residue −1 mod 4C for the smallest C-family.

title: Quadratic-form representations through continuants
connection: Arxiv:1203.0347 extends H. J. S. Smith's continuant approach to proper binary quadratic-form representations and gives deterministic algorithms; this matches ES F16/F17/F31 and F32.
why: ES's negative-continuant and continued-fraction formulations invite a constructive bridge from continuant identities to integral representations.
first_step: Take p≡1 mod 4, compute its two-square representation using the paper's algorithm, and inspect whether the output naturally supplies ES denominator congruences.

title: Continuant recurrences as bounded ES word identities
connection: Arxiv:2501.06512 derives a continuant formulation for second-order recurrences and associated identities, matching ES F16/F17/F19 and F32's short certificate theme.
why: Its recurrence-to-continuant translation may offer a systematic way to generate and verify short ES word identities.
first_step: Extract the recurrence identity and check whether the ES trilinear polynomial is a specialization of a continuant recurrence or determinant expansion.

title: Stern-sequence extremals and witness-count analogies
connection: Arxiv:1608.08322 proves results on largest values in Stern rows using alternating binary expansions and continuants; it matches ES F16/F17/F32 and offers a structured-word counting analogue for F04.
why: Its ordering argument is an explicit model for controlling extremal values among many short representations, not a generic heuristic.
first_step: Read its reduction of ordering to continuants and test whether the same normalization orders ES certificates for a fixed prime by denominator size.

title: Parity control in Egyptian-fraction rewrites
connection: Arxiv:2003.13229 explicitly discusses parity in Egyptian fractions, matching ES F12/F27/F29 and the denominator parity constraints underlying ES.
why: Parity-sensitive identities could be tested directly against the 2-adic cases that distinguish ES denominator types.
first_step: Extract its parity rules and check whether one rewrite preserves the 2-adic valuation pattern of the denominators in known ES triples (e.g. 4/7 = 1/2+1/21+1/42 has no denominator divisible by 4).

title: Matrix encoding of Markoff solution orbits
connection: Arxiv:0709.1499 encodes Markoff triples in integral upper-triangular matrices and connects them to the Markoff tree, matching ES F18/F38/F39 and surface-family feature F13.
why: An explicit matrix encoding can turn a nonlinear witness-generation problem into an orbit/reachability question.
first_step: Read the matrix correspondence and see whether ES's fixed-entry SL₂(Z) formulation admits analogous generators preserving the ES equation.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Positive solution orbits versus positivity in ES
connection: The positive-integer Markov–Hurwitz solution study in arXiv:2605.05075 matches ES F01/F13/F27 and F38, where positivity is part of the arithmetic orbit structure.
why: It gives a concrete comparison for whether involutions preserve the positive cone or require discarding signed solutions.
first_step: Inspect the orbit-generation recurrence and check whether an ES analogue preserves all denominator positivity constraints.

title: Stern continuants and orbit-growth bounds
connection: The explicit transformation/order methods for continuants in arXiv:1608.08322 match ES F16/F17/F38 and the tree-like certificate organization F39.
why: If ES word transformations form a graph, extremal continuant growth could bound the size and depth of its search tree.
first_step: Build the graph of length-three ES word moves induced by continued-fraction identities and test whether the extremal operation from the paper bounds depth at fixed n.

title: Smooth-number equidistribution and ES divisor classes
connection: Soundararajan's theorem (arXiv:0707.0299) shows that y-smooth integers below x are equidistributed in reduced residue classes mod q for q < y^{4√e−ε}. This matches ES F10/F20/F21, while ES needs a pointwise tied divisor.
why: Restricting the tied integer to smooth values might permit stronger residue control and expose a dense subfamily of primes.
first_step: Read the modulus range in the theorem and test whether an ES family's tied integer can be forced smooth at a compatible modulus.

title: Problem 300: Croot and Liu–Sawhney density bounds
connection: Problem 300 ↔ ES F04, F05, F12, F21, F33: count of reciprocal-sum representations, density bounds, and pointwise-versus-average tension.
why: The site records Croot’s improvement and the Liu–Sawhney bound; the mechanisms controlling abundance of unit-fraction sums are close in flavor to counting ES witnesses.
first_step: Read Croot [Cr03] and Liu–Sawhney [LiSa24] as linked from the page; extract the counting inequality and ask whether its variables can be restricted to three denominators summing to 4/p.

title: Problem 302: density forces a reciprocal relation
connection: Problem 302 ↔ ES F01, F05, F12, F33: density-to-existence, finite reciprocal sums and additive structure.
why: The page describes bounds on sets avoiding a unit-fraction equation, a potential way to show candidate ES-denominator sets cannot all be sparse.
first_step: Read the cited elementary argument and determine whether its density threshold can be applied to residues of candidate ES denominators modulo p.

title: Problem 306: multiplicative prime-factor Egyptian decompositions
connection: Problem 306 ↔ ES F01, F12, F14, F33: universal decomposition format, fixed reciprocal sums and symmetric terms.
why: The problem’s decomposition constraints concern reciprocal sums over products of primes, potentially suggesting ways to construct ES denominators with controlled factorization.
first_step: Read Butler–Erdős–Graham [BEG15] linked from the page and isolate the construction; test whether its prime-factor allocation can impose 4/p as the sum.

title: Problem 311: Tang’s least nonzero reciprocal subset sum
connection: Problem 311 ↔ ES F04, F12, F21, F32: a least positive reciprocal sum, controlled denominators and explicit certificates.
why: The page reports Tang's upper bound δ(N) ≤ exp(−cN/(log N·log log N)³), i.e. very close near-misses to 1 exist; the trivial lower bound is 1/lcm(1..N). This calibrates how close reciprocal subset sums can come to a target, which is relevant to near-miss ES searches.
first_step: Read Tang’s linked note; identify the exact least-sum construction and test whether it can force a remainder of the form 4/p−1/x.

title: Problem 316: divisor-set partition counterexample
connection: Problem 316 ↔ ES F03, F10, F12, F33: divisor structure, partition obstructions and reciprocal sums.
why: The page’s counterexample uses proper divisors; divisor-set geometry is central to ES’s divisor reformulations and may reveal useful structured coverings.
first_step: Study Sándor’s proper-divisor counterexample and check whether analogous divisor partitions constrain divisors of 4Cp+1 in ES.

title: Problem 327: unit-fraction characterization of odd sets
connection: Problem 327 ↔ ES F03, F12, F27, F33: reciprocal-equation equivalence, parity and additive structure.
why: The page explicitly links a unit-fraction equation to a parity condition and points to an elementary density argument; parity/congruence restrictions are fundamental in ES.
first_step: Read the van Doorn argument linked through problem 301 and determine whether its forced pair construction can generate an ES triple for each prime residue class.

title: Problem 308: threshold versus individual target
connection: Problem 308 ↔ ES F01, F04, F12; feature flip F01: eventual threshold statement rather than all n.
why: Croot's result shows that for large N every integer up to about H_N − (9/2+o(1))(log log N)²/log N is a sum of distinct 1/n with n ≤ N, and that this fails a little below H_N. Isolating this threshold mechanism may suggest how to handle finite exceptional sets in ES.
first_step: Read [Cr99] and identify how the least missed integer is bounded; test whether the argument yields a threshold for residual targets after one ES term.

title: Problem 304: Vose bound and denominator-size stress test
connection: Problem 304 ↔ ES F04, F12, F32: bounded-length representation, denominator growth and certificate size.
why: The page records Vose's improvement N(b) ≪ √(log b) for the number of terms (not denominator size). The contrast between term-count bounds and ES's fixed three terms can benchmark certificate-size questions.
first_step: Read Vose [Vo85] and identify how denominators grow in his construction; compare with the polynomial-in-p size of any three-term ES certificate.

title: Problem 313: prime reciprocal equation and local congruences
connection: Problem 313 ↔ ES F03, F06, F12, F29: prime denominators, local conditions and fixed reciprocal identity.
why: The equation forces arithmetic restrictions on a prime set; deriving these restrictions may offer a quick local filter or construction clue for ES.
first_step: Reduce the 313 identity modulo each prime and modulo 8, then compare the resulting local constraints with the ES p-adic checks.

title: Problem 316: explicit minimal obstruction and feature flip
connection: Problem 316 ↔ ES F03, F10, F12; feature flip: a finite divisor-set obstruction versus ES’s universal prime family.
why: A concrete minimal counterexample shows exactly how a divisor structure can defeat a reciprocal partition, suggesting explicit obstruction searches for ES parametrizations.
first_step: Check the cited minimal set and compute which congruence classes its divisors occupy; compare with the ES divisor-class criterion.

title: Problem 301: disjoint blocks and divisor-fiber decomposition
connection: Problem 301 ↔ ES F10, F12, F15, F33: disjoint reciprocal blocks, fixed-variable divisor fibers and additive-multiplicative structure.
why: The elementary disjoint-block argument may translate into a fiber decomposition after fixing one ES denominator, where the remaining pair lies on a split hyperbola.
first_step: Fix x in 4/p=1/x+1/y+1/z and rewrite the y,z equation as a divisor product; compare its fibers to the disjoint sets in the 301 argument.

title: Problem 319: reciprocal-set construction and residue-class balance
connection: Problem 319 ↔ ES F03, F05, F12, F20: reciprocal sets, density, congruence balance and character-like averaging.
why: Croot’s set construction produces a reciprocal-sum phenomenon; testing its distribution in residue classes can reveal whether real-character biases help ES.
first_step: Compute residue-class reciprocal sums for the constructed set modulo 4 and 8 and compare with the real-character main terms in ES counts.

title: Problem 308: subset-sum threshold as a two-term completion probe
connection: Problem 308 ↔ ES F01, F12, F15, F32: universal tail coverage, reciprocal sums and fixed-variable hyperbola completion.
why: Croot’s threshold result suggests abundant tails after a partial choice; the ES-specific question is whether a tail can be compressed to exactly two terms.
first_step: Fix a candidate x and test whether the reciprocal subset-sum interval guaranteed by the theorem contains the residual 4/p−1/x using only two terms.

title: Squarefree obstruction list for xy+yz+zx
connection: OEIS A055745 is the squarefree subset of integers not represented by xy+yz+zx, sharing F25/F08w/F13 and F04: a concrete finite-looking exceptional set arises within an algebraic family and representation counts are computable.
why: Comparing obstruction types rather than just the overall existence theorem may reveal whether ES failures cluster on squarefree or squareful inputs.
first_step: Compute ES failure counts separately for squarefree n and n with square factors over a modest prime range, and compare the apparent exceptional pattern with A055745's finite-list phenomenon.

title: Idoneal numbers and sparse failures of a cubic representation
connection: A025052 cross-references A000926 (Euler idoneal numbers) as integers not of the strict form ab+ac+bc with 0<a<b<c. This shares F08w/F13/F25/F31: a thin algebraically structured exceptional set tied to quadratic forms.
why: The quadratic-form reformulation offers a concrete bridge to ES's own quadratic-form/lattice perspectives, without assuming the obstruction mechanisms coincide.
first_step: Read the A000926 cross-reference and test whether the ES divisor-witness count on primes is better organized by discriminant/class data in Q(i) than by raw residue classes.

title: More-than-three unit fractions and numerator-dependent exceptions
connection: The MO question asks about k/n as a sum of a fixed number of unit fractions when k>4. This shares F01w/F11/F12/F25 and flips the exact numerator 4: fixed-term existence may become easier or harder with k.
why: A controlled numerator comparison can test whether ES's hard residue classes arise from a special small numerator or persist across nearby numerators.
first_step: On primes p in a small interval, compare the number of three-term representations of k/p for k=3,4,5 and tag each missing k against p's residue classes.

title: Prime-minus-one characterization of a bilinear-form complement
connection: OEIS A005097 identifies the complement of values represented by 2xy+x+y as n with 2n+1 prime. This shares F01/F02/F10/F16w: an exact prime-indexed criterion, a simple polynomial representation, and a complementary exceptional set.
why: An exact arithmetic characterization of representability through a linear transform of n is a useful model for turning ES witness existence into a primality/divisor condition.
first_step: Rewrite the ES divisor certificate conditions as an equivalent primality or factorization test if possible; first search for an affine transform analogous to 2n+1 in the simple bilinear identity.

title: A prime criterion hidden in a missing-value sequence
connection: A005097 is simultaneously a prime transform and a complement of a polynomial value set. It shares F10/F16w/F24/F25: one can enumerate witnesses by factor pairs and the nonrepresented values have an exact, computable criterion.
why: It shows how an apparent open-ended omission problem can collapse to a sharp criterion; search for an analogous characterization of any ES subfamily's omitted primes.
first_step: Select a natural ES subfamily (e.g. one denominator divisible by p), calculate its omitted primes, and check whether omission is equivalent to primality of a low-degree transform.

title: Stern primes and a second notion of additive nonrepresentation
connection: The A060003 comments identify several small exceptions as odd Stern primes, i.e. primes not of the form p+2b². This combines prime inputs with a restricted additive representation and finite exceptional values, matching F01p/F10/F25/F29.
why: Separating prime inputs from composite exceptions might reveal whether ES prime witnesses are governed by a different density or local obstruction than composite n.
first_step: Run the same candidate-generation code on ES primes and composites separately, comparing first-witness distributions and residue classes with the Stern-prime subset in A060003.

title: Exceptional small values in a square-factor covering theorem
connection: The square-factor theorem for xy+yz+zx has the explicit exceptions 4 and 18. This shares F08w/F25/F27: a universal positivity-constrained representation has algebraic-family exceptions, and positivity matters to the theorem.
why: The exceptional small values may be artifacts of positivity or low-parameter degeneracy, distinctions also relevant to ES denominator positivity.
first_step: In ES parameter identities, list every boundary case where a denominator is zero, negative, or repeated; compare whether the remaining failures are similarly confined to low parameter values.

title: Counting distinct unit-fraction solutions, not just proving existence
connection: MathOverflow 229514 asks for the number of strictly increasing tuples with reciprocal sum 1 and reports the unique 3-term solution 1/2+1/3+1/6. This shares F04/F12/F14/F21: an exact representation-count problem with symmetry removed and pointwise counts rather than existence alone.
why: A canonical count framework can clarify what ES's R(p) should count (ordered, unordered, or distinct denominators) and how symmetries affect estimates.
first_step: Adopt the increasing-denominator convention from the MO question and recompute small-prime ES representation counts, comparing them to ordered counts after dividing by S3 orbit sizes.

title: Group class equations naturally generate reciprocal sums
connection: MO 229514 notes that a finite group with n conjugacy classes gives a reciprocal sum equal to 1 using centralizer orders. This shares F01/F12/F14/F33: a structured family of unit-fraction representations arises from a symmetry object and its orbit stabilizers.
why: Although centralizer denominators are usually repeated, the orbit-stabilizer construction offers a structural source of identities and a possible way to build ES certificates from group actions.
first_step: Check whether any finite-group class equation can be normalized to 4/p with three distinct centralizer orders; start with small groups and inspect the resulting divisibility constraints.

title: Unique-representation locus as a low-multiplicity test
connection: A093669 lists integers with exactly one strictly ordered representation as ab+ac+bc, sharing F04/F13/F25 and contrasting ES's expected polylogarithmic abundance with a rigid one-point fibre.
why: A unique-witness locus is a sensitive place to test whether an ES construction proves mere existence or can force multiple genuinely distinct solution orbits.
first_step: Enumerate ES primes with exactly one unordered solution orbit up to a modest cutoff and compare their factorization and residue signatures to the one-representation trilinear terms.

title: Collatz parity vectors as finite-word certificates
connection: The Collatz problem shares F16w, F22, F32, F23: finite parity words encode trajectories and permit certificate-style computation for a universal integer claim. ES has fixed polynomial/word forms and short certificates (F16,F32).
why: The disciplined separation of word constraints, congruences, and positivity may inspire an ES certificate search with independently checkable proof objects.
first_step: Write a tiny enumerator for ES n=tuv−u−v certificates by bounded word/parameter height and compare its pruning by congruences with Collatz parity-vector pruning.

title: Lonely runner: finite-dimensional torus avoidance
connection: Lonely runner shares F01, F06, F23, F24: a universal integer-speed assertion has no simple local obstruction, strong finite verification, and geometric/torus heuristics. ES similarly combines local solubility with a global integral point question (F06,F07).
why: Its reduction to simultaneous fractional-part inequalities may offer a model for separating local admissibility from global witness existence.
first_step: Read Perarnau’s survey and identify a solved small-runner argument using a finite covering of the torus; translate the covering step into ES residue classes.

title: EFL: approximate coloring plus absorbing reservoir
connection: EFL’s proof shares F01,F03,F05w: universal coverage is achieved by a global bound, finite local compatibility, and an absorption step. ES’s finite congruence covering and exceptional square classes have the same cover-then-patch outline (F03,F08).
why: It provides a concrete proof architecture to test: cover almost all classes cheaply, then reserve flexible certificates to repair the remainder.
first_step: Extract the EFL approximate-decomposition/absorption interface and test a toy version on ES residue classes modulo 840 with square classes left uncovered.

title: Apollonian curvatures: local-global density one versus every integer
connection: The Apollonian curvature problem shares F03,F05,F10,F23: congruence-allowed values, density-one local-global results, and arithmetic orbit structure. Its known density-one scope contrasts with ES’s pointwise target (F21).
why: The local-global methods combine thin orbits and congruence sieving, a close model for ES where congruence coverage is necessary but not sufficient.
first_step: Read Bourgain–Kontorovich's density-one theorem (arXiv:1205.4416) and isolate its sieve/expansion step; then read the 2024 Annals counterexample paper and ask whether ES's p-tied divisor parametrization can supply an analogous orbit.

title: Addition chains: certificate search with rigorous lower bounds
connection: Addition chains match ES through F01,F32,F23,F24: finite verifiable certificates, computer searches, and a global existence/bound problem. The Scholz–Brauer problem also illustrates the gap between finding certificates and proving optimality.
why: ES witnesses are NP-style certificates; addition-chain exact-search methods could improve reproducible bounded ES searches and expose hard residue classes.
first_step: Build a bounded-depth ES certificate enumerator that canonicalizes symmetric triples and records the first uncovered prime at each depth.

title: Three-generator Frobenius numbers as sparse witnesses
connection: The 3-generator Frobenius problem shares F01,F10,F23,F32: arithmetic objects are characterized by integer parameters and modular/divisibility constraints, with finite certificates and computational catalogs. ES similarly searches thin divisor witnesses for each prime.
why: Apéry-set methods convert semigroup membership into finite residue-class data, potentially useful for organizing ES divisors by residue.
first_step: Read a three-generator Frobenius formula and test an Apéry-style residue table for ES’s tied divisor integer 4Cp+1.

title: SL₂(Z) semigroup membership as bounded-word reachability
connection: Matrix-semigroup membership shares F16w,F18,F32,F23: existence asks for a finite word producing a target matrix, with short certificates and decidable bounded searches. ES has a prescribed-entry SL₂ formulation and bounded certificate length.
why: Automata/word-search tools can enumerate structured ES matrix products and exploit congruence states before large integers arise.
first_step: Encode the ES matrix identity as generators and run breadth-first search modulo small moduli, retaining only states compatible with the target entry.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Odd greedy algorithm feature flip: unbounded term count
connection: Greedy Egyptian expansion shares ES’s positive unit fractions, universal input, and integer certificates (F01,F12,F27), but typically permits a variable number of terms rather than fixed three. This flip pinpoints bounded-term termination as ES’s core difficulty.
why: The algorithm may yield a baseline decomposition from which terms can be compressed or paired into a three-term representation.
first_step: Compare the first three greedy terms for 4/p against a complete ES certificate and identify a local compression identity.

title: Ringel’s tree packing: complementarity and finite obstruction checks
connection: Ringel's conjecture (proved for large n by Montgomery–Pokrovskiy–Sudakov and Keevash–Staden) and the open graceful-tree problem share F01,F23,F34: universal finite-structure coverage, computation, and families whose union must cover all edges/labels. ES similarly unions thin prime-covering families.
why: Complementary decompositions may inspire pairing ES certificate families so their uncovered sets cancel or shrink systematically.
first_step: Identify the smallest uncovered residue class after a standard ES covering and see if a complementary parametrized line covers it.

title: Erdős–Faber–Lovász: finite colorings as congruence coverings
connection: EFL shares F01,F03,F34: every finite input must be covered by one of finitely many compatible color classes, paralleling ES’s finite residue covers and infinite certificate-line union.
why: The proof’s conflict-graph decomposition may suggest a systematic way to organize overlapping ES certificate lines without double-counting.
first_step: Map ES certificate families to vertices in a conflict graph (edges for incompatible residue coverage) and test whether a coloring gives a finite cover.

title: Apollonian thin-orbit sieve and congruence expansion
connection: Apollonian packings share F03,F05,F10,F22: a thin orbit is sifted among locally allowed integers, yielding density-one coverage. ES’s witness divisors are thin and congruence constrained.
why: The orbit-sieve viewpoint directly addresses why local admissibility may fail to imply a witness for individual primes.
first_step: Read the density-one theorem’s sieve dimension and test whether an ES parameter orbit has comparable equidistribution modulo squarefree moduli.

title: Egyptian fraction identities as local witness transformations
connection: Egyptian fraction problems share F12,F14,F16w,F27: positive reciprocal equations have permutation symmetry and algebraic transformations between representations. ES has the same three-term symmetric witness geometry.
why: Classical splitting identities may transform a failed two-term or constrained witness into a valid three-term one while preserving denominator congruences.
first_step: Enumerate unit-fraction splitting identities preserving denominator divisibility by p and check if they close a missing ES square class.

title: Group word-problem feature flip: equality versus existence
connection: Group word problems share ES’s finite words, matrix structure, and short certificates (F16w,F18,F32), but often ask whether two given words are equal, rather than whether some witness word exists. This feature flip marks a decision-versus-search distinction.
why: Normal-form methods help only if ES’s matrix semigroup has a usable normal form; testing this prevents conflating word equality with target reachability.
first_step: Check whether the ES generator set admits a normal form in SL₂(Z); if not, test the simpler congruence quotient search first.

title: Zaremba and ES: finite alphabet versus finite word length
connection: Both Zaremba and ES use continued fractions and SL₂ words (F17,F18,F32), but Zaremba constrains the digit alphabet while ES constrains word length and matrix entries. This feature flip isolates alphabet complexity from length complexity.
why: Comparing the two constraints may show whether ES can be attacked using a finite alphabet despite variable intermediate parameters.
first_step: Compute partial quotients of the ES₅ representations for small primes and test for a finite digit alphabet covering a positive fraction.

title: Egyptian fraction counts and sieve moments
connection: ES shares F04, F12, F21, F22 with counting representations by unit fractions. The transferable object is a count of divisor parametrisations rather than mere existence.
why: A lower-tail estimate for representation counts could turn average abundance into pointwise existence.
first_step: Read Elsholtz–Tao, identify their count parametrisation, and test whether the second-moment argument localizes to prime n.

title: Hasse norm principle and norm-form equations
connection: Norm-form local-global problems share F06, F07, F20, F29; quadratic characters encode splitting and local constraints.
why: A norm-form reparametrisation could clarify the role of Gaussian splitting without assuming a new obstruction exists.
first_step: Rewrite the hard p≡1 mod 4 case using norms from Q(i), then compare local-global criteria for the resulting norm equation.

title: Vieta jumping on cubic Diophantine surfaces
connection: Cubic surface Diophantine problems share F13, F14, F38, with solution-preserving swaps or involutions.
why: Height-reducing involutions might explain parity of ES representations and connect otherwise separate solution families.
first_step: Check whether the ES involution graph has a canonical reduced representative for each orbit by minimizing max(x,y,z).

title: Polynomial identity methods for Diophantine coverings
connection: Polynomial identity problems share F03, F09, F34, F35: finite algebraic families cover some classes but may provably miss others.
why: Their obstruction proofs could sharpen understanding of what an infinite covering must add beyond finite congruences.
first_step: Formalize ES identity families as polynomial maps and compute the algebraic locus they cover modulo several small primes.

title: Integral points and effective height bounds
connection: Effective integral-point problems share F13, F32 and the tension between small certificates and uniform existence.
why: A bound on minimal witness height polynomial in p could permit a structured search or finite reduction.
first_step: Check known effective bounds for integral points on the ES surface and identify whether they are uniform in the parameter p.

title: Parity problem in sieve theory
connection: Sieve parity problems share F21, F22, F40 and explain why robust average estimates may fail to detect a single required arithmetic type.
why: Diagnosing a parity obstruction can direct effort toward extra structure rather than stronger sieve weights alone.
first_step: Check whether ES's restricted-divisor sequence has a parity-insensitive distribution indistinguishable from a counterexample sequence.

title: Multiplication-table divisor distribution
connection: Multiplication tables share F10, F15, F21: ES needs a divisor in a specific congruence class of a tied integer.
why: Fine-scale divisor distribution could improve over generic divisor-count estimates.
first_step: For the forms 4Cp+1, tabulate divisors by residue class and interval for a bounded sample of primes, then compare with known multiplication-table bounds.

title: Quadratic reciprocity obstructions in parametrised identities
connection: Reciprocity-limited parametrisations share F08, F09, F29: a natural family fails on a quadratic-residue locus.
why: Alternative reciprocity symbols or multiple parameters may cover complementary loci.
first_step: For each known ES family, record its Legendre-symbol condition and test whether two families have complementary failure sets.

title: SAT/SMT certified search for finite identity menus covering residue classes
