connection: SAT solvers settled Boolean Pythagorean triples, Schur number 5 and Keller's conjecture in dim 7 with certified proofs; ES identity families mod M form a finite covering problem per modulus (B1 says no finite menu covers all, but menus can be optimised).
why: SAT/ILP can find minimal identity menus and certify which residue classes mod M are uncoverable by identities of bounded degree — sharp data for B1-type statements.
first_step: Encode 'polynomial identity families with coefficients ≤ K cover class r mod M' as SAT/ILP for M = 840·k and certify the uncovered set.

title: Modular forms and nonvanishing of Fourier coefficients
connection: Coefficient-nonvanishing problems share F19, F20, F36; analytic average nonvanishing may fall short of every prime coefficient.
why: Methods proving nonzero coefficients in specified progressions could give a pointwise route for ES's generating function.
first_step: Identify the modular object, its Eisenstein/cusp decomposition, and available nonvanishing theorems for the relevant prime subsequence.

title: Branching processes for solution-tree growth
connection: Solution-tree problems share F24, F38, F39 and model repeated involutive moves as branching orbits.
why: Tree growth statistics could predict the number of distinct witnesses generated from a seed, while exposing cycles.
first_step: Determine whether the ES transformation graph is locally tree-like at bounded height and calculate its first-return probabilities.

title: Local solubility without integral global points
connection: Local-global counterexamples share F06, F07, F27 and test whether local conditions suffice under positivity and integrality.
why: A catalogue of mechanisms helps distinguish a hidden obstruction from a genuinely hard global construction.
first_step: Compare ES with integral conic and norm-form examples having solutions at every completion but no integral point.

title: Branching of prime representations by quadratic forms
connection: Quadratic-form representation problems share F29, F31, F36 and encode prime classes through splitting and lattice points.
why: Representation by several related forms might give complementary prime classes analogous to a family-cover strategy.
first_step: List the quadratic forms in ES reformulations and compare their represented prime classes via genus characters.

title: Residue-class divisor sums and real-character bias
connection: Divisor sums share F10, F20, F37; exceptional real characters can create one-sided fluctuations.
why: Understanding bias helps avoid a false expectation that generic cancellation forces every class to receive a divisor.
first_step: Compute the real-character contribution to the ES divisor count separately and see when it can dominate the error terms.

title: Adelic methods for integral points in families
connection: Arithmetic families share F06, F07, F13, F20; local densities may vary with the parameter and influence global integral points.
why: Uniform adelic analysis could identify parameter classes with systematically stronger integral-point counts.
first_step: Compute local densities of ES surface points at primes dividing 2p and compare with the global expected count across p residue classes.

title: Zwegers/Appell–Lerch: Kronecker's θ(x²)/θ(x)²-type quotients as Appell–Lerch sums with completions
connection: Quotients of Jacobi theta functions in the elliptic variable are Appell–Lerch sums (Kronecker's identity); Zwegers' completion makes them harmonic Maass–Jacobi forms. ES's (K1′) normal form is such a quotient (F19).
why: Bringmann–Ono-style methods give exact formulas/asymptotics for coefficients of mock objects; a sign-definite exact formula at prime indices would be ES-relevant.
first_step: Match (K1′) of METAPLECTIC_ES with Zwegers' μ(u,v;τ) and compute its completion; check whether the nonholomorphic part is supported on squares (T1).

title: Hurwitz 84(g−1) / the spectrum of 1 − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z: gaps near 0 vs ES's values (n−4)/n
connection: The set {1 − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z} has the minimum positive value 1/42 and a well-studied accumulation structure (Hurwitz). ES asks whether every (n−4)/n belongs to {1 − Σ1/x_i} (n ≥ 5).
why: The order structure of the triangle-group 'area spectrum' (it is well-ordered with known limit points) is classical; ES is a membership question for an explicit sequence in it.
first_step: Compute the area spectrum up to denominator 10⁶ and its intersection with {(n−4)/n}; visualise where the hard n sit in the spectrum.

title: Mihnea & Bogdan (arXiv 2509.00128, 2025): ES verified to 10¹⁸ with solution-count data f(p) — data for signature calibration
connection: The paper extends verification to 10¹⁸ and evaluates the solution-counting function f(p) (F23, F04); check what count statistics are reported.
why: Independent count data to calibrate the log²p model against an outside source.
first_step: Compare their reported count statistics with M_BM(p) predictions at matching heights.

title: Feature flip F13 (cubic → quadric): 4/n = 1/x + 1/y is a hyperbola — fully solved by divisors
connection: The 2-term equation is a split conic; its solvability is a divisor-in-class condition and fails on a positive-density set. ES adds one variable and becomes a cubic surface with hyperbola fibres (F15).
why: Exactly measures what the extra dimension buys: from a single divisor condition (fails often) to a union over the fibre parameter (fails maybe never).
first_step: Compute the density of primes failing the 2-term condition for 4/p − 1/x as x ranges over the first K admissible values; plot the decay in K.

title: Feature flip F24: sub-problems where the heuristic predicts infinitely many failures (single lines) — calibrate the union
connection: Each single ES line (e.g. (★) at a fixed level C) is expected to fail infinitely often (e.g. whenever 4Cp+1 is prime — infinitely often under Dickson/Schinzel); (★) overall fails at 14 primes ≤ 10¹⁰; ES itself is verified to 10¹⁸.
why: The transition 'infinitely many failures → finitely many → none' along the union is a measurable phase diagram; its rate is the key heuristic input.
first_step: Plot, for unions of the first k lines (ordered by density), the count of failures ≤ X for X = 10⁶..10⁹; fit failure counts ~ X·exp(−c k).

title: Feature flip F39: Stern–Brocot / Calkin–Wilf trees enumerate every rational exactly once — is there a tree enumerating ES words with p at a bounded depth?
connection: Universality of a tree enumeration is trivial for rationals; ES's word forest (F39) has connectivity results. A tree in which every prime appears within bounded depth would prove ES₅-type statements.
why: Gives a combinatorial reformulation: bounded-depth covering in an explicit tree (like λ(p) ≤ 3 in the Euclid tree).
first_step: Compute the depth of each hard prime in the Stern–Brocot-type tree generated by the ES₅ moves; check bounded depth up to 10⁸.

title: Smallest-solution size statistics: max denominator of the best ES solution vs. p^θ
connection: ES witnesses have size ≤ poly(p) (F32). The distribution of the minimal possible max-denominator (or minimal level C) over hard primes is an observable comparable to 'least witness' problems (least nonresidue ≪ log² p under GRH, least prime in AP). Note (★) has no level at all for 14 primes ≤ 10¹⁰, so the level statistic needs the union with other lines.
why: If the least witness is always ≤ (log p)^A (in level coordinates) a bounded-search proof shape becomes plausible — B1 says no fixed bound works, but a log-power bound is untouched by B1.
first_step: For hard primes ≤ 10⁹ record the minimal C with R_C(p) > 0 and minimal max(x,y,z)/p; fit against log p.

title: Feature flip F31: Gauss's three-squares count r₃(n) ~ class number — a lattice count with a class-number main term
connection: r₃(n) = 12h(−4n)-type formulas give pointwise lower bounds via Siegel. If any ES count is (even partially) a class number, Siegel-type lower bounds apply (ineffectively).
why: Search for a lattice/genus formulation where an ES sub-count equals a class number or a sum of class numbers of discriminants tied to p.
first_step: Compute R(p) and Σ_{small D} h(−Dp) for hard primes ≤ 10⁶ and regress; any exact relation would be striking.

title: Feature flip F36: problems where GRH IS known to give the pointwise result (least nonresidue, Artin, Ramanujan's form) — common structure
connection: Check whether in each GRH-success case (least nonresidue, Ramanujan's form x²+y²+10z², …) a single L-function or bounded family controls the event at the given n; caveat: Hooley's GRH proof of Artin uses infinitely many Kummer-field zeta functions and gives a density, so the criterion needs refinement. ES's event needs a family of size ≍ p of characters χ_{−4uB} at once.
why: Gives a structural criterion: count how many L-functions must be simultaneously controlled; ES needs too many for GRH-type explicit formulas.
first_step: For each GRH-success sibling, record the number of L-functions and the conductor range used; tabulate vs ES.

title: Feature flip F27 (cone): 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with x,y,z ∈ ℤ_{≠0} and at most one negative — count grows polynomially
connection: Allowing one negative denominator turns the problem into an indefinite one; check whether the solution count then grows like n^δ (it stays finite unless 4/n is a unit fraction). The positive cone cuts it down to polylog.
why: Counting solutions in sub-cones (e.g. one denominator 'barely negative') interpolates between trivial and ES; a continuity/sign-change argument across the cone boundary could be a route.
first_step: Count signed solutions with |negative denominator| ≤ p^θ for hard p and see how the count decays as θ → 0.

title: Additive energy of {1/x} and three-fold sums: Bourgain-type sum-product for reciprocals of integers ≤ N
connection: How many rationals of height ≤ H lie in {1/x + 1/y + 1/z}? Counting 3-fold reciprocal sums is a sum-product/energy question (F33).
why: A lower bound showing the 3-fold reciprocal sumset hits a large fraction of rationals a/n with small numerator would be a density version of ES-type statements.
first_step: Compute |{1/x+1/y+1/z : x,y,z ≤ N}| ∩ {4/n} for N up to 10⁴ and the energy of the reciprocal set.

title: Sierpiński/Riesel numbers: k·2^n + 1 composite for all n via covering — a 'shifted integer always composite' phenomenon
connection: Covering congruences force k·2^n + 1 to be composite for all n. ES needs p-tied integers 4Cp + 1 to be composite WITH a divisor in a class; a covering forcing compositeness is a step in the right direction for a fixed p.
why: If for each hard p a covering-type argument forced some 4Cp + 1 (C ≤ K) to have a SMALL prime factor q ≡ −1 mod 4C·…, a witness might follow (small prime factor in the right class ⇒ witness when cofactor class matches).
first_step: For hard primes, find small primes q with q | 4Cp + 1 and q ≡ −1 (mod 4C) for some C < q (i.e. C ≡ −(4p)⁻¹ mod q with the class condition); count such (q, C) pairs with q ≤ log²p.

title: Maynard 'dense clusters of primes in subsets' for certificate families
connection: Maynard (Compositio 2016) shows any positive-density subset of admissible linear forms contains many simultaneously prime values; ES certificates are indexed by a dense set of linear forms in the C-parameter (4Cp+1, Cp+...).
why: Gives a combinatorial robustness: we need not control which certificate fires, only that a dense sub-family of forms is admissible at p.
first_step: Check whether the family {4Cp+1 : C ≤ X} with the divisor-in-class event can be recast as primality of auxiliary linear forms f = (4Cp+1)/d for d in a fixed finite set; test admissibility mod small primes.

title: Lichtman beyond-square-root Goldbach/AP methods for tied moduli
connection: Lichtman (2023) improves level of distribution for primes in APs with well-factorable weights to x^{0.617…} and uses it for Goldbach-type counts; ES Type I/II counts are linear-sieve-like sums over moduli 4C.
why: Any improvement in the level for the ES counting function shrinks the exceptional set exponent (repo's E(N) ≪ N exp(−c(log N)^{3/4})).
first_step: Check whether Lichtman's well-factorable weights can be placed on the C-variable (4C | modulus) in the repo's exceptional-set argument (paper/es-threequarter-note.tex).

title: Guth–Maynard large values of Dirichlet polynomials → short-interval exceptional sets
connection: Guth–Maynard (2024) improve zero-density (Ingham 12/5 → 30/13) via large-values estimates; ES exceptional-set bounds pass through prime counts in short intervals/APs.
why: Zero-density improvements translate to shorter intervals where almost all ES-good primes are detected; could sharpen E(N) or the size of windows where every prime is covered.
first_step: Locate in the repo's exceptional-set notes which zero-density exponent is used and recompute the window exponent with A = 30/13.

title: Helfgott–Radziwiłł expansion of divisibility graphs
connection: Helfgott–Radziwiłł (2021) prove expansion of graphs on integers where n ~ n+p if p | n (prime p in a range), improving log-Chowla; ES witnesses are divisibility relations d | N with N in a p-tied family.
why: A divisibility-graph expander on {4Cp+1 : C ≤ X} could transport 'some witness' along edges, the kind of local-to-global step ES lacks.
first_step: Build the graph on C ≤ 10^5 (fixed p) with edges C ~ C' if a common prime ℓ ≤ H divides both 4Cp+1 and 4C'p+1 and compute its spectral gap.

title: Linear correlations of restricted divisor functions (Matthiesen-type) with p as a coefficient
connection: Matthiesen proved asymptotics for Σ_t Π_i f(L_i(t)) for divisor-type f via the Green–Tao machinery. R(p) is Σ_C of a restricted divisor function of the linear form 4pC + 1; with more structure (several levels) it becomes a correlation.
why: Gives asymptotics with uniformity questions in the coefficient p — the precise point to check.
first_step: Matthiesen, 'Linear correlations of multiplicative functions', Proc. LMS 121 (2020), arXiv:1606.04482 — verified: fixed linear forms only, coefficients may NOT grow with the range; so the needed input is a uniform-in-coefficients version — state it precisely and look for partial results (e.g. for τ-type functions via Kloosterman methods).

title: Maynard 'primes represented by incomplete norm forms' for ES norm forms
connection: Maynard (Forum Pi 2020) counts primes as norms N(a1ω1+…+akωk) with missing coordinates, using a sieve beyond classical parity; ES Type I divisor event is a norm-divisibility event in quadratic fields.
why: Incomplete-norm-form technology handles thin sets of algebraic integers, relevant to certificates where only a few coordinates vary (c,d at fixed p).
first_step: Check whether 'N𝔞 for 𝔞 | (p+2c√−d)' with c,d in boxes is an incomplete-norm-form set in Maynard's sense.

title: de la Bretèche–Drappeau level of distribution of quadratic polynomials
connection: de la Bretèche–Drappeau (JEMS 2020) prove level of distribution beyond 1 for #{n ≤ x : q | n² + D} averaged over q; ES Type I is 'f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p (mod 4cd)'.
why: Exactly the object (divisors of a quadratic value) with level > 1 — needed when f is larger than the square root.
first_step: Check whether their result allows a residue condition f ≡ a (mod 4cd) on the modulus f itself, and whether the polynomial variable can be c (with p fixed).

title: Fouvry–Kowalski–Michel trace functions over primes for ES residue indicators
connection: FKM show algebraic trace functions K(n) mod q have Σ_{p≤x} K(p) = o(π(x)) for x ≥ q^{3/4+ε}; ES conditions like '(−p mod 4C) ∈ some set' are trace-function-type functions of p.
why: Gives equidistribution of primes p against arbitrary algebraic weights — e.g. the set of p for which a given finite menu fails mod q.
first_step: Check whether the 'menu failure' indicator mod a prime q (FIXED_MODULUS_SHOTS.md) is a bounded-conductor trace function and apply FKM to get prime densities.

title: Granville–Koukoulopoulos–Matomäki 'when the sieve works'
connection: GKM (Duke 2015) characterise when sifted sets by a set of primes have the expected density; the 'divisors avoid a coset structure' condition in ES is a sifted-set condition on prime factors of 4Cp+1.
why: Precise conditions for sieve heuristics to be correct are what a pointwise lower-tail claim needs.
first_step: Check whether the sifting set 'primes ℓ whose class mod 4C lies in a subgroup H not containing −1' satisfies GKM hypotheses uniformly in C.

title: Erdős primitive-set / Lichtman: ES-covered n as a set of multiples
connection: Since a solution for n gives one for every multiple of n, the set of n covered by any fixed family of identities is a set of multiples ℳ(B) of a primitive set B; Lichtman (2022) proved the Erdős primitive set conjecture Σ 1/(b log b) ≤ Σ_p 1/(p log p).
why: Sets-of-multiples theory (Besicovitch, Erdős, Hall) quantifies how much a family covers and how the uncovered set (divisor-closed) can look.
first_step: For the repo's identity menus up to modulus M, compute the primitive generator set B among primes ≤ 10^7 and the density of ℳ(B); test whether Σ_{b∈B} 1/(b log b) tracks the uncovered density.

title: Random multiplicative function model of (·/p) on divisor-generated sets (Harper's low moments)
connection: Model (·/p) restricted to S₃(p) by a random multiplicative function f. Then ES₅ failure is 'f ≡ 1 on a structured set'. Harper showed better-than-square-root cancellation for Σ f(n) (low moments), so multiplicative structure reduces fluctuations.
why: It is the native probabilistic model for character values with multiplicative constraints; it gives a heuristic failure probability that respects multiplicative dependencies among elements of S₃(p).
first_step: Compute the multiplicative dependency rank of S₃(p) (dimension of the F₂-span of its exponent vectors over primes). The failure probability under the model is 2^{−rank}; compare with observed.

title: Harel–Mousset–Samotij upper tails via entropic stability (dual for R(p))
connection: HMS 'Upper tails via high moments and entropic stability' gives sharp upper tails for subgraph counts; for ES, upper-tail control of the *failure* indicator counts translates into exceptional-set bounds.
why: Exceptional-set results are upper tails of a 'number of uncovered p' variable.
first_step: Write E(N) as a polynomial count and check whether HMS-type moment methods give anything beyond Vaughan-type bounds.

title: Ustinov's Kloosterman-sum method for continued-fraction length statistics
connection: Ustinov computes asymptotics of the number of a/b with prescribed CF statistics by reducing to lattice-point counts with Kloosterman sums; ES₅ is λ(p) ≤ 3 (a length-3 CF event).
why: Gives exact averaged main terms with power savings for CF-length events, possibly pointwise-in-p with a C-average.
first_step: Reproduce Ustinov's count of (a,b) with a/b having CF length 3 and specialize to b tied to p.

title: Y. Zhang's Landau–Siegel preprint (claimed) as alternate effectivity input
connection: Yitang Zhang's 2022 preprint claims L(1,χ) ≫ (log D)^{−2022}; same effectivity consequences as above.
why: A second independent route to effective Siegel-type input.
first_step: Check the current status (errata, refereeing) of Zhang's arXiv:2211.02515 before relying on it.

title: Pascadi exceptional Maass form large sieve → ES dispersion
connection: Pascadi (2024) proves large sieve inequalities for exceptional Maass forms improving dispersion estimates (primes in APs to large moduli); the repo's exceptional-set argument uses dispersion-type steps.
why: Better exceptional-eigenvalue control improves level of distribution in the Type II dispersion step.
first_step: Locate in EXCEPTIONAL_TYPEI_LOGLOG2.md where θ = 7/64 enters and recompute with Pascadi's bounds.

title: Bloom–Sisask log-barrier Roth bound and its almost-periodicity
connection: Bloom–Sisask broke the logarithmic barrier in Roth's theorem using Croot–Sisask almost periodicity; ES certificate sets are sumsets/product sets of divisor sets.
why: Croot–Sisask almost-periodicity is a general tool for showing A·B (here divisor quotients) contains long structured pieces.
first_step: Apply Croot–Sisask to the convolution 1_D * 1_{D^{-1}} on (ℤ/e)^× with D = divisor set of N and quantify the approximate periods.

title: Bourgain–Glibichuk–Konyagin exponential sums over small multiplicative subgroups
connection: BGK: subgroups H ⊂ 𝔽_p^× with |H| > p^δ have nontrivial exponential sums; the subgroup generated by small primes / prime factors of N mod e is such an H.
why: Additive equidistribution of H mod e could feed into counts of e with −1 ∈ ⟨factors of N⟩.
first_step: For e prime, compute |⟨prime factors of (p+e)/4⟩| in 𝔽_e^× at hard primes and check how often −1 ∈ H fails (equivalently |H| odd).

title: Sum-product in ℤ/q for composite q (Bourgain) for ES moduli 4C
connection: Bourgain's sum-product and exponential-sum bounds for arbitrary q handle composite moduli; ES moduli 4C, 4cd are composite and smooth.
why: The ES condition mixes additive (4Cp+1) and multiplicative (divisor class) structure — a sum-product configuration.
first_step: State the ES Type I condition as 'A + B ∩ product set' in ℤ/4C and check whether Bourgain's composite-modulus results say anything at C ≈ p^θ.

title: Is ES critical or supercritical? Fractional expectation threshold of the level hypergraph
connection: Park–Pham relate thresholds to expectation thresholds. The repo measures ≈ (0.44 → 0.97)·log p expected hit levels (critical regime). Compute, in a random model matching ES's level statistics, the threshold for 'some level hits' and see whether ES sits above it by a growing margin.
why: If ES is only 'critically' above threshold in natural models, any proof must exploit non-random structure; if supercritical, second-moment-type methods are favoured.
first_step: Simulate the matched random model and compute P(no hit) as a function of the scaling parameter; compare with data for hard primes.

title: Alweiss–Lovett–Wu–Zhang sunflowers among minimal ES solutions → identity families
connection: ALWZ improved sunflower bounds to (log w)^{w(1+o(1))}; families of ES solutions across many n, encoded as sets of prime-power factors of (x,y,z), contain sunflowers, which correspond to shared 'cores' i.e. parametric identity families.
why: Mechanically extracts polynomial identities (Mordell-type) from solution data.
first_step: Encode the minimal solutions for primes p ≤ 10^6 in a fixed Mordell class as sets of (prime, exponent, slot) and search for sunflowers with ≥3 petals.

title: Absorption method (Keevash / Kwan–Sah–Sawhney–Simkin) — 'almost all → all' gadgets
connection: Iterative absorption converts near-perfect structures into perfect ones by pre-reserving absorbers; ES knows almost-all results, and the missing step is exactly almost-all → all.
why: If ES solutions for n could be built from solutions of auxiliary numbers with an 'absorber' reserving flexibility, the exceptional set could be absorbed.
first_step: Look for an ES operation combining solutions of several auxiliary integers (m1,…,mk tied to p) into a solution for p; test on data whether such auxiliary sets always contain a solvable member.

title: Szemerédi regularity / arithmetic regularity (Green; Green–Tao) for the failure set
connection: Arithmetic regularity decomposes any set into structured + pseudorandom parts; the ES failure set E is divisor-closed and scales from q ≡ 3 (mod 4) can't fill an AP.
why: Arithmetic regularity applied to E (if nonempty, hypothetically) would force structure contradicting known closure properties — a disproof-shape calibration.
first_step: List all closure properties E must satisfy (divisor-closed, avoids identity classes, density zero) and check whether arithmetic regularity yields a contradiction for positive relative density in primes.

title: Green–Tao–Ziegler linear equations in primes for prime-denominator ES solutions
connection: GTZ count prime solutions of finite-complexity linear systems; ES solutions with prime denominators reduce to linear equations after fixing products (e.g. Type II with x = (p+e)/4 prime-parametrised).
why: Counting prime-denominator ES solutions across p gives averaged statements with primes in all slots.
first_step: Enumerate ES solution shapes where all three denominators are of the form (linear form in parameters) and identify a finite-complexity linear system in primes.

title: OAI 025 short Egyptian fractions O(log log b) (claimed) — length-3 specialization
connection: OAI family 025 claims every a/b is a sum of O(log log b) distinct unit fractions, sharp; ES asks for exactly 3 terms at a = 4.
why: The construction's mechanism (how denominators are chosen) could expose a 'small number of terms' greedy-plus-smooth technique; calibration of what length is cheap.
first_step: Read the OAI 025 build sources and record which step needs Θ(log log b) terms; check whether for a = 4 the construction degenerates to fewer terms.

title: Campos–Griffiths–Morris–Sahasrabudhe 'book algorithm' as a structured search heuristic
connection: The exponential improvement for diagonal Ramsey uses a book-building algorithm controlling red/blue densities; ES certificate search is a two-colour (residue/non-residue) structure problem on divisor sets.
why: The book algorithm is a template for finding large structured objects in a 2-coloured complete structure.
first_step: Colour pairs of prime factors of N by whether their product ratio class is a QR mod e; search for a 'book' configuration implying −1 ∈ Q.

title: Expander mixing on Cayley graphs of (ℤ/e)^× generated by prime factors of N
connection: Alon–Roichman: O(log|G|) random generators give an expander; the ES e-slice uses the Cayley graph on (ℤ/e)^× generated by the ω(N) ≈ log log N prime factors of N.
why: Quantifies precisely why one integer's factors are too few to force −1 (B2) and what extra generators (other slices) would need to be pooled.
first_step: Compute spectral gaps of Cayley graphs of (ℤ/e)^× with generators = prime factors of N and also with pooled generators from several slices sharing e.

title: Golsefidy–Varjú superstrong approximation for the ES₅ semigroup
connection: Salehi Golsefidy–Varjú prove expansion for perfect groups' congruence quotients; ES₅ words generate a semigroup in SL₂(ℤ) whose Zariski closure and congruence images are computable.
why: Determines whether the ES₅ semigroup has full congruence image mod every q (local-global input).
first_step: Compute the Zariski closure and mod-q images of the semigroup generated by the ES₅ letters for small q.

title: Kontorovich–Nakamura crystallographic packings ↔ ES integral geometry
connection: Kontorovich–Nakamura classify crystallographic sphere packings via integral Lorentzian reflective lattices; ES has lattice/quaternion reformulations and a cubic integral surface.
why: Packing local-global problems (Apollonian) are the main family with proved reciprocity obstructions akin to T1.
first_step: Check whether any ES lattice L_ρ (LATTICE_MEETING.md) is a reflective Lorentzian lattice.

title: Erdős–Szemerédi sum-product / Solymosi for ES additive-multiplicative mixing
connection: Sum-product phenomenon: A+A or A·A large; the ES integer families {4Cp+1} are additive shifts while certificates are multiplicative.
why: Sum-product heuristics predict that additive families can't stay multiplicatively structured, supporting divisor-class equidistribution.
first_step: Measure multiplicative energy of {4Cp+1 : C ≤ X} vs random integers of the same size.

title: Decoupling/energy for the hyperbolic ES surface {4uBC − u − B}
connection: BDG decoupling bounds moments of exponential sums over curves. Additive energy of the ES-word set (#{w₁ = w₂} with w = 4uBC−u−B ≤ N) controls the second moment Σ_n R(n)².
why: Second-moment control is the ingredient of every almost-all → pointwise attempt via variance; decoupling-type bounds for this specific surface could be sharp.
first_step: Compute the energy E(N) = Σ_{n≤N} R(n)² for N up to 10⁷ and fit N·(log N)^a; compare with what a decoupling inequality for (u, B, uB) would predict.

title: U_n as a Looijenga pair: Gross–Hacking–Keel theta functions on the ES log CY surface
connection: The projective closure 4xyz = nw(xy+yz+zx) minus the triangle w = 0 is a log Calabi–Yau surface with a toric model: P² blown up at three collinear boundary points (GEOMETRY_ES Prop 2.1). GHK construct a canonical basis of theta functions on the mirror family of any Looijenga pair, indexed by integral points of the tropicalisation.
why: Theta functions give canonical regular functions with positive structure constants. If positive integer points of U_n correspond to positivity of some theta function's values, the native existence tools are scattering diagrams.
first_step: Read GHKS 'The mirror of the cubic surface' and check whether the nodal (Cayley) degeneration with boundary through nodes is covered; compute the tropicalisation of U_n.

title: Skorobogatov–Sofos: Schinzel's Hypothesis on average → ES certificate families
connection: SS prove Schinzel's Hypothesis H for 100% of polynomials in families ordered by coefficient height and deduce Hasse principle for 100% of fibred varieties; ES certificates are values of polynomials in (c,d,e) tied to p.
why: Gives a rigorous 'almost all polynomials in a family behave' statement, the polynomial analogue of 'almost all p'.
first_step: Embed the ES Type I certificate polynomial family into a family indexed by coefficients and check which statement of SS transfers (likely 'ES for 100% of a coefficient family', not ES itself).

title: Browning–Matthiesen norm forms equal to products of linear polynomials
connection: BM prove HP/weak approximation for N_{K/ℚ}(x) = ∏ L_i(t) using additive combinatorics (GT linear equations machinery); ES Type I reads f | N(p + 2c√−d) — divisors of norms of linear forms in (c,d).
why: Additive combinatorics replaced sieve hypotheses in BM — the same could make averaged ES certificate counts in (c,d) unconditional.
first_step: Rewrite the Type I event as the solubility of N_{ℚ(√−d)/ℚ}(α) = f·g with α linear in parameters and match to BM's setting.

title: Whang: nonlinear descent on moduli of local systems → is U_n a relative character variety?
connection: Whang proves structure theorems for integral points on moduli of SL₂ local systems on surfaces (Markoff-type) via mapping class group descent; the Cayley cubic is the SL₂ character variety of the four-holed sphere at special boundary traces.
why: If U_n is (an integral model of) a relative character variety, mapping-class-group descent gives finiteness of orbits of integral points.
first_step: Match U_n to the Fricke cubic of the four-holed sphere: find boundary traces (a,b,c,d) making the Fricke cubic projectively equal to 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) with the ES boundary.

title: Lawrence–Venkatesh p-adic period maps for families of ES curves
connection: LV prove finiteness of S-integral points on hypersurfaces/curves via big monodromy of p-adic period maps; ES Type I/II fibres (fix one denominator) are genus-0 curves, but auxiliary curves (fix two certificate parameters with extra integrality) may have higher genus.
why: LV-type finiteness would be a disproof-shape tool (bounding structured solution families) rather than an existence tool.
first_step: Identify any naturally occurring higher-genus curve in the ES certificate space (e.g. requiring two simultaneous ES solutions with a shared denominator) and compute its genus.

title: Pila–Wilkie / Binyamini–Novikov sharply o-minimal counting for ES real-analytic families
connection: Pila–Wilkie counts rational points on transcendental parts of definable sets; Binyamini–Novikov(–Zack) give effective polylog versions for sharply o-minimal structures. ES counting functions involve log-like main terms in a definable family (the real points of U_n as n varies).
why: The count M_BM(p) ≍ log² p is polylogarithmic — the same scale as sharply o-minimal point counts; a structural explanation of 'polylog' could come from there.
first_step: Check whether the set {(n, x/n, y/n, z/n)} is definable in ℝ_exp after a log-scaling and whether its algebraic part is all of it (then Pila–Wilkie says nothing).

title: Santens / Wilsch integral Manin conjecture applied to U_n
connection: Santens proves Manin's conjecture for integral points on toric varieties; Wilsch counts integral points on log Fano threefolds; Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel give the predicted shape. f(n) is a count of integral points on the log CY U_n (not log Fano) with growing n.
why: The log CY case predicts polylog growth — matching M_BM ≍ log²; an integral-Manin framework could give a conceptual main term.
first_step: Compute Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel's predicted exponent of log B for integral points on the Cayley cubic minus triangle and compare with log² p.

title: Sections of the ES fibration over 𝔽_q(t) via free rational curves (Browning–Sawin)
connection: Browning–Sawin use the function-field circle method to count/describe spaces of rational curves on hypersurfaces; ES polynomial identities are sections of U → A¹_n, i.e. rational curves on the total space.
why: Counting sections of bounded degree over 𝔽_q(t) quantifies the Mordell–Schinzel barrier and might find all identity families of a given degree.
first_step: Set up the moduli of degree-d sections of the ES total space over 𝔽_q(t) and compute its dimension; compare with known Mordell/Schinzel identity families.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Bhargava–Gauss composition of x²+4dy² values in Type I
connection: Type I needs f | p² + 4c²d: values of the form X² + 4dY² at (p,c); divisors of represented values are represented by forms in the same genus/class group (composition).
why: Recasts the Type I event as a class-group statement about the ideal above f in the order of discriminant −16d — where Bhargava cubes / composition laws act.
first_step: For hard primes, compute the class-group element of each prime divisor of p²+4c²d and see whether the failure is explained by class-group parity.

title: Smith's Rédei-symbol / governing-field method for distributions of 'sterility' across p
connection: A. Smith's work on 2^∞-Selmer and class groups uses governing fields and additive combinatorics on Boolean cubes of twists to get distributions of higher Rédei symbols; ES T1 is a reciprocity (Rédei-type) obstruction and repo memos treat Rédei matrices.
why: Could prove that 'sterility patterns' up to depth k have the predicted distribution across p — a structured 100%-type statement.
first_step: Model ES sterility at depth k (fixed moduli) as a Rédei-matrix event and compute its distribution over p ≤ 10^8; compare with a Smith-type uniform model.

title: Pierce et al. ℓ-torsion & Ellenberg–Venkatesh lemma: many small split primes ⇒ small torsion
connection: The EV lemma converts many small split primes into ℓ-torsion bounds; ES Type I needs small split primes in Q(√−d) in specific classes.
why: Reverse direction: class-group structure (small 2-torsion) forces many small primes in many classes, possibly including the ES-needed class.
first_step: For d ≤ 100 and hard p, compute the classes of small split primes in Cl(−16d) and whether the Type I-needed class is hit.

title: Cremona symmetries of the Cayley cubic and ES solution moves
connection: The Cayley cubic's automorphism/birational symmetry group includes S₄ on the nodes and quadratic Cremona maps (inversion x ↦ 1/x relates to the reciprocal plane); ES only uses S₃ permutations.
why: Any extra symmetry preserving the integral structure would give the missing ES 'group action' (cf. Chen/Markoff).
first_step: List the birational automorphisms of σ₃ = 0 commuting with w′ = const and test their action on ES solutions for small n.

title: Perfectoid tilting Q_p(p^{1/p^∞}) ↔ 𝔽_p((t^{1/p^∞})) for local ES statements (honest low-value item)
connection: Scholze's tilting equivalence relates étale covers in mixed and equal characteristic; ES over 𝔽_q[T] has proved variants, but tilting is a local (p-adic) statement and ES's difficulty is global.
why: Recorded for completeness: the only ES-side objects it can touch are local solubility and local densities, which are already known.
first_step: Check whether any repo statement uses a local-at-p fact over 𝔽_q((t)) that lacks a mixed-characteristic counterpart; if none, close this item.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Fargues–Scholze / local Langlands — no natural ES object (recorded)
connection: Geometrisation of local Langlands (Fargues–Scholze) concerns representations of p-adic groups; ES has no evident reductive-group or Galois-representation object attached.
why: Recording the null result prevents later re-proposal; the nearest real link would go through automorphic forms attached to ES counts (theta series), which are GL₂/GL₁ and need no geometrisation.
first_step: Ask whether any ES count is a Fourier coefficient of an automorphic form on a group of rank ≥ 2; if not, close.

title: Motivic / Grothendieck-ring class of U_n and its point counts
connection: The class [U_n] in K₀(Var) and its point counts #U_n(𝔽_ℓ) are computable (Cayley cubic minus triangle); integral-point main terms are built from such local counts.
why: Exact point counts mod ℓ give exact local densities and identify any 'local sterility' structure for free.
first_step: Compute #U_n(𝔽_ℓ) symbolically as a function of n mod ℓ and verify it's ℓ² − 3ℓ + c(n,ℓ) style.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Type II as SL₂(ℤ) matrices with prescribed off-diagonal product (hyperbolic lattice counting)
connection: ff′ − ab = 1 with ab = 4c²dp: Type II certificates are integer matrices of determinant 1 with diagonal ≡ −1 (mod 4cd) and off-diagonal product fixed — a hyperbolic lattice-point problem in Γ(4cd)-cosets.
why: Spectral counting in congruence subgroups (Selberg 3/16, Kim–Sarnak 7/64) applies; the fixed product ab is a 'divisor-split' constraint.
first_step: Count matrices in a coset of Γ(4cd) with |entries| ≤ T and ab = 4c²dp numerically, compare with the spectral main term.

title: Duke's theorem / torus packets (OAI 015 higher-dim Duke, claimed) for ES lattices
connection: Duke's theorem: class-group orbits (CM points, closed geodesics) equidistribute as discriminant → ∞; OAI 015 claims higher-degree torus-packet equidistribution. ES Type I lives in class groups of discriminant −16d tied to p.
why: Equidistribution of class-group packets is a pointwise-in-discriminant statement — at one discriminant, all of the packet equidistributes.
first_step: Find a discriminant D(p) → ∞ such that ES(p) follows from some ideal class in the packet hitting a fixed open set of the modular surface.

title: Li–Zhang's theorem on Kudla–Rapoport: unitary special cycles and an arithmetic Diff-parity
connection: KUDLA_ES links T1 to oddness of Kudla's Diff(T). In the unitary setting, Li–Zhang proved the Kudla–Rapoport conjecture (arithmetic intersection numbers = derivatives of local densities).
why: If ES certificates are special cycles on a unitary Shimura variety, intersection numbers have exact local formulas, and positivity is geometric.
first_step: Identify which ES count, if any, appears as a degree of a special cycle (positive by geometry), per KUDLA_ES.md.

title: Shifted convolution sums (Blomer, Holowinsky) for Σ_C r(4Cp+1)-type ES sums
connection: Shifted convolution sums Σ a(n)b(n+h) of automorphic coefficients have spectral asymptotics; ES Type I/II correlate divisor-class counts at N and N + (shift) across slices.
why: Second moments of ES counts over C at fixed p are shifted convolutions of Eisenstein coefficients.
first_step: Express Σ_C R_C(p)² as a shifted convolution and compute its main term numerically vs data.

title: Hecke-like transport between f(n) and f(ℓn)
connection: Solutions for n lift to ℓn (multiplicativity); a Hecke operator T_ℓ on solution sets would also need an adjoint pulling solutions from ℓn back to n, which is exactly the missing direction for primes.
why: If solution counts satisfied Hecke-type relations (f(ℓ²n) related to f(n), f(ℓn)), one could deduce f(p) > 0 from composite data.
first_step: Compute f(n), f(ℓn), f(ℓ²n) for n prime ≤ 10^5, ℓ ≤ 13 and fit linear relations; check whether any Hecke-type identity holds.

title: Marcus–Spielman–Srivastava interlacing families: existence of one good member
connection: MSS proved bipartite Ramanujan graphs of every degree exist by showing the expected characteristic polynomial's root bounds the root of some member (interlacing families); ES needs one good member (certificate) among a family.
why: Interlacing gives existence beyond first-moment counting when the quantity is a polynomial root — an unusual existence mechanism worth checking for ES polynomial encodings.
first_step: Encode ES certificates at p as roots/zeros of a family of real-rooted polynomials (e.g. via the lattice L_ρ's theta function restricted to a line) and test interlacing.

title: Geodesic-flow coding (Series) of γ_w: ES₅ as a closed geodesic with 3 cusp excursions of prescribed depths
connection: Caroline Series' coding links the cutting sequence of a geodesic to its CF expansion, so cusp-excursion depths correspond to partial quotients. A word gives a closed geodesic whose (HJ) coding has 3 blocks of depths (v, t, u), plus a p-condition.
why: Shrinking-target and logarithm-law results (Sullivan) describe cusp excursions statistically. Prescribed exact-depth triples relate to 'periodic orbits with prescribed excursions' counts (Pollicott, Lalley).
first_step: Count closed geodesics whose coding is exactly a 3-block HJ word with depths in given ranges; compare with the word count via the p-constraint.

title: Murmurations for ES counts (He–Lee–Oliver–Pozdnyakov; Zubrilina)
connection: Murmurations: averages of Frobenius traces a_p over families ordered by conductor show oscillations in p/N, explained by Zubrilina via trace formula; ES counts f(p) averaged over p in a window with normalisation by a scale (e.g. 4C ~ p^θ) might show analogous oscillations.
why: A murmuration-type oscillation would reveal a hidden spectral term in ES counts — new structure for heuristics.
first_step: Plot normalised ES counts f(p)/log²p averaged over p in windows against p mod M / p modulo small structures and against p/X for X ranges; look for oscillatory patterns.

title: Rudnick–Soundararajan lower bounds for moments → 'at least one large term'
connection: Rudnick–Soundararajan prove lower bounds for moments of L-function families by a simple Hölder trick; ES needs lower bounds for a count of certificates.
why: Moment lower bounds (≥ expected order) for R(p) over a C-family at fixed p would show certificates are not all absent — but only if the family is at fixed p.
first_step: Apply the RS Hölder trick to Σ_C R_C(p) with weights and see whether it gives Σ_C R_C(p) ≫ main term at a single p.

title: Nicolas–Serre Hecke algebra mod 2 for parity of ES counts
connection: Nicolas–Serre describe coefficients of modular forms mod 2 via a nilpotent Hecke algebra; the repo PROVED complement pairing makes level counts even and R(p)/2 mod 2 looks like a fair coin.
why: If ES counts relate to Eisenstein coefficients, their parities might be governed by mod-2 modular forms rather than randomness.
first_step: Compute R(p)/2 mod 2 and the parity of class-divisor counts at 4Cp+1 and compare with the mod-2 behaviour of the corresponding Eisenstein coefficients.

title: Pila–Shankar–Tsimerman André–Oort heights for the CM tetrahedron of the Cayley cubic
connection: PST proved André–Oort via canonical height bounds; the Cayley cubic/Markoff CM dictionary in the repo (cayley_markoff_cm) relates special points to CM data.
why: Height bounds for special points might constrain which CM points carry ES solutions (a finiteness/distribution statement).
first_step: Locate the CM-point parametrisation in cayley_markoff_cm.md and check whether ES integral points map to special points of bounded height.

title: Effective Oppenheim (Lindenstrauss–Margulis–Mohammadi–Shah) for indefinite ternary ES forms
connection: LMMS give effective density of values of indefinite ternary forms at integer points; the quadratic part n(xy+yz+zx) of U_n is an indefinite ternary form.
why: Effective value-distribution of the quadratic part near targets proportional to xyz may constrain solution geometry.
first_step: Write ES as Q(x,y,z) = (4/n)·xyz with Q = xy+yz+zx and see whether effective Oppenheim-type counting with a cubic weight is meaningful.

title: Theta quotient / eta-quotient identities for ES counts (exact formulas)
connection: Eta-quotient identities give exact divisor-sum formulas for representation numbers (e.g. r₄, r₈); ES has theta-quotient reformulations in the repo.
why: An exact formula (sum of divisor functions) for some ES-adjacent count would make positivity checkable.
first_step: Search the ES theta-quotient reformulation for a modular form of small level whose coefficients equal an ES sub-count; test by computing 200 coefficients.

title: LLL / Coppersmith small roots for ES Type I certificates at fixed p
connection: Coppersmith's method finds small roots of modular polynomials; Type I asks for f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p (mod 4cd), a small-root problem for a polynomial in (c,d) modulo an unknown divisor (Howgrave-Graham variant).
why: Turns certificate search into lattice reduction with provable size ranges; complements factoring-based search at 10^18–10^25.
first_step: Implement Howgrave-Graham's 'approximate common divisor / unknown divisor' lattice for N(c) = p² + 4c²d, d fixed, and compare its hit rate with brute force at p ~ 10^20.

title: Lean-checked certificate verifier for ES solutions at specific hard primes
connection: A Lean `decide`/`norm_num` proof that 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z for explicit p is trivial; a verified checker for large batches (with external computation) mirrors certified-SAT practice.
why: Turns computational evidence (e.g. 10^18 claims) into checkable artefacts — important since the 10^18 claim is an unrefereed preprint.
first_step: Write a Lean function checking ES solutions given (p,x,y,z) and run it on the repo's hard-prime certificates.

title: PatternBoost / Wagner RL for counterexamples to ES sub-conjectures
connection: Wagner (2021) and PatternBoost (Charton–Ellenberg–Wagner–Williamson 2024) find counterexamples to combinatorial conjectures via RL/transformer-guided local search; ES sub-conjectures (U(n) sporadic set, S_{n,k} zero patterns, sibling failures) are searchable.
why: Finding new sporadic exceptions in siblings refines the zero law; finding none strengthens conjectural lists.
first_step: Run local-search guided by a learned score over n ≤ 10^12 restricted to low-count residue cells for U(n) and S_{n,−4}.

title: Hilbert's tenth problem over ℚ (OAI 004, claimed) and Koenigsmann: logical status of ES variants
connection: OAI 004 claims H10 over ℚ is undecidable; Koenigsmann defined ℤ in ℚ by a universal formula. ES is a Π₁ statement once solution sizes are bounded (x ≤ 3n/4, etc.).
why: Being Π₁, ES is 'decided by a counterexample if false'; logic tools say nothing about truth, but undecidability results for families (e.g. 'given polynomial family, does every n have an Egyptian representation') calibrate generality.
first_step: Write ES explicitly as a bounded-quantifier Π₁ sentence and note which generalisations (k/n with arbitrary k, unbounded term count) cross into undecidable territory.

title: Complexity of finding an ES solution: factoring-oracle reduction
connection: Given p, an ES solution is found by factoring a few p-tied integers until a divisor lands in the class; expected polylog many integers. So ES-search is (heuristically) in ZPP^{FACTOR}, and in BQP via Shor.
why: A complexity statement 'ES search is as hard as factoring' (or easier) would be a novel angle; a proof that search is easy for all p would be a constructive ES proof.
first_step: Formalise the reduction and test whether ES certificates can be found without any factoring (e.g. via Coppersmith) for random large p.

title: Interval/ball arithmetic certified analytic constants (Arb/FLINT) for explicit exceptional sets
connection: Arb provides rigorous numerics; explicit versions of the repo's exceptional-set or main-term constants need certified evaluation of Euler products and integrals.
why: Needed for any explicit statement (calibration with verification).
first_step: Compute M_BM(p)'s Euler-product constant with Arb to 30 digits with certified error.

title: Equational-theories-project-style crowdsourced + automated exploration of ES variants
connection: Tao's Equational Theories Project (2024) combined ATPs, Lean and crowdsourcing to settle ~22 million implications; ES has a large lattice of variants (k/n, number of terms, sign constraints, rings) with implication structure.
why: Mapping the implication lattice among ES variants (which imply which; which fail where) is mechanical and ATP-friendly.
first_step: List 50 ES variants in the repo (siblings, coprime/non-coprime, Type I/II, ES₅, I3) and compute an implication matrix with counterexamples from data.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Distributed GPU search for counterexamples in Mordell-hard cells beyond 10^18 (targeted, not exhaustive)
connection: Exhaustive verification is at 10^18; targeted search in the lowest-count residue cells (DISPROOF_AVENUES) at 10^20–10^30 is feasible on GPUs with Type II e-slice tests.
why: Calibration of the zero law at much larger scales where expected counts are still polylog.
first_step: Port the e-slice test to CUDA for a fixed cell and benchmark primes per second at 10^24.

title: Fake-ES models: same local statistics, almost-all holds, infinitely many failures
connection: Kahane–Katznelson show a.e. results can be sharp for any null set. Build synthetic 'ES-like' problems (random divisor data with ES's congruence statistics, or ES with a perturbed rule) where Vaughan's proof goes through verbatim but failures are infinite; the real proof must use a feature the fakes lack.
why: Identifies which properties of the integers any ES proof must use — the constructive face of the barrier map.
first_step: Construct a random model of 'divisors of 4Cp+1' with independent prime-factor classes, run the almost-all argument, and check what pointwise statement fails.

title: Persistent data releases + OEIS-style sequence mining for ES statistics
connection: Many breakthroughs came from noticing sequences (OEIS); ES statistics (min-count primes, record-hard primes, sibling failure lists) could be matched against OEIS.
why: Cheap: an OEIS hit could connect ES failure sets of siblings to known sequences (e.g. S_{n,−4} failures {2,9,21,165,945,1197}).
first_step: Query OEIS for the sibling failure lists and U(n)'s sporadic set {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145}.

title: OAI 012 joint Dickman law for consecutive integers ↔ consecutive Type II slices
connection: OAI 012 claims log P⁺(n)/log n and log P⁺(n+1)/log n are asymptotically independent (Erdős–Pomerance). At fixed p the Type II slices N_e = (p+e)/4, e = e₀, e₀+4, …, are consecutive integers N, N+1, N+2, …
why: Joint anatomy of consecutive integers is exactly the joint law of successive ES slices at one p; independence-type theorems for consecutive integers are the right genre (though they average over n, here n ≈ p/4 + small).
first_step: Measure, at hard primes, the joint distribution of (ω, P⁺, smoothness) of N, N+1, …, N+K for the first K slices vs random consecutive integers near p/4; read OAI 012's method for short-range uniformity.

title: OAI 029 Artin primitive roots for every admissible base (claimed) — order-2-adic statistics
connection: OAI 029 claims ≫ x/log²x primes p < 2x with a primitive mod p; for the ES e-slice with prime e, −1 ∈ ⟨ℓ⟩ ⟺ ord_e(ℓ) even, and a primitive root ℓ | N gives −1 = ℓ^{(e−1)/2} (but the exponent must be realised inside N).
why: Primitive-root abundance controls how often a single prime factor generates −1 multiplicatively — a precondition (not sufficient) for e-slice success.
first_step: For hard primes, count slices where some prime factor of N is a primitive root mod e, and how often −1 is then in Q.

title: Iwaniec / Ford–Green–Konyagin–Maynard–Tao Jacobsthal & large-gap sieves for sterile windows
connection: Large-gap constructions (FGKMT) sieve out long intervals by choosing residue classes cleverly; ES sterile windows (all slices in a window fail) are analogous 'sieved-out' intervals.
why: The machinery (hypergraph covering, Maynard weights) for building long sifted intervals tells how long a sterile slice window could be.
first_step: Compute the longest run of failing e-slices at hard primes and compare with a FGKMT-type construction of residue classes killing a window.

title: OAI 020 squarefree values of quartics (claimed) — squarefreeness of p-tied quadratics
connection: OAI 020 claims squarefree density for irreducible quartics; ES p-tied integers p² + 4c²d are quadratic/quartic in parameters, and square factors matter for divisor structure (T1 is a square phenomenon).
why: Squarefreeness of p² + 4c²d in c is classical (quadratic); quartic families arise when c and d are tied (d = c² etc.).
first_step: Check the frequency of square factors in Type I values at hard primes and whether failures correlate with square divisors.

title: OAI 013 Ostmann inverse Goldbach (claimed) — additive irreducibility of ES-good sets
connection: OAI 013 claims the primes are not A+B up to finite modification; ES-type sets (n with Type I solution of a shape) have additive/multiplicative decomposition questions.
why: Not a route to ES, but a structural fact about sets of n defined by divisor events: the set of n covered by a family is a set of multiples (multiplicatively decomposable).
first_step: Record and close unless an additive decomposition of the covered set appears.

title: OAI 006 Goldfeld densities (claimed) — rank-parity as a model for ES parity layers
connection: OAI 006 claims Goldfeld's conjecture for quadratic twists; ES's parity layers (R(p)/2 mod 2 fair coin) resemble root-number parity statistics in twist families.
why: Root numbers are local products — a fully local parity; ES parity looks random — comparing clarifies whether an ES 'root number' exists.
first_step: Test whether R(p)/2 mod 2 is predicted by any product of local symbols (p/ℓ) for small ℓ via logistic regression.

title: OAI 018 Margulis–Platonov (claimed) — normal subgroups of SL₂ over global fields for ES words
connection: OAI 018 claims Margulis–Platonov over number fields; normal-subgroup structure of arithmetic groups matters for congruence-subgroup and thin-group questions about ES₅ words.
why: Very indirect; listed for completeness of the SL₂-word line.
first_step: Close unless an ES SL₂ formulation needs non-congruence normal subgroups.

title: OAI 024 asymptotic count of totients (claimed) — value-set counting technique
connection: OAI 024 claims an asymptotic for V(x) = #{φ(n) ≤ x}; Ford's anatomy of totients machinery counts value sets of multiplicative functions — ES's 'set of n with an ES solution of shape S' is a value set problem.
why: Value-set counting with structured preimages mirrors 'set of 4/n reachable by shape S'.
first_step: Read OAI 024 introduction for the method and see if 'n = 4xyz/(xy+yz+zx)' value-set counting fits.

title: Katz monodromy of the function-field ES certificate cover
connection: Over 𝔽_q(t), the variety of ES certificates over the space of prime polynomials of degree n has a monodromy group; big monodromy ⇒ equidistribution ⇒ positive counts for large q.
why: Computing this group exposes the function-field analogue of T1 (failure at squares = monodromy degeneracy?).
first_step: Compute Frobenius cycle types of the certificate cover over 𝔽_q for small q,n numerically to guess the monodromy group.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Kubilius model / PD anatomy for the p-tied integer 4Cp+1
connection: The Kubilius model replaces ω-type statistics of integers by independent prime indicators; Granville's anatomy shows prime factors follow PD(1).
why: A precise anatomy model of 4Cp+1 (C varying, p fixed) predicts the full distribution of R(p), including the lower tail.
first_step: Simulate R(p) under a Kubilius/PD model with the exact local factors at small primes and compare its lower tail with data at p ≤ 10^8.

title: Smooth-number restriction (Vaughan–Wooley) with smooth moduli in APs (Drappeau/Harper)
connection: Smooth numbers drove progress on G(k). ES: restrict certificates to smooth (u,B) or smooth 4C, where distribution in progressions to large moduli is better (friable Bombieri–Vinogradov beyond 1/2).
why: Smooth moduli are where the strongest level-of-distribution results live; ES certificates are numerically often smooth.
first_step: Drappeau, 'Théorèmes de type Fouvry–Iwaniec pour les entiers friables', Compositio 151 (2015), arXiv:1307.7554 (verified) gives beyond-√ distribution for friable integers; check whether it applies to sums Σ_{C smooth} #{d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 (4C)}; measure numerically the fraction of (★) solutions with y-smooth C for y = p^{0.1}.

title: Turán–Kubilius inequality for R(p) across C: second-moment pointwise statements
connection: Turán–Kubilius bounds variance of additive functions; R_C(p) summed over C is a sum of divisor-class indicators, whose variance over C at fixed p might be bounded by a Turán–Kubilius-type argument.
why: A variance bound Var_C ≪ (mean)² /K at fixed p would imply many C succeed — pointwise in p, averaged over C.
first_step: Compute mean and variance over C ≤ X of R_C(p) at hard primes; test whether Var/mean² decays with X.

title: Granville–Harper–Soundararajan Halász with explicit structure for failure-indicator twists
connection: GHS give a quantitative Halász theorem with explicit dependence on the pretentious distance; failing slices have divisor sums conspiring with characters mod 4C.
why: A quantitative pretentiousness bound for class-divisor sums would say failures are 'character-pretentious' only on thin sets.
first_step: Compute, for failing N, max_χ |Σ_{d|N} χ(d)|/τ(N) over χ mod 4C and its distribution.

title: Weighted dilation graphs / smooth shifted primes (OAI 'Weighted dilation graphs', claimed)
connection: The OAI paper claims x^{1−o(1)} primes p ∈ (2x,5x] with p−1 being x^δ-smooth via weighted dilation graphs; ES slices benefit from smooth N_e (many small generators).
why: Smooth shifted primes in abundance give structured slices; the dilation-graph technique is a new combinatorial counting tool.
first_step: Read the dilation-graph construction; test whether it can produce primes p with a smooth slice N_e for some small e.

title: Littlewood–Offord in finite abelian groups (Juškevičius–Šemetulskis) — exact anti-concentration
connection: Sharp LO bounds in arbitrary abelian groups bound max_x P(Σ ε_i v_i = x) given that steps avoid small subgroups; ES needs a LOWER bound on P(= −1), the converse direction.
why: Clarifies that LO gives upper (anti-concentration) bounds; for ES a 'local limit theorem' (equidistribution of the walk) is needed — a different but standard tool.
first_step: Compute the local-limit error for the ±1/0 walk with ω ≈ log log N steps in (ℤ/e)^×; note the step count is far below the mixing time ~ log e.

title: Word-map surjectivity (Larsen–Shalev; Ore conjecture) for ES₅ word shapes
connection: Larsen–Shalev show word maps w: G^k → G are surjective (or nearly) for large finite simple groups; ES₅ is a specific word shape with constrained letters in SL₂.
why: Surjectivity of the ES word map on SL₂(𝔽_q) (with letter constraints) is the local-at-q statement; failures at small q explain local obstructions.
first_step: Define the constrained ES₅ word map over 𝔽_q and compute its image size for q ≤ 100.

title: Bourgain–Lindenstrauss–Michel–Venkatesh effective ×a×b for multiplicative semigroups mod q
connection: BLMV give effective equidistribution of orbits of the multiplicative semigroup ⟨a,b⟩ acting on ℤ/q (Furstenberg ×2×3 discrete analogue); ES e-slices ask whether −1 lies in a product set built from a few multiplicative generators mod e.
why: Shows when a 2-generator multiplicative semigroup fills (ℤ/q)^× — the 'enough generators' threshold relevant to pooling slices.
first_step: Compute, for e-slices at hard primes, the size of the semigroup generated by the two smallest prime factors of N mod e.

title: Heath-Brown delta-method circle method for Σ_{n≤N} f(n) with power saving
connection: Heath-Brown's delta method counts integral points on quadrics/cubics with Kloosterman refinement; the total count of ES solutions over n ≤ N is an integral-point count on the 3-fold 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx).
why: Power-saving asymptotics for the total count, and for counts restricted to n in APs, feed variance and exceptional-set arguments.
first_step: Set up the delta-method count for #{(n,x,y,z): n ≤ N} with a smooth weight and identify the singular series (should match ET's main term).

title: Tao's Collatz 'almost bounded orbits' technique for greedy-with-choice Egyptian algorithms
connection: Tao (2019) analysed a 3-adic Syracuse random variable to show almost all Collatz orbits attain almost bounded values; ES solutions are produced by greedy-type algorithms (choose x ≈ n/4, recurse on the remainder) whose residue dynamics resemble Syracuse.
why: A stabilisation argument for the remainder's residue distribution could show 'greedy with bounded look-ahead succeeds for almost all n in log density' — and identify the structure of failures.
first_step: Implement the greedy-with-choice algorithm (x = ⌈n/4⌉ + k, k ≤ K) and record the residue distribution of remainders at each step for p ≤ 10^7.

title: Tao–Teräväinen odd-order log-Chowla & Klurman–Mangerel–Teräväinen sign patterns
connection: Tao–Teräväinen proved odd-order log-averaged Chowla; KMT studied sign patterns of multiplicative functions; ES certificates at consecutive slices involve λ/divisor patterns of consecutive integers N, N+1, …
why: Patterns of multiplicative data on consecutive integers are exactly what Type II slices are.
first_step: Tabulate (λ(N_e), λ(N_{e+4}), …) patterns at hard primes vs random and test for bias.

title: Host–Kra / Frantzikinakis ergodic structure for multiplicative ES colourings
connection: Host–Kra factors describe multiple ergodic averages; Frantzikinakis–Host apply them to multiplicative functions; the colouring of n by 'ES shape type' is multiplicatively closed (solutions lift to multiples).
why: A Furstenberg-correspondence model of the ES shape colouring could show forced configurations in each colour class.
first_step: Define the colouring n ↦ (minimal certificate type) and test partition-regularity-type configurations numerically.

title: Adiprasito–Huh–Katz Hodge theory for matroids: positivity from combinatorial Hodge–Riemann
connection: AHK proved log-concavity (Rota/Heron/Welsh) via Hodge–Riemann relations on matroid Chow rings; U_n in reciprocal coordinates is a hyperplane-arrangement object (matroid of {u,v,w,u+v+w}).
why: Matroid Hodge theory gives positivity of combinatorial invariants of the arrangement; whether any ES count is such an invariant is the question.
first_step: Compute the characteristic polynomial / Chow ring of the arrangement for U_n and check whether any coefficient relates to solution counts (likely not; record).

title: Shearer / entropy inequalities for joint divisibility of slices
connection: Shearer's lemma bounds joint entropy by marginals; the joint divisibility profile of slices (N_e mod small primes for e in a window) is a random vector whose entropy controls how many 'independent chances' ES gets.
why: Quantifies effective number of independent slices at a fixed p.
first_step: Compute empirical entropies of divisibility profiles across windows of slices at hard vs typical primes.

title: Gallagher's larger sieve with prime-power moduli to bound sterile p
connection: The larger sieve bounds sets missing many residue classes modulo prime powers; sterile primes must lie in non-covered classes modulo many moduli 4C simultaneously.
why: A direct quantitative bound on the number of primes ≤ X sterile to depth K.
first_step: Compute, for each modulus m ≤ M, the number of residue classes of p that are sterile for certificates of modulus m, and plug into the larger sieve.

title: Siegel's theorem on integral points of curves for one-parameter ES slices
connection: A curve C ⊂ U_n (e.g. x fixed as polynomial in a parameter) has infinitely many integral points only if genus 0 with ≤ 2 points at infinity; ES certificate curves are genus 0 with specific boundary.
why: Counting points at infinity classifies which 1-parameter certificate families can be infinite — a structural census.
first_step: For each certificate family in the repo, compute genus and number of points at infinity of the associated curve.

title: Selberg Λ² upper-bound sieve for the number of sterile p ≤ X at depth K
connection: Λ² sieve gives sharp upper bounds for sifted sets; 'p sterile for all certificates with C ≤ K' is a sifting condition on p modulo the moduli 4C and auxiliary primes.
why: Gives E_K(X) ≪ X/(log X)^{g(K)} with explicit g, the cleanest depth-K exceptional bound.
first_step: Compute the sieve dimension of the depth-K sterility condition from the densities of sterile classes mod primes ℓ.

title: Ramaré's local models / Ramaré–Walker for one-integer certificate densities
connection: Ramaré's local-model technique gives explicit lower bounds for sifted sums by matching local densities; the deep catalogue lists Ramaré–Walker as a thin-count precedent.
why: Template for explicit lower bounds with a small number of witnesses.
first_step: Re-read the deep catalogue entry and check whether ES's one-integer event fits Ramaré's 'local model' assumptions.

title: PARI/Magma class-field computations: explicit 'ES ray class fields' for small (c,d)
connection: Computer algebra computes ray class fields explicitly; ES Type I certificates for fixed (c,d) correspond to primes f splitting in a specific ray class field with a twist by p.
why: Explicit fields allow Chebotarev-density computations of the per-(c,d) success probability, sharpening M_BM.
first_step: Compute with PARI bnrinit for d ≤ 10, c ≤ 5 and list Frobenius conditions.

title: Target-Davenport constants for I3 at small t: forcing −1 from enough prime factors
connection: In (ℤ/t)^× with t ≤ 20, a sequence of prime factors of tn+1 of length ≥ D(G) has a nonempty subproduct ≡ 1; the I3 event needs a divisor ≡ −1, so a 'target' Davenport constant is the forcing threshold.
why: Combined with 'tn+1 has many prime factors for some t ≤ T' (provable for most n?), could give I3 for many n deterministically.
first_step: Compute target constants for G = (ℤ/t)^×, t ≤ 30, and the fraction of n where some t ≤ 30 has ω(tn+1) above the threshold.

title: Function-field transfer of T1: odd squares in 𝔽_q[T] and the reciprocity obstruction
connection: T1 (no Type I/II at odd squares) should have a function-field analogue with polynomial reciprocity; FF_ODD_ABSENCE/FF_STERILE memos study function-field sterility.
why: In function fields the obstruction might be explained by monodromy, giving a conceptual T1 proof that could suggest a 'prime T1' test.
first_step: Verify T1 for squares of irreducible polynomials over 𝔽_3, 𝔽_5 numerically and compute the monodromy of the certificate cover at a square.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Gaussian ES_Q1 count growth log³N vs log²N: Lang–Weil / local densities explanation
connection: z52 found ES_Q1 counts grow like log³N (EVIDENCE) against the board's log²N; integral-Manin-type predictions depend on the rank of the relevant Picard/boundary data over ℚ(i).
why: A geometric explanation (extra boundary component splitting over ℚ(i)) would validate the log-power heuristics used for ES itself.
first_step: Compute the Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel exponent for U_n over ℚ(i) vs ℚ (Galois action on boundary/nodes) and compare with 3 vs 2.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Matomäki–Radziwiłł for divisor-class functions on the slice window (N, N+H) at fixed p
connection: The Type II slices are the short interval [p/4, p/4 + H]; MR-type theorems give almost-all-short-interval behaviour, but here the interval is one specific interval (fixed by p).
why: Precisely localises the B2-type gap as 'one specific short interval near p/4' — any 'all short intervals' theorem for the divisor-class function would prove ES.
first_step: Check the strongest known 'all intervals of length H' result for multiplicative functions (e.g. Teräväinen/MR 'every interval' results for smooth numbers) and compare H with ES's polylog window.

title: Duke–Imamoḡlu–Tóth-style traces for I3's t-family (closed geodesics of discriminant t²n²+…)
connection: (tu−1)(tv−1) = tn+1 relates to binary forms of discriminant depending on (t,n); traces over these classes could be mock-modular generating functions.
why: Same speculative mechanism as for ES₅, but I3's single free parameter t makes the family cleaner.
first_step: Identify the binary quadratic form whose representation gives I3 at (t,n) and compute its discriminant.

title: Rosser–Iwaniec semi-linear sieve for I3 at t = 4: 'tn+1 has a divisor ≡ 3 (mod 4)'
connection: At t = 4, the I3 event needs a divisor of 4n+1 that is ≡ −1 (mod 4) (plus size constraints): it fails iff all prime factors of 4n+1 are ≡ 1 (mod 4) — a semi-linear sifted set of density ≍ (log n)^{−1/2}.
why: Exact density of the t = 4 failure set; combining t = 4, 8, 12 … failures gives a sieve-dimension computation for I3's exceptional set.
first_step: Compute the joint failure probability for t ∈ {4, 8, 12, 16} under independence and compare with data.

title: Extreme-value prediction of ES's 'last hard prime' scale from sibling data
connection: Siblings with known last exceptions (I3: 2 433 600; U(n): 978145?) calibrate extreme-value models mapping expected count μ(n) to the largest failing n.
why: If the same model predicts ES's last failure below 2 (i.e. none), it quantifies P(ES false) consistently across siblings.
first_step: Fit log P(fail at n) ≈ −μ(n)·κ on siblings, then evaluate Σ_{p > 10^18} exp(−κ μ(p)).

title: SAT/ILP search for a 'prime T1': a non-square class where all certificates of bounded shape fail
connection: A 'prime T1' (structured family of primes with no Type I/II certificates of a bounded shape) is the campaign's sought disproof-shape; SAT/ILP can search residue systems where all bounded-shape certificates fail.
why: Either finds sterile families to a given depth or certifies none exist below a modulus — sharp data for the sterility question.
first_step: Encode depth-K sterility for certificate shapes with C ≤ K as a CRT-consistency SAT instance and search moduli up to 10^6.

title: Murmuration-type averages of I3 counts against n mod t
connection: Average I3 counts as a function of n's residue pattern across t could show oscillations analogous to murmurations.
why: Exposes hidden structure that residue-class fits might miss.
first_step: Plot normalised I3 counts averaged in windows vs n/X and residues mod 840.

title: Effective Chebotarev in the ES Type I ray class fields (explicit success density per (c,d))
connection: For fixed (c,d), the density of primes p having a Type I certificate with that (c,d) and a prime f is a Chebotarev density in a field tied to (c,d); summing gives M_BM's constant.
why: Explicit densities let one compute the exact main term and the variance contributed by each (c,d).
first_step: Compute the Chebotarev density for (c,d) ∈ {(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)} via PARI and compare with empirical frequencies.

title: Spectral sparsification / effective resistance on certificate dependency graphs
connection: Spielman–Srivastava sparsification approximates graphs by sparse ones preserving quadratic forms; the Janson Δ is a quadratic form on the certificate dependency graph.
why: Allows computing/approximating Δ for huge certificate families at large p.
first_step: Compute Δ exactly for p ~ 10^7 and approximately via sparsification at p ~ 10^12.

title: Bloom/Liu–Sawhney machinery for few-term Egyptian representations with dense denominators
connection: Bloom: positive density sets contain S with Σ1/n = 1, via counting with main term + exponential sums on integers with structured anatomy. Ask what the machinery gives for k-term representations of 4/p (k fixed, small) with denominators restricted to structured sets (multiples of p with smooth cofactors).
why: Bloom's framework is the modern Fourier-analytic engine for unit-fraction existence; checking where it breaks for k = 3 localises ES's difficulty.
first_step: Read Bloom's §§2–4 and identify the minimal number of terms the method needs; check if it can handle 4/p = Σ_{i≤k} 1/n_i with k ~ 10 and n_i in a set of density zero.

title: ES₅ as a sandpile-group pairing condition on a 4-vertex fan multigraph
connection: The chain matrix M = [[v,−1,0],[−1,t,−1],[0,−1,u]] is the reduced Laplacian of the multigraph: path a–b–c plus a sink s joined to a, b, c by v−1, t−2, u−1 parallel edges. It has det M = tuv−u−v = p spanning trees, a cyclic sandpile group ℤ/p, and its discriminant (monodromy) pairing has self-pairing (M⁻¹)₁₁ = A/p. So ES₅(p) (∃ t,u,v ≥ 2, tuv−u−v = p, (A/p) = −1 with A = tu−1; sufficient for ES(p)) ⇔ some fan multigraph of this shape with p spanning trees has a sandpile pairing in the non-square class.
why: Sandpile groups with their pairings are a mature field (Lorenzini, Shokrieh, Bosch–Lorenzini) with classification results for pairings on cyclic critical groups; this gives ES₅ a purely graph-theoretic statement.
first_step: Script: for p ≡ 1 (4) < 10⁵, enumerate all graphs on ≤ 5 vertices with p spanning trees and record which pairing classes occur; is the non-square class reached by 4-vertex fans exactly when ES₅(p) holds, and always by 5-vertex graphs?

title: Spanning-tree values and Zaremba (Chan–Kontorovich–Pak) applied to fan graphs
connection: Chan–Kontorovich–Pak prove exponential growth of the set of spanning-tree counts of n-vertex planar graphs via continued fractions, thin orbits and Zaremba. ES₅ asks the same kind of question for continuants of length 3 with a sign condition.
why: It is the nearest proved theorem in which spanning-tree counts and continued fractions are linked through thin-orbit methods. Their graphs realise numerators of CFs, as our fan does for HJ length 3.
first_step: Read arXiv:2411.18782 §2 (graph ↔ CF dictionary). Check whether their construction realises a prescribed numerator p with a prescribed denominator class (A/p) = −1 at bounded length.

title: Idoneal numbers in spanning-tree extremal problems vs U(n)/I3 sporadic lists
connection: Azarija–Škrekovski: α(n) ≤ (n+4)/3 iff n ∉ {3,4,5,6,7,9,10,13,18,22}, a subset of Euler's idoneal numbers. U(n)/I3 have finite sporadic failure lists for tuv−u−v representations, also continuant/spanning-tree statements.
why: The appearance of idoneal numbers (class-group exponent ≤ 2) in a spanning-tree problem suggests the U(n) sporadics {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145} might have a class-group characterisation.
first_step: Compute the class groups Cl(−4n), Cl(−n) for the U(n) sporadics and for I3 failures; test exponent-2 / genus-one patterns.

title: Linking form of the double branched cover of a 2-bridge link with a 3-vertex plumbing description
connection: L(p,A) is the double branched cover of the 2-bridge link b(p,A). The ES₅ sign is the isometry class of the linking form of Σ₂(b(p,A)), and HJ length 3 means a 3-vertex linear plumbing (negative-CF) description. Note this is not an 'even' continued fraction: three even HJ digits would give an even determinant.
why: Knot theory has exact formulas tying linking forms, Goeritz matrices and signatures (Gordon–Litherland). If σ mod 8 detects (A/p), the ES sign becomes a knot signature on a 3-parameter knot family.
first_step: Compute σ(b(p,A)) by Murasugi's formula Σ_{i<p} (−1)^{⌊iA/p⌋} for p < 500. Check whether σ mod 8, together with p mod 8, determines (A/p) (a van der Blij / Gauss-sum reciprocity).

title: Rational balls bounded by lens spaces (Lisca) vs 3-chain plumbings
connection: Lisca classified lens spaces bounding rational homology balls (p = m², specific q). Square p is exactly where ES-type certificates vanish (T1), and rational-ball bounding is tied to the linking form being metabolic.
why: T1 (obstruction at odd squares) and 'bounds a rational ball' are both 'linking form is split/hyperbolic' phenomena. A Lisca-style lattice-embedding argument could explain T1 topologically and show why primes escape it.
first_step: Read Lisca math/0701610 §§2–3 (lattice embeddings). Check whether the T1 square-class obstruction is equivalent to the metabolic linking form of L(m², A) for the relevant A.

title: Cyclic quotient singularity 1/p(1,A) with a 3-curve resolution and non-residue A
connection: p/A = [[v,t,u]] is the minimal resolution chain (−v,−t,−u) of the cyclic quotient singularity 1/p(1,A). ES₅(p) ⇔ some 1/p(1,A) with (A/p) = −1 has exactly 3 exceptional curves.
why: Singularity theory controls resolution lengths via Riemenschneider duality, P-resolutions and smoothing components (KSB). The ES sign is a Galois-type datum: is 1/p(1,A) isomorphic over a quadratic twist to 1/p(1,1)?
first_step: Compute embedding dimension and Riemenschneider dual lengths for A ∈ L₃(p); test whether the dual-chain length distribution differs between (A/p) = ±1.

title: Hacking–Prokhorov degenerations of P² to P(a²,b²,c²) and Markov-type equations for ES
connection: Hacking–Prokhorov: toric degenerations of P² to weighted projective planes with T-singularities are governed by Markov triples a²+b²+c² = 3abc, generated by mutations. ES's Markoff-type surface S_{n,D}: nA²+B²+D = ABC is a twisted analogue.
why: Mutation trees of degenerations give an infinite combinatorial structure over a Markov-type equation, and U_n has no comparable mutation structure (only coordinate permutations), while S_{n,D} has only Vieta-type involutions such as B ↦ AC − B (and A ↦ BC/n − A when n | BC). This is a place to look for a hidden mutation.
first_step: Check whether S_{n,D} solutions arise as weights of Q-Gorenstein degenerations of some del Pezzo (degree depending on n); start from HP's classification table.

title: Frobenius-class form: uv | n+u+v ⇔ n is in the 'Frobenius shadow' of the numerical semigroup ⟨u,v⟩
connection: n = tuv−u−v ⇔ n ≡ −(u+v) (mod uv). If gcd(u,v) = 1 (automatic for interior words at a prime n), Popoviciu's formula gives exactly t−1 representations of n as au+bv (a,b ≥ 0), and uv−u−v is the Frobenius number. Without coprimality this fails (t = u = v = 2, n = 4). ES₅ words are pairs (u,v) whose denumerant at n is in the Frobenius residue class, plus a sign condition.
why: The theory of numerical semigroups and denumerants (Popoviciu, Sylvester, Ramírez Alfonsín) gives a new vocabulary for the forest F_p (uv | p+u+v), with generating-function tools.
first_step: Express the ES₅ sign in terms of (u,v,n) via denumerant data; check whether Σ_{(u,v)} sign·q^n has a Popoviciu-type generating function (∏ 1/(1−q^u)(1−q^v) restricted to a class).

title: Christoffel/Sturmian word of slope A/p with three runs
