connection: HJ length r(p/A) is a run-length statistic of the Christoffel word of slope A/p (equivalently the cutting sequence of the segment to (p,A)). ES₅ asks for a non-residue A whose Christoffel word has the minimal 3-block structure.
why: Combinatorics on words has exact results on Christoffel words, palindromes and standard factorizations, which might give explicit constructions of A with prescribed structure, for instance via palindromic closure.
first_step: Express r(p/A) = 3 as a factorisation condition on the Christoffel word; test whether the Lothaire standard factorisation relates the two halves to (A/p).

title: Quantum (WRT) invariants of lens spaces: Gauss sums carrying (A/p)
connection: Jeffrey's formula for the Witten–Reshetikhin–Turaev invariant of L(p,q) involves Dedekind sums and quadratic Gauss sums whose evaluation produces Jacobi symbols in q. The ES sign may appear as a phase of a quantum invariant of L(p,A).
why: Quantum topology has exact formulas (and quantum modularity results) for WRT invariants of Seifert/lens spaces. A sum over words of a quantum invariant could be a computable object.
first_step: Write τ_r(L(p,A)) (Jeffrey 1992). Check whether some level r makes the phase equal to (A/p), and evaluate Σ_{A ∈ L₃(p)} τ_r(L(p,A)).

title: Hyperbolic triangle billiards / Veech triangles with prescribed area
connection: Billiards in the hyperbolic (π/x, π/y, π/z) triangle unfold to the triangle group's tiling of H² (not to Euclidean translation surfaces). Separately, Euclidean rational triangles unfold to translation surfaces, and Veech's lattice triangles are special shapes there. ES is a statement about the area spectrum of reflection-group triangles.
why: A genuine dynamics translation of the original equation, but probably only a restatement. Recorded for breadth.
first_step: Check whether the area/angle condition has any known role in Veech-group classification (Kenyon–Smillie, Ward triangles).

title: Domino/strip tilings counted by continuants with a parity weight
connection: Positive continuants count tilings of a strip by monominoes and dominoes with weights. The negative continuant K(v,t,u) = tuv−u−v is a signed count, equivalently det of the chain matrix as a weighted path-matching count. The ES sign is the class of the cofactor.
why: Tiling enumeration has transfer-matrix and involution machinery. A sign-reversing involution on tilings might isolate a non-residue cofactor.
first_step: Write tuv−u−v and tu−1 as tiling counts of a 3-cell strip with weights; look for a sign-reversing involution whose fixed points carry the class of tu−1 mod p.

title: Isoperimetry/expansion of the forest components vs character-sum smoothness
connection: If the component of 1 in F_p has edge expansion h and contains a QNR, then a bichromatic edge exists. Combinatorial expansion of an arithmetic forest is a graph-theory question.
why: 'The component containing 1 reaches a QNR' is a sufficient (not necessary) condition for ES₅, the arithmetic analogue of a percolation/connectivity statement. FRONTIER §3 records that under Dickson it fails infinitely often (e.g. p = 409 has a monochromatic component of 1 but a negative word (15,4,7)).
first_step: Compute the component sizes of F_p and the least QNR inside the component of 1, for p < 10⁶.

title: ℤ/2 gauge field on F_p plus multiplicative edges: the Legendre colouring as a flat connection
connection: F_p is a forest, so its own critical group is trivial and colourings carry no holonomy. Adding 'multiplicative' edges u ~ qu (q a small prime, weight (q/p)) creates cycles. The Legendre colouring is then a ℤ/2 gauge configuration that is flat around every cycle by multiplicativity, and ES₅ failure means it is also constant along every forest edge.
why: Speculative: combining the forest's divisibility edges with multiplicative edges might force a contradiction for a flat ℤ/2 connection that is trivial on forest edges, i.e. a global consistency obstruction that a single forest cannot carry.
first_step: Build the augmented graph for p < 2000 (forest + edges u ~ 2u, 3u, 5u); compute the space of ℤ/2 colourings that are multiplicative on the added edges and constant on forest edges, and its dimension.

title: Ford circles: A/p lies in a horoball of 'depth-3' chain
connection: r(p/A) = 3 means the Ford circle chain from ∞ to A/p has three tangency steps of HJ type. ES₅ becomes: some non-residue A has A/p inside the union of depth-3 Ford horoball chains.
why: The Ford circle picture makes the condition a covering-by-horoballs statement, where hyperbolic volume arguments live.
first_step: Draw/compute the union of depth-3 HJ horoball chains intersected with {A/p}; measure its proportion and its correlation with QR.

title: A¹-curves on U_n and log Gromov–Witten counts vs polynomial ES identities
connection: GHK's theta functions are built from counts of A¹-curves (log GW invariants) meeting the boundary at one point. Integral A¹-curves in U_n are polynomial parametric families of (signed) solutions, the fixed-n analogue of Mordell identities.
why: Mordell–Schinzel says no polynomial families cover square classes. Log GW counts are an enumerative invariant of the same objects, so they might give a geometric reason for which classes are covered.
first_step: Count low-degree A¹-curves on U_n for a few n by direct polynomial search (deg ≤ 3); compare with the GHK broken-line counts.

title: Frieze patterns with coefficients (Cuntz–Holm–Jørgensen) for boundary (1,1,1,1,N)
connection: CHJ develop friezes with coefficients and prove finiteness: for given boundary there are finitely many friezes with entries in a discrete set. They also obtain them by cutting subpolygons out of triangulated polygons. ES₅ words are exactly the positive integral friezes of the pentagon with boundary (1,1,1,1,N) (FRIEZE_ES).
why: Their 'cutting out subpolygons from Conway–Coxeter friezes' construction could realise each ES₅ word inside a classical triangulation of an (N+…)-gon, giving a triangulation model of the sign.
first_step: Read arXiv:1909.02332 §§3–5. Represent each word for p < 200 as a cut-out from a Conway–Coxeter frieze and check whether the sign (4 | quiddity entry) is visible on the triangulation.

title: Lyness 5-cycle with a coefficient: integrable map whose integer orbits are ES₅ words
connection: The pentagon Ptolemy relations with one frozen side N give a period-5 birational map (a Lyness-type recurrence x_{k+1}x_{k−1} = x_k + c_k with c ∈ {1,N}). Integer orbits are words. Lyness maps have an invariant cubic (elliptic) fibration.
why: Discrete integrable systems give invariants and elliptic fibrations of such maps; the invariant of the coefficient-N Lyness cycle gives each word a 'conserved energy', possibly with arithmetic meaning.
first_step: Compute the invariant rational function of the (1,1,1,1,N) Lyness cycle (sympy). Evaluate it on words and look for a link with the sign or with t.

title: SL₂-tilings (Bergeron–Reutenauer) containing a row of five with boundary N
connection: SL₂-tilings are infinite arrays of 2×2 minors 1; friezes are bounded tilings. A word gives a finite SL₂-pattern; Bergeron–Reutenauer parametrise tilings by bi-infinite paths in the Farey graph.
why: It turns words into Farey-graph path pairs, where the ES sign might be a holonomy in SL₂(ℤ/4) along the path pair (SVZ already looked at mod-4 contractibility).
first_step: Compute the Bergeron–Reutenauer path pair of each word; check whether the mod-4 holonomy distinguishes signs.

title: Quiver representations of A₂ with dimension-vector data equal to a word
connection: Friezes of type A_n categorify via Caldero–Chapoton maps on cluster categories of A_n. Frieze entries are Euler characteristics of quiver Grassmannians. Coefficients correspond to frozen vertices (Frobenius categories).
why: Categorification gives representation-theoretic meaning to every entry, so 'entry ≡ 0 mod 4' becomes 'Euler characteristic of a quiver Grassmannian ≡ 0 mod 4'.
first_step: Find the Frobenius 2-CY category categorifying friezes with coefficients (Holm–Jørgensen line of work), and identify which objects give entries t,u,v,tu−1,tv−1.

title: Total family U → A¹_n: integral points on a threefold and Manin–Peyre for the total space
connection: The total space 𝒰 = {4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx)} ⊂ A⁴ is a threefold. ES says the projection 𝒰(ℤ_{>0}) → ℤ_{≥2} is surjective. Integral points on the threefold are counted asymptotically (Elsholtz–Tao averages), so surjectivity is a 'fibre-wise' strengthening.
why: This is the standard 'surjectivity of a morphism on integral points' question, related to Serre's thin-set / Hilbert irreducibility for integral points. The fibres here are log CY rather than rational curves.
first_step: Look up results on 'integral points: surjectivity onto the base' (e.g. Corvaja–Zannier thin sets, integral Hilbert irreducibility) to locate the nearest theorem.

title: Integral points via the universal torsor: ES as lattice points satisfying a system of coprime divisibilities
connection: Torsor descent turns 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) into the classical parametrisation x = abd·…, which has the shape of ET's (a,b,c,d) Type I/II data. Torsor coordinates are the standard native coordinates.
why: It explains the ET parametrisations as torsor coordinates, and opens the use of the torsor's own symmetry group, a torus.
first_step: Match ET (2.1)–(2.7) with the Cox ring of the minimal desingularisation of the closure; list any extra torus action not used so far.

title: ES over number fields with unit-rank ≥ 1 (unit orbits as infinite families)
connection: Over O_K with infinite unit group, U_n(O_K) may have unit-orbit families. UNIT_ORBIT_ES studied these; the native field is Diophantine equations over rings of integers (unit equations, S-unit theorems).
why: Shows what infinite symmetry does to the problem. The S-unit equation theory (Evertse–Győry) gives finiteness or infinitude results for the related unit equations.
first_step: Check whether some ES equivalent form is an S-unit equation in disguise (e.g. after fixing a factorisation pattern) and apply the S-unit counting bounds.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Vojta/abc for integral points on U_n: what does 'log Kodaira dimension 0' predict
connection: Vojta's conjecture predicts degeneracy of integral points only for log general type. U_n is log CY (κ̄ = 0), so integral points may be dense, and no prediction of existence follows.
why: This is a calibration: it explains why no conjectural Diophantine machine gives ES, unlike Markoff (log CY too) where Ghosh–Sarnak found failures.
first_step: Note as calibration. Check whether 'log CY with BM set non-empty but positive points absent' is known to occur infinitely often in a family (Loughran–Mitankin for Markoff).

title: Motivic/Igusa zeta function of U_n: local densities and the BM main term
connection: The BM main term is a product of local densities, each the limit of #U_n(ℤ/p^k)/p^{2k}. Igusa's local zeta function encodes these densities as rational functions with poles governed by an embedded resolution.
why: The exact local factors (especially at 2) control the T1/sign phenomena. Igusa poles might give a uniform closed form for the BM constant, which is already exact.
first_step: Compute Igusa zeta of 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) at p = 2 and p | n via the toric resolution; compare with BM_CORRECTED_COUNT local factors.

title: Integral points on the affine quadric family: Type I as a sum-of-squares/norm condition in ℤ[√−d]
connection: QUATERNION_ES Lemma 1.1: Type I at level d ⇔ (1+2aw)(1+2bw) = e(2cw − p) in ℤ[w], w = √−d. This is a factorisation problem in an imaginary quadratic order.
why: Factorisation in quadratic orders is governed by the class group and genus theory, and the repo uses it in LATTICE_MEETING. The native next step is a Heegner-point/CM-points equidistribution input.
first_step: Express the condition as 'a specific ideal of norm e lies in a class of order ≤ 2·something'; test which genus characters are forced.

title: Prehomogeneous vector space view: averages are easy, pointwise is the problem (calibration)
connection: Orbit-counting on prehomogeneous spaces gives averages over discriminants (Davenport–Heilbronn style). ES's averages are known (Vaughan, ET), and the pointwise question has no prehomogeneous analogue.
why: This calibrates what arithmetic statistics can give: possibly a positive-proportion statement in the n-aspect with explicit constants, not ES.
first_step: Skip unless a pointwise parametrisation arises. Note as a calibration entry.

title: Olson/Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv-type theorem for 'subset product = −1' in (ℤ/4C)^×
connection: Zero-sum theory has inverse theorems: sequences with no zero-sum subsequence are structured (lie in a coset). ES failure at fixed C forces the prime factors of 4Cp+1 to lie in an index-2-type structure that avoids −1.
why: Inverse zero-sum theorems give explicit structure of failing configurations, which is a different angle from sieve counting.
first_step: State: the subset products of ω primes avoid −1 ⇒ all lie in a subgroup H not containing −1 or the configuration is short. Check against data for p < 10⁶.

title: Sum-product / Bourgain–Glibichuk–Konyagin for the set S_L(p) as L grows
connection: S_L(p) = {A : r(p/A) ≤ L} grows like p^{c(L)} for L ≫ log p. Sum-product theory says sets of size p^δ generate F_p in bounded steps. ES₅ fixes L = 3, where |S₃| ≈ log²p.
why: It is the native additive-combinatorics frame for why L = 3 is hard (polylog sets have no sum-product leverage) and where L-ladders become easy.
first_step: Tabulate |S_L(p)| and the least L with S_L(p) ⊄ QR for p < 10⁶ (this is λ(p)); fit L_min growth.

title: Klein polygons / sails of the cone for p/A: HJ length = number of sail vertices
connection: The HJ digits of p/A are read off the boundary of the convex hull of the non-zero lattice points in the cone of the toric model of 1/p(1,A) (e.g. cone((0,1),(p,−A)) up to orientation convention; Klein's sail). The boundary lattice points are the HJ convergents (r(p/A) + 2 Hilbert-basis points), and geometric vertices are the points with digit ≥ 3. So r(p/A) = 3 means exactly 3 interior boundary points.
why: Arnold's statistics of sails and multidimensional continued fractions are a native toolbox. Sails with few vertices are rare and structured.
first_step: Express 'sail of cone(p,A) has 3 interior vertices' and count over A ∈ QNR; compare with Arnold's predictions for random cones.

title: Mayer/Gauss–Kuzmin–Wirsing transfer operator twisted by (·/p): spectral gap for character sums over CF sets
connection: Character sums over sets defined by CF conditions can be studied by transfer operators with a character twist (as in Bourgain–Kontorovich and Dolgopyat). A spectral gap gives cancellation in Σ_{A: CF condition} χ(A).
why: It is the native way to get cancellation for CF-defined sets, but works for growing lengths, not length 3. Recorded as the nearest tool.
first_step: Record the length threshold L(p) beyond which twisted transfer-operator methods give non-trivial Σ_{A ∈ S_L(p)} (A/p); compare with λ(p) data.

title: Knauf's number-theoretic spin chain and Riemann ζ: a ζ-like Dirichlet series for HJ lengths
connection: Knauf's spin chain partition function is ζ(s−1)/ζ(s). An analogous chain with HJ (by-excess) matrices and a quadratic-character field might have a Dirichlet-series partition function whose coefficients encode λ(p).
why: If the partition function is an L-function quotient, analytic properties (zeros/poles) would control its coefficients.
first_step: Compute Σ_{p,A} p^{−s} x^{r(p/A)} (A/p) numerically and try to identify it as an L-function combination.

title: Kudla Diff-parity and T1: incoherent Eisenstein series derivative as a 'certificate counting function'
connection: KUDLA_ES: T1 ⟺ oddness of Kudla's Diff(T). The derivative of an incoherent Eisenstein series at the centre has Fourier coefficients that are arithmetic degrees of special cycles (Kudla–Rapoport–Yang).
why: If ES certificate counts were arithmetic degrees on a Shimura curve or variety, the arithmetic Siegel–Weil formula would give exact identities, with positivity coming from geometry.
first_step: Check whether certificates of level d correspond to special 0-cycles Z(T) on a quaternionic Shimura curve; compare degrees with KRY's formula numerically.

title: Brandt matrices: theta series of ternary lattices of maximal orders and the representation number of certificates
connection: Brandt matrix entries are representation numbers of the norm forms of ideals in B_{p,∞}; their traces relate to class numbers of imaginary quadratic orders (Eichler trace formula). Certificate counts at level d may be Brandt-matrix entries.
why: Eichler's trace formula is an exact class-number identity. If certificate counts are traces, they become class-number sums, and class numbers are positive.
first_step: Compute Brandt matrices B(m) for p < 200 (Sage/Magma) and correlate entries with ES level counts.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Gauss's three-squares theorem as a template: r₃(n) ≍ h(−n) and the ES sign as a genus character
connection: Gauss: r₃(n) = 12h(−4n) (n ≡ 1,2 mod 4, squarefree) is an exact class-number formula for a pointwise existence theorem. THREE_SQUARES links the ES sign to three-squares data.
why: It is the canonical example where pointwise existence follows from an exact identity plus positivity of class numbers. ES lacks such an identity (SIGN_IDENTITY).
first_step: Look for a combination Σ_level c_t·(certificate count at level t) that equals a positive class-number expression (e.g. h(−tp) type) at primes; fit numerically.

title: Waldspurger/Kohnen–Zagier: squares of half-integral-weight coefficients as central L-values
connection: SIGN_IDENTITY Prop 2.4 restricts the Waldspurger route. In native terms: if the ES count (or its sign part) were |c(p)|² for a weight-3/2 form, nonvanishing would be L(f⊗χ_p, 1/2) ≠ 0, which is known for positive proportions (Iwaniec–Sarnak type) but not pointwise.
why: Calibration: shows the best automorphic route yields positive proportion, unless a root-number obstruction is absent and an exact formula exists.
first_step: Record calibration; check whether any weight-3/2 form's coefficients correlate with N₋(p) on p < 10⁵ (it should be ruled out by size).

title: Markoff-type surface S_{n,D}: Vieta jumping (olympiad technique) as a descent on certificates
connection: S_{n,D}: nA² + B² + D = ABC has the Vieta involution B ↦ AC − B (always integral) and A ↦ BC/n − A (integral only when n | BC). Where the involutions stay integral and positive, Vieta jumping descends solutions towards fundamental ones (IMO 1988 Q6 style); unrestricted integral descent is not automatic here.
why: Vieta jumping is the elementary native tool for Markoff-type equations. It gives finite fundamental sets per (n, D) and transports positivity along orbits.
first_step: For n = p < 500, compute the fundamental (minimal) solutions under Vieta jumping on S_{p,D} and check whether ES certificates (2D | C) appear among fundamental solutions or in their orbits.

title: Heegner points / CM points equidistribution (Duke) for the lattice meeting point
connection: LATTICE_MEETING moves the slice inside Cl(−4p); Duke's theorem says CM points of discriminant −4p equidistribute on the modular curve. Certificates are CM points landing in a thin region (near the cusp, Y small).
why: Duke's theorem with explicit rates (Iwaniec's bound for half-integral-weight coefficients) is a pointwise-in-p existence statement for regions of size ≫ p^{−δ}. ES needs regions of size ≈ p^{−1/2}·polylog.
first_step: Compute the hyperbolic area of the 'certificate region' for CM points of disc −4p and compare with the best-known equidistribution error p^{−1/28}-type.

title: Genus theory and the 2-part of Cl(−4p): ES sign as a genus character value
connection: For p ≡ 1 (4), Cl(−4p) has 2-rank 1, and genus characters are (·/p) and χ_{−4}. Certificate ideals of norm e must lie in a principal genus or its complement; the slot lemma's mod-4 condition may be the 4-rank (Rédei) symbol.
why: Rédei symbols and 4-ranks are explicit and computable. If the ES sign is a Rédei symbol of the certificate ideal, the structure is governed by governing fields (Stevenhagen, Smith).
first_step: For p < 10⁵, compute the Rédei-matrix data of Q(√−p), Q(√−2p) and compare with p's ES₅ certificate statistics (sign distributions by level).

title: Dedekind eta multiplier and the ES sign: (A/p) as an eta-multiplier value on γ_w
connection: The eta multiplier ε(γ) is given by Dedekind sums, and Rademacher's formulas relate it to Jacobi symbols. The ES sign is the theta multiplier on γ_w (bsB_theta_multiplier), and θ and η multipliers are related (θ = η⁵/(η²η²)-type identities).
why: Expressing the sign via η multipliers gives a conjugacy-invariant (Rademacher Φ function / class invariant), which might be easier to sum over words.
first_step: Compute Rademacher's Φ(γ_w) (and separately the Rademacher symbol) for words at p < 1000 and check whether either, mod 8 or 24, determines the sign.

title: Bounded arithmetic: is the Mordell covering (ES for n ∉ hard classes) provable in IΔ₀ + Ω₁?
connection: Bounded arithmetic proves elementary NT statements whose witnesses are polynomial-time computable. ES for the easy residue classes has explicit polynomial witnesses (Mordell identities), so it is provable in very weak systems.
why: Proof-complexity calibration: a proof of full ES in a weak system would yield a polynomial-time witness algorithm (Buss witnessing). Conversely, if no poly-time deterministic witness algorithm exists, any proof must use strong axioms or non-constructive steps.
first_step: State the witnessing theorem consequence: ES provable in S¹₂ ⇒ a poly-time algorithm outputs (x,y,z) from n. Check whether any deterministic poly-time ES algorithm is known (likely not without factoring).

title: Quadratic residue codes: ES₅ failure as S₃(p) ⊂ support of the QR idempotent
connection: The QR code of length p is defined by the QR set. ES₅ fails at p iff S₃(p) ⊆ QR. Coding theory studies which structured sets sit inside QR (e.g. minimum-weight words, automorphism group PSL₂(p) acting on QR codes).
why: The QR code's automorphism group PSL₂(F_p) is large. Words (as SL₂ data) act naturally, so S₃(p) ⊆ QR might be translated into a code-automorphism statement.
first_step: Check whether S₃(p) is a union of orbits of some subgroup of PSL₂(F_p) stabilising QR; if so, failure would be forced or forbidden group-theoretically.

title: F₂-linear algebra: ES₅ failure ⇔ a linear system over F₂ in the Legendre symbols of small primes
connection: (A/p) = ∏ (q/p)^{v_q(A)}. ES₅ failure ⇔ all A ∈ S₃(p) have Σ v_q(A)·ε_q ≡ 0 (mod 2), where ε_q = [(q/p) = −1]. This is a linear system over F₂ in the unknown vector ε (the 'quadratic character of p on primes').
why: The exact linear-algebra form shows that failure is consistent iff the exponent-vector matrix of S₃(p) has the actual ε in its right kernel. Rank considerations give a sharp combinatorial necessary condition.
first_step: For p < 10⁶ compute rank_F₂ of the exponent matrix of S₃(p) (over primes dividing elements) and the codimension of the failure space; record the minimum over p.

title: Large deviations / lower-tail of the certificate count: Poisson vs Gaussian regime
connection: The certificate count N(p) has mean ≍ log²p. P(N(p) = 0) is a lower-tail large deviation. In random-graph theory (Janson–Łuczak–Ruciński) lower tails are governed by Janson's inequality and are exponential in the mean.
why: The lower-tail exponent ≈ mean gives P(0) ≈ p^{−c log p}, summable over p: ES true heuristically. Native LDP theory would quantify the needed dependence structure.
first_step: Fit log P(N = 0 | mean M) from data (repo has it) against the Janson prediction −M/(1+Δ/M); record Δ.

title: Percolation on the forest F_p: giant component reaching a QNR
connection: If F_p behaves like a random graph above the percolation threshold, the component of 1 is giant and contains a QNR. ES₅ (p ≡ 1 mod 8) follows from 'the component of 1 contains a QNR'.
why: Percolation-native: thresholds are sharp, and arithmetic graphs (divisor graphs) have percolation results (e.g. random divisor graphs). The forest might be supercritical in a window of small vertices.
first_step: Compute the degree distribution and component structure of F_p restricted to vertices ≤ X for p < 10⁷; locate the effective percolation threshold.

title: Kolmogorov-complexity view of the sporadic lists (U(n) and Rickards–Stange-type exceptions)
connection: Finite sporadic lists in local-global problems (U(n): six values; RS: 15) have low Kolmogorov complexity only if explained by structure. An algorithmic-information test can flag 'structured' vs 'random' sporadics.
why: Exploratory: a compressible sporadic list suggests a hidden obstruction that might also act at primes.
first_step: Factorisations (computed): 105 = 3·5·7, 2961 = 3²·7·47, 3985 = 5·797, 25305 = 3·5·7·241, 111969 = 3³·11·13·29, 978145 = 5·7·27947. All are ≡ 1 (mod 8); mod 840 they are 105, 441 = 21², 625 = 25², 105, 249, 385, so two lie in square classes mod 840. Next: test whether every sporadic lies in a class mod 840·k that is 'square-like' for U's local model.

title: Garsia–Milne involution principle for a bijective ES-count identity
connection: The involution principle builds a bijection from two sign-reversing involutions. If N₋(p) = (count of a simple positive set) − (count of another) via explicit involutions, Garsia–Milne yields a bijection and hence positivity whenever the simple set is bigger.
why: It is the enumerative-combinatorics native machine for turning signed identities into injections. Positivity of ES would follow from an injection from a set of known size ≥ 1.
first_step: Look for any signed identity for N₋ (SIGN_IDENTITY lists the known ones); check whether its terms are counts of explicit finite sets amenable to involutions.

title: Discrete Morse theory / matching on the poset of near-solutions
connection: Acyclic matchings on a poset (Forman) count critical cells, and Euler characteristic = alternating count of critical cells. If an ES-defined poset has Euler characteristic ≠ 0, a critical cell (certificate) must exist.
why: It is a combinatorial-topology tool that generalises sign-reversing involutions with a global acyclicity condition, a strictly richer version of the windmill route.
first_step: Define a poset of partial certificates (e.g. levels/divisor pairs ordered by divisibility) and compute its Euler characteristic as a function of p (small p).

title: Class-number-one-type ineffectivity: is I3's exceptional list finite by a Siegel-type argument?
connection: Chowla proved finiteness of idoneal numbers via Siegel's (ineffective) class-number bound. If I3 failure at n forced a large class group to have a small exponent (an 'idoneal-type' condition), Siegel–Tatuzawa would give finiteness of exceptions up to one.
why: It is the only known mechanism turning a 'polylog-witness' representation problem into a pointwise theorem (with ineffectivity). It is the (R)-rigidity type of FRONTIER's meta-finding.
first_step: Look for a map: I3 failure at n ⇒ the class group of some order of disc −D(n) has exponent ≤ 2 (or bounded); test on the known I3 exceptions.

title: Drinfeld modules / Carlitz module: ES_q certificates as torsion points
connection: DRINFELD_ES: degree-k Diff-parity over F_q(T) via rank-k Drinfeld modules. Carlitz torsion gives cyclotomic function fields where Frobenius of P is explicit.
why: In function fields, 'divisor of 4CP+1 in a class' is a Chebotarev statement in Carlitz cyclotomic extensions, with effective Chebotarev (Weil). This is the native tool.
first_step: State the function-field Type II at fixed level C as a Chebotarev condition in F_q(T)(Λ_{4C}) and compute the effective error.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Power ladder ES_(k): cubic and higher rungs collapse to finite coverings
connection: POWER_LADDER_ES: for odd k, ES_(k) (x, y integers; the third term 1/z with z RATIONAL whose reduced denominator is Q^k, Q odd, gcd(Q,n) = 1; equivalently a third term Q^k/Z) is a finite congruence covering mod 4, while even k returns to ES^□. The native field is power-residue symbols and Waring-type coverings.
why: Calibration item: it shows exactly which relaxations are trivially true. A new rung (e.g. denominators in a norm group of a cyclic field) can be tested the same way.
first_step: Generalise: third denominator in N(K^×) for an abelian field K; find the index condition that makes the rung a finite covering.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Erdős #306-type Fourier counts (Li 2609.32140) and why abundance is needed
connection: Recent AI/Lean-assisted solutions of Erdős problems (e.g. Li's #306) use Fourier counts over exponentially many configurations. ES has polylog witnesses.
why: Calibration: these tools apply to ES variants with many more terms (k ≥ log n unit fractions). They locate the minimal k where Fourier methods work.
first_step: Find the smallest k(n) for which '4/n is a sum of k unit fractions with denominators ≤ n^C' is provable by a Fourier count; compare with k = 3.

title: q-deformed rationals [p/A]_q (Morier-Genoud–Ovsienko) and Jones polynomials of 2-bridge links
connection: MGO's q-rationals have numerator polynomials with positive coefficients, which equal (up to normalisation) Jones polynomials of 2-bridge links (Kogiso–Wakui). The fan graph is the Tait graph, so the Jones polynomial is a Tutte specialisation. ES₅ concerns the class of A, i.e. which 2-bridge link has numerator p.
why: A root-of-unity specialisation detecting (A/p) would make the ES sign a quantum invariant with positivity structure (q-rationals), possibly giving inequalities.
first_step: Compute [p/A]_q numerators for p < 300 and evaluate at q = i, e^{iπ/4}, e^{2πi/8}; test whether any evaluation's phase equals (A/p) on words.

title: Stern's diatomic sequence: (p, A) = (s(k), s(k+1)) and HJ length as a binary-run statistic of k
connection: Every coprime pair occurs exactly once as consecutive Stern values, and the CF of p/A is encoded by the run lengths of k's binary expansion. ES₅ ⇔ some k with s(k) = p, s(k±1) ≡ non-residue, and k's binary word in a 3-run HJ pattern.
why: This makes ES₅ a statement about binary words, so automata/regular-language tools (automatic sequences, Stern's sequence is 2-regular) apply.
first_step: Find the exact HJ-run encoding (LORENZINI_W §7 has a Stern coding); enumerate k with ≤ 3 HJ-runs and s(k) = p, check the sign.

title: Hilbert basis of a 2-dimensional cone: ES₅ ⇔ a cone of index p in the non-residue class with a 5-element Hilbert basis
connection: The Hilbert basis of cone((0,1),(p,−A)) consists of the HJ convergents, so it has r(p/A) + 2 elements. ES₅ ⇔ some cone of type 1/p(1,A) with (A/p) = −1 has Hilbert basis of size 5.
why: Integer-programming/commutative-algebra native: Hilbert-basis sizes and normal semigroup rings (embedding dimension). Toric-ideal theory gives explicit invariants.
first_step: Compute the semigroup-ring invariants (Hilbert series, a-invariant) of the 5-element cones and test whether the sign is a ring-theoretic invariant (e.g. class group element of the toric ring).

title: Multiplicative generation of F_p^* by forest edge products
connection: A = (p+u)/v ≡ u/v (mod p), so (A/p) = (uv/p) on forest edges. ES₅ fails ⇒ every edge product uv lies in the QR subgroup ⇒ the group generated by edge products is ≠ F_p^*. So ES₅(p) ⇐ 'edge products generate F_p^*'.
why: Generation of (ℤ/q)^× by small structured sets is now proved for almost all q (Klurman–Shparlinski–Teräväinen). Edge products are small integers with a divisibility constraint; this links ES₅ to the 'small sets generate' literature.
first_step: Compute the index of ⟨uv : (u,v) edge of F_p, u,v ≤ X⟩ in F_p^* as X grows, p < 10⁶; compare the least X needed with the least QNR.

title: Fair-division reading (Rhind papyrus): 4 loaves among n people, each share as 3 unit fractions (not necessarily distinct)
connection: ES(n) ⇔ 4 loaves can be split among n people so that each share is exactly three unit-fraction pieces. This is the historical Egyptian 2/n-table problem generalised.
why: It is a pure restatement, recorded once. It suggests looking at the scribes' algorithms (choose the first denominator from n's divisors-plus-offset), which match Type I/II choices.
first_step: Compare the Rhind 2/n table's rules with Type I/II certificate selection rules (historical algorithms as certificate selectors).

title: Erdős–Kac jointly over levels: dependence of ω(4Cp+1) across C via shared small primes
connection: Level failures are dependent because 4Cp+1 and 4C′p+1 share small prime factors when C ≡ C′ mod q-structures. The joint distribution of (ω(4Cp+1))_C is a Kubilius-model question.
why: It quantifies how independent the per-level events are, the input any probabilistic or sieve approach needs.
first_step: Compute empirical correlations of 1[level C fails] across C ≤ 50 for p < 10⁷ and fit a Kubilius-type model.

title: Lattice-based crypto SIS/LWE hardness as a heuristic for certificate existence in relation lattices
connection: The relation lattice Λ_q(S) = {x : ∏ g_s^{x_s} = 1} is an SIS-type lattice. Its short vectors relate to subset products hitting targets. Crypto worst-case to average-case reductions say random such lattices have short vectors of predictable length (Gaussian heuristic).
why: Gaussian-heuristic predictions for short vectors give a model of certificate existence that respects lattice structure, more refined than Poisson.
first_step: Compare the Gaussian heuristic for λ₁(Λ_q(S)) with actual values for q < 10⁵, S = first k primes; quantify the deviation.

title: Fermionic/spin TQFT: the parity condition '4 divides an entry' as a spin-structure obstruction
connection: In 3-manifold topology, spin structures on L(p,q) and plumbings are tracked by characteristic sublinks (Wu sets). 'Some pentagon entry ≡ 0 (mod 4)' may say the plumbing admits a spin structure with a given Rokhlin invariant mod 16.
why: Rokhlin's theorem (σ ≡ 0 mod 16 for spin closed 4-manifolds) is a rigid integrality statement. If the ES sign is a Rokhlin invariant, T1 might be a Rokhlin-type obstruction.
first_step: Compute μ-invariants (Neumann–Siebenmann) of L(p,A) via plumbing for all words with p < 500 and compare with the sign.

title: Zolotarev: (A/p) = sign of the permutation x ↦ Ax on ℤ/p — ES₅ as 'an odd multiplication permutation with a length-3 HJ structure'
connection: (A/p) = sgn(π_A), π_A(x) = Ax mod p. ES₅(p) ⇔ some A ∈ L₃(p) gives an odd permutation. Permutation-group language: the parity of π_A can be computed from the cycle type (order of A in F_p^*).
why: (A/p) = −1 ⇔ ord(A) is even with the full 2-part of p−1, i.e. A generates the 2-Sylow quotient. So ES₅ becomes a statement about the 2-adic valuation of multiplicative orders of elements of L₃(p).
first_step: For p ≡ 1 (8), compute v₂(ord_p(A)) for A ∈ L₃(p); ES₅ ⇔ some A has v₂(ord A) = v₂(p−1). Look at the distribution of v₂(ord A) on words.

title: Fixed-letter word families as Chebotarev sets: density of p covered by words with (t,u) fixed
connection: Fixing (t,u) makes A = tu − 1 fixed, and the word exists iff v = (p+u)/A is an integer, i.e. p ≡ −u (mod A). The sign condition (A/p) = −1 is then fixed by reciprocity together with the 2-adic supplement when A is even: given p ≡ −u (mod A) and p mod 4 (and mod 8 if A is even), (A/p) = ±(−u/A) is determined. So each fixed (t,u) covers either a whole residue class mod 4A of primes or nothing (that is, it is the Mordell/B1 structure).
why: It is the cleanest 'fixed-menu' native form, and B1 says finitely many never suffice. The densities and their union bound give the exact covering deficit in Chebotarev language.
first_step: Compute the union density of fixed-(t,u) families with tu ≤ T as T grows (inclusion–exclusion via CRT), and the rate at which the uncovered density decays.

title: Parity barrier (Selberg) check: is ES's sign condition a parity-sensitive sieve problem?
connection: Selberg's parity problem prevents sieves from distinguishing integers with an even or odd number of prime factors. The ES sign (A/p) = ∏ (q/p)^{v_q} is a 'twisted parity' of A's factorisation, which suggests sieve methods face a parity-type barrier.
why: It is the sieve-theory native diagnosis. Repo PARITY_AUDIT may cover it; the twisted-parity framing via (·/p) might be new.
first_step: Check PARITY_AUDIT.md; formalise the 'twisted parity' barrier: construct a weight that agrees with sieve axioms but kills (A/p) = −1 terms.

title: Kneser's theorem on D(px) + D(px) mod (4x − p) and its stabiliser
connection: If 0 ∉ D + D (mod m), Kneser gives |D + D| ≥ 2|D| − |H| for the stabiliser H. Divisor sets of px are multiplicatively structured (D(px) = D(p)·D(x)), so the additive stabiliser is likely trivial, giving a size condition.
why: It is the cleanest additive-combinatorics translation of 'certificate exists at x'. Only size and structure of D(x) mod m enter.
first_step: Compute, over x, the ratio |D(px) mod m|/m; find the x where 2|D| > m (Cauchy–Davenport forces D + D = ℤ/m when m is prime). Record whether such x exist for all p.

title: Torus bundles T_{γ_w}: H₁ order |tr γ_w − 2| and Anosov dynamics
connection: The mapping torus of γ_w on T² has H₁ = ℤ ⊕ coker(γ_w − I) with |coker| = |tr γ_w − 2| = tu + tv − 4. Its linking form and Sol geometry are explicit.
why: A 3-manifold carrier where the trace, not p, is the order. The ES sign may appear as a linking-form class at a different modulus, which gives a new dictionary for transport between p and traces.
first_step: Compute the linking form of T_{γ_w} for words at p < 300 and look for a relation between its square class and (A/p).

title: Weak del Pezzo of degree 3 from the nodal ES cubic: Weyl-group orbits of the 9 lines
connection: The minimal resolution of the closure is a weak del Pezzo surface of degree 3 whose (−2)-curves form a root system. The Weyl group of the complement acts on lines/conic bundles. GEOMETRY_ES records 9 rational lines.
why: The lattice-theoretic structure (Pic ≅ I_{1,6}, roots) organises all conic fibrations, i.e. all 'Type I/II-like' families, in one Weyl orbit picture.
first_step: Compute the root system of the nodes and the orbit structure of conic classes; list the conic fibrations defined over ℚ and match them to known certificate types.

title: Gcd structure across levels: gcd(4Cp+1, 4C′p+1) | 4(C′−C)·… as a coupling axiom
connection: For two levels, gcd(4Cp+1, 4C′p+1) divides C′(4Cp+1) − C(4C′p+1) = C′ − C. So prime factors are shared between levels only through C′ − C. This is the exact coupling of the family {4Cp+1}.
why: This 'gcd-coupling' is the arithmetic analogue of the dependency graph in LLL/Janson. Any pointwise argument across levels must exploit it.
first_step: Build the level-dependency hypergraph for p via shared primes q | C′ − C, and test whether failure patterns in data are explained by it.

title: ES over imaginary quadratic rings (ℤ[i], ℤ[ω]): does unit freedom make it easy?
connection: Potential-automorphy-style arguments work over extensions first. For ES over O_K (K imaginary quadratic), 4/π = 1/ξ + 1/η + 1/ζ with ξ, η, ζ ∈ O_K and no positivity (no real place): the extra units and the lack of positivity might allow identity-based proofs for every prime π. Determine what makes ℤ-ES hard (positivity at the real place? the square classes?) by seeing which ring versions are easy.
why: Isolating the role of the archimedean positivity constraint tells whether the difficulty is archimedean or arithmetic.
first_step: Search the literature ('Erdős–Straus number field', 'Gaussian integers Egyptian fractions'); experimentally find identities for 4/π over ℤ[i] covering all Gaussian primes up to norm 10⁶.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Gaussian periods / cyclotomic: (A/p) via the quadratic Gauss sum and certificates as cyclotomic units
connection: (A/p) = σ_A(√p*)/√p* in Q(ζ_p). Words give A with AA* = tp + 1, i.e. A·A* ≡ 1 (mod p), so σ_A σ_{A*} = id. The ES sign is the action of σ_A on the quadratic subfield.
why: Galois-theoretic language: ES₅ ⇔ some word's Galois element σ_A ∈ Gal(Q(ζ_p)/Q) is non-trivial on Q(√p). This connects to Galois-module structure of cyclotomic units (Sinnott) if words relate to units.
first_step: Look for a cyclotomic unit or Gauss-sum expression naturally indexed by words (e.g. (1 − ζ^A)/(1 − ζ)) whose norm to Q(√p) is sign-sensitive.

title: Integer matrices with prescribed characteristic polynomial: ES words as conjugacy classes
connection: Words correspond to γ ∈ SL₂(ℤ) with b = p and a ≡ d ≡ −1 (mod c). Counting SL₂(ℤ) matrices with given trace and a fixed entry is a classical problem (Eskin–McMullen counting in affine symmetric varieties).
why: Eskin–McMullen/Duke–Rudnick–Sarnak give asymptotic counts in growing balls, which shows the shape of the main term but with no fixed-p pointwise content (B3).
first_step: Note calibration; compute the count of γ with b = p and trace ≤ T as T grows, and its sign-weighted version.

title: Fourier–Dedekind sums / Beck–Robins: lattice points in the word region via Dedekind–Rademacher sums
connection: Counting lattice points in rational polytopes yields Fourier–Dedekind sums (Beck–Robins). The ES₅ sign involves Dedekind sums (DEDEKIND_ES). Combining the two might express Σ_{words} (sign) as a finite combination of Dedekind–Rademacher sums.
why: Dedekind–Rademacher sums satisfy reciprocity laws that allow fast evaluation and sometimes positivity statements.
first_step: Express |L₃(p)| and Σ (A/p) for p < 1000 in terms of Dedekind–Rademacher sums r_n(a,b;c) by linear fitting; look for exact identities.

title: Gross–Zagier singular moduli: Type I as p | N(j(τ₁) − j(τ₂))
connection: Gross–Zagier: p divides N(j(τ₁) − j(τ₂)) iff the two CM orders embed simultaneously into a maximal order of B_{p,∞} (with an explicit formula). QUATERNION_ES shows Type I(p) ⇔ an 'x = 2 collision' of CM orders in B_{p,∞}.
why: It may give a closed criterion: ES Type I at p ⇔ p divides a specific singular-moduli difference. The Gross–Zagier formula expresses the exponent as a sum over representations of binary forms.
first_step: Check numerically for p < 500 whether Type I certificate existence at level d matches p | N(j(√−d)·…) for the orders appearing in Λ_{d,m}.

title: Continued fraction of √f, f = μ² − n: Lagrange's |value| < 2√f and V_n points among convergents
connection: Small values of an indefinite binary form occur at convergents of its roots (Lagrange: |Q(A,B)| < 2√f/… ⇒ (B,A) is a convergent-type pair). V_n points with small D are therefore convergents of (μ ± √f)/n.
why: This makes V_n points a CF computation, with period-length and Pell-unit structure, and connects to ES's other CF forms (HJ length).
first_step: Verify that every V_n point at μ with D < √f comes from a convergent of (μ + √f)/n; then express the B = 1 condition as a condition on the convergent index.

title: Pencil fibres with non-square k: does any Brauer class survive, and what are the zero statistics?
connection: The Z52 theorem covers k = m². For non-square k, Br S_{n,k} may differ, and the k = 0 limit is approached through both square and non-square k. Data on zeros of S_{n,k} for non-square k is the natural sibling table.
why: If non-square fibres have no obstruction and no zeros, the k = 0 fibre's behaviour is 'squares-only obstructed', mirroring T1 in the k-direction.
first_step: Tabulate S_{n,k}(ℕ) = ∅ for n < 10⁴, k ∈ {2, 3, 5, 6, 7}; compare with BM predictions computed from the conic-bundle structure.

title: Heilbronn's average CF length with a quadratic-character twist
connection: Heilbronn: the average number of steps of the Euclidean algorithm on a/p is (12 log 2/π²) log p. Twisting by (a/p), the difference between average lengths over QR and QNR a is a 'character-correlated CF statistic'.
why: If QNRs have systematically shorter/longer expansions (in HJ form), that is a global bias relevant to λ(p) ≤ 3. Twisted Heilbronn sums reduce to Kloosterman-type sums (Ustinov's methods).
first_step: Caveat from a cheap test (scripts/z52b_translate_cheap.py, p < 3000): the plain mean of HJ length is dominated by a near p (p/(p−1) = [[2,…,2]] has length p−1, and (−1/p) = 1 puts it in QR), so QR − QNR mean differences are large noise (0.2 to 9.7). Use regular-CF length, log-HJ length or the count of A with r(p/A) ≤ L instead, for p < 10⁵.

title: Configuration-model random graph for F_p with the divisor-degree sequence
connection: Model F_p as a random graph with the same degree sequence (degrees = numbers of valid partners). Component-size predictions (Molloy–Reed criterion) show whether the component of 1 should be giant.
why: It gives a quantitative null model for forest connectivity, and deviations would show the arithmetic is non-random in a usable way.
first_step: Compute the degree sequence of F_p and the Molloy–Reed quantity Σ d(d−2); compare predicted and actual component sizes for p < 10⁶.

title: Ibukiyama's explicit maximal orders O(q,r) in B_{p,∞} vs the ES orders Λ_{d,m}
connection: Ibukiyama gives explicit maximal orders of B_{p,∞} in terms of q ≡ 3 mod 8 with (−q/p) = −1 and r² ≡ −p mod q. ES's Λ_{d,m} are orders in definite algebras defined by u² = −d, v² = −m, uv + vu = 1. Embedding Λ_{d,m} into O(q,r) links certificates to the choice of auxiliary prime q.
why: Ibukiyama orders are the standard computational model. The auxiliary-prime choice resembles ES's least-QNR dependence (q with (−q/p) = −1).
first_step: For p < 200, test which Λ_{d,m} embed into Ibukiyama orders with small q and compare with certificate levels.

title: Gauss composition of the word forms: is there a group law on words of fixed level t?
connection: Words of level t correspond to factorisations N_t = A·A* with A ≡ A* ≡ −1 (mod t), i.e. to ideal-like objects. If they correspond to ideals in an order (e.g. of disc −4t or t² − 4), composition may combine words of p₁ and p₂ into words of p₁p₂-related N.
why: A composition law gives a multiplicative structure on certificates, the missing 'algebraic rigidity' (R-type) in FRONTIER's meta-finding.
first_step: Test: given words of level t at n₁ and n₂, is there a natural word of level t at some n₃ = f(n₁,n₂) (e.g. via (tn₁+1)(tn₂+1) = t·n₃ + 1 with n₃ = tn₁n₂ + n₁ + n₂)? Check sign multiplicativity.

title: Lens space surgery obstruction: QNR lens spaces are never integral surgeries on knots in S^3 (linking-form/homotopy obstruction)
connection: p-surgery on a knot K ⊂ S³ gives H₁ = ℤ/p with linking form ±1/p, so a lens space L(p,q) arising this way has ±q a square mod p. For p ≡ 1 (4) that means (q/p) = +1. Hence ES₅(p) ⇔ some lens space that is homotopically not an integral knot surgery bounds a 3-chain plumbing. Greene's solution of the lens space realisation problem uses exactly plumbing-lattice embeddings.
why: It locates the ES sign in a famous problem: Greene's lattice-embedding classification (via changemaker lattices) gives a complete description of the square class side. The ES side is its complement.
first_step: Read Greene (Ann. Math. 2013), §§1–3. Check whether the changemaker-lattice machinery has a version for the non-square linking class (e.g. surgeries on knots in other 3-manifolds) that yields 3-chain plumbings.

title: Cohen–Lenstra for sandpile groups (Wood; with pairings: Hodges) and the distribution of pairing classes on random graphs
connection: Wood proved sandpile groups of random graphs follow a Cohen–Lenstra-type law, and Hodges (arXiv:2311.07078) extended this to the groups together with their pairings (as conjectured by Clancy–Kaplan–Leake–Payne–Wood conjectures; et al.). For graphs with cyclic group ℤ/p, the pairing class is ±square (as opposed to non-square) with predictable probabilities; for p ≡ 1 (4) the two classes are 'square' and 'non-square'.
why: It gives a theorem-level random model for ES₅'s sign: 'random small graphs with τ = p have a non-square pairing with probability ≈ 1/2'. ES₅ is a fixed-shape (fan) specialisation.
first_step: Read Wood, The distribution of sandpile groups of random graphs (JAMS 2017); compute the empirical pairing-class frequency over all fan words for p < 10⁵ vs the CL prediction.

title: The L-ladder in cluster language: λ(p) ≤ L ⇔ an (L+2)-gon frieze with one coefficient side N = p (sign rule for L ≥ 4 still to be found)
connection: Words of HJ length L are friezes of the (L+2)-gon with all boundary sides 1 except one side N. CHJ prove finiteness for given boundary. The naive generalisation of the slot lemma is FALSE (reviewer counterexample: chain [2,2,2,5] has det 17 and cofactor 13 with (13/17) = +1, while its length-3 subcontinuant is 4); a correct sign rule for L ≥ 4 has to come from the van der Blij / characteristic-vector formula. Discarded phrasing: 'some diagonal ≡ 0 mod 4'.
why: It gives a uniform family of cluster-algebraic statements (types A_{L−1} with coefficient). L = 3 is ES₅, and λ(p) ≤ L for growing L is Zaremba-adjacent and provable.
first_step: Find the correct sign rule for L = 4 numerically (sign of A vs 4-divisibility of frieze diagonals) for p < 10⁴.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Schreier graph of SL₂(ℤ) on P¹(F_p) (Selberg's 3/16): HJ length as a path length with unbounded generators
connection: The HJ step A ↦ ⌈p/A⌉A − p is a move on P¹(F_p)-type data, and r(p/A) is a path length from A to 0 in a graph with generators M(b) for all b. The bounded-generator Schreier graph is an expander (Selberg's eigenvalue bound).
why: It explains (B3) why expansion does not give length-3 paths: unbounded generators collapse the diameter, and existence of length-3 paths into a coset is not spectral. It is recorded as the native picture.
first_step: Compute, in the bounded-generator Schreier graph (b ≤ B), the distance from ∞ to the QNR set as a function of B and p; compare with λ(p).

title: Integer-relation search (PSLQ/LLL) for N₋(p) or the slot-count in a basis of arithmetic functions
connection: Try to express N₋(p), N₊(p) or the ES₅ word count as an integer combination of standard arithmetic functions of p and p-tied integers (τ(p+k), class numbers h(−kp), r₂, r₃(kp), …).
why: A found identity is a candidate exact formula (an R-type rigidity). A null result over a large basis is evidence against simple formulas. SIGN_IDENTITY did a version; the basis can be widened.
first_step: Build a basis of 200 functions evaluated at 2000 primes; run integer relation detection (LLL on the evaluation matrix) for N₋(p).

title: Effective Chebotarev in the compositum of Q(√−t, ζ_t) over all small t: the joint Frobenius of p
connection: ES certificate existence at levels t ≤ T is a function of p's Frobenius in a large compositum K_T (genus fields, ray class fields) plus the factorisation of tp+1. The first part is Chebotarev; the second is not Galois-theoretic.
why: It cleanly separates the Galois-theoretic layer (handled by Chebotarev/GRH) from the 'factorisation of one integer' layer, which is where B2 lives.
first_step: Define K_T explicitly for T ≤ 12; compute which Frobenius classes guarantee a certificate (from the Galois layer alone) and their density.

title: Elkies-style 'search for structure' in large-height ES solutions via lattice reduction
connection: Elkies's ABC/Euler-conjecture searches use lattice reduction to find large solutions with structure. For ES, solutions with exceptionally large minimal x (hardest p) might be found by targeted lattice search, giving data on 'how hard' primes look.
why: It is the computational-NT native way to probe extreme cases, giving better test cases than random primes.
first_step: Search primes p < 10¹⁵ near pseudosquares for the maximal least-certificate level using lattice-guided sampling; record extremes.

title: Montesinos relaxation: Euler number −4/n with arbitrary numerators β_i (M(0; β₁/x, β₂/y, β₃/z))
connection: Allowing Seifert invariants (x,β₁),(y,β₂),(z,β₃) gives β₁/x + β₂/y + β₃/z = 4/n, which is trivially solvable. Requiring all β_i = 1 is ES; requiring β_i ∈ {1, 2} is an intermediate rung.
why: It gives a relaxation ladder native to Seifert/Montesinos knots, where the rung β_i ≤ 2 might be provable and might reveal which numerator constraint carries the difficulty.
first_step: Test 'β_i ∈ {1,2}' (i.e. 4/n = Σ ε_i/x_i with ε_i ∈ {1,2}) for all primes < 10⁷; find whether a uniform construction exists.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Markov uniqueness at prime powers (Baragar, Button, Schmutz) as a pointwise-at-primes precedent
connection: The Markov uniqueness conjecture is proved when the largest Markov number is a prime power (Baragar; Button; Schmutz), using the factorisation/roots of x² ≡ −1 (mod m) and the arithmetic of 9m² − 4. It is a pointwise statement at primes about a Markoff-type equation, proved via the arithmetic of a p-tied integer.
why: It is a rare (R)-type rigidity result at primes for a Markoff-type surface; ES's S_{n,D} is Markoff-type. Its mechanism (counting square roots of −1 mod p) is cheap and might transfer to counting certificate roots mod p.
first_step: Read Button, 'The uniqueness of the prime Markoff numbers' (J. LMS 1998); identify the step where primality is used and check whether an analogous root count constrains S_{p,D} solutions.

title: SL₂-character variety of the punctured torus / pair of pants: S_{n,D} as a relative character variety
connection: Markoff-type cubics x² + y² + z² − xyz = k are relative SL₂-character varieties of the once-punctured torus (k = boundary trace + 2). The mapping class group acts, and that action drives BGS/Chen. S_{n,D} might be a character variety of a different surface or with a twisted boundary condition, or might not be one at all.
why: If S_{n,D} is a (twisted) character variety, a mapping-class-group action exists, which is exactly the missing infinite group action; if not, that is a structural reason for the difference from Markoff.
first_step: Test whether nA² + B² + D − ABC can be transformed (rescaling, sign changes over ℚ(√n)) into a character-variety cubic x² + y² + z² − xyz − k; compute the invariants (discriminant, singular points) to decide.

title: Meta: the chain matrix M(t,u,v) as a common carrier in ≥ 8 fields — a transfer table of nearest theorems
connection: M(t,u,v) is simultaneously a reduced Laplacian, an electrical network, a ternary Gram matrix, a plumbing intersection form, a cyclic-quotient resolution graph, a FQH K-matrix, an A₂ frieze with coefficient and an SL₂ word. For each field, record the strongest pointwise existence theorem about this object.
why: It organises the translation work so that a single new theorem in one field can be checked for transfer to all others.
first_step: Build the table (field, object, nearest pointwise theorem, what it would need) from items in this lane; mark empty cells as targets.

title: Tetrahedral analogue: 1/r = Σ 1/h_i over four faces (four-term Egyptian in 3D)
connection: For a tetrahedron, 1/r = Σ_{i=1}^4 1/h_i (inradius vs altitudes). The triangle identity 1/r = Σ 1/h_i (three terms) is the 2D version behind the altitude form of ES. Higher-dimensional simplices give k-term Egyptian equations with geometric realisability conditions.
why: It places ES in a dimension ladder of simplex geometry, where realisability (simplex inequalities) adds constraints. Low priority, but it is a natural family.
first_step: Record; optionally test whether 4/n = Σ 1/h_i (4 terms) with tetrahedron realisability is always solvable.

title: Riemenschneider point diagram: dual chains and the sign under p ≡ 1 (4)
connection: The Riemenschneider dual of p/A is p/(p − A), and (p−A/p) = (A/p) for p ≡ 1 (4). Duality maps length-3 chains (v,t,u) to chains of length v + t + u − 5. So ES₅ is also a statement about QNR fractions whose dual chain has a specific long shape.
why: The dual picture (long chains of 2's and a few larger entries) is where Zaremba-type 'bounded digits' tools live. ES₅ becomes 'some QNR has a dual with ≤ 3 non-2 blocks'.
first_step: Express ES₅ via the dual: QNR B with p/B = [[2,…,2, a, 2,…,2, b, 2,…]] of a specific block shape; count such B via digit-structure.

title: Frobenius number analogue for three generators: n = tuv − u − v as a three-generator semigroup statistic?
connection: For coprime u, v, uv − u − v is the Frobenius number of ⟨u,v⟩. For three generators there are formulas (e.g. for ⟨u, v, w⟩ with structure, Rødseth). Is tuv − u − v the Frobenius number of a natural 3-generated semigroup (for instance ⟨u, v, tuv⟩ is trivial)? If so, I3 becomes 'every large n is a Frobenius number of a semigroup of a given shape'.
why: 'Which integers are Frobenius numbers of 3-generated semigroups' is a studied question; a match would bring that literature in.
first_step: Search small cases: for given n = tuv − u − v, compute Frobenius numbers of ⟨a,b,c⟩ with a,b,c ≤ 50 and test whether some natural family reproduces tuv − u − v.

title: Positive definite binary forms of discriminant −4(tp+1)… and the A/A* pairing as an ambiguous-form question
connection: Factorisations N = A·A* correspond to ambiguous forms/ideals of discriminant related to N. Words are factorisations with A ≡ A* ≡ −1 (mod t). Genus theory of disc −4N tells which ambiguous classes exist.
why: Gauss's genus theory counts factorisations as ambiguous classes, and the mod-t condition becomes a genus-character condition, a native class-group statement.
first_step: For small t, compute the genus characters of the ambiguous forms of disc −4N_t and identify which genus the word factorisations occupy.

title: Kernel-checked verification tables (Lean/Coq certificates) for ES up to large bounds
connection: Store per-prime certificates (x,y,z) or compact Type I/II data and verify them inside a proof assistant (by computation via norm_num/decide or a verified checker).
why: Infrastructure: a formal ES-up-to-N theorem makes formal T1, slot lemma and the reductions usable together with numeric bounds. It is cheap relative to its reuse value.
first_step: Prototype: verify ES for p < 10⁶ in Lean 4 from a certificate file with a verified checker; measure time.

title: Bohr-set formulation: L₃(p) as elements of a multiplicative Bohr set intersected with an exact divisibility condition
connection: A ∈ L₃(p) ⇔ A ≡ u·v⁻¹ (mod p), A = (p+u)/v, so, precisely, A/p = 1/v + u/(pv), the right endpoint of (1/v, 1/v + u/(pv)], so A lies in a union of short intervals near 1/v (a Bohr-type set for the frequencies 1/v) and is exactly determined there. ES₅ asks for a QNR in this union with exact landing.
why: Character sums over Bohr sets (Burgess-type in short intervals near rationals with small denominators) are native. Exact landing is again the divisor condition, but the interval structure may give partial control.
first_step: Compute the union of intervals I_v = (p/v, p/v + u/v)-type for all (u,v) and its total length vs p; compare with Burgess thresholds.

title: Conway–Coxeter count analogue: number of positive friezes with boundary (1,1,1,1,N) as an arithmetic function of N
connection: Classical friezes of the n-gon are counted by Catalan numbers. With coefficient N on one side, the number of positive integral pentagon friezes is an arithmetic function F(N) (≈ number of words incl. boundary words ≍ log²N). ES₅ refines it by the sign.
why: Generating functions of frieze counts with coefficients might be more structured (e.g. in terms of divisor functions or class numbers) than word counts, with a combinatorial (triangulation) interpretation via CHJ.
first_step: Compute F(N) and F₋(N) for N < 10⁵; search OEIS and fit to divisor-function combinations.

title: Integral Apollonian-type packing whose curvatures are ES-word data
connection: Apollonian packings have curvature quadruples satisfying Descartes's equation. A packing or a thin-group orbit whose curvatures include p exactly when ES₅(p) holds would put ES in the Apollonian local-global framework (where reciprocity obstructions are understood).
why: Speculative construction target; QUESTION_R and apollonian_reciprocity explored nearby ideas.
first_step: Look for a quadratic form F (Descartes-like, signature (3,1) or (2,1)) and a thin orbit whose entries realise (t,u,v)-data with p as a coordinate.

title: Algebraic geometry of the word surface W: tuv − u − v = p as a cubic surface family over the p-line
connection: W_p : tuv − u − v = p is an affine cubic surface (a log CY of the same 'xyz + linear' type as Markoff-like surfaces). Its integral points are words. Its Brauer group and BM obstruction for integral points with the sign condition give an ES₅-native arithmetic-geometry statement.
why: It gives ES₅ its own arithmetic geometry, distinct from U_n, possibly with a cleaner Brauer group (the sign condition might be a Brauer class evaluation).
first_step: Compute Br(W_p) for the compactification (sympy/Magma); test whether (A/p) = (tu − 1 / p) is the evaluation of a quaternion algebra class (ramified along tu = 1; see the Brauer item) (tu − 1, p) on W_p.

title: Global by-excess (HJ) tree of all length-3 pairs and the forest colouring
connection: The HJ algorithm acts on pairs: (p, A) → (A, u) → (u, 1) → (1, 0) for p/A = [[v,t,u]] (A = tu − 1, vA − p = u). Reading it backwards, all pairs (m, a) of HJ length 3, over all m, form level 3 of one global tree rooted at (1, 0) (a Stern–Brocot-type tree for the by-excess algorithm). Mod p, u ≡ vA, which recovers (A/p) = (uv/p), the forest colouring.
why: It places all words for all p in one tree, so that the ES₅ question 'level-3 node with first coordinate p and QNR colour' becomes a tree-colouring question across p. Tree statistics such as the number of level-3 nodes with first coordinate m (≍ log²m) are explicit.
first_step: Generate the level-3 layer of the global tree for m < 10⁶; for each prime m record the colours; look for inherited colour patterns from level-2 parents (u,1) → (tu−1, u) that are independent of m.

title: Sparsity index: why binary Goldbach is stuck and ES is worse
connection: Binary Goldbach has a main term n/log²n among ~n terms and never got pointwise; ES has main term ≍ log²p among ≍ p log p 'trial events' (PARITY_AUDIT trial form).
why: Quantifies how far ES is from any problem ever upgraded; directs search to reformulations with denser events (fewer trials, larger main term).
first_step: Define sparsity = log(main term)/log(#trials) for each ES reformulation (★, b=1, ES₅, e-slice, I3 words) and tabulate; look for the least sparse one.

title: Chen switching for ES: Type I ↔ Type II role switch to upper-bound 'near misses'
connection: Chen bounded the bad P₃ contribution by sieving the switched set. ES: a 'near miss' at level C is a divisor of 4Cp+1 in a wrong class; switching d ↔ (4Cp+1)/d and C ↔ another parametrisation (Type I ↔ Type II) may convert hard lower bounds into upper bounds of a switched count.
why: Lower bound = (computable total) − (upper-bounded bad part) is the only robust way sieves get existence.
first_step: List all involutions/bijections between ES certificate sets (Type I/II, (★)↔b=1, level switching) and check whether any maps near-misses of one family to near-misses with a computable total in another.

title: Schnirelmann/Mann in the space of fractions: ES as U + (U+U) ∋ 4/n
connection: Schnirelmann turned a positive density for P+P into 'every n'. ES asks 4/n ∈ U+U+U (U = unit fractions). Translate to: 4/n − U meets U+U, and look for Mann-type sumset theorems for sets of rationals with structured denominators.
why: 4-term ES is trivial (4/p = 1/(k+1) + 3/(p(k+1)) and 3/m always splits into ≤ 3 terms), so the problem is exactly the 'order 3 vs order 4' gap of a basis — a classical additive-combinatorics shape.
first_step: Formalize U+U as {a/b : b has a divisor pair (d,e) with d+e ≡ 0 mod a}; study the measure/density of 4/n − U ∩ (U+U) for n in a dyadic range.

title: Powers-of-two slice: ES solutions with x = 2^k
connection: Goldbach–Linnik used the lacunary set of powers of 2. ES slice: 4/p = 1/2^k + 1/y + 1/z needs (2^{k+2} − p)/(p·2^k) to split into two unit fractions; e.g. via the divisor p it needs (2^{k+2} − p) | (2^i + 1) for some i ≤ k+2.
why: A lacunary, explicit family of candidate first denominators with rich multiplicative structure (2^i+1 factors via cyclotomy) — the ES analogue of Linnik's 2^v.
first_step: Compute, for p ≡ 1 (mod 24) up to 10⁷, the fraction of p having an ES solution with a power-of-2 denominator and the distribution of the least k.

title: g(4)=19 descent: analytic threshold + greedy reduction to the verified range
connection: BDD reduced every n below 10³⁶⁷ to the verified range by subtracting biquadrates. ES has no subtraction structure, but the e-slice form reduces ES(p) to a property of N = (p+e)/4 < p; formalize a 'descent' that moves a hard instance to a smaller one.
why: If certificate existence at p could be read off from data at N ≈ p/4 that is itself verifiable recursively, verification scales.
first_step: Measure: for the hardest primes (DISPROOF_AVENUES list) how many e ≤ 1000 give N = (p+e)/4 with ≥ k divisors; is there always an e with N highly composite?

title: Divisor counts in a class as coset theta series of the split form xy
connection: Watson's trick works with sums of squares in arithmetic progressions (coset theta series). D_t^−(N) = #{xy = N, x ≡ −1 (t)} is a representation number of the indefinite binary form xy on a lattice coset.
why: Puts ES level counts into the language of (indefinite) lattice cosets where theta-lifts and Siegel–Weil apply; METAPLECTIC_ES already gives the generating function.
first_step: Write Σ_N D_t^−(N)q^N as a coset theta series of xy and compare with METAPLECTIC_ES Thm K; then try a theta lift to a ternary/quaternary positive form.

title: Lagrange descent on near-certificates via a composition law
connection: Lagrange got every p by producing m·p = sum of 4 squares with m < p and descending m using Euler's identity. ES needs a composition law on 'defective' certificates (defect m) that lowers |m|.
why: Descent is the oldest almost→every mechanism; ES lacks an obvious composition, but the SL₂ form (matrices [[a,p],[c,d]]) has matrix multiplication.
first_step: Define defect for SL₂-form near-certificates (e.g. congruence a ≡ −1 only mod c/m); test whether products/quotients of two near-certificates with the same defect yield smaller defect.

title: Pigeonhole over complementary divisor sets: |Div(N₁)| + |Div(N₂)| > φ(e) forces a certificate
connection: Lagrange's lemma: the sets {x²} and {−1−y²} each have (p+1)/2 elements so they meet. ES e-slice: for a coprime split N = N₁N₂ (N = (p+e)/4), if |Div(N₁) mod e| + |Div(N₂) mod e| > φ(e), some a | N₁ and b | N₂ satisfy a ≡ −b, so −1 ∈ Rat_e(N).
why: A clean sufficient condition reducing ES to finding e with N highly composite relative to φ(e).
first_step: For p in the hard list, search e ≤ 10⁴ maximising (|Div(N₁)|+|Div(N₂)|)/φ(e) over coprime splits; report how close to 1 the best ratio gets.

title: Thue's lemma / short vectors in lattices L_{p,λ} producing (★) triples
connection: Thue's pigeonhole gives |x|,|y| ≤ √p with x ≡ λy (mod p). Choose λ from ES structure (e.g. λ ≡ −4⁻¹ or ratios from Rat_e) and test whether short vectors produce positive (★) data.
why: Pigeonhole-in-a-box is the cheapest every-p mechanism; ES's linear congruence p ≡ −(u+B) (mod 4uB) has a modulus depending on the unknowns, so a 2-D lattice must be found for each candidate level.
first_step: For fixed C (or u), (★) says 4uC − 1 | p + u: build the lattice {(x,y) : x ≡ y·λ_C mod (something)} and check numerically whether LLL-short vectors give solutions.

title: Cauchy-lemma analogue: simultaneous control of (u+B, uB)
connection: Cauchy's lemma represents a number and its 'trace' simultaneously. (★) in pair form: s = u+B, q = uB with s ≡ −p (mod 4q) and s² − 4q a square. Seek an inequality region in (s,q) where existence is forced, as Cauchy's b² < 4a, 3a < b²+2b+4 does.
why: Simultaneous norm/trace representation is the mechanism behind every-n polygonal theorems; ES's (s,q) formulation is of the same shape (sum and product of two unknowns).
first_step: Plot, for many p, the set of (s,q) satisfying the congruence and check where the 'square discriminant' condition is hit; look for a region of guaranteed hits.

title: Correlate f_I(p), R(p) with class numbers h(−4p), h(−kp)
connection: Duke/Iwaniec: representation numbers of ternary forms ≈ class numbers. If some ES count correlates with h(−kp) for small k, a class-number-sized main term may be hidden in a weighted ES count.
why: Cheap test of whether ES counts carry class-number information beyond the BM/genus layer.
first_step: For primes p ≤ 10⁷, regress R(p)/log²p and f_I(p)/log²p on h(−4p)/√p, h(p)·reg/√p and L(1,(·/p)); report partial correlations.

title: Always-existing objects (CM points / closed geodesics of discriminant tied to p) landing in a target region
connection: Duke's theorem works because Heegner points of discriminant −d always exist (h(−d) ≥ 1) and equidistribute. ES needs existence; find objects attached to every p (e.g. CM points of disc −4p, geodesics of disc p) such that landing in an explicit cusp/congruence region ⟺ an ES certificate.
why: Equidistribution then forces existence for all large p (possibly ineffectively) — the general almost→every template of Duke/Linnik.
first_step: Try: reduced forms [a,b,c] of disc −16p or −4(4Cp+1); check whether 'a ≡ −1 (mod 4C), a small' type conditions encode (★); measure how deep in the cusp the region lies (it may be too deep — the B2 issue).

title: Per-level explicit thresholds: R_t(n) is exactly a divisor count — make each level's failure set explicit
connection: 290 theorem: explicit per-form cusp bounds + finite checks. ES levels have no cusp part (METAPLECTIC Thm K: R_t = D_t^− − β_t), so each level's failure set is an explicit multiplicative condition on tn+1. Compose them escalator-style.
why: Explicit per-level failure sets turn the menu escalation into a computation on multiplicative sets (thin sets S_t).
first_step: For t ≤ 64 describe {n : D_t^−(tn+1) = 0} as 'no sub-multiset product of the prime factors of tn+1 is ≡ −1 mod t' (prime factors in a subgroup avoiding −1 is sufficient but not necessary — e.g. t = 28, N = 141 = 3·47) and compute the densities of intersections.

title: Many-variable relaxations: ES with an extra term tied to the others
connection: Hasse principle holds for forms in many variables (Davenport, Heath-Brown, Hooley). 4-term ES is trivial; find intermediate 'k-term ES with constraints' (e.g. 1/x+1/y+1/z+1/w with w forced to equal xyz·k, or two terms merging 1/a+1/b = 1/c) that are circle-method accessible and imply 3-term ES.
why: Interpolates between trivial (4 free terms) and hard (3 terms); the implication step is the interesting part.
first_step: List 4-term constrained families and for each check (i) does a solution give a 3-term solution, (ii) number of variables after eliminating constraints.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Integral-point fibration on U_n by the curves x = const (two-term problems)
connection: Fibration method for rational points; integral versions exist for some schemes fibred into affine conics (Harpaz, JEMS 2019, conditional on stated hypotheses). Fixing x makes ES a two-term problem 1/y + 1/z = 4/n − 1/x, a divisor problem.
why: U_n is a log K3-type affine cubic surface (check); an integral fibration method with a BM-type local condition would be a structural every-n mechanism.
first_step: Harpaz, 'Integral points on conic log K3 surfaces', JEMS 21 (2019), arXiv:1511.04876 (verified: sufficient conditions under stated arithmetic/geometric hypotheses, not unconditional); check whether U_n fits the framework and which hypotheses fail.

title: Dirichlet's product trick: a product of all level series with nonnegative coefficients
connection: Dirichlet: Π_χ L(s,χ) = ζ_K(s) has nonnegative coefficients, so no L(1,χ) vanishes. ES: look for a product/combination of the twisted level series Σ_χ σ_χ(tn+1) whose coefficients are nonnegative and whose value 'at s = 1' (or at the p-th coefficient) is forced positive.
why: Positivity of a combination is how non-vanishing statements are proved for every modulus; METAPLECTIC Thm K gives exactly these character-twisted series.
first_step: From Thm K, form Σ_{χ mod t} σ_χ(N) products over a few levels t and test numerically which combinations have nonnegative coefficients that vanish at p only when R(p) = 0.

title: Prime-factor census by CRT: q | 4Cp+1 iff C ≡ −(4p)⁻¹ (mod q)
connection: In Bertrand/Chebyshev the prime factorisation of a binomial coefficient is explicit. Here every prime q ∤ 2p divides 4Cp+1 exactly on one class C ≡ c_q (mod q); a single-prime certificate exists iff 4c_q | q+1 for some q ≡ 3 (mod 4) (C = c_q < q). Higher certificates combine several q's at a common C.
why: Makes the certificate problem an explicit combinatorial problem on the residues c_q(p); single-prime certificates have probability ≈ τ((q+1)/4)/q, summing to ≍ log²p — the main term in a transparent form.
first_step: Compute the single-prime-certificate count S₁(p) = #{q ≡ 3 (4) prime : 4c_q(p) | q+1} for p ≤ 10⁸ and its share of R(p); check whether S₁(p) alone ever vanishes for p in the hard list.

title: Large-values / 'zero-density' estimate for levels at fixed p
connection: Hoheisel's every-interval theorem needed that few zeros are far right (zero density). ES analogue: at fixed p, show that only few levels C have a large deviation of the level count D_C(p) from its expected 2/φ(4C)·(…), so the many 'good' levels carry R(p) > 0.
why: Large-values estimates are statements about one object (here one p) and many 'frequencies' (levels) — the right quantifier order.
first_step: Compute the empirical distribution of level deviations for fixed p ~ 10⁹ and test a large-values inequality of the shape #{C ≤ X : |dev_C| > V} ≪ X·(stuff)/V².

title: Least non-residue lens: ES failure ⇒ p is a QR modulo every small prime (via the BM layer)
connection: Linnik's large sieve shows n(p) ≪ p^ε for almost all p; Burgess gives n(p) ≪ p^{0.152} for all p. If 'no certificate at levels ≤ L' forced (p/ℓ) = 1 for all ℓ ≤ L^c, then Burgess would contradict failure once L^c > p^{0.152}.
why: SYNTHESIS_SPARKS9 already shows BM-level positivity via ℓ(n); the question is how far the forcing extends when certificates (not just main terms) are required.
first_step: Test empirically: among primes with no (★) certificate at levels C ≤ K, what is the distribution of ℓ(p)? (If ℓ(p) is not forced large, the lens fails for (★).)

title: Audit EH/BV-conditional ES statements for smooth-moduli (MPZ) versions
connection: Zhang got bounded gaps by replacing EH with an equidistribution statement for smooth moduli only. Check each conditional ES result in CONDITIONAL_ES.md: which moduli does it need, and would Polymath8's MPZ(ϖ,δ) (smooth moduli, fixed residues) suffice?
why: Turns a list of conditional results into unconditional ones whenever the moduli can be taken smooth — exactly the Zhang move.
first_step: Read CONDITIONAL_ES.md and tabulate: hypothesis, moduli used, residues fixed or varying, whether smooth restriction loses only a constant.

title: Use p = a² + b² to create bilinear structure (Friedlander–Iwaniec style)
connection: FI broke parity using Gaussian-integer arithmetic for x² + y⁴. Primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) are norms ππ̄; rewrite certificate conditions (e.g. 4Cp+1 = dd′) in terms of (a,b) and Gaussian integers to obtain Type II bilinear sums with structure.
why: Mordell-hard primes are all ≡ 1 (mod 4), so this extra structure is always available and unused in divisor formulations.
first_step: Express 4Cp + 1 = 4C(a²+b²) + 1 and look for factorisations over ℤ[i] or ℤ[√−C] (4Ca² + 4Cb² + 1) that align with d ≡ −1 (mod 4C).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Switching d ↔ (4Cp+1)/d: only d ≤ √(4Cp+1) needed, then the trial form
connection: Titchmarsh/Linnik handle large divisors of p−1 by switching to the complementary divisor. For ES both d and N/d are ≡ −1 (mod 4C), so R(p) = 2·#{small d}, and for small d, C is forced: C = c_d := −(4p)⁻¹ mod d with 4C | d+1 and d² ≤ 4Cp+1 (trial form).
why: Shows that R(p)/2 = #{d : 4c_d(p) | d+1, d² ≤ 4c_d(p)p + 1} with c_d(p) = −(4p)⁻¹ mod d (reviewer repair: the size condition selects the smaller of the two complementary divisors) — a single explicit arithmetic condition per d, ready for Type I equidistribution in d.
first_step: Implement the d-indexed formulation and test whether the events {4c_d(p) | d+1} for d in dyadic ranges behave like independent events with probability τ((d+1)/4)/d.

title: Transference principle: dense subsets of ES certificates relative to a pseudorandom majorant
connection: Green–Tao: a dense subset of a pseudorandom set inherits linear patterns. ES certificate sets for varying p sit inside the majorant {all factorizations of 4Cp+1}; transference could show a positive-density subset of p's certificate data forces patterns that are certificates for other p's.
why: Odd: it moves information between different p, which is not ES; but a pattern-based closure (certificate for p₁,p₂ ⇒ certificate for p₃) would be an every-type mechanism.
first_step: Search the (★) data for linear patterns: triples (p₁,p₂,p₃) in AP whose certificates are linearly related.

title: Siegel's two-character trick for ES: a positive-coefficient product over two primes
connection: Siegel bounds L(1,χ₂) below by using ζ L(χ₁) L(χ₂) L(χ₁χ₂) ≥ 0 together with an exceptional χ₁. ES: combine the certificate counts at p and at an auxiliary prime p′ (or the characters (·/p), (·/p′), (·/pp′)) in a positivity identity, so that failure at p would force excess at a related object which is bounded.
why: Positivity products across two objects are how individual lower bounds were first obtained from average information.
first_step: Look for an identity: Σ over certificates of pp′ (composite!) = (certificates of p)·(…) + (certificates of p′)·(…) + mixed; check numerically whether the mixed term is small/positive.

title: Inverse Frey: encode the failure of ES at p as an object with impossible properties
connection: Frey/Ribet/Wiles: a hypothetical solution yields an elliptic curve whose mod-ℓ representation would come from a nonexistent level-2 form. ES failure gives no point, but it gives a huge family of constraints (no divisor of 4Cp+1 is ≡ −1 mod 4C, for all C). Package these constraints as a Galois/automorphic object (e.g. a 'character' on level structures) and seek a rigidity contradiction.
why: The FLT pattern 'counterexample ⇒ object ⇒ contradiction' is the archetypal every-n proof; ES's failure data are rich enough to define objects.
first_step: Formalise the failure data as a function F_p(C, a) = 1[class a mod 4C contains a divisor of 4Cp+1]; check whether ES failure makes F_p multiplicative/character-like in C (it would be in the square-mimicking profinite model).

title: Wieferich-type congruences forced on a hypothetical counterexample
connection: Mihăilescu showed a Catalan solution forces p^{q−1} ≡ 1 (mod q²) — strong congruences on the unknowns. ES: a counterexample p must be a square modulo every M for which bounded certificates cover the non-square classes (Mordell: mod 840). Push the list of forced congruences as far as possible and combine with the least-non-residue bound.
