why: If 'no certificate with parameters ≤ L' forces (p/ℓ) = 1 for all ℓ ≤ L^c, Burgess (n(p) ≪ p^{0.152}) gives a contradiction for L^c > p^{0.152}.
first_step: For moduli M = 840·m, compute the residues uncovered by certificates with all parameters ≤ L; test whether they are exactly squares mod M and how L must grow with M.

title: Cyclotomic size argument: 'non-certificate part' of Π_C(4Cp+1) must be small
connection: Bang–Zsigmondy: Φ_n(a) is large but its non-primitive part is tiny (only the largest prime of n), so a primitive prime exists. ES analogue: bound the part of Π_{C≤X}(4Cp+1) made of primes that cannot participate in any certificate, and show it is smaller than the whole.
why: A size argument needs no equidistribution; it uses only the explicit CRT census of prime factors (cf. Erdős–Bertrand item).
first_step: Define 'certificate-capable' primes q (those with 4c_q | (q+1)k-type relations) and compute log of the incapable part vs. Σ log(4Cp+1) for test p.

title: Dirichlet–Pell pigeonhole on near-certificates in M₂(ℤ)
connection: Pell is solvable for every non-square D by: infinitely many (x,y) with bounded norm defect, two with the same defect k and residues mod k, divide them to get norm 1. ES Type I/II fail exactly at odd squares — the Pell exception shape. In the SL₂ form, look for near-certificate matrices with bounded defect; two congruent ones give a quotient that is an exact certificate.
why: Pigeonhole + group law is the cleanest every-n mechanism whose only failures are squares; T1 must appear as the reason the quotient fails at squares.
first_step: Define defect for matrices [[a,p],[c,d]] (e.g. det = 1 + δ, or a ≡ −1 only mod c/δ); generate many for a given p and test whether quotients of pairs with equal defect yield exact certificates.

title: Smith-type distribution of 'certificate-free levels' in twist families
connection: Smith's method computes distributions of Selmer groups in quadratic-twist families. The set of levels C at which p has no certificate is a 'Selmer-like' local-global object varying with p; its distribution over p could be computed by Smith/Koymans–Pagano-style methods.
why: Exact distributional knowledge of the failing-level profile is stronger than the zero-law heuristics now used.
first_step: Define the profile vector (1[level C fails])_{C ≤ K} and tabulate its empirical distribution over p; compare with a product-of-local-factors model.

title: Hecke-type relations between ES counts at p, pℓ, pℓ² (Soundararajan's no-escape-of-mass)
connection: Soundararajan prevented escape of mass using λ(ℓ)² = λ(ℓ²) + 1, which forbids both λ(ℓ) and λ(ℓ²) small. ES: find exact or approximate relations between certificate counts f(p), f(pℓ), f(pℓ²) (solutions for composite n come from p, from ℓ, and 'mixed') that make f(p) = 0 incompatible with the controlled values at pℓ, pℓ².
why: Multiplicative relations at related integers are a way to get pointwise information from quantities that are easier to bound.
first_step: Compute f_II(n) (or R(n)) for n = p, pℓ, pℓ² for p ≤ 10⁵, ℓ ≤ 50, and fit f(pℓ) ≈ a·f(p) + b·f(ℓ) + c·f(p)f(ℓ) + mixed; study the mixed term.

title: Complementary failure sets: two ES methods whose exceptions are incompatible
connection: Holowinsky's and Soundararajan's methods each fail only for forms with atypical eigenvalue statistics, in opposite directions; combined they cover every form. ES: the (★) line and the b=1 line never fail simultaneously ≤ 10⁸; find statistics S_A, S_B such that (★) failure forces S_A(p) extreme and b=1 failure forces S_B(p) extreme in an incompatible way.
why: A two-method union is an every-p proof template that does not need either method to be pointwise by itself.
first_step: Compute a battery of statistics (ℓ(p), T(p), L(1,(·/p)), M_BM, level-failure profile) for the 14 (★)-failures, the 3 b=1 failures and controls; look for anticorrelated pairs.

title: Amplified second moment over a short family around p
connection: Friedlander–Iwaniec amplification: bound an individual member by a family moment weighted with an amplifier peaked at the target. ES: Σ_{|n−p|≤H} |R(n) − M(n)|²·|A_p(n)|² with A_p(n) = Σ_{ℓ≤L} c_ℓ (n/ℓ)(p/ℓ); if this is ≤ (M(p)|A_p(p)|)²/2, then R(p) > 0.
why: The bookkeeping (family size H vs amplifier length L ~ H) is not immediately hopeless; the hard input is the twisted second moment of R − M over short intervals.
first_step: Numerically evaluate the amplified moment for p ~ 10⁶–10⁷, H ~ 10³–10⁴, Legendre-symbol amplifiers, and compare with the diagonal term.

title: Potential ES: count solutions over a quadratic field and use Galois parity
connection: Potential automorphy proves things over extensions and descends via Brauer induction. ES over O_K for real quadratic K: Gal(K/ℚ) acts on K-solutions of 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z with totally positive x,y,z; fixed points are ℚ-solutions. If the number of K-solutions in a Galois-stable finite window is odd, a rational solution exists.
why: Parity across a Galois action is a descent mechanism that needs no analysis over ℚ.
first_step: For K = ℚ(√2), ℚ(√5) and small p, enumerate totally positive integral solutions with norms bounded (finite after fixing a fundamental domain for units) and compute the parity of the count of non-rational ones.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Killing ramification: remove small-prime structure from a counterexample
connection: KW lower the level by passing through compatible systems. ES: a counterexample p is a square mod 840; transform the problem (via the e-slice or by passing to n = p·m for auxiliary m) to a 'less ramified' instance where certificates are easier, without losing the failure.
why: Speculative; but ES(pm) → ES(p) fails in general, so the transfer must use primitive certificates of pm (those not coming from m).
first_step: Count primitive (non-inherited) Type II solutions of 4/(pm) for small m and test whether they ever yield information about p's certificates.

title: Birational automorphisms of U_n preserving integral points (Markoff-style moves)
connection: Markoff surfaces have Vieta involutions generating a group whose orbits structure all integral points; BGS/Chen then work. ES 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is linear in each variable (no Vieta involution); X = 1/x makes it a plane. Search Bir(U_n) for maps preserving integrality (beyond permutations).
why: If a nontrivial group acts on integral points of U_n, orbit/strong-approximation methods (and Chen's divisibility) become available.
first_step: Compute a few Cremona-type maps of the ES surface (e.g. from the Type I/II parametrisations) and test integrality preservation on known solutions.

title: Congruences for certificate counts (Chen's divisibility mechanism)
connection: Chen proved Markoff components have size ≡ 0 (mod p), which with BGS's 'giant component' gives connectivity. ES: find a congruence R(p) ≡ r(p) (mod m) (or for a refined count) with r(p) ≠ 0 determined by p's residue class; then the count cannot vanish.
why: A congruence mod a fixed m is a pointwise statement; R(p) is even, so look at R(p)/2 mod 2, mod 3, or counts weighted by characters.
first_step: Compute R(p)/2 mod m and several refined counts mod m (m = 2,3,4,8) for p ≤ 10⁷ and test whether any is determined by p mod M for small M.

title: Almost-all does not imply every: a structured-exception audit for ES
connection: Bourgain–Kontorovich proved density one for Apollonian curvatures, yet infinitely many exceptions exist. ES's almost-all theorems (Vaughan) are compatible with an infinite thin exceptional family; list the families where every known ES mechanism is weakest (odd squares for Type I/II; Mordell-hard classes; large ℓ(p)) and check ES (any type) explicitly far along them.
why: Disproof-side hygiene: the Apollonian story shows the almost-all→every step can fail exactly through reciprocity.
first_step: Extend adversarial searches along n = m² · (small k) and primes with large ℓ(p) beyond 10¹⁸ using the cheapest e-slices.

title: Niederreiter's recursive constructions for prime powers → ES exponential families
connection: Niederreiter proved Zaremba for every power of 2, 3, 5 by explicit recursive constructions. The repo proved ES for 3·2^s + 1, 7·4^s + 9, 63·2^s + 1; open: 15·2^s + 1, 4^s + 297. Import the recursive (q → 2q, q → 3q) construction idea: produce certificates at n_{s+1} from those at n_s.
why: Recursive constructions along exponential families are the only way Zaremba got 'every member' for infinite families.
first_step: For 15·2^s + 1, list known certificates for s ≤ 60 and look for a recursion (u,B,C)_s → (u,B,C)_{s+k}.

title: Values of rational quadratic forms with congruence: does ES's (degenerate) quadric relate to the exceptional rational case of EMM?
connection: Eskin–Margulis–Mozes: for irrational forms counts are asymptotic, while rational forms of signature (2,1)/(2,2) have exceptional logarithmic behaviour. ES's quadric ad − pc is rational but degenerate (rank-2 quadratic part, linear in c), so EMM does not apply directly; ask whether a nondegenerate model (e.g. after eliminating c via a ≡ d ≡ −1 mod c) falls in the EMM exceptional regime and whether the log-excess there mirrors the log²p main term.
why: A dictionary between ES's polylog main term and the known exceptional counts of rational quadrics could import their methods.
first_step: Read EMM's treatment of rational forms (Annals 1998) and compute the predicted count for ad − pc ∈ {1} with |a|,|d| ≤ T, c ≤ T.

title: Weyl/van der Corput differencing on the exponential-sum form of R(p)
connection: Weyl upgraded to every irrational polynomial by differencing. R(p) = Σ_{u,B} (4uB)⁻¹ Σ_{h mod 4uB} e(h(p+u+B)/(4uB)); apply van der Corput differencing in u (or B) to the nonzero frequencies to extract cancellation for fixed p in smoothed ranges.
why: Standard tool not obviously tried at fixed p; at least gives the true size of the error term in smoothed (★) counts.
first_step: Run the differencing on a smoothed model and compare the predicted error with the numerically observed |R_w(p) − M_w(p)|.

title: SAT search for the smallest profinite obstruction to bounded certificate menus
connection: Konev–Lisitsa used SAT for EDP's C=2. Encode 'no certificate with parameters ≤ K' as residue constraints on p modulo M and use SAT/ILP to find all residue classes mod M consistent with failure; verify that they are exactly squares (B1) and find the minimal K for each M.
why: Cheap automated confirmation of the B1 picture and a generator of hard test cases.
first_step: Encode for M = 840·q (q ≤ 50 prime) and K ≤ 200; compare SAT solutions with the square classes.

title: ±1-weighted zero-sum theory in (ℤ/e)*: when do many distinct factor classes force −1?
connection: Olson's group-ring proof computes D(G). ES window certificate: Π q_i^{ε_i} ≡ −1 (mod e) with ε ∈ {−1,0,1} over prime factors q_i of N_e (with multiplicity). Reviewer repair: length alone does not force coverage (mod 7, the sequence 3,1,1,… generates everything but its signed subproducts are only {1,3,5}); zero-sum/covering theorems need many distinct (or well-spread) classes, so the right parameter is the number of distinct classes and their multiplicities.
why: Zero-sum theory gives exact thresholds; ES then needs only 'enough prime factors' + 'the right subgroup', separating combinatorics from arithmetic.
first_step: Compute, for (ℤ/e)* with e ≤ 200, the minimal number of distinct classes (with multiplicity data) guaranteeing that signed subproducts contain −1 when −1 ∈ ⟨classes⟩, and compare with typical ω(N_e) ≈ log log p.

title: Reiher's double counting: subsequences of fixed length with prescribed sum
connection: Reiher combined Chevalley–Warning with counting of subsequences of each length. ES analogue: count divisors of N of each 'length' (number of prime factors) in each class mod 4C; parity/divisibility constraints between lengths might force the class −1 to be hit.
why: Fine-grained counts by number of prime factors carry more structure than the total divisor-class set.
first_step: For N = 4Cp+1 with ω(N) ≥ 4, compute the table (k, class) ↦ #{divisors with k prime factors in class}, and look for identities mod 2 or mod 3.

title: Nibble + absorber: random greedy first denominator, absorber for the two-term remainder
connection: Designs exist for all large admissible n via an approximate (nibble) decomposition plus a prepared absorber fixing leftovers. ES: choose x so that m = 4x − p is small and smooth (nibble-like), then 'absorb' via the two-term condition (m/(px) = 1/y + 1/z iff px has divisors a, b with a + b ≡ 0 mod m).
why: Separates ES into a flexible step (many x) and a rigid step (two-term splitting); quantifies how often the absorber succeeds.
first_step: For hard primes, enumerate x near p/4 with m ≤ M and measure the success rate of the two-term step as a function of the smoothness and divisor count of x.

title: Closure maps: certificate(p) ∧ certificate(q) ⇒ certificate(r) for some r(p,q)
connection: Wilson's PBD-closure and Graham's 2n+2/2n+9 maps produce 'every large n' from finitely many seeds. ES is closed under n → kn only; search for genuinely bilinear closure operations producing certificates for new primes r from certificates of p and q.
why: Any nontrivial closure operation on certificate-carrying primes would be a completely new structural fact about ES.
first_step: Brute-force search: for pairs of (★) triples (u₁,B₁,C₁), (u₂,B₂,C₂), test small bilinear/polynomial combinations for producing triples of other primes.

title: Unavoidable configurations + discharging over levels
connection: Four colour theorem: every planar graph contains one of 633 reducible configurations (found by discharging). ES: define 'configurations' as local data (p mod small M, factorisation pattern of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ K); show by a discharging/averaging argument that every p contains one of a finite list, each of which forces a certificate.
why: B1's Thm M says bounded procedures follow formal runs at square-mimicking points, so the configuration list must include unbounded data; still the method gives a framework for structured case analysis.
first_step: Collect, for p ≤ 10⁸, the minimal 'certificate-forcing' local configurations and see whether a small set covers all p empirically.

title: Entropy inequality for the union of certificate families
connection: Gilmer's entropy argument shows some element is frequent in a union-closed family. ES certificate families are 'union-like' (if a family works for p it works for multiples); an entropy inequality on the joint distribution of certificate indicators across families might force a frequently-successful family.
why: Odd, but entropy methods recently produced constant-factor every-family results from nothing.
first_step: Compute the empirical joint distribution of success indicators of 10 certificate families over primes ≤ 10⁷ and the entropy of their union.

title: Graham's 77-theorem mechanism for ES-like partition problems
connection: Graham: if n is representable then so are 2n+2 and 2n+9, plus a finite check (78–333). The mechanism is affine closure maps. ES is closed under n → kn but no affine map n → an + b preserves solvability in general (it would be a Mordell-type identity). Determine all affine maps that preserve Type II solvability on some residue class.
why: Classifying affine closure maps tells exactly how far identity-based closure can go (Mordell–Schinzel-type limit).
first_step: Search a, b ≤ 100 for which ES-solutions of n map to solutions of an + b on a residue class, via the Type II parametrisation.

title: Minimum-modulus-type statement: every certificate system covering a class must use a small modulus
connection: Hough: every distinct covering has a modulus ≤ 10¹⁶. ES analogue: for each Mordell-hard class r mod 840, any finite set of (★) congruences covering all primes in r ∩ [X, 2X] must include moduli of a certain size or divisibility (e.g. divisible by many small primes). Gives structural information on what certificates must look like.
why: Constraints on the moduli of any covering are a form of 'forced structure' usable in a proof by contradiction.
first_step: Empirically compute, for each hard class and dyadic X, the greedy minimum set of moduli covering all primes; record its smallest modulus and prime-divisibility profile.

title: Modular forms mod ℓ for the ES word series
connection: Ono used half-integral weight forms mod m and Serre's Hecke-nilpotence/Chebotarev results to get congruences for every prime modulus. Reduce the ES word series W(q) = Σ_{t,u,v≥2} q^{tuv−u−v} (or the level series of Thm K) mod 2 or 3 and look for congruences with eta/theta quotients that determine R(p) mod m from p's class.
why: A modular congruence 'R(p) ≡ nonzero (mod m) on a class' is an every-p statement on that class.
first_step: Compute W(q) mod 2, mod 3 to 10⁶ terms and test linear relations with products of θ(q^k), η(q^k) modulo 2/3.

title: Strengthen to induct: a stronger ES statement with an inductive parameter
connection: Thomassen proved 5-choosability by proving a much stronger precoloured statement that inducts. ES candidates: 'for every p and every prescribed residue r of x mod 8 (or of C mod 3), a certificate with that property exists' — check numerically which strengthenings hold, then look for an induction parameter (number of prime factors of 4Cp+1, size of e).
why: Often the right strengthening is what makes induction possible; numerics cheaply filter candidates.
first_step: Compute, for p ≤ 10⁶, which prescribed-property versions of (★)/ES hold for all p; keep the strongest surviving ones.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Type I via binary forms: divisors of p² + 4c²d in classes mod 4cd
connection: Class field theory decides which primes are represented by which forms. Type I: f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p (mod 4cd). Divisors of values of X² + 4dY² are constrained by genus/class-group characters of disc −16d; the condition f ≡ −p couples them to p. Compute exactly which classes mod 4cd are possible for divisors, and show −p is excluded exactly when p is a square (T1).
why: Puts Type I in CFT language where every-p statements (Chebotarev, ring class fields) are standard.
first_step: For small d, c enumerate possible classes of divisors of p² + 4c²d mod 4cd via genus characters, and compare with −p's class; verify the T1 exclusion at squares.

title: Gradient ladder: infinitely many → positive proportion → 100% → every, for ES sub-statements
connection: Hardy→Selberg→Levinson→Conrey climbed the ladder for zeros on the line. For ES sub-routes (e.g. 'certificate with C ≤ (log p)^A', 'Type II with u = 1'), place each on the ladder (infinitely many / positive proportion / 100% / every) to find the highest rung reachable for a restricted family.
why: Restricted families at '100%' rung are cheap wins; the transition points show which restriction kills 'every'.
first_step: Tabulate known/expected rungs for 10 restricted sub-routes using repo results and quick numerics.

title: Miller → AKS: deterministic certificate search for every p, with a provable bound
connection: Miller's test needed ERH to bound the search; AKS removed the hypothesis by a different certificate. ES certificate searches are fast in practice; a provable polynomial-time (in log p) algorithm that always returns a certificate would prove ES. Even a conditional one (under GRH) would be a new result.
why: Algorithmic formulations sometimes admit unconditional proofs via a cleverer certificate.
first_step: State precisely what a GRH-conditional 'ES certificate in time (log p)^A' would need (BM_CORRECTED says GRH gives only M_gen ≥ log log p) and what kind of different certificate could avoid that.

title: Euler's false conjecture: an 'obstruction class' that turned out solvable
connection: Euler believed n ≡ 2 (mod 4) had no orthogonal Latin squares; only 2 and 6 fail. Mordell-hard square classes look like an obstruction class for identities, yet ES holds there numerically. BSP's recursive constructions crossed the class barrier — look for recursive (product) constructions for ES certificates that move from easy classes into square classes.
why: Product/recursive constructions are exactly what identities (polynomial in p) cannot do; ES(n) ⇒ ES(kn) is a product construction but goes the wrong way.
first_step: Search for constructions producing certificates for p from certificates for auxiliary integers in easy classes (e.g. via the e-slice N = (p+e)/4 structure).

title: Covering-system obstructions: could a finite set of primes block all certificate families at once?
connection: Erdős showed infinitely many odd n are not p + 2^k because a covering system makes every candidate divisible by a small prime — invisible to density heuristics and not Brauer–Manin. ES has no BM obstruction (BL), but check whether ES certificate families admit a covering-type obstruction on some infinite set (all certificates forced to be non-integral by a finite set of primes).
why: Disproof-side hygiene: covering obstructions are the classical way heuristically-true statements fail infinitely often.
first_step: Argue structurally: ES certificate existence is not a 'primality of many shifts' condition, so covering obstructions should not apply; make this precise by checking that certificate conditions are open in the profinite topology for non-squares.

title: Dual certificates: an exact 'magic function' proving positivity of a weighted ES count
connection: Viazovska's proof found an exact auxiliary function (from modular forms) satisfying sign conditions — a dual certificate. ES: seek weights w on certificate shapes and an exact identity Σ w·(certificates of p) = (explicit positive function of p) + (manifestly nonnegative terms), with the identity coming from modular forms (Thm K level series).
why: Positivity via an exact identity with sign conditions is a way to bypass error terms entirely.
first_step: Using the Thm K series, search linear combinations of level series (with q-expansion coefficients) whose p-th coefficient is a nonnegative combination of R_t(p) plus a known positive term.

title: Positivity from an exact divisor-sum formula: where the tail can be bounded
connection: For the partition function, positivity is trivial but Lehmer bounded the Rademacher tail explicitly. ES level counts are exact divisor-class sums (R_t(n) = D_t^−(tn+1) − β_t(n)); summing over t with weights, the 'tail' is the order-≥3 character part X(n). Ask for the explicit size of X(n) relative to M_BM in the exact formula at small levels.
why: Even without analysis, the exact formula tells which levels dominate and how much the tail can at most remove.
first_step: Compute M_BM(p) and X(p) separately for p ≤ 10⁷ and plot X(p)/M_BM(p); identify primes where it approaches −1.

title: Σ over the first denominator of a two-term representation function (ternary-Goldbach shape)
connection: Ternary Goldbach averages a binary problem over one prime: Σ_p r₂(n − p). ES: R_ES(p) = Σ_x r₂^{EF}((4x − p)/(px)), where r₂^{EF}(m/N) = #{1/y + 1/z = m/N} is a divisor-pair count (a + b ≡ 0 mod m over divisor pairs of N). The average over x is the extra variable that made Goldbach-type problems pointwise.
why: Makes the 'three-variable' structure explicit with a sum over a long free variable x ∈ (p/4, 3p/4), whose length is power-size even if the main term is not.
first_step: Compute for hard p the distribution of r₂^{EF} over x and the correlation between consecutive x; check whether the x-sum behaves like a sum of independent rare events.

title: Weak subconvexity: ES needs only an ε-saving over the trivial bound R ≥ 0
connection: Soundararajan's weak subconvexity extracts a (log)^{−δ} saving from multiplicativity and mean values alone. ES: R = M_gen + X with X ≥ −M_gen trivially (R ≥ 0); ES is exactly 'X > −M_gen', any saving over the trivial bound. Seek a multiplicativity-driven argument producing X ≥ −(1 − δ)M_gen.
why: Frames ES as the weakest possible improvement over a trivial bound, the regime where 'soft' multiplicative arguments sometimes succeed.
first_step: Identify the multiplicative structure of the coefficients in X(p) (characters of order ≥ 3 mod 4uB evaluated at p) and test whether a Halász-type mean-value argument applies.

title: Critical exponent of the ES word set on the Bourgain–Kontorovich dimension scale
connection: BK's density-one Zaremba needs the Hausdorff dimension of the bounded-quotient Cantor set above 5/6 (positive proportion above 1/2, etc.). The ES word set (minus-continuants of length 3 with t ∈ 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ − p)) has #words ≤ X ≈ X log X; compute its effective 'critical exponent' and where it sits relative to BK thresholds.
why: Places ES in the thin-orbit hierarchy: it is 'fat' (exponent 1 with log), explaining density one, and shows the every-p question is about the log factor.
first_step: Count ES words ≤ X for X up to 10⁹ and fit X^δ (log X)^a; compare with the semigroup Hausdorff-dimension heuristics.

title: Modular units / Weber functions as certificate generators
connection: Heegner and Stark solved class number one through values of modular functions at CM points giving explicit Diophantine equations. Look for modular functions whose values at CM points related to p (disc −4p, −16p) are algebraic integers that factor into ES certificate data.
why: CM values give 'always-existing' algebraic objects attached to p; if their norms produce divisors in the right classes, existence follows.
first_step: Compute norms of Weber-function values f(√−p) or of singular moduli j((1+√−p)/2) differences for small p and check their prime factors against −1 (mod 4C) classes for the relevant C.

title: Group-ring/Fourier formula for the window certificate count
connection: Olson's method works in group rings. For window e and N = Π q_i^{a_i} (coprime to e), the number of coprime divisor pairs (a, b) with ab | N and a ≡ −b (mod e) (the −1 branch; the full window condition also allows the target −p, PARITY_AUDIT §0 — reviewer repair) equals (1/φ(e)) Σ_{χ mod e} χ(−1) Π_i (1 + Σ_{1≤j≤a_i} (χ(q_i)^j + χ̄(q_i)^j)). A positive value gives an ES certificate at window e; the analogous formula with χ(−p) in place of χ(−1) handles the −p branch.
why: An exact character-sum formula for each window; non-vanishing is a statement about one finite character sum, open to zero-sum/Fourier techniques.
first_step: Implement the formula, verify against brute force, then study which characters dominate when the count is 0 for hard (p, e) pairs.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Dvir-type bound for certificate-free residue sets modulo q
connection: Dvir's polynomial argument shows Kakeya sets are large. Dual question for ES: how large can a set A of residues r mod q (q prime) be such that no r ∈ A admits a (★)-type certificate with parameters in a box (u, B, C ≤ Q)? A low-degree polynomial vanishing on A and its 'directions' could bound |A|.
why: Upper bounds on certificate-free residue sets mod q translate into 'most residues are covered' statements with explicit polynomial-method constants.
first_step: Compute certificate-free residue sets mod q for q ≤ 10⁴ and box sizes Q; compare their sizes with q·(1 − c) and check for algebraic structure (squares?).

title: Splitting-condition families: ES for all p with (p/ℓ) = −1 for a fixed small ℓ
connection: Linnik's ergodic method proved Duke-type equidistribution under a fixed splitting condition. Intermediate ES goal: prove ES (or (★)) for all p in the set {p : (p/ℓ) = −1} for one fixed ℓ (e.g. ℓ = 3 excluded by Mordell classes; ℓ = 11, 13, …), where the BM main term at levels involving ℓ is guaranteed.
why: A fixed non-residue gives a guaranteed positive BM contribution (SYNTHESIS_SPARKS9); a theorem for one fixed ℓ would be the first infinite every-p family of Mordell-hard primes.
first_step: For ℓ = 11, 13, 17 compute the (★) and ES₅ counts restricted to levels using ℓ, over primes with (p/ℓ) = −1; check whether these restricted counts ever vanish.

title: Pell-shaped conjecture: Type I ∪ II for all odd non-squares beyond a finite list
connection: Pell is solvable exactly for non-squares. ES Type I/II fail at all odd squares (T1) and, per the repo, U(n) fails at odd squares plus {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145}. Formulate the precise 'Pell-shaped' conjecture (Type I ∪ II solvable for every odd non-square n outside an explicit finite list) and treat it as the natural target with the right exception set.
why: A conjecture whose exception set is exactly squares + finite list has the shape of classical every-n theorems (Pell, three squares).
first_step: Extend the Type I ∪ II census over odd non-squares (not just primes) to 10⁹ and confirm the exception list.

title: Affine-group encoding: (★) as a product-covering statement in Aff(ℤ/q)
connection: In small groups (affine group of F_q, order q(q−1)) the Gowers/Nikolov–Pyber thresholds are less demanding. The (★) condition (4uC − 1) | (p + u) can be read as an affine relation x ↦ 4uC·x − u evaluated mod divisors; look for a formulation as 'target ∈ A·B·C' in an affine group with sets of size ≈ q^{2/3}.
why: If an encoding into a small quasirandom-enough group exists, the 'one more factor' trick could cover every target mod q; integrality still needs a size argument.
first_step: Search encodings: map (u, C) ↦ affine maps mod q and check whether the product set of three natural sets covers Aff(F_q) for q ≤ 101.

title: Basis of order 3 vs order 4: Egyptian 'order' of 4/p is ≤ 4 trivially
connection: Schnirelmann bounds the order of a basis. For unit fractions, 4/p is always a sum of 4 unit fractions (4/p = 1/(k+1) + 3/(p(k+1)), and 3/m splits into ≤ 3 terms); ES asks for order 3. Study the 'order-3 deficiency': which 4-term representations of 4/p are 'one merge away' from a 3-term one (two terms with 1/a + 1/b a unit fraction)?
why: Turns ES into a merging problem on abundant 4-term representations, a different combinatorial entry point.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵ enumerate 4-term representations with bounded denominators and count mergeable pairs; compare with the number of 3-term solutions.

title: Genus-theory exclusion at squares mirrors the 4^a(8b+7) exclusion
connection: Three squares fail exactly on 4^a(8b+7) — a local obstruction at 2. T1 is a global (reciprocity) exclusion at odd squares for Type I/II. Look for a ternary/quaternary encoding where the T1 exclusion becomes a local obstruction (at 2 or at an auxiliary prime) after a change of variables, which would make it 'genus visible'.
why: If T1 could be made local in some encoding, the remaining problem would be a pure genus-to-class question.
first_step: Test encodings: n ↦ 4Cn + 1 for small C; at odd squares n = m², check whether 4Cm² + 1's divisor-class failure is explained by local conditions at 2 or at primes dividing C.

title: Large-degree analogue: ES for m/p as m grows with p
connection: Tao's Sendov proof works for sufficiently high degree, using the degree as a large parameter. ES has a natural large parameter family: m/p for growing m (ES_m). Uniform-in-m results exist for the exceptional set ((D)31: E_m(I) ≪ H exp(−c(log H)^{3/4} m^{−1/4})); study the regime m ≈ log p where Schinzel-type exceptions appear, as a 'large-parameter' analogue.
why: The large-m regime has genuine exceptions; the transition region may show which mechanism protects m = 4.
first_step: Compute the least m(p) for which m/p fails (3-term) for primes p ≤ 10⁵, and the distribution of m(p)/log p.

title: Croot's 'one target, all colourings' as a pointwise model for ES
connection: Croot's theorem is pointwise in the target (exactly 1) and uniform over colourings — the quantifier structure ES needs (one target 4/p, every p). Study Croot's proof for which step converts averaged Fourier information into a single-target statement.
why: Croot's argument is one of the few in Egyptian fractions where a specific target is hit for every configuration; its key lemma may transfer to 'every p' with a family of targets.
first_step: Read Croot (Ann. Math. 2003) and isolate the single-target step; test whether its numerics (number of terms, smoothness) can be squeezed to 3 terms for targets 4/p.

title: Family of twists by characters mod p: R as a coefficient of a p-twisted object
connection: Subconvexity in the q-aspect uses the family of all characters mod q. ES at p involves characters mod p evaluated at small integers ((−m/p) in T(p)); consider the family {R_χ(p) : χ mod p} of character-twisted certificate counts and its moments, where orthogonality mod p is available.
why: The q-aspect family is the natural family for a fixed p (it does not need varying p), so moment methods apply without leaving p.
first_step: Define R_χ(p) = Σ_{certificates} χ(u)… for χ mod p; compute Σ_χ |R_χ(p)|² exactly by orthogonality and see whether it controls the trivial-character term.

title: Distribution of certificates across dyadic level ranges
connection: Primes in every short interval vs almost all: the analogue at fixed p is whether certificates appear in every dyadic level range [K, 2K] (K ≤ p^{1/2}) or cluster. With R(p) ≍ log²p spread over ≍ log p dyadic ranges, ≍ log p certificates per range are expected.
why: If every dyadic range typically carries certificates, a proof could target one range of convenient size (e.g. C ≈ p^{1/3}) where tools are best; if they cluster, that range is fixed by the data.
first_step: For p ≤ 10¹⁰ in the hard list, histogram certificates by ⌊log₂ C⌋ and record the empty ranges.

title: Integral Brauer–Manin for the fixed-p (u,B,C) surface as a family of affine conics over the C-line
connection: For fixed C, (★) is the hyperbola (4uC − 1)(4BC − 1) = 4Cp + 1, an affine conic. Integral Hasse/BM results for families of affine quadrics (Colliot-Thélène–Xu, strong approximation with BM) treat such fibrations; analyse the total space over the C-line.
why: BL computed Br for the ES surface; the fixed-p (u,B,C) surface (a threefold when p varies) is a different model where fibrewise integral BM is classical.
first_step: Compute the Brauer group of the generic fibre (a split conic? then trivial) and the integral obstruction for the total space; compare with BL's ℤ/2.

title: Kummer-style 'regular' primes for ES: an invariant κ(p) that makes ES provable
connection: Kummer proved FLT for regular primes (p ∤ class number) long before Wiles. Look for an arithmetic invariant κ(p) (class number of ℚ(√−p), 2-rank/4-rank, parity of the fundamental unit norm of ℚ(√p), ℓ(p)) such that ES (or a sub-route) is provable for all p with κ(p) in some set, giving an infinite every-p family.
why: Partial every-p theorems on natural infinite sets of Mordell-hard primes do not yet exist; Kummer's theorem is the historical model.
first_step: Correlate (★)/ES₅ counts with κ(p) candidates for p ≤ 10⁸ and look for an invariant whose small/large values guarantee many certificates.

title: Ramanujan-type congruences for ES counts on progressions
connection: Ramanujan/Ono congruences say p(An + B) ≡ 0 (mod m). Search for progressions An + B on which f_II(n) or R(n) is always ≡ 0 (mod m) (m = 2, 3, 4, 8) beyond the trivial evenness; such congruences would reveal modular structure that might also produce nonzero congruences at primes.
why: Systematic congruence mining is cheap and has historically uncovered hidden modular structure.
first_step: Compute f_II(n), R(n) for n ≤ 10⁷ and test all A ≤ 840, B mod A for congruences mod 2, 3, 4, 8.

title: Genus-theoretic parametrisations: Mordell-hard primes as values of principal-genus forms
connection: Gauss's genus theory: p is a square mod 840-type moduli iff p lies in principal genera of the relevant discriminants, so p = Q(x, y) for a form Q in a principal genus (disc −4·210 etc.). Seek certificate families polynomial in (x, y) for p = Q(x, y), exploiting that Mordell-hard classes are exactly where these representations exist.
why: Turns 'square classes' from an obstacle into a parametrisation: hard primes come with extra representations.
first_step: For Mordell-hard primes ≤ 10⁷, compute representations by forms of discriminants dividing −4·840 and correlate (x, y) with known certificates (u, B, C).

title: Legendre-formula bookkeeping for Π_C(4Cp+1): which primes can make up the product?
connection: Sylvester–Schur works by bounding the contribution of small primes via Legendre's formula. For Π_{C≤K}(4Cp+1) the contribution of each prime q is explicit by CRT (q divides the terms with C ≡ c_q mod q). Compute the share of the product coming from primes q that could serve as single-prime certificates, versus the rest.
why: Makes the 'size argument' quantitative: if certificate-capable primes must contribute a definite share of log Π, one of them must divide some term in the right class.
first_step: Compute Σ_{q} (number of C ≤ K with q | 4Cp+1)·log q split by whether 4c_q | q+1-type conditions can hold.

title: Wielandt-style orbit counting: a group action whose non-certificate orbits have size ≡ 0 (mod m)
connection: Wielandt proves Sylow existence because |X| = C(p^a m, p^a) ≢ 0 (mod p), so some orbit has size prime to p. ES: find a finite set X_p (e.g. 4-term or 'imprimitive' representations, or divisor configurations) with a group G (ℤ/3 permuting coordinates, S₃, or a dihedral group of moves) acting so that every orbit not containing a certificate has size divisible by m while |X_p| ≢ 0 (mod m).
why: Generalises the Zagier involution (m = 2) to larger groups where the needed congruence of |X_p| may be easier to establish.
first_step: Enumerate candidate (X_p, G) pairs for small p and check orbit-size divisibility; look for one where |X_p| mod m is given by a formula in p.

title: Interlacing families over windows: real-rooted averages certify a good window
connection: MSS: if a family of real-rooted polynomials has a common interlacer, some member's largest root is ≤ that of the average. Define for each window e a polynomial f_e(t) (e.g. Π over prime factors q of N_e of (t − Re χ(q)) for a character χ mod e with χ(−1) = −1) whose root location detects certificates; average over e.
why: Converts 'some e works' into a statement about an averaged polynomial, which can be computed or estimated.
first_step: Construct toy f_e for small e, test interlacing numerically for hard p, and check whether the average polynomial's root implies a certificate for some e.

title: Precoloured version: ES with a prescribed denominator divisible by a given small prime
connection: Thomassen's induction works for a stronger precoloured statement. Candidate strengthening: for every prime p and every small prime r, there is an ES solution with r | x (or r ∤ any denominator). If such a refined statement holds numerically, its extra structure might allow an induction over r or over the e-slice.
why: Strengthenings with an inductive parameter are how many every-n combinatorial theorems were proved.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶, check which (r, condition) refinements hold for all p; record the first failure for each.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Variance-to-mean ratio of R(p) as a quasi-independence diagnostic
connection: Koukoulopoulos–Maynard's key was showing overlaps are small on average (quasi-independence). For ES, the variance of R(p) over primes near X relative to its mean measures overlap; Poisson-like behaviour (ratio ≈ 1 after removing the genus fluctuation) indicates quasi-independent events.
why: If the residual variance after the BM/genus layer is ≈ mean, the second-moment method is near-optimal and the remaining obstacle is purely the 'single realisation' issue.
first_step: Compute Var(R(p) − M_BM(p))/E[R(p)] in windows at 10⁶, 10⁸, 10¹⁰.

title: From Tijdeman (effective finiteness) to Mihăilescu (exact): bound first, then algebra
connection: Catalan moved from 'finitely many, bounded effectively' to 'exactly one' via algebra that did not need the bound. For ES-type finiteness targets (e.g. finitely many (★)-failures), an algebraic characterisation of failures (all 14 known (★)-failures share a property P) might give the exact list without analysis.
why: The 14 known (★)-failures ≤ 10¹⁰ are a finite data set where an exact algebraic description is testable.
first_step: List the 14 primes with their factorisations of 4Cp+1 for small C, residues mod 840·k, and ℓ(p); look for a shared algebraic property and test it as a predictor above 10¹⁰.

title: Furstenberg-set analogue: certificate 'lines' in the (C, d) plane
connection: Kakeya/Furstenberg estimates bound unions of lines/tubes from below. For fixed p, each prime q gives the 'line' {C ≡ c_q (mod q)} of levels where q | 4Cp+1; certificates are incidences of these lines with the conditions 4C | (product of chosen q's) + 1. An incidence-geometry lower bound might force a certificate.
why: Incidence bounds are robust every-configuration statements; ES at fixed p is an incidence problem between residue lines and divisibility conditions.
first_step: Plot, for small p, the incidence structure (q, c_q) and the certificate incidences; ask for the right incidence theorem (Szemerédi–Trotter over ℤ/q? Bourgain–Katz–Tao in F_q?).

title: Classify all 'transfer maps' between ES instances via the e-slice
connection: Graham's closure maps transfer representability from n to 2n+2, 2n+9. For ES, the e-slice transfers between p and N = (p+e)/4. Classify maps T: (N, e) ↦ (N′, e′) such that a certificate for (N, e) yields one for (N′, e′); a rich enough transfer system could connect every instance to verified ones.
why: Transfer systems are the engine of closure-type every-n proofs.
first_step: Search small linear maps (N, e) ↦ (aN + b, ce + d) preserving −1 ∈ Rat_e(N) on all data with N ≤ 10⁶.

title: Antipodal structure: the swap involution u ↔ B as a free ℤ/2-action on near-certificates
connection: Borsuk–Ulam/Tucker need a free ℤ/2-action. The (★) data (u, B) ↦ (B, u) is a ℤ/2-action, free off the diagonal u = B; certificates come in swap pairs (R(p) even). Study the ℤ/2-index of the space of near-certificates (a cell complex over levels) — a non-trivial index would force a fixed configuration, i.e. a certificate.
why: Uses a symmetry ES already has (R(p) even) in a topological rather than parity way.
first_step: Build a small complex for p ≤ 10³ (cells = near-certificates, faces = relaxations) and compute its ℤ/2-index.

title: Rédei-type reciprocity explains T1 — look for its 'higher' analogues in ES sub-routes
connection: Negative Pell's obstructions beyond local ones come from Rédei symbols (higher reciprocity). T1 is a quadratic-reciprocity cancellation. Search for Rédei-symbol-type (quartic/biquadratic) conditions that predict extra failures of sub-routes ((★), b=1, ES₅) among primes, beyond what the BM/genus layer explains.
why: If found, such conditions refine the main term (like Stevenhagen's refinement) and sharpen targets; if absent, the genus layer is complete.
first_step: Compute Rédei symbols [a, b, p] for small a, b and correlate with (★) failures / low counts.

title: Fourier interpolation/uniqueness: ES data at primes determine a function vanishing somewhere?
connection: Radchenko–Viazovska Fourier interpolation shows a function is determined by values at √n. Odd idea: the function n ↦ R(n) (or its smoothed version) is determined by data on a sparse set via modular identities (Thm K); if R vanished at p, interpolation formulas would force a contradiction with positivity elsewhere.
why: Interpolation/uniqueness theorems from modular forms are a way to transfer information between sparse and dense sets of n.
first_step: Check whether Thm K level series admit Rademacher/Fourier-interpolation-type formulas expressing R(p) via values at other n with explicit kernels.

title: Power-size main terms are not enough: p + m² is open with a √n main term
connection: Hardy–Littlewood's conjecture that every large non-square n is p + m² has main term ≍ √n/log n, yet is open pointwise (binary). So 'lift ES to a count with a power-size main term' (TART items) is necessary but not sufficient: the lifted problem must also have enough free variables (ternary-or-more) for minor-arc control.
why: Self-correction for the power-main-term items: specifies the extra requirement (dimension) any lift must meet.
first_step: For each proposed lift V_p of ES, count the number of free variables after fixing p and compare with the Kloosterman/circle-method thresholds (≥ 4 for quadratic-type, more for cubic).

title: Exact characterisation of sub-route success sets (Brjuno-type)
connection: Yoccoz showed the Brjuno condition is exactly the linearisable set, turning 'almost every' into 'iff'. For ES sub-routes, seek the exact arithmetic characterisation of the success set (e.g. Type I ∪ II succeeds iff n is not an odd square and n ∉ finite list; (★) succeeds iff …), including a mechanism producing the failures.
why: An exact 'iff' is the strongest form of an every-type theorem and forces understanding of the failure mechanism.
first_step: For (★) and b=1, fit the failure sets ≤ 10¹⁰/10¹¹ to candidate closed-form conditions and look for a constructive mechanism that produces the failures (as Yoccoz constructed non-linearisable examples).

title: Congruence mod ℓ from a mod-ℓ Galois image: ES counts with large-image structure
connection: Swinnerton-Dyer's classification of exceptional primes for τ gives congruences τ(p) ≡ explicit function of p (mod ℓ). If ES counts (or a weighted combination of level series, Thm K) were coefficients of a form with a mod-ℓ Galois representation, congruences R(p) ≡ g(p) (mod ℓ) would follow, and ES would hold wherever g(p) ≢ 0.
why: Turns ES non-vanishing into a congruence problem with explicit exceptions — the τ approach.
first_step: Check whether the theta-quotient/Eisenstein parts of Thm K have coefficients satisfying Eisenstein-type congruences mod small ℓ (they are divisor sums twisted by characters, so congruences like σ_χ(N) ≡ … mod ℓ may exist).

title: Sign/size arguments on special values: choose auxiliary objects whose values have forced factors
connection: Elkies chose D so that H_D(j(E)) has a controlled sign and size. ES: choose auxiliary integers built from p (values of polynomials P(p) or norms from auxiliary fields) whose sign/size/Jacobi symbol forces a prime factor in a class tied to a level C, with the factor also dividing 4Cp + 1.
why: A systematic search space for 'forcing' constructions that guarantee prime factors in classes.
first_step: Search quadratic polynomials P with P(p) | (4Cp+1)·(something) for families of C and compute Jacobi-symbol constraints on their prime factors.

title: Uniformity obstruction for linear-forms-in-primes certificate schemes at fixed p
connection: For fixed p, ES has finitely many solutions with denominators bounded polynomially in p (not O(p²): z can be ≍ p⁴, reviewer example x = (p+3)/4, y = (px+2)/3, z = pxy/2 for p ≡ 5 mod 24), and a fixed certificate parametrisation with auxiliary primes typically needs prime tuples of linear forms in a box polynomial in p with coefficients depending on p (many-to-one parametrisations need separate care). Green–Tao–Ziegler asymptotics are not uniform in coefficients comparable to the box, so they do not apply directly (correcting the BHS item).
why: Records precisely why the conditional→unconditional (Harpaz–Skorobogatov–Wittenberg) move does not transfer to ES as stated, and what uniformity would be needed.
first_step: State the needed uniform version: count of t ≤ T with L_i(t) all prime for forms with coefficients ≤ T^{1+ε}; compare with known uniform results (e.g. for a single form: Brun–Titchmarsh / Siegel–Walfisz ranges).

title: The b=1 line as a 'Goldbach's other conjecture' model with sporadic failures
connection: The b=1 line fails at 193, 2521, 66529 and nowhere else ≤ 10¹¹ — like 5777 and 5993 for Goldbach's other conjecture. Fit the expected b=1 count at these primes and test whether failures are 'explained' by small expected counts; calibrate the same model on (★) (14 failures ≤ 10¹⁰).
why: Validates the heuristic models on sub-routes with real failures before trusting them for ES.
first_step: Compute the b=1 model main term at all p ≤ 10⁷ and the empirical P(fail | main term); check that the three failures sit at the extreme low end.

title: Non-vanishing on the line Re s = 1 analogue: a level Dirichlet series that cannot vanish
connection: PNT/Dirichlet need L(1 + it, χ) ≠ 0 via the 3-4-1 positivity trick (Mertens). For fixed p consider F_p(s) = Σ_C D_C(p) C^{−s} (finite sum): (★)(p) ⟺ F_p ≢ 0, and (★)(p) ⇒ ES(p) (not conversely: p = 409 fails (★) but satisfies ES). A '3-4-1'-type positivity combination of F_p, its twists, and F at related p might force non-vanishing.
why: Odd, but 3-4-1 is the archetype of extracting non-vanishing from positivity of a trigonometric polynomial.
first_step: Look for nonnegative trigonometric polynomials in a 'twist' variable (characters mod 4C) such that the combination of twisted level counts is ≥ c·(untwisted total) − (controlled).

title: Hecke operators on ES counts as functions of n: R(nℓ) vs R(n) for split/inert ℓ
connection: QUE uses Hecke operators T_ℓ acting on eigenfunctions. Define T_ℓ on functions of n by (T_ℓ f)(n) = f(nℓ) + (character)·f(n/ℓ) and test whether R (or f_II) is approximately an eigenfunction of some T_ℓ on Mordell-hard n, with eigenvalue depending on (n/ℓ).
why: An approximate Hecke structure would give the multiplicative relations needed for Soundararajan-type arguments.
first_step: Regress f_II(nℓ) on f_II(n) for n prime and ℓ ≤ 50, separately for (n/ℓ) = ±1.

title: Uniform spectral gap for the 'ES move graph' on residues mod q
connection: Bourgain–Gamburd give uniform expansion of Cayley graphs mod q. Define a graph on (ℤ/q)³ (or on SL₂(ℤ/q)) by ES-preserving moves (change of one word parameter) and test for a uniform spectral gap in q; uniform mixing would give quantitative equidistribution of words mod q with archimedean size control.
why: Uniform-in-q expansion is the input for affine-sieve/Bourgain–Kontorovich-type counting, which is how thin-orbit local-global results are proved.
first_step: Compute the spectral gap of the move graph for primes q ≤ 200 and look for uniformity.

title: Effective equidistribution scale vs the required cusp depth (quantify the B2 gap)
connection: Every-orbit equidistribution theorems come with effective rates (Strömbergsson, Venkatesh). ES₅/word formulations require hitting regions of measure ≈ (log p)²/p-ish; compute the smallest measure of target region that current effective rates for closed horocycles of length p can resolve.
why: Turns 'B2' into a number in the dynamics language: the exponent gap between the required and available resolution.
first_step: From Strömbergsson's effective rate (Duke Math. J. 123 (2004): subsegments longer than ℓ^{1/2+ε} of a closed horocycle of length ℓ equidistribute; verified), compute the minimal region measure resolvable at length p and compare with the ES₅ target measure.

title: Non-lacunary semigroups of levels: multiplicative closure of 'working levels'
connection: Furstenberg's ×2×3 rigidity uses non-lacunarity of {2^a 3^b}. If level C works for p, does level C·k work for p for many k? (If d | 4Cp + 1 with d ≡ −1 mod 4C, then nothing obvious at level Ck.) Study whether the set of working levels for p is close to a multiplicative semigroup.
why: If working levels had semigroup structure, rigidity theorems for multiplicative semigroups could constrain failure.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁷ compute the set of working levels and test closure under multiplication by small k.

title: Absorbers from Mordell identities: reserve identity-covered structure to fix square classes
connection: Absorption reserves a structure that can repair any leftover. Mordell identities cover non-square classes; for a hard p, consider auxiliary integers N related to p (e.g. N_e = (p + e)/4, which may lie in easy classes) whose identity-certificates can be 'absorbed' into a certificate for p via the e-slice.
why: Transfers the power of identities (which fail only on square classes) to hard p through an auxiliary object.
first_step: For hard p, compute which N_e lie in identity-covered classes and whether their identity certificates translate into window certificates for p.

title: Sun-style refinements as data: four-square-like refinements of ES
connection: Sun formulated many 'refined Lagrange' conjectures by computer search; several were proved. Generate ES refinements automatically (x + y or z constrained to be a square, a prime, ≡ r mod m, etc.), test them to 10⁷, and keep those that never fail — new conjectures whose extra structure may make them provable or reveal hidden symmetries.
why: Automated conjecture generation found provable statements for sums of squares; ES has never been mined this way systematically (check repo).
first_step: Write a search over ~200 refinement predicates P(x, y, z, p) and test on all p ≤ 10⁶; report survivors.

title: Recursive product constructions: certificates for p from certificates for pieces of 4Cp + 1
connection: Bose–Shrikhande–Parker built orthogonal Latin squares of composite orders from smaller ones. For ES, 4Cp + 1 = N₁N₂ (coprime): if N₁ has a divisor ≡ a (mod 4C) and N₂ one ≡ b with ab ≡ −1, the product is a certificate. Study 'recursive' constructions splitting N and combining class information from each piece.
why: Product constructions are the combinatorial counterpart of the Kneser/product-set items, with an explicit recursive structure.
first_step: For hard p, enumerate coprime splittings of 4Cp + 1 and compute the class sets of divisors of each piece; count combinations giving −1.

title: Current-graph-style explicit constructions for one residue class mod a large modulus
connection: Ringel–Youngs used 'current graphs' — compact algebraic data generating a whole family. For one Mordell-hard class r mod M (M large, e.g. 840·1001), search for compact algebraic data (a finite list of certificate templates with parameters depending on p's residues mod M′) covering all primes in that class up to 10⁹.
why: Even if B1 forbids bounded templates for all p, the minimal template count per class reveals growth rates and hidden structure.
first_step: Run a greedy set-cover of primes in the class by parametric templates (Type II with C | M′) and plot template count vs X.

title: Polynomial congruence certificate: an identity in ℤ[X]/(X^r − 1, p) detecting ES
connection: AKS used a polynomial congruence that holds iff n is prime. Ask whether ES(p) has a characterisation by a polynomial identity modulo (X^r − 1, p) or modulo auxiliary moduli (e.g. a product over levels of polynomials whose evaluation detects certificates), testable deterministically.
why: Odd: algebraic characterisations sometimes admit clean counting proofs (as in AKS's group-size argument).
first_step: Construct the generating polynomial P_p(X) = Π_{C ≤ K} (1 − X^{[level C fails]}) style objects and look for algebraic relations they satisfy for all p.

title: Strong approximation mod p for the ES surface fibre U_p (BGS-style) — sanity check
connection: BGS proved Markoff surfaces satisfy strong approximation mod p for most p. For ES, check the analogous local statement: does U_n(ℤ) → U_n(ℤ/q) have dense image for various q (it is BM-obstructed for strong approximation by BL)? Quantify the BL obstruction concretely on data.
why: Makes BL's 'BM obstruction to strong approximation always exists' concrete and shows which residue patterns ES solutions avoid.
first_step: For small n with many solutions, compute the reductions of solutions mod q and compare with U_n(ℤ/q).

title: Divisor sum over shifted primes reversed: Σ_{q prime} 1[q | p + m] for structured m
connection: The Titchmarsh divisor problem counts divisors of shifted primes. The trial form needs prime (or general) divisors of p + u in the class −1 mod (stuff tied to u); reverse the roles: for fixed p, count primes q ≡ 3 (4) with q | p + u and q = 4uC − 1 for some C — a 'Titchmarsh problem with a tied modulus' at a single p.
why: Relates single-prime certificates to the distribution of prime divisors of p + u, a classical object.
first_step: Count, for fixed p, pairs (u, q) with q | p + u, q ≡ −1 (mod 4u), q prime; compare with heuristic Σ_u τ*/φ(4u).

title: No minor arcs: positivity lets ES discard all but the smallest levels
connection: Goldbach-type proofs must bound minor arcs because terms cancel. ES counts are sums of nonnegative level counts, R(p) = Σ_C D_C(p) ≥ Σ_{C ≤ K} D_C(p); so ES ⟸ a certificate among levels C ≤ K = (log p)^A, where the expected count is still ≍ (log p)·(log K) → ∞. The whole problem is a lower bound for a short, explicit 'major-level' sum.
why: Reframes which part of the analytic machinery is needed: only lower bounds on a few explicit structured counts, no cancellation estimates for the bulk.
first_step: For p in the hard lists, find the least K(p) such that some level ≤ K(p) carries a certificate, and fit K(p) against (log p)^A.

title: Sieve of growing dimension: when do the thin sets S_C (C ≤ K) exhaust all primes?
connection: Failing levels 1..K means 4Cp + 1 ∈ S_C for all C ≤ K, an intersection of thin multiplicative sets of total 'dimension' Σ_{C≤K} δ_C. Upper-bound sieves for such intersections are standard for fixed K; ES needs K growing with p until the expected number of survivors near X is < 1 — a sieve problem of growing dimension.
why: Puts the ES exceptional-set question in the language of high-dimensional sieves (Diamond–Halberstam–Richert), where the dependence on dimension is explicit.
first_step: Compute Σ_{C≤K} δ_C as a function of K and the K(X) at which X·(log X)^{−Σδ} < 1; compare with the observed least K(p).

title: Affine-sieve strengthening: certificates with prime or almost-prime parameters
connection: Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak's affine sieve produces almost-primes in orbits once expansion is known. Ask whether every p has a (★) certificate with u, B (or 4uC − 1, 4BC − 1) prime or with ≤ r prime factors; if true numerically, sieve methods on the word set apply and the strengthened statement has more structure.
why: Strengthenings with prime parameters connect ES to the affine-sieve toolkit and to Chen-type almost-prime results.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁸ compute the least r such that a certificate with Ω(4uC − 1) ≤ r and Ω(4BC − 1) ≤ r exists; find primes needing large r.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Large deviations of Euclid's algorithm at a fixed denominator (Hensley, Baladi–Vallée)
connection: The CF length of a/v is asymptotically Gaussian with mean ≍ log v (Heilbronn for the mean at fixed denominators; Hensley, Baladi–Vallée via transfer operators — reviewer repair: Baladi–Vallée average over denominators v ≤ N with rate O(1/√log N), not a fixed denominator). ES₅ (λ(p) ≤ 3) asks for an extreme left-tail event (length 3, prescribed shape). Large-deviation estimates for fixed p from the dynamical analysis of Euclid's algorithm would give lower bounds in exactly this quantifier order.
why: The dynamical analysis of Euclid's algorithm is 'every p' by construction (it averages over a, not p); the question is how far into the tail its estimates reach.
first_step: Find fixed-denominator large-deviation statements (Hensley's work on fixed-denominator Euclid statistics; check) beyond Baladi–Vallée's denominator-averaged ones; compare the reachable tail with length-3 events (count ≍ log²p out of p).

title: Search for F_q[T] counterexamples to the direct ES analogue at small q
connection: Function-field analogues sometimes fail at small q (as Artin's C₂ fails for small p). If the direct analogue of ES over F_q[T] (with a suitable positivity replacement, e.g. degree constraints) fails for some small q, the failure mechanism is an explicit structure that ℤ-ES must avoid; if it holds for all tested q, the F_q[T] proof (repo) is the template.
why: Cheap exhaustive computation with high information value (8/131-type test in the function-field world).
first_step: For q = 2, 3, 4, 5 and irreducible P of degree ≤ 12, search solutions of 4/P = 1/X + 1/Y + 1/Z (with the repo's degree conventions) and list failures.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Third-method insurance: find a family whose success is uncorrelated with both (★) and b=1
connection: Holowinsky–Soundararajan needed exactly two complementary methods. ES data show (★) ∪ b=1 never fail together ≤ 10⁸, but a proof-grade argument may need a third family whose success correlates with neither (e.g. ES₅, Type I lines, small windows). Measure correlations of success indicators among 6–8 families.
why: Identifies the minimal robust family set for a complementary-methods proof.
first_step: Compute the correlation matrix of family success indicators (and of their counts) over primes ≤ 10⁸ in Mordell-hard classes.

title: Kaplansky-type ternary forms with conditional (GRH) complete lists as structural analogues
connection: Beyond Ramanujan's form, several ternary forms have GRH-conditional complete lists of exceptions (Ono–Soundararajan type). Their exception lists are finite but sporadic; ES-adjacent statements with sporadic exceptions (U(n) list, b=1 failures) might be 'ternary-form-like'. Test whether the U(n)/b=1 exceptions are represented/non-represented by specific ternary forms.
why: A direct dictionary between sporadic ES-adjacent exceptions and ternary-form exceptions would import Waldspurger/GRH technology.
first_step: For the known sporadic exception lists, test representability by all reduced positive ternary forms of discriminant ≤ 500.

title: Commutator-style 'every element' from character ratios: target −1 in (ℤ/e)* via products of few divisor classes
connection: Ore-type results show every element is a product of few commutators using character bounds. Analogue for windows: when the prime-factor classes of N_e generate a large subgroup H ∋ −1, show −1 is a product of a bounded number of them (with ±1 exponents) using additive-combinatorics in abelian groups (Cauchy–Davenport/Kneser iterated), i.e. a bound on the 'diameter' of H w.r.t. the generating multiset.
why: Reduces window certificates to a diameter bound in a Cayley graph of an abelian group — fully finite and checkable.
first_step: Compute the ±1-diameter of (ℤ/e)* w.r.t. the multiset of prime-factor classes of N_e for hard (p, e), versus ω(N_e).

title: Syracuse-type random variable for ES: the 2-adic/3-adic structure of minimal certificates
connection: Tao's Collatz proof analysed the distribution of a 3-adic 'Syracuse random variable'. ES certificates carry 2-adic data (4 | t; 8ℤ − p branch) and 3-adic data (Mordell classes mod 3). Define the analogous random variable (residues of minimal certificate parameters mod 2^k, 3^k) and study its distribution and mixing as p varies.
why: Fine-scale mixing of certificate residues is the kind of statement that powers almost-all → 'almost every scale' improvements.
first_step: Compute the distribution of minimal certificate parameters mod 2^k·3^j over primes ≤ 10⁸ and test for Fourier decay.

title: Stickiness analogue: certificates at nearby levels share prime factors
connection: Wang–Zahl handled 'sticky' Kakeya sets where tubes cluster coherently across scales. For fixed p, near-certificates at levels C and C + kq share the prime q (CRT); study whether certificate data are 'sticky' across levels (coherent families sharing primes) and whether non-sticky configurations are easier to force.
why: A structural dichotomy (sticky vs non-sticky) that may split the problem into two tractable halves.
first_step: Measure, for fixed p, the clustering of certificate-bearing levels modulo primes dividing their divisors.
